title: LP-1 | Required Margin Miscalculated
content: The vulnerability is a miscalculation of the required maintenance margin in the margin‑adjustment logic of the protocol. The root cause lies in an argument swap when the contract calls the positionMaintenanceMargin routine: it passes the option premium where the spot price of the underlying asset should be supplied, and passes the spot price where the premium should be supplied. Because the margin formula expects the spot price as the X input and the premium as the Y input, swapping them dramatically changes the resulting maintenance margin. This incorrect margin propagates to the utilizationRatio calculation, which then produces either excessively high or insufficiently low interest rates and breaks the validation that checks the maxUtilizationRatio constraint. An attacker who can influence either the premium or the spot price can therefore force the protocol to accept positions with too little collateral, exposing the liquidity pool to under‑collateralised loans, or can inflate the required collateral, causing legitimate users to be over‑charged or to have their positions liquidated prematurely. The impact includes potential loss of user funds, distorted interest accrual, and a breach of the economic guarantees of the platform. The condition occurs every time a new position is opened or an existing one is adjusted, because the faulty function call is invoked as part of the margin‑checking path. All participants that rely on the margin calculation – liquidity providers, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit performed by the Guardian team, who noted the mismatched parameter order. It can be hard to notice because the resulting utilizationRatio may still appear numeric and, in many market scenarios, the error does not immediately cause a revert, making the bug subtle until extreme price or premium values are observed. The recommended remediation is to correct the call so that the spot price is supplied as the first argument (X) and the premium as the second argument (Y), thereby restoring the intended margin formula and ensuring that utilizationRatio and maxUtilizationRatio checks behave as designed. In broader terms, this is a classic case of a parameter‑ordering bug that compromises financial calculations, leading to incorrect accounting, unexpected zero or negative balances for users, and a mismatch between the expected refund or margin requirement and the actual outcome observed on the UI.
summary: When computing the position maintenance margin required, the maintenance margin is miscalculated because the positionMaintenanceMargin is called with the option premium as the spot price of the asset and the spot price of the asset as the option premium. This drastically miscalculates the required positionMaintenanceMargin and results in an invalid utilizationRatio, causing inflated or insufficient interest rates and undermines the maxUtilizationRatio validation.

title: DIEM-1 | Liquidations Halted Due To DoS
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded growth bug in the portfolio management component of the DIEM protocol that allows a single user to accumulate an unlimited number of open trades within their portfolio. Because the contract does not enforce a maximum total count of trades, a malicious or careless user can create enough trade entries that any function which needs to iterate over the full list—most notably the liquidation routine—exceeds the block gas limit and therefore fails to execute. The root cause is the absence of a global cap on the size of the trade array; the existing maxBatchTrading check only limits the number of trades that can be added in a single transaction, not the cumulative total after many separate calls. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling the openTrades function with small batches, gradually inflating the portfolio until liquidation, margin calls, or any batch‑processing operation runs out of gas and is effectively halted. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents the protocol from liquidating under‑collateralized positions, which can leave lenders’ funds exposed and may lead to systemic risk if large positions remain un‑cleared. This scenario manifests when a portfolio contains a very high trade count, typically after many successive calls to openTrades; the liquidation function then reverts with an out‑of‑gas error, and users observing the UI will see messages such as "liquidation failed" or simply no action despite the protocol indicating that a position should be liquidated. All participants who rely on the protocol’s risk management—borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the safety mechanisms are disabled. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the team simulated large portfolios and observed that liquidation could not be completed. It is difficult to notice in production because the failure appears as a generic transaction revert rather than an explicit vulnerability, and the contract’s design does not emit a clear error indicating that the trade list is too large. The recommended remediation is to introduce a hard limit on the total number of trades that any single portfolio may hold, enforcing this constraint on every trade‑creation path, thereby ensuring that iteration‑based functions remain within feasible gas bounds. Conceptually, this is a classic resource‑exhaustion or unbounded array bug that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each position can be processed in a bounded amount of time and gas, leading to a scenario where funds disappear from the risk engine without being liquidated, breaking the expected refund or collateral recovery flow.
summary: There is no limit to the amount of trades a user may open in their portfolio. Therefore it is possible for a user to open so many trades that functions that need to iterate through all of them multiple times, such as liquidation, cannot occur. The maxBatchTrading validation fails to protect against this DoS as it limits only the amount of trades that can be opened in a single openTrades function call.

title: DIEM-2 | Sell Premium Paid Twice
content: The vulnerability is a double‑credit of the option seller’s premium. When a user opens a sell (short) option trade, the protocol immediately transfers the total premium to the user’s portfolio. Later, during settlement of the same trade, the _calculatePnl function adds the value of _trade.averageEntry.mulDivUp(closedUnits, 1e18) – which is exactly the premium that was already paid out – to the profit‑and‑loss (PNL) amount that is subsequently transferred back to the user. This erroneous addition occurs only when the option expires with a premium of zero, i.e., when the option finishes out‑of‑the‑money. The root cause is the logic that treats the original premium as if it were a profit at trade closure, without checking whether it has already been disbursed. An attacker can exploit this by opening a short position, receiving the premium, waiting for the option to expire worthless, and then collecting the same premium a second time as PNL, effectively withdrawing funds from the contract that were never owed. The impact is a direct loss of assets from the protocol’s liquidity pool, a breach of accounting invariants, and an inflated profit display for the attacker, which may go unnoticed because the UI typically shows a positive balance after settlement and the zero‑premium condition is often assumed to be harmless. The bug manifests under the specific condition of a sell trade (!isBuy) that settles with a zero premium, and it affects any user who can open such a trade as well as the overall protocol’s financial integrity. It was discovered through a systematic audit that traced the flow of premium funds from the openTrades function through the settlement routine and identified the unintended second transfer. The issue is subtle because the transfer is performed by a generic PNL credit routine, making it appear as a legitimate profit rather than a duplicated payout. To remediate, the contract should exclude the initial premium from the PNL calculation when closing a sell trade that expires with zero premium, for example by tracking whether the premium has already been paid or by conditioning the PNL addition on a non‑zero settlement premium. This adjustment restores the correct accounting model where the seller’s premium is paid once at trade initiation and not treated as additional profit on settlement, thereby preventing unauthorized fund extraction and preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees.
summary: In the openTrades function, when a user opens a !isBuy trade their portfolio receives the totalPremium immediately. However upon settling and closing the expired trade, when the premium of the expired option is 0 the _trade.averageEntry.mulDivUp(closedUnits, 1e18), which represents the totalPremium upon opening the sell trade, is credited as PNL in the _calculatePnl function and later transferred to the user’s portfolio a second time.

title: PORT-1 | swapMargin Used To Game The AMM
content: The vulnerability resides in the swapMargin function of the IVXLP protocol, which permits a user to transfer margin balances out of their portfolio without any verification that the portfolio remains solvent after the transfer. The root cause is the absence of a post‑swap solvency check: the contract allows users to first sell option contracts to the automated market maker (AMM) and immediately collect the premium, then repeatedly invoke swapMargin to move the deposited margin (including the newly received premium) back to their own address. Because the protocol does not ensure that the portfolio retains enough collateral to cover the outstanding option obligations, the user can empty the margin while still holding the premium, leaving the portfolio unable to meet exercise or settlement requirements at expiry. Exploitation proceeds step‑by‑step: (1) the attacker opens a position by selling options to the AMM, receiving a premium; (2) the attacker calls swapMargin to withdraw the entire margin, including the premium; (3) the attacker repeats the sale‑and‑swap cycle, "sandwiching" the portfolio and draining almost all value; (4) the portfolio ends with zero usable margin but still records the sold options, making it liquidatable; (5) the protocol’s liquidation mechanism then liquidates the insolvent portfolio, effectively transferring the drained funds to the attacker and depleting the IVXLP contract’s liquidity. The impact is severe: the attacker can siphon nearly all assets from the liquidity pool, other users lose their ability to rely on the pool’s capital, and the protocol’s financial integrity is compromised. This condition occurs whenever a participant can call swapMargin after any option sale and there is no check that the resulting portfolio is not liquidatable. The affected parties include all liquidity providers, option buyers, and the protocol itself, since the drained funds reduce overall pool health and may cause broader market instability. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that exercised the swapMargin path in conjunction with option sales, revealing that repeated calls allowed the portfolio’s margin to drop below the liquidation threshold without triggering an error. The bug is difficult to notice because swapMargin appears to be a legitimate utility for rebalancing, and the immediate receipt of premium masks the underlying loss of collateral until liquidation occurs. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “insufficient post‑operation validation” or “margin‑drain” bugs, where a contract allows state‑changing operations that render the system under‑collateralized. From the user's perspective, the UI would show a normal premium receipt after selling an option, but subsequent balance queries would display a zero or dramatically reduced margin, and attempts to exercise the option would fail or result in unexpected liquidation, effectively making the funds disappear. To remediate, the function should either be removed entirely or be hardened with an explicit validation step that reverts if the portfolio would become liquidatable after the margin swap, ensuring that collateral always remains sufficient to cover outstanding obligations.
summary: Users are able to use the swapMargin function to siphon funds from their portfolio well past the point of insolvency. A user can sell options contracts to the AMM and collect the premium in their portfolio immediately. The user can then repeatedly use the swapMargin function on their portfolio and sandwich themselves to extract roughly all the value from the portfolio. The user retains their initial margin deposit as well as the premium from selling the options contracts to the AMM, without having any margin remaining in their portfolio to exercise these contracts upon expiry. A malicious user can use this attack to drain nearly all of the available funds in the IVXLP contract, after removing the balance from their portfolio they will then be insolvently liquidated.

title: DIEMT-1 | DeltaT Rounds Down To 0 Bricking Trades
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol computes the time step deltaT for option pricing. The contract derives deltaT by dividing the remaining seconds to expiry (secondsToExpiry) by a constant of 15. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, any option with less than 15 seconds remaining yields a deltaT of 0. Several core financial functions – calculateCosts(), interestRate(), utilizationRatio() – depend on deltaT to compute the number of pricing periods N as N = secondsToExpiry / deltaT. When deltaT is zero, the division triggers a division‑by‑zero revert inside the Binomial._optionPrices routine. The revert propagates up the call stack, causing calculateCosts(), interestRate() and utilizationRatio() to fail. These functions are invoked during opening, closing, liquidation and profit‑and‑loss calculations, meaning that as soon as an option with a sub‑15‑second expiry is added to the activeOptionIds list, the entire pricing engine becomes inoperable. Consequently, the protocol cannot open new trades, cannot settle existing positions, and cannot liquidate under‑collateralised trades. Liquidity providers and traders experience stalled operations, their balances appear unchanged while the UI shows no available markets, and funds may become effectively locked until the offending option is manually removed or the contract is upgraded. The issue was uncovered during an audit when a test case exercised an expiry of 10 seconds, revealing that deltaT was rounded down to zero and the subsequent division caused a revert. The bug is subtle because it only manifests for extremely short‑lived options, which are uncommon in normal usage, and the revert may be attributed to a generic “calculation error” rather than a systemic flaw. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum deltaT (for example, defaulting to 1) or validate that secondsToExpiry is at least 15 before computing deltaT. Additionally, the protocol should regularly settle and remove expired options from the active list to prevent the accumulation of malformed entries. By preventing a zero divisor and ensuring the active options set is cleaned, the protocol restores its ability to price options correctly, open and close trades, and protect user funds.
summary: secondsToExpiry is divided by 15 to produce deltaT. Options with <15 seconds of expiry will have deltaT rounded down to 0 and will cause functions such as calculateCosts(), interestRate() and utilizationRatio() to revert. The above functions call Binomial._optionPrices which calculates N period for binomial pricing: uint256 N = inputs.secondsToExpiry / inputs.deltaT; Because inputs.deltaT is 0 after rounding down, a division by 0 revert occurs. While the option is included in the activeOptionIds, all other options will be impacted: interestRate() and calculateCosts() are needed for pnlOperations, which will completely prevent closing and liquidation trades from occurring due to the revert. This will negatively impact liquidity providers and traders. calculateCosts() and utilizationRatio() are called when opening a trade, completely preventing trades from being opened in the protocol.

title: PORT-2 | Incorrect Approval Prevents Liquidation
content: The vulnerability resides in the margin‑removal routine of a DeFi lending protocol where the contract prepares a token swap before releasing a user’s collateral. The routine first calls the ERC‑20 approve function to allow the swap router to spend the tokens that will be sold. Instead of approving the exact quantity of tokens that will be swapped, the code mistakenly approves an amount derived from the USD value of those tokens. This subtle conversion error creates a mismatch: when the market price of the token is below one US dollar, the USD‑derived allowance is smaller than the actual token amount required for the swap. As a result, the swap transaction cannot pull the needed tokens, the call reverts, and the surrounding removeMargin operation aborts. Because liquidation in this protocol is performed through removeMargin, the failure blocks any liquidation attempt on under‑collateralised positions. From a user’s point of view, a liquidator invoking the function receives a transaction error such as “insufficient allowance” or a generic revert, while the borrower’s position remains open despite being under‑collateralised. The impact is that the protocol’s risk‑management mechanism is effectively disabled for assets priced under $1, potentially allowing bad debt to accumulate and jeopardising the overall solvency of the system. The condition occurs whenever a token with a price below one US dollar is used as collateral or for margin removal, and it affects any user who relies on liquidation to enforce margin calls, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer from un‑liquidated unhealthy positions. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit that inspected the approval logic of the removeMargin function. It is hard to notice because the allowance call appears syntactically correct; only when testing with low‑price tokens does the insufficient allowance surface, and the error does not manifest for higher‑priced assets. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of "token amount vs. value conversion errors" where financial calculations use a fiat‑denominated figure to set token‑level permissions, leading to under‑approval. To remediate, the contract should compute the exact token amount that will be transferred in the swap and approve that quantity, ensuring the allowance matches the swap’s requirements regardless of the token’s USD price. By aligning the approved amount with the actual token amount, the swap can succeed, liquidation can proceed, and the protocol’s accounting invariants remain intact.
summary: In the removeMargin function, before a swap occurs an amount is approved. This is supposed to be the token amount that is being swapped. However the USD value of the token amount is approved instead. This is especially detrimental when a token’s USD value is less than $1 because the approval will be insufficient for the swap causing a revert and making liquidations via removeMargin impossible.

title: DIEM-3 | Liquidation will fail due to insufficient funds
content: The vulnerability lies in the liquidation routine of the Diem contract, where the amount of USDC expected to be transferred to the IVXLP contract is calculated as the total dollar‑denominated balance of the trader's portfolio. This calculation assumes that the portfolio value is already expressed in USDC and does not take into account that, for any non‑USDC token held, the contract must perform an on‑chain swap to obtain USDC. The swap introduces protocol fees and market slippage, which reduce the actual USDC received compared with the pre‑swap portfolio valuation. Because the liquidation logic proceeds with the original (inflated) amount, the Diem contract frequently ends the operation with less USDC than required to satisfy all downstream payouts. When the contract attempts to transfer the shortfall, the transaction reverts due to insufficient balance, causing the liquidation to fail entirely. This failure can occur whenever a position is insolvent and the portfolio contains assets other than USDC, making the liquidate() function dependent on external price conversion that is not accounted for in its accounting. The affected parties include the trader whose position cannot be closed, lenders or stakeholders who expect to receive liquidation proceeds, and the protocol itself, which may become unable to enforce margin calls and could suffer a buildup of stuck insolvent positions. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that traced the flow of funds in the liquidate() function and identified a mismatch between the expected USDC amount and the amount actually received after token swaps. It is hard to notice because the code appears to transfer the full portfolio balance, and the reduction caused by fees and slippage only manifests after the swap, which may not generate an obvious error flag until the final transfer step. Conceptually, this bug belongs to the class of “insufficient funds after external conversion” or “accounting mismatch due to ignored swap costs” vulnerabilities, where a contract assumes that a nominal value will be preserved across a conversion step. Users experience this as a liquidation transaction that silently reverts, with no funds being moved, often seeing messages such as “insufficient USDC balance” or simply observing that their position remains open despite being under‑collateralized. The expected behavior—successful liquidation and distribution of proceeds—is replaced by a failed transaction, leading to the perception that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is unable to enforce its rules. The recommended remediation is to base the liquidation payout on the actual USDC amount received after the swap, or to incorporate a safety buffer that accounts for swap fees and slippage, thereby guaranteeing that the contract holds enough USDC to complete all required transfers.
summary: In the liquidate function when a position is insolvently liquidated the PnL amount transferred to the IVXLP contract is determined to be the total balance of the portfolio in a dollar amount. If a token in the portfolio is not USDC, it will be swapped for USDC and incur a fee as well as slippage before the USDC amount is received in the Diem contract. Because the Diem contract receives less USDC, it will not have sufficient funds to transfer to all necessary stakeholders. The lack of funds will lead to the transaction reverting, making it impossible to liquidate a position that requires a swap.

title: C-01 | Rebalancer Position Closed Twice
content: The vulnerability concerns the Rebalancer contract’s initiateClosePosition function, which can inadvertently invoke the rebalancer logic while it is already processing a close request. The root cause is the absence of a re‑entrancy guard or state flag that prevents the Rebalancer from being triggered a second time from within the same transaction. When a user or an external caller executes _usdnProtocol.initiateClosePosition, the call propagates to Rebalancer.initiateClosePosition; this call then performs operations that update the position’s balance and call Rebalancer.updatePosition. Because the rebalancer is not protected against being re‑entered, the same close logic runs again before the first execution finishes, causing the closed amount to be deducted twice, the balance to be double‑counted, and the state updates performed by updatePosition to be overwritten. An attacker can exploit this by initiating a close order and causing the contract to execute the rebalancer twice, leading to an inaccurate accounting state where the protocol believes more assets have been removed than actually exist. The impact includes erroneous balance reports, potential loss of funds for users, and a breakdown of the protocol’s accounting invariants, which rely on a single, atomic deduction of the closed amount. The issue manifests only when the close initiation path traverses the rebalancer, so normal operations that do not close positions remain unaffected, making the bug subtle and hard to spot during routine testing. It was discovered during a third‑party audit that examined the close‑position flow and noticed that the state after a close did not match the expected invariant. Because the double deduction occurs within the same transaction, no external event flags the problem, and the contract may appear to have processed the close successfully while silently corrupting internal balances. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑reentrant pattern: either revert the call if the rebalancer is already active, introduce a mutex flag that blocks a second entry, or refactor the logic so that initiateClosePosition cannot trigger the rebalancer from within the same execution context. This ensures that the balance is deducted exactly once, the position state is updated correctly, and the protocol’s accounting guarantees are preserved.
summary: When initiating a close order for the rebalancer position with the initiateClosePosition function it is possible that the initiation of the close triggers the rebalancer itself. This results in many issues, including but not limited to: • Double counting the balance which is being closed • Removing the closed amount from the rebalancer's previous tick twice • Overwriting the state updates which were made in the Rebalancer.updatePosition function

title: C-02 | Validate Withdraw Uses Current Total Shares
content: The vulnerability arises in the withdrawal validation routine of the protocol. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract records the vault's asset balance (balanceVault) but it does **not** record the total number of shares outstanding at that moment. Instead, during the later validation step the function recomputes the entitled asset amount by multiplying the user’s share proportion with the **current** totalShares value. Because totalShares can change between the initiation of the withdrawal and its validation – for example when a previous withdrawal reduces the share supply – the per‑share value used in the calculation becomes larger than it should be. An attacker can exploit this by depositing funds, creating multiple pending withdrawals that together represent the full share balance, and then allowing the first withdrawal to decrease totalShares. The second withdrawal is still calculated against the original vault balance but now with a smaller totalShares denominator, which results in the attacker receiving more assets than their share entitlement. Repeating this pattern drains the vault without any price movement, because each cycle repeats the same snapshot‑balance versus a reduced share count. The impact is a loss of protocol liquidity and possible total fund exhaustion, affecting all users and investors who rely on the vault’s accounting. The issue manifests only when there are at least two pending withdrawals that are validated sequentially while the totalShares variable changes between them; a single withdrawal does not expose the bug. It is difficult to notice because each individual withdrawal appears to return the correct amount based on the current state, and the over‑payment only becomes evident when the cumulative effect is observed. The bug belongs to the class of *state‑snapshot* or *inconsistent accounting* vulnerabilities, where mutable global state is used for financial calculations instead of immutable snapshots taken at the time of the action. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after initiating a withdrawal they may receive more tokens than expected, or conversely the protocol may end up with a zero balance while the user’s share balance remains unchanged. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of the _validateWithdrawalWithAction function and identified that the totalShares parameter was not saved at init. To remediate, the contract should capture the totalShares value at the moment the withdrawal request is created and use that immutable snapshot throughout the validation and settlement phases, ensuring that the asset‑to‑share ratio remains consistent regardless of later share modifications.
summary: The _validateWithdrawalWithAction function does not use the totalShares amount saved at init in the pending action. Instead, it calculates the amount of assets a user should receive by using the current totalShares amount, together with the available balanceVault from init. Therefore reducing the totalShares amount between init and validation of a withdrawal will give the user more assets than the user should receive and vice versa. This can be exploited in the following way: • Attacker deposits funds • Attacker initiates multiple withdrawals of part of his shares for example two withdrawals of 50% of his shares • The first withdrawal is validated and reduces the totalShares amount • The second withdrawal is validated and uses the balanceVault from init but the reduced totalShares amount to calculate how many assets the attacker receives and therefore sends the attacker more assets than he should receive • Attacker repeats the process to drain the protocol All of this is independent of price changes allowing the attack to be performed swiftly and consistently.

title: ORDA-1 | Wrong amount deposited into the DegenBox
content: The vulnerability is a unit‑conversion bug that causes an incorrect amount of tokens to be deposited into the DegenBox when the function sendValueInCollateral is executed. The function receives a parameter that represents a collateralShare amount, specifically GM shares, and then it calculates the equivalent shortToken amount (amountShortToken) using the current exchange rate between GM shares and the short token. However, instead of depositing amountShortToken, the code mistakenly passes the original GM share amount to degenBox.deposit. Because the GM share amount and the short token amount can differ dramatically depending on the exchange rate, the protocol records a deposited balance that does not reflect the true value of the collateral. This mismatch can lead to several exploitable consequences: the protocol’s accounting assumes a higher (or lower) collateral value than actually provided, causing liquidation checks to fail and revert transactions; users may see their deposit appear to be accepted while the underlying collateral is insufficient, leading to unexpected liquidation or loss of funds; and the overall risk model of the protocol is broken, violating the business logic that collateral value should be accurately represented. The issue manifests whenever a user or a contract calls sendValueInCollateral with GM shares as the input, which is a normal operation for depositing collateral. Affected parties include any depositor of GM shares, the protocol’s liquidation engine, and downstream lenders who rely on correct collateralization ratios. The bug was discovered during a manual audit performed by the Guardian team, and it is subtle because the deposit transaction succeeds on‑chain and emits no obvious error, making the valuation discrepancy hard to detect without deep inspection of the conversion logic. The class of bug corresponds to a “unit mismatch” or “incorrect variable usage” pattern, where a variable intended to represent one unit (shares) is erroneously used as another (token amount). From a user perspective, the UI may show that the deposit succeeded, but the expected collateral value is missing, causing liquidation attempts to revert with messages like “insufficient collateral”. In reality, the protocol receives far fewer short tokens than intended. To remediate the issue, the deposit call must be amended to use the correctly converted amountShortToken instead of the raw share amount, ensuring that the value recorded in the DegenBox matches the actual short token quantity. This change restores proper accounting, prevents unintended liquidation reverts, and aligns the protocol’s behavior with user expectations of how much collateral they have supplied.
summary: In the sendValueInCollateral function the amount provided as a parameter is a collateralShare amount (GM shares in the degen box), that amount is then converted to a shortToken amount via an exchange rate. The amountShortToken is then sent to the degenBox, however the amount (GM shares) is what is deposited. Therefore a GM token Shares amount will be treated as a short token amount, which may have severely different valuations depending on the exchange rate. Additionally this can often cause the liquidation to revert if the GM token is a lower value than the short token.

title: GMXC-1 | Liquidations Prevented By Request Expiration
content: The vulnerability consists of a denial‑of‑service condition on the liquidation mechanism that can be triggered by a malicious actor who creates a new order for a user who is already liquidatable. The protocol normally cancels any open order belonging to a liquidatable account in order to retrieve the underlying collateral before performing the liquidation. However, the cancel‑order function is blocked for a period defined by the constant REQUEST_EXPIRATION_BLOCK_AGE, which on Arbitrum is set to 1200 blocks (approximately five minutes). When the GMX deposit or withdrawal feature is disabled, the keeper that would normally execute or cancel orders becomes inactive, so the pending order remains uncancelled for the full expiration window. An attacker can front‑run the liquidation transaction, open an order on the same account, and because the order falls within the expiration window it cannot be cancelled. The liquidation routine then fails to retrieve the collateral, leaving the position under‑collateralized and effectively immune to liquidation for up to five minutes. This situation can cause the protocol’s risk parameters to be violated, leading to potential loss of funds, inaccurate accounting, and a breach of the business expectation that any under‑collateralized position will be promptly liquidated. The issue is observed only when a user’s account becomes liquidatable while the deposit/withdrawal feature is turned off, a combination that is rare in normal operation, which makes the bug hard to notice during routine testing. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the order‑cancellation logic and the conditions under which the keeper operates, revealing the logical flaw that the request expiration check prevents forced cancellation. The bug falls into the class of front‑running and time‑locked request‑expiration vulnerabilities that deny critical protocol actions. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include a liquidatable position that does not get liquidated, balances that stay unchanged despite insufficient collateral, and pending orders that linger for several minutes instead of being resolved within seconds. To remediate the problem the protocol should forbid the creation of new orders for accounts that are already liquidatable and must enforce that the deposit/withdrawal feature is enabled before allowing order creation. Additionally, the cancellation routine should be allowed to bypass the request‑expiration restriction for liquidation‑critical paths, or the keeper should remain active for order cancellations even when deposits and withdrawals are disabled. Implementing these changes restores the guarantee that liquidations can always proceed when required, aligning actual behavior with the intended accounting and risk management model.
summary: During liquidation, if a user has an open order, the order is cancelled in order to retrieve the underlying tokens. However orders cannot be cancelled while within the REQUEST_EXPIRATION_BLOCK_AGE. Therefore a malicious user can front-run liquidations and create an order to prevent liquidations. The REQUEST_EXPIRATION_BLOCK_AGE is currently configured to 1200 blocks on Arbitrum. In practice, the time to execute an order in GMX should be ~2 seconds, however when the deposit or withdrawal feature is disabled on GMX the keeper will not execute or cancel orders. Therefore a malicious user can gain a ~5 minute grace period where they cannot be liquidated due to the REQUEST_EXPIRATION_BLOCK_AGE when the deposit or withdrawal feature is disabled as the order will not be executed or cancelled by the keeper.

title: CRT-1 Shorted root hash can be brute forced
content: The vulnerability is a cryptographic weakness in the cumulative Merkle‑drop implementation that uses a truncated (128‑bit or 160‑bit) root hash instead of the full 256‑bit hash. Because the root hash is shortened, the collision resistance of the hash function is dramatically reduced, allowing a malicious actor to brute‑force a valid Merkle proof for a chosen leaf that encodes the attacker’s address and a fabricated token balance. The root hash is calculated as keccak256 of the Merkle tree, but only the lower 128 or 160 bits are stored, so an attacker can iterate over possible leaf values – essentially address and balance pairs – until the truncated hash matches the stored root. Once a matching leaf is found, the attacker can submit the corresponding Merkle proof to the contract’s claim function and receive tokens that they are not entitled to. The impact is the potential unauthorized draining of the airdrop or distribution pool, causing funds to disappear from the contract and leaving legitimate users without their expected allocations. This condition occurs only when the contract is deployed with the short‑hash cumulative Merkle‑drop variant; any contract that relies on the full 256‑bit version is not affected. The affected parties include the protocol developers, token holders expecting a fair distribution, and any users who interact with the claim function. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the Merkle‑drop verification logic and noticed the use of an abbreviated hash length. It is hard to notice in routine testing because the contract will still correctly verify proofs that happen to fit the shortened hash, and normal usage does not expose the low entropy of the root. To remediate, the contract should be rewritten to use the full 256‑bit cumulative Merkle‑drop implementation, which guarantees that hash collisions are computationally infeasible. In conceptual terms, the fix removes the possibility of brute‑forcing a Merkle proof by ensuring the Merkle root has full cryptographic strength. From a user’s perspective, the symptom would be that the total token balance of the distribution contract suddenly shrinks or that claimed amounts exceed what was advertised, because an attacker can claim extra tokens. The bug belongs to the class of “insufficient hash length” or “truncated hash collision” vulnerabilities that break the integrity guarantees of Merkle proofs and violate the fundamental accounting assumption that each leaf uniquely maps to a single token allocation.
summary:
Malicious user can brute force proof for case leaf = keccak128(abi.encodePacked(address(malicioususer), token.balanceOf(address(this)))) because root hash is shorted:
CumulativeMerkleDrop128.sol#L95
CumulativeMerkleDrop160.sol#L95

title: CRT-1 Transactions frontrunning
content: The vulnerability resides in a fee‑collection contract that calculates the amount of tokens to return to a trader with the expression `returnAmount = amount * tokenBalance / value(erc20)`. This formula mistakenly multiplies the requested trade size (`amount`) by the total balance of the pool (`tokenBalance`) and then divides by the stored price (`value(erc20)`). Because the pool balance is used instead of a per‑unit price, the contract effectively locks a fixed price for the entire remaining balance rather than the price for a single token. The root cause is the misuse of a global state variable (`tokenBalance`) in a price calculation that should be based on a unit price derived from the ratio of value to balance. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a legitimate user’s transaction: first calling a function such as `updateReward` that artificially inflates `tokenBalance`, then submitting a trade that uses the corrupted price. The victim’s trade is executed with a higher effective price, so the user receives fewer tokens than expected (for example, receiving ~8.6 WETH instead of the full 10 WETH) while the attacker profits from the price difference (approximately 1.4 WETH). The same error also breaks partial‑trade accounting; when two users trade sequentially for the same amount, the second trader receives an incorrect amount (e.g., 5 WETH purchased for 100 1Inch instead of the expected 50 1Inch), causing the original reward provider to receive either no compensation or an over‑payment. The issue manifests only when multiple transactions are packed in the same block and an adversary can insert a state‑changing call before the victim, making it hard to notice in routine testing because the arithmetic looks plausible and the deviation is modest. The impact includes lost funds for honest traders, unfair profit for manipulators, and a breakdown of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, potentially eroding trust in the fee‑collector mechanism. The flaw was discovered during a MixBytes audit that inspected the contract’s arithmetic logic and identified the incorrect use of `tokenBalance`. To remediate, the return amount should be calculated using a per‑unit price, for example `returnAmount = amount * value(erc20) / tokenBalance` or an equivalent expression that isolates the unit price before applying the trade size, thereby restoring correct proportional pricing and preventing front‑run price manipulation.

title: C-01 | Collateral Removed On Position Adjustment
content: The vulnerability is a collateral‑withdrawal flaw that allows an address holding the fee‑collector role to remove all of its deposited collateral simply by adjusting a liquidity position. The contract enforces a special rule for fee collectors that their positions are considered to have a zero collateral requirement. When a fee collector calls either increaseLiquidityPosition or decreaseLiquidityPosition, the internal updateCollateral routine interprets the existing collateral as excess because the required amount is calculated as zero. Consequently the routine removes the entire collateral balance and transfers it back to the caller. This behaviour contradicts the protocol specification, which states that a fee collector must never be able to back out of the collateral it has provided, even when the position is being modified. The root cause is the combination of a privileged‑role check that sets the required collateral to zero and a generic collateral‑rebalancing function that blindly returns any surplus to the caller. An attacker can exploit the issue by first depositing the minimum collateral needed to open a position, then invoking a position‑adjustment function; the contract will instantly refund the full amount, effectively letting the attacker withdraw collateral that should remain locked for the duration of the epoch. The impact is a direct loss of funds for the protocol because the withdrawn collateral may be needed to cover under‑collateralized positions, potentially leading to liquidation of other users’ positions or a shortfall in the fee pool. The flaw manifests only when a fee collector modifies a position during an active epoch; normal users are not affected because their required collateral is computed correctly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that exercised the fee‑collector workflow and observed that the collateral balance became zero after a position adjustment. It is hard to notice because the same functions work as intended for regular participants, and the transfer of collateral back to the caller may be mistaken for a legitimate refund after a position close. To remediate the problem the contract should either prevent updateCollateral from being executed for fee‑collector accounts when a position is adjusted, or prohibit fee collectors from modifying positions until the epoch ends, thereby ensuring that collateral remains locked for the required period. This class of bug falls under improper handling of privileged roles in accounting logic, where a special‑case rule unintentionally triggers a generic refund mechanism, breaking the intended invariant that collateral stays locked for the duration of the position.
summary: Fee collectors can create under-collateralized positions and collateralize them using depositCollateral. However, when calling increaseLiquidityPosition or decreaseLiquidityPosition, the zero collateral requirement for fee collectors causes updateCollateral to mistakenly remove and transfer all collateral back to the fee collector. This allows fee collectors to withdraw collateral after depositing, potentially any loss at the end of the epoch. This is against protocol spec that the fee collector should never be able to back out of provided collateral, even if adjusting positions.

title: C-01 | Total DoS Of Epochs
content: The vulnerability is an accounting and state‑management flaw in the vault’s redemption workflow that allows a malicious actor to inflate the totalPendingWithdrawals counter and eventually trigger an underflow in the _reconcilePendingTransactions routine, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service for the whole protocol. The root cause is that the requestRedeem function only checks that the caller’s share balance is sufficient but does not transfer or lock the shares at the moment the request is created. Because the shares remain fully transferable, an attacker can submit a redemption request, then move the same shares to another address, submit another request, and repeat this cycle arbitrarily many times. Each call adds the requested amount to totalPendingWithdrawals while the underlying token supply and the pendingSharesToBurn bookkeeping remain unchanged. Over time the inflated pending total diverges from the actual share supply, and when the vault later attempts to reconcile pending transactions it performs arithmetic that assumes the two values are consistent. The mismatch can cause a subtraction that underflows, reverting the transaction and preventing any further processing of withdrawals for the current epoch. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected failures when trying to redeem, missing or zero refunds, and a vault UI that may display an unusually large pending withdrawal amount or a frozen state where no withdrawals are processed. The impact is severe: any user can manipulate the accounting, potentially drain the vault of usable liquidity, and the protocol can become completely unusable until the state is manually corrected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of share handling and identified that shares were never transferred or burned at request time, a pattern that contradicts the deposit flow where tokens are moved immediately. Because the bug only manifests when the reconciliation logic runs, it can be difficult to notice during normal operation, especially if the totalPendingWithdrawals grows slowly. The recommended mitigation is to align the redeem workflow with the deposit workflow: transfer the caller’s shares to the vault when a redemption request is created, and later burn those shares from the vault’s balance rather than from the user’s address. This ensures that the pending withdrawal amount always reflects actual locked shares, preventing the arithmetic mismatch and eliminating the possibility of an underflow‑induced denial‑of‑service.
summary: Users can create redemption requests for their vault shares using the requestRedeem function, which will increase the totalPendingWithdrawals variable. The only requirement regarding the request amount is that the users' balance must be sufficient. Users’ shares are neither transferred nor burned at the creation of the request. Since these shares are transferable, a user can create a request using requestRedeem, transfer shares to another address, create another request, and repeat this process as many times as desired. As a result, totalPendingWithdrawals will be inflated. This allows users to manipulate pendingSharesToBurn and totalSupply, or even cause a complete DoS in the system due to an underflow [here](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-1/blob/5b3416a28dfaa24ba3844e10081e55425d0a286a/packages/protocol/src/vault/Vault.sol#L301C13-L307C15) in the _reconcilePendingTransactions function.

title: C-02 | Bond Cannot Be Returned
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the bond that a user must lock when calling submitMarketSettlementPrice in the Vault contract. The contract forwards the price submission to an UMA oracle and, by design, registers the Vault itself as the asserter of the price. When the oracle resolves the assertion, the UMA protocol automatically returns the locked bond to the address that was recorded as the asserter. Because the Vault is hard‑coded as the asserter, the bond is transferred back to the Vault contract rather than to the original caller who supplied the bond. The Vault contains no function that allows the original caller to claim or recover the returned bond, and there is no bookkeeping that records which user supplied the bond. Consequently, the bond becomes permanently trapped in the Vault’s balance. This flaw originates from a logical design error: the contract assumes that the entity that posted the bond (the user) is also the entity that should receive it back, but it instead records the contract itself as the beneficiary. An attacker does not need to exploit code execution; any honest user who submits a market settlement price will lose the bond they paid, and a malicious actor could force others to submit prices to drain their funds. The impact is a direct loss of user capital, erosion of trust in the protocol’s settlement mechanism, and the permanent reduction of available liquidity in the Vault. The issue manifests every time submitMarketSettlementPrice is invoked and the UMA assertion settles successfully; under those conditions the bond is returned to the Vault and never becomes accessible again. Users are affected because they see a successful transaction but later notice that the amount they locked disappears from their wallet with no refund or error message. The problem was identified during a manual security audit (by the auditor “Guardian”) that examined the settlement flow and noticed the missing recovery path. It can be hard to detect because the contract does not emit an event indicating that the bond was returned to the Vault, and the Vault’s internal balance is not exposed to users, so the loss appears as a silent deduction. To remediate, the settlement function should allow the caller to specify the asserter address (or automatically set the caller as the asserter) so that the UMA protocol returns the bond directly to the user. Additionally, the Vault should maintain a mapping of bond owners and provide a withdrawal or claim function that lets users retrieve any bond that the contract receives, ensuring that funds are never permanently locked due to a design oversight. This class of bug is a “bond‑locking without refund” or “asset‑recovery omission” flaw, where a contract receives a token or ether as collateral but lacks a mechanism to return it to the rightful owner after the intended operation completes.
summary: When submitMarketSettlementPrice is called in Vault.sol, the vault is set as the asserter in the UMA oracle. Upon successful settlement of the assertion price, the bond is returned to the vault. However, there is no mechanism to refund this bond to the user who submitted the price and paid for it. Additionally, there is no recovery function, causing the bond to remain permanently stuck in the vault.

title: C-02 | tradeRatio Can Be Manipulated To Wipe Debt
content: The contract calculates a proxy price called tradeRatio from the amount received in a Uniswap‑style swap when a trader modifies an existing position. TradeRatio is then used to compute the value of virtual gas (vGas) and to determine the amount of virtual ETH (vETH) that must be borrowed for the new position. The vulnerability arises because the calculation does not guard against the situation where the swap involves a dust amount of vGas. Due to Uniswap’s rounding rules, a very small amountIn or amountOut can be rounded down to zero, which makes tradeRatio evaluate to zero. The protocol only checks that tradeRatio stays within a configured minPrice / maxPrice range, but the check is performed after the ratio has already been used to set the borrowed vETH amount. Consequently, a zero tradeRatio leads to a borrowedVEth value of zero, effectively erasing the debt associated with the position. An attacker can open a long position, then decrease the position by a single wei, forcing tradeRatio to zero, which is below the minPrice threshold. The system records the position as having no borrowed vETH, creating bad debt. When the attacker subsequently closes the position, they retrieve their original collateral and any accrued profit, while the protocol absorbs the loss as unrecoverable debt. This exploit can be carried out whenever a trader modifies a position with a tiny vGas amount, and the contract does not enforce a non‑zero tradeRatio or revert on ratios below the minimum price. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the trade modification flow and identified the rounding edge case. It is difficult to notice because the zero‑ratio condition only occurs for dust‑size swaps that appear harmless, and the contract’s error handling does not flag a zero tradeRatio as abnormal. To remediate, the contract should validate that the computed tradeRatio is greater than or equal to the configured minimum price (and less than or equal to the maximum price) before it is used to calculate borrowed amounts, and should revert the transaction if the ratio is zero or otherwise invalid. Additionally, enforcing a minimum swap size or using a safe‑division routine that guarantees a non‑zero denominator would prevent the rounding‑to‑zero scenario. The bug belongs to the class of price‑oracle manipulation and rounding‑error vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions, leading to situations where users receive more funds than they should and the protocol incurs unrecoverable debt.
summary: When modifying a trade position, the output of a swap is used to calculate tradeRatio, which serves as a proxy price to determine the value of vGas. This ratio is essential for calculating PnL and setting the borrowed amounts for the new position. However, if a small (dust) amount of vGas is swapped, amountIn or amountOut for vETH may round to zero due to Uniswap’s rounding behavior, causing tradeRatio to also be zero. This allows for potential exploitation: in a long position, borrowedVEth becomes zero, effectively wiping the position's debt and creating bad debt in the system. Attack Scenario: 1. Alice opens a long position. 2. Alice decreases the position by 1 wei, setting tradeRatio to zero, which is below minPrice, creating bad debt by wiping all borrowedVEth. 3. Alice closes the position, recovering all previously deposited collateral plus additional funds, effectively stealing from the system.

title: C-01 | Claims By The Collector Prevented
content: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the size of the collectors array that is built in the internal _getClaimChecksFromVestingConfigs routine and the actual entries that are written into that array. The routine first counts the number of vesting configurations whose collector field equals the zero address and uses that count (numCollectors) to allocate a fixed‑length checks.collectors array. Later, entries are only written when two conditions are true: the claim is intended for a collector (isForCollector) and the collector address stored in the configuration matches the caller (c.collector == msg.sender). Because the initial count includes configurations that have a zero collector, the allocated array contains slots that are never populated for those configurations. Those empty slots retain the default zero address value. When the populated array is handed over to the L1 ClaimChecker contract, each element is validated with a call to _checkCollectorClaim(claimer, collectors[i]). The zero address cannot be approved in the delegate registry, so the validation for those empty slots fails automatically. As a result, any claim that relies on this verification path is rejected, even though the caller may be a legitimate collector. The bug manifests whenever a collector attempts to claim vested tokens and the vesting configuration includes any entry with a zero collector address. Users experience a denial of service: they submit a claim transaction, the UI reports success of submission but the claim never finalises, balances remain unchanged and the expected refund or token transfer never arrives. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that each collector entry corresponds to a valid address are violated, breaking the business logic that collectors should be able to retrieve their allocations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the logic for building the collectors array and noticed the inconsistent condition used for sizing versus populating the array. It is subtle because the contract does not revert; it simply returns a false verification result, making the failure appear as a generic claim error rather than a clear programming mistake. To remediate the problem the array length must be derived from the same predicate that determines whether an entry will be written – i.e., increment numCollectors only when isForCollector && c.collector == msg.sender – or the array should be resized (e.g., using a dynamic push or trimming after the loop) so that no zero‑address entries are passed to the ClaimChecker. In conceptual terms the fix removes the mismatch between expected and actual collector entries, ensuring that only valid collector addresses are validated and that legitimate claims can be completed without unexpected zero‑address rejections.
summary: In the _getClaimChecksFromVestingConfigs function the checks.collectors array is assigned a length based on the numCollectors which is purely the number of conﬁgs which satisfy c.collector = address(0). However the criteria for an address to be added to the checks.collectors array is isForCollector & co.collector = msg.sender. Therefore the checks.collectors array will have empty entries for the conﬁgs that are claimed by the collector address themselves. The checks.collectors array with empty entries is then used to verify the claim with the ClaimChecker contract on L1. The _checkCollectorClaim(claimer, collectors[i]) check will trivially fail because no claimer can be approved in the delegate registry for the zero address. Therefore these claims cannot be veriﬁed and cannot be completed.

title: C-01 | Messaging Channel Blocked By Locked Chain Reads
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises in the cross‑chain messaging channel of a LayerZero V2 OApp when the function that determines the exclusive owner of an NFT on a remote chain reverts because the token is locked on that chain. The root cause is the use of a hard revert in unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights as a control‑flow mechanism; when the NFT is locked the function throws, which propagates to the Destination Verification Node (DVN) that attempts to process the read request. The DVN then emits an UnresolvableCommand error and cannot verify the response for the associated nonce. The EndpointV2 contract checks that every nonce has a verified response before allowing further processing in lzReceive, so the failure to verify blocks any subsequent read messages for that OApp on the originating chain. An attacker or even a legitimate user who triggers a lock on the target chain can therefore stall the entire read channel, preventing ownership synchronization and any other read‑only cross‑chain operations. The impact is a complete DoS of the ownership‑syncing feature: users see no updates, cross‑chain transfers appear stuck, and the protocol may be unable to process further messages until the blocked nonce is manually skipped. The condition occurs whenever unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights is called on a chain where the NFT is locked, which is common on high‑gas networks such as Ethereum where the delegate may be unwilling or unable to pay the cost of calling the skip function on the endpoint. The affected parties include the OApp developers, protocol operators, and end‑users who rely on timely ownership updates. The issue was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team when tracing the flow of a revert through the messaging channel and observing that the EndpointV2 validation prevented further lzReceive calls. It is hard to notice because the revert happens deep inside the read path and the only symptom visible to users is the absence of expected updates; no explicit error is shown in the UI, only a silent stall of messages. The bug belongs to the class of improper error handling in cross‑chain messaging, where a revert is used for business‑logic decisions instead of returning a status flag, leading to a chain‑wide blockage. To remediate, the unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights function should be changed to return a boolean indicating whether the remote chain is locked, alongside the exclusive owner address, allowing the caller to handle the locked state without reverting. This change enables the delegate to safely invoke the skip function and resume normal message processing, restoring the expected flow of ownership synchronization and preventing the DoS scenario.
summary: The unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights function reverts for chains that have the NFT locked. However this will cause the read messaging channel for the OApp on that chain to be blocked, preventing all subsequent reads on the chain. This occurs because the DVNs cannot process the read request, producing an error of UnresolvableCommand which prevents the DVN from verifying their response for the nonce. When DVNs have not verified the response for a nonce, validation in the EndpointV2 contract prevents any subsequent messages for the OApp from being processed in lzReceive: [https://github.com/LayerZero-Labs/LayerZero-v2/blob/7da76840e41dc593d3c2007ce35b911b1d816b4b/packages/layerzero-v2/evm/protocol/contracts/MessagingChannel.sol#L138](https://github.com/LayerZero-Labs/LayerZero-v2/blob/7da76840e41dc593d3c2007ce35b911b1d816b4b/packages/layerzero-v2/evm/protocol/contracts/MessagingChannel.sol#L138) This produces a block of read messages on the chain which the invalid read request was triggered from. The delegate of the OApp can call the skip function on the endpoint in order to skip the affected nonce which cannot be veriﬁed and resume lzReceive processing. However with the commonality of reverts in the target unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights the delegate will not successfully be able to unstuck the read channels, especially on chains where gas costs are high like Ethereum. As a result the ownership syncing feature is completely DoS'd by either malicious or normal use.

title: C-03 | gmxUnlockDate And glpUnlockData Should Be Updated On Every Deposit
content: The vulnerability resides in the vault’s handling of vesting schedules and accounting after deposits. The contract records two timestamps, gmxUnlockDate and glpUnlockDate, only when the first deposit occurs. Because the code checks for a zero value before assigning the one‑year future timestamp, any later deposits never refresh these dates. Consequently, once the initial one‑year period expires, the vault owner can invoke earlyOwnerExit even though tokens deposited later are still within their vesting window. EarlyOwnerExit withdraws all vested tokens and signals a transfer of the vault’s ownership, but it fails to adjust the internal supply counters (gmxSupply and glpSupply) that represent the total amount of GMX and GLP held. These counters feed the per‑share reward calculations (accumulatedGmxWethPerShare and accumulatedGlpWethPerShare). When the supply values remain stale, the contract believes more reward shares exist than the actual WETH balance can cover. Users attempting to claim rewards or withdraw their stake trigger a distribution that exceeds the contract’s balance, causing a revert and effectively a denial‑of‑service. From a user’s perspective the UI may show zero rewards, a transaction that reverts with an “insufficient balance” error, or an inability to withdraw funds. The issue is a classic example of improper state management: vesting dates are not updated per deposit and accounting variables are not reconciled after an owner‑initiated exit. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the deposit and earlyOwnerExit logic and noticed that the unlock timestamps were only set once. The bug is subtle because the initial deposit behaves correctly, masking the problem until additional deposits are made and the owner triggers an early exit after the first year. The impact is critical: depositors can lose access to their rewards, experience failed withdrawals, and the owner can potentially transfer all GMX‑related assets after a year, even though some of those assets belong to later depositors. To remediate, the contract should update the unlock timestamps on every deposit, recalculate gmxSupply and glpSupply inside earlyOwnerExit to reflect the withdrawn amounts, and separate the owner’s share from the users’ share, possibly by using an escrow mechanism that protects user‑deposited tokens during ownership transfers. This would restore accurate reward accounting and prevent premature exits that violate the intended vesting schedule.
summary:
In the ExitVault contract, the variables gmxUnlockDate and glpUnlockDate are initialized only during the first deposit to mark the
end of one-year vesting period for the esGMX tokens. Specifically, they are set in the deposit function when these variables are
zero:
if (s.gmxUnlockDate = 0) {s.gmxUnlockDate = block.timestamp + SECONDS_IN_YEAR;
emit GMXVestingStarted(msg.sender, s.gmxUnlockDate);} if (s.glpUnlockDate = 0) {s.glpUnlockDate = block.timestamp +
SECONDS_IN_YEAR; emit GLPVestingStarted(msg.sender, s.glpUnlockDate);}
However, these unlock dates are not updated on subsequent deposits. This means that if additional deposits are made after the
initial deposit, the gmxUnlockDate and glpUnlockDate remain unchanged. As a result, the vault owner can call earlyOwnerExit
once the initial unlock dates have passed, even if not all esGMX tokens from the later deposits have been fully vested into
GMX. This allows the owner to exit earlier than expected before the vesting period for the new deposits is complete.
When the owner calls earlyOwnerExit, the vault withdraws all vested tokens and signals the transfer of the vault's account to a
specified receiver. However, during this process, the state variables gmxSupply and glpSupply are not updated to reflect the
withdrawal. These variables continue to represent the total supply as if the tokens were still in the vault.
As a consequence, the accumulated reward per share variables s.accumulatedGmxWethPerShare and
s.accumulatedGlpWethPerShare become inaccurate because they rely on gmxSupply and glpSupply for their calculations. When
users attempt to claim rewards or interact with the vault, the contract may attempt to distribute more WETH rewards than what it
actually possesses reverting due to insufficient balance.
This inconsistency in the vault's accounting can cause a Denial of Service for users, preventing them from withdrawing their funds
or claiming rewards. Finally, it should also be taken into consideration that the vault owner can use earlyOwnerExit to signal an
account transfer and move out all the GMX-related funds.
This is only possible if one year has passed the first user deposit. When the acceptTransfer is executed, it will unstake all
the user's funds from the vester contracts and transfer them to the receiver, receiving funds that belong to the depositors.

title: C-04 | ExitVault Overcollects GMX/GLP Tokens From Users
content: The vulnerability is an over‑collection logic error in the ExitVault contract that determines how many GMX tokens a user must deposit to vest a given amount of esGMX. The contract uses a proportional formula that multiplies the user’s GMX deposit by the maximum vestable amount and divides by the vault’s GMX capacity. This formula does not match the GMX Vester’s official getPairAmount calculation, which bases the required GMX on the user’s combined average staked amount and the maximum vestable esGMX. Because of this mismatch, the contract computes a larger GMX requirement than actually needed. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the code; any user who follows the normal deposit flow will be forced to send more GMX than necessary. The excess GMX is locked in the vault without providing any additional vesting benefit, effectively causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective. The issue manifests when a user initiates a deposit through the _depositWithGmx function; the transaction succeeds, but the user’s GMX balance is reduced by an amount that exceeds the amount required for the intended esGMX vesting. Users may notice that after the transaction their GMX balance is lower than expected, while the amount of esGMX they receive is unchanged. This discrepancy can be hard to spot because the contract does not emit a warning and the UI typically only shows the amount deposited, not the theoretical minimum. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect financial accounting” or “mis‑aligned token pairing” bugs, where a contract uses an inaccurate formula to calculate a required counterpart token, leading to over‑payment. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the Vester’s pairing logic and the use of a simplistic proportional calculation instead of the precise getPairAmount formula. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared the ExitVault’s calculation with the Vester contract’s specification. To remediate, the _depositWithGmx function should be rewritten to call the Vester’s getPairAmount (or replicate its exact arithmetic) so that the required GMX amount is derived from the combined average staked amount and the maximum vestable esGMX, ensuring users only lock the exact amount needed for vesting. Aligning the calculation eliminates the unnecessary locking of GMX, restores correct accounting, and prevents users from losing capital without benefit.
summary:
In the ExitVault contract, users are required to deposit GMX tokens to vest esGMX tokens. The intention is
that users contribute the precise amount of GMX needed to vest a corresponding amount of esGMX, based on the
vesting mechanics defined by the GMX protocol.
However, the current implementation in the ExitVault miscalculates the required amount of GMX, and therefore, forces
the users to deposit more GMX tokens than necessary. The core of the issue lies in the _depositWithGmx function
within the ExitVault contract, which determines the amount of esGMX to vest (esGmxToVest) based on the user's GMX
deposit. The calculation is as follows:
(uint256 maxVestWithGMX, uint256 maxGMXCapacity, uint256 maxGLPCapacity) =
getMaxVestAmountForVault(address(this)); uint256 esGmxToVest = (_amount * maxVestWithGMX) /
maxGMXCapacity;
This formula attempts to proportionally assign esGMX to vest based on the amount of GMX deposited. However, it
does not accurately reflect the vesting requirements defined in the GMX Vester contract, specifically the
getPairAmount function, which calculates the exact amount of GMX required to vest a given amount of esGMX.
In the GMX Vester contract, the getPairAmount function ensures that the amount of GMX needed is proportional to the
user's combined average staked amount and the maximum vestable amount of esGMX, following this formula:
pairAmount = esAmount * combinedAverageStakedAmount / maxVestableAmount;
By not aligning with this formula, the ExitVault overestimates the amount of GMX needed for vesting. This results in
users depositing more GMX tokens than required. Users are locking up excess GMX without receiving additional
vesting benefits, which is inefficient and can discourage participation.
The overcollection not only misaligns user expectations but also contradicts the protocol's goal of optimizing resource
utilization. Users contribute more capital than necessary and the excess GMX remains idle within the vault, providing
no additional advantage in terms of vesting esGMX. This same concept also affects the GLP/GLPVester flow.

title: C-05 | Faulty ownerDeposit Mechanism
content: The vulnerability resides in the ownerDeposit routine of the vault contract, where the accounting of the owner’s initial GMX and GLP balances is flawed. During contract initialization the variables representing the owner’s initial GMX and GLP holdings are set to record the total amount that should be returned to the owner after the vesting period. However, the ownerDeposit function increments these variables each time the owner calls the function, regardless of whether the owner actually transfers new tokens. As a result the recorded initial balances are added twice – once at initialization and again on the first deposit – causing the contract to believe the owner is entitled to withdraw more tokens than were ever supplied. This double‑counting directly reduces the share of other participants because the excess amount is taken from the pool of funds that belong to all depositors. In addition, the function reduces the owner’s share count before the internal deposit logic restores it, meaning that any yield generated between the reduction and the restoration is calculated on a smaller share base. Consequently the owner receives less yield on new deposits, while the remaining yield is distributed to other users, breaking the intended accounting model. A third, related flaw is that the owner’s initial GMX and GLP stakes are automatically staked at deployment but are not included in the accumulated reward per‑share variables until the owner invokes ownerDeposit. During this window the accrued rewards are incorrectly allocated to other depositors, and the owner cannot increase their position with additional GLP because the function lacks a token transfer step for GLP. The issue manifests whenever the owner performs a deposit after initialization, which can be triggered by any normal user interaction that calls the function. The affected parties include the contract owner, who can unintentionally (or maliciously) withdraw more than their rightful amount, and all other vault participants, whose balances and expected yields are diminished. The problem was identified during a formal security audit that examined the accounting flow of the vault’s deposit and reward mechanisms. It is subtle because the contract’s state variables appear to be updated correctly on the surface, yet the timing of share adjustments and the omission of reward inclusion create a hidden discrepancy that only becomes evident when the owner’s withdrawal is processed after a year. To remediate the flaw, the ownerDeposit function should be removed and the owner’s initial balances should be vested directly at contract creation, or the function should be rewritten to update the initial balance variables only when a genuine token transfer occurs and to adjust share counts after reward calculations. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state variables are incorrectly mutated, leading to double counting, premature share reduction, and reward misallocation, all of which violate the protocol’s financial guarantees and can cause users to see their balances shrink or their expected refunds disappear.
summary:
The function ownerDeposit and its implementation brings many problems for the system. It creates several
issues for both sides of the vault. Firstly and most critical issue is: "Double Counting ownerInitialGMX
and ownerInitialGLP in ownerDeposit". During vault initialization, ownerInitialGMX and ownerInitialGLP
variables are initialized with the comment: “Store the total balance so that we know how much to transfer
back to the owner after a year exits.”
Which means owner will be able to withdraw this amount after the end of vesting. However in the
function ownerDeposit these values are incremented regardless if owner makes a new deposit or not.
Hence the initial amounts that are transferred via full account transfer will be double counted when owner
makes the deposit for them. Which means owner can withdraw more than what he actually has and this
withdrawal will come with a cost to other users, as the cost will be taken from their share.
Secondly: "Diminished Yield When Owner Deposits". When an owner deposits their shares are reduced in
anticipation of them being increased later on in the respective internal deposit function. However, before
they are increased the account will get yield based on shares. Since it was reduced early the yield will also be
reduced. Leading to a loss of yield for the owner whenever they deposit. And finally, another issue is: "Initial
Stakes Of Owner Won't be Counted in Reward Calculation".
During initialization, Owners GMX's and GLP's will be staked automatically but these won't be counted in
accumulatedGmxWethPerShare and accumulatedGlpWethPerShare until owner does a ownerDeposit. Hence
the yield accrued in between will be given to other depositors. Moreover it won't be possible for owner to
deposit more than their share amounts in one step because amount will be withdrawn from share.
Furthermore, it is not even possible to deposit new GLP tokens to the vault by the owner because there is no
transfer capability in ownerDeposit function for GLP.

title: C-06 | Utilizing Vault Transfer To Steal Funds
content: The vulnerability resides in the ExitVaultEntryPoint contract where the transferFrom function allows the current vault owner to change the NFT ownership and the owner field stored in the GmxAStorage struct without synchronising any of the accounting state that is tied to that owner. Specifically, the variables that track the initial GMX and GLP balances allocated to the owner (ownerInitialGMX and ownerInitialGLP) and the streaming structures (GMXStream and GLPStream) remain bound to the original address even after the NFT is transferred. Because the protocol assumes that ownership transfer also transfers the right to claim the future vesting and streaming rewards, the mismatch creates a situation where the new owner can trigger a withdrawal request, then the original owner regains the NFT, and the original owner still retains the unclaimed ownerInitialGMX/GLP amounts that will be released after the vesting period. An attacker can therefore inflate the amount of claimable tokens, sell their shares, and later collect the vesting payouts that rightfully belong to other participants.
