The flaw is triggered whenever the transferFrom function is called, which can be done by any address that currently holds the vault ownership. Users who rely on the contract to correctly attribute rewards and vesting to the current owner are affected, including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself because the mis‑allocation reduces the total funds available to legitimate participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the state changes performed by the ownership transfer with the expected accounting updates. It is subtle because the contract does emit an ownership change event and updates the NFT owner, giving the impression that all rights have moved, while the hidden accounting variables stay unchanged. The impact is a potential loss of vested GMX and GLP tokens, effectively allowing an owner to steal funds that should be distributed to other users. To remediate the problem the contract should, as part of any ownership transfer, settle pending rewards for both the outgoing and incoming owners, update the GMXStream and GLPStream structures to reflect the new owner, and ensure that ownerInitialGMX and ownerInitialGLP are either transferred or reset according to the protocol’s accounting rules. In other words, the transfer operation must be atomic with respect to all financial state tied to the owner, preventing a scenario where ownership changes but reward balances do not.
summary:
Owner can transfer the ownership of the entire vault to any other address via transferFrom function
in ExitVaultEntryPoint contract. However this transfer only changes the owner of the NFT and owner
value in GmxAStorage struct, but does not update any other user related values (GMXStream and
GLPStream values).
This creates an important attack vector and also some unexpected scenarios because of the
ambiguity of the action. Firstly, ownerInitialGMX and ownerInitialGLP are variables that will be
transferred back to owner after a year exits. And owner can use ownership transfer mechanism to
increment these values and steal funds from other users.
Here is the attack path:
1. Transfer ownership to your second address.
2. createWithdrawRequest, so that when it is matched, your address won't be the owner anymore
and ownerInitialGmx won't be updated.
3. Transfer ownership back main address.
4. You sold your shares but still holding ownerInitialGmx and ownerInitialGlp which you can get
those amounts back when vesting ends.
Apart from this issue it is also not clear what this ownership transfer tries to achieve. For example,
when token distribution happens, Vested GMX distribution will go to the new owner because the
transfer is done directly to the s.owner, hence the part that is not donated will go to new owner, but
reward accumulation still happens to old owner because owners' reward related variables are not
updated.
Another thing is while the shares are not transferred, ownerInitialGMX/GLP will belong to new owner
now. So while it is not clear what new owner will receive from this ownership transfer, it will also
create an attack vector to steal funds from other users.

title: C-01 | User Info Not Updated During Matching
content: The vulnerability originates from the matchWithdrawRequest function and the GMXYieldStrategy contract where a matcher’s share balance is increased without first updating the associated reward accounting. Specifically, the contract increments the matcher’s shares but does not invoke the internal _depositGMX or _depositGLP routines that would claim pending WETH rewards and refresh the wethRewardDebt field. As a consequence, the userInfo entry that tracks the matcher’s GLP stream last claim timestamp remains unchanged while the shares field grows. The same omission occurs for the esGMX vesting information, which is never adjusted when the matcher’s position is matched. The root cause is therefore a missing state‑update step that should synchronize reward debt with the new share amount. An attacker, or even a regular user, can trigger the flaw by withdrawing a portion of their tokens after their shares have been increased but their reward debt is stale. The pending WETH calculation uses the formula pendingWeth = shares * accumulatedTokensPerShare / 1e18 - wethRewardDebt. When the stored wethRewardDebt reflects a higher share count than the current shares (because shares have decreased after a withdrawal), the subtraction underflows, causing the transaction to revert. This underflow creates a denial‑of‑service condition for the affected user: further withdrawals or reward claims fail until the contract somehow doubles the user’s rewards, an event that may never happen if the contract owner exits the system. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal request but the transaction reverts, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and no WETH reward received, which appears as “my funds disappeared” or “my reward is always zero”. The issue is hard to notice because the share increase succeeds and no immediate error is emitted; the problem only surfaces later when a share reduction triggers the underflow check. The impact includes locked funds for the affected matcher, potential permanent loss of rewards, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees that rewards should be claimable proportionally to shares. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who observed that the matcherInfo update only touched the shares field and omitted the corresponding reward‑debt and vesting updates. To remediate the bug, the contract should ensure that all relevant accounting variables—GMX shares, esGMX vesting data, and wethRewardDebt—are refreshed before any share modification. This can be achieved by calling the _depositGMX/_depositGLP functions to settle pending rewards, storing the accumulated token amount instead of the debt in the user struct, and then recomputing the user’s share of the stake based on the difference between the current accumulated amount and the saved snapshot. By aligning reward debt with the actual share balance, the underflow condition is eliminated and the protocol’s reward distribution logic is restored.
summary:
In the matchWithdrawRequest function, the matcher's shares are incremented without first invoking the
_depositGMX or _depositGLP functions. This prevents the wethRewardDebt from being updated. As a result, the s.userInfo[matcher].glpStream.lastClaim mapping remains unchanged for the matcher, even though his s.userInfo[matcher].glpStream.shares have increased.
In the GMXYieldStrategy contract, when updating the matcherInfo during position matching, the contract
only updates the shares field in the gmxStream structure but fails to update the corresponding esGMX
vesting information.
This results in several issues such as a permanent DoS or drained funds. Furthermore, The WETH reward
calculation can underflow if the share amount decreased since the last claim.
Here we can see the reward calculation:
uint256 pendingWeth = shares * s.accumulatedTokensPerShare / 1e18 - wethRewardDebt;
Therefore an underflow DoS occurs if:
shares * s.accumulatedTokensPerShare / 1e18 < wethRewardDebt
The WETH reward debt is calculated in the same way:
wethRewardDebt = shares * s.accumulatedTokensPerShare / 1e18;
That means if a wethRewardDebt is stored, the shares amount of the user decreases and it tries to calculate
the pendingWeth amount again resulting in an underflow DoS. A decrease in shares can happen regularly
when users withdraw their tokens.
If a user withdraws half their tokens a DoS of the system occurs for this user until the user's rewards are doubled which could never happen if the owner exits the system in the meantime.

title: C-02 | Current Constants.GMX_REWARD_ROUTER Was Disabled By GMX Team
content: The vulnerability stems from the ExitVault contract referencing a hard‑coded address for the GMX reward router (GMX_REWARD_ROUTER) that was deprecated by the GMX team. The constant in Constants.sol still points to the old router address 0x159854e14A862Df9E39E1D128b8e5F70B4A3cE9B, which has been disabled on‑chain through a governance transaction. Because the router contract no longer implements the expected staking, unstaking and reward‑claim functions, any call from ExitVault to this address reverts. This situation occurs whenever a user attempts to stake GMX, unstake GMX, or claim GMX rewards through the protocol; the transaction fails and the user receives a revert error instead of the expected state change. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that a staking action was submitted but the on‑chain balance remains unchanged, or that a withdrawal attempt returns a generic “transaction reverted” message, leading to confusion and the impression that funds have disappeared. The impact is critical because it blocks core protocol functionality, prevents users from earning or retrieving rewards, and can lock assets in the contract if the protocol does not provide an alternative path. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared on‑chain router addresses with the values stored in the source code and identified the mismatch. It is hard to notice because the constant appears syntactically correct and the contract compiles without errors; only runtime execution reveals the revert. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of configuration or address‑binding errors where a contract relies on an external contract that has been upgraded or deprecated without updating its reference. To remediate, the constant GMX_REWARD_ROUTER should be updated to the new router address 0x5E4766F932ce00aA4a1A82d3Da85adf15C5694A1, and the ExitVault logic should be verified to work with the new ExtendedGmxTracker that now distributes GMX rewards. After the update, staking, unstaking and reward claims should succeed, restoring the expected accounting flow and user experience.
summary:
The current reward router GMX_REWARD_ROUTER =
0x159854e14A862Df9E39E1D128b8e5F70B4A3cE9B; present in the Constants.sol file has been
deprecated by GMX in a recent [transaction.](https://arbiscan.io/tx/0xcb8f8ada8d9f4afb9e49f25f55d06fd46f40ef9453c1a9e7700f10459cb23174)
A [new reward router](https://arbiscan.io/address/0x5E4766F932ce00aA4a1A82d3Da85adf15C5694A1) is now being used. Consequently, any operation on the old
reward router will revert, affecting the functionality of contracts that rely on it. The ExitVault contract
uses the deprecated reward router address for various operations, such as staking and unstaking
GMX tokens.
This reliance on the outdated address will cause these operations to fail. Do also note that the [new
reward router](https://arbiscan.io/address/0x5E4766F932ce00aA4a1A82d3Da85adf15C5694A1)
interacts with a new RewardTracker (ExtendedGmxTracker) which includes GMX tokens as reward.

title: C-01 | getPositionPnl Always Returns 0
content: The vulnerability resides in the profit‑and‑loss reporting routine of a position manager that interfaces with GMX. The function intended to return the current PnL of a position calls GMX’s getPositionPnlUsd but supplies a sizeDeltaUsd argument equal to zero. GMX’s calculation logic derives profit and loss from the change in position size; when the supplied size delta is zero the internal formula treats the operation as having no exposure and therefore returns a PnL of zero. Consequently the wrapper function always reports zero profit or loss regardless of the actual market movement of the position. This logical mismatch leads to margin and price‑per‑share (PPS) calculations that omit the real PnL, causing the protocol to underestimate required collateral and to display inaccurate account balances. The bug manifests whenever the position manager queries PnL, which is a routine operation performed during margin checks, liquidation assessments, and UI updates. All users holding positions through this manager are affected because the displayed PnL is constantly zero, making them believe their positions are flat when they may be deeply in profit or loss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared on‑chain PnL values with off‑chain expectations and noticed a consistent discrepancy. It is subtle because the function call succeeds and returns a numeric value, so no revert or error is emitted; the symptom is simply an unexpected zero in the UI or in accounting reports, which can be easily overlooked if the developer assumes the underlying GMX call is correct. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter propagation” or “logic error in financial calculation”, where a function forwards an argument that does not represent the intended quantity. To fix the issue the wrapper should pass the total size of the position, not the delta, to GMX’s getPositionPnlUsd, thereby allowing the external library to compute the true PnL. After correction, margin checks will reflect the actual profit or loss, users will see accurate balances, and the protocol’s risk model will operate as designed.
summary: The getPositionPnl function is utilized to verify the current profit and loss of a position. However, when it calls GMX's getPositionPnlUsd, the sizeDeltaUsd parameter is set to 0. The issue with this is that the getPositionPnlUsd function calculates profit and loss based on the amount of size change. Therefore, in cases where the sizeDelta is zero, it indicates that no profit or loss has occurred for that portion of the position since the portion is 0. This results in margin calculations being inaccurate by the amount of profit and loss the position currently has, impacting PPS.

title: C-02 | Insufficient Access Control On Callbacks
content: The vulnerability is an insufficient access‑control check in the afterOrderExecution callback of the position manager contract. The function assumes that the callback key originates from a legitimate order created by the Umami protocol, but it never validates this assumption. Because the contract does not verify the source of the key, any external user can supply a malicious key and force the contract to treat Umami as the callback contract. When the attacker triggers afterOrderExecution, the callback logic sets the current key for the position. By supplying a key that points to an empty or mismatched collateral token, the contract updates its internal accounting so that the price‑per‑share (pps) value drops instantly by the full external position value. This creates a situation where the external position becomes effectively unreachable without an admin‑only operation. Moreover, the admin function that re‑adds a position can be abused: after the attacker forces the pps to collapse, the admin’s re‑addition causes a stepwise jump in pps. An attacker can deposit funds just before the admin action and redeem immediately afterwards, extracting value from the external position that should have been protected. The impact is a loss of user funds, incorrect accounting, and the possibility of draining the protocol’s external assets. The bug manifests whenever afterOrderExecution is called with a crafted key, which can happen during normal order execution or any external call that triggers the callback. All users who rely on the protocol’s accounting, as well as the protocol itself, are affected because the pps distortion leads to unexpected zero balances or reduced redemption amounts. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the callback flow and noticed the missing validation. It is hard to notice because the contract’s external interface appears normal; the incorrect accounting only becomes visible after a malicious callback causes the pps to collapse, which may be mistaken for a market movement or a normal loss. The vulnerability belongs to the class of access‑control bypasses in callback mechanisms, where unchecked external inputs allow state manipulation. To remediate, the contract should explicitly verify that the key supplied to afterOrderExecution corresponds to an order created by Umami, rejecting any keys that do not match the expected provenance. This validation restores the intended trust boundary and prevents arbitrary users from hijacking the callback logic, thereby protecting the price‑per‑share calculation and ensuring that external positions remain reachable and correctly accounted for.
summary: The afterOrderExecution function is missing a check to see if the key is one from Umami. The issue with this is that arbitrary users can currently set Umami as the callback contract and execute the logic within this callback. Part of this logic is setting the current key. If this were to change either by the attacker using a different collateral token or the opposite trading direction, the key would point to an empty position, resulting in the pps instantly decreasing by whatever the external position value is as well as making the actual external position unreachable without admin intervention. To add to this any admin intervention can then be exploited, since re-adding a position would cause a stepwise jump in pps a user could deposit prior to the action and then redeem right after to extract value from the external position.

title: C-01 | Inﬂation Attack Steals First Deposit
content: The vulnerability is an inflation‑type attack on a collateral pool that follows the ERC‑4626 accounting model. The pool calculates a share price (lpPrice) as total assets divided by total shares, and the addLiquidity function mints shares for a depositor based on this price. Because the donateLiquidity function can add assets to the pool without minting any corresponding shares, an attacker can artificially inflate the lpPrice. The attack proceeds by first depositing a negligible amount (1 wei) so that the attacker owns a tiny share balance. When a legitimate user later submits a large liquidity order, the attacker front‑runs the transaction and calls donateLiquidity with a large amount of the same token. This donation raises the total assets while the share count remains unchanged, causing the computed lpPrice to increase dramatically. When the victim’s addLiquidity call is executed, the share amount is calculated as deposit amount divided by the inflated lpPrice; due to integer division the result rounds down to zero, so the victim receives no shares despite the transaction succeeding. After the victim’s order is filled, the attacker withdraws the shares they originally received; because the share price is now inflated, those shares represent the attacker’s original tiny deposit plus the victim’s large contribution, effectively stealing the victim’s funds. The bug manifests only for tokens with 18‑decimal precision because the internal _toWad conversion truncates values, and it relies on the ability to front‑run the victim’s order, which is possible in the pool’s two‑step order flow on Arbitrum. Users affected are any depositors, especially the first legitimate depositor after the attacker’s front‑run, who may see their balance unchanged or receive zero shares, leading to a loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the MUX Perps collateral pool where the interaction between addLiquidity and donateLiquidity was examined. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the UI may simply show a successful deposit with no change in share balance, which can be mistaken for a negligible amount. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “share‑price manipulation” or “inflation attacks” where external asset injections are not coupled with share adjustments, allowing zero‑share issuance. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum share issuance threshold so that any positive deposit yields at least one share, or adjust the share calculation to round up, and restrict the donateLiquidity function to privileged accounts or disable it after the first genuine deposit, thereby preventing arbitrary inflation of the share price.
summary:
An inﬂation attack, commonly seen in ERC-4626 vaults, allows a malicious actor to steal deposits
from the ﬁrst depositor. This vulnerability exists in the collateral pool and can be executed as
follows:
• The attacker deposits 1 wei of liquidity into the pool (e.g., ARB).
• The attacker observes a victim placing a liquidity order for 1000 ARB.
• The attacker front-runs the victim and donates 1000 ARB using the donateLiquidity function,
inﬂating the lpPrice.
• The broker ﬁlls the victim's liquidity order, but due to the inﬂated lpPrice, the victim receives 0
shares.
• The attacker withdraws their shares, reclaiming the donated amount along with the victim's
deposit.
The two-step order ﬂow allows for 'front-running' which is usually not feasible on Arbitrum. This
attack is also feasible only with 18-decimal tokens due to the _toWad conversion in addLiquidity.

title: C-01 | Mishandled Donated Liquidity Breaks Rebalance
content: The vulnerability originates in the liquidity removal routine of the BPOOLv1 contract, specifically the removeAllFrom function that is supposed to treat unexpected donated liquidity as regular liquidity and move the corresponding amount together with its accrued fees into the bAssetFees_ accumulator for later transfer to the fee recipient. In practice the function forwards the donated amount to an internal removeLiquidity call that permanently burns the tokens, while the same amount is nevertheless added to the bAssetFees_ total. This creates a bookkeeping inconsistency: the protocol records more fee tokens than actually exist in the MarketMaking contract’s bAsset balance. When the rebalance routine later attempts to transfer the accumulated fees, the contract detects that its internal balance is insufficient and triggers a revert. The revert aborts the entire rebalance operation, preventing the market‑making engine from adjusting its liquidity positions in response to price changes. A malicious participant can exploit the flaw by deliberately sending a donation to the pool; the donation is burned, the fee counter is inflated, and the subsequent fee transfer always fails, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition for the rebalance function. From a user’s perspective the protocol appears unresponsive: expected rebalancing actions do not occur, balances displayed in the UI may show zero or missing fees, and users may see that their deposits are not being reallocated as advertised. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that a donation caused the fee transfer to revert. The problem is subtle because the donation path is rarely exercised in normal operation, and the mismatch between burned tokens and recorded fees does not surface until the fee transfer step, making it easy to overlook during casual testing. To remediate the bug the contract should be changed so that donated liquidity is not burned; instead the donated amount should be retained, correctly accounted for, and transferred to the fee recipient together with legitimate fees, ensuring that the bAssetFees_ accumulator never exceeds the actual token balance. This correction restores the invariant that the contract’s internal fee accounting matches its real token holdings, allowing rebalance to succeed and preventing a potential DOS vector.
summary:
The removeAllFrom function in the BPOOLv1 contract is intended to handle any unexpected liquidity
(i.e., donations) by removing it from the position and then accounting for both the liquidity amount
and its fees in the total bAssetFees_, which is subsequently sent to the fee recipient.
However, the current implementation does not behave as intended. Instead, the donated amount is
burned in the internal removeLiquidity function while that same burned amount is also counted in
bAssetFees.
This discrepancy causes the MarketMaking contract’s bAsset balance to be lower than the total
bAssetFees_, leading to a revert when fees are transferred.
Because of this revert, the rebalance function fails to execute, preventing the protocol from adjusting
its liquidity to changing market conditions. Additionally, a malicious actor could intentionally exploit
this ﬂaw by donating, causing a DOS to the rebalance function.

title: C-01 | Collateral-Free Borrows
content: The vulnerability is a cross‑contract reentrancy flaw in the borrow workflow of the Impermax V3 protocol that allows a borrower to obtain a loan while retaining full ownership of the NFT liquidity‑provider (NFTLP) collateral. The root cause is that the ImpermaxV3Borrowable.borrow function performs an external callback (impermaxV3Borrow) before it updates the internal borrow balance for the tokenId. During this callback the borrower can invoke ImpermaxV3Collateral.redeem and withdraw the entire NFTLP because the contract still believes the position is fully collateralised. Because the borrow balance is still recorded as zero at that moment, the redemption checks that the borrow balance for the tokenId on all linked borrowable contracts is zero and therefore succeed. After the callback returns, the borrow function proceeds to the canBorrow check, which still sees sufficient liquidity in the NFTLP position – even though the NFT has already been transferred to the borrower – and therefore allows the loan to be finalized. The impact is that an attacker can borrow a non‑zero amount of assets while walking away with the complete NFTLP collateral, effectively creating a collateral‑free loan and potentially draining the protocol’s liquidity. This condition occurs whenever a borrow is initiated with a positive amount and the borrower’s NFTLP collateral is sufficient, and the protocol’s code executes the external callback before updating the borrow balance. The affected parties include any borrower who can trigger the reentrancy, the protocol itself (which loses collateral and may become insolvent), and lenders whose funds are at risk. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the ordering of state changes and external calls. It can be hard to notice because the contract appears to perform the usual borrow checks, but the state mutation order hides the fact that the collateral can be withdrawn in the same transaction. To remediate, the protocol should lock the NFTLP collateral for the duration of the borrow, update the borrow balance before any external calls, and/or employ a reentrancy guard that prevents the collateral contract from being called during the borrow callback. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of reentrancy and improper state‑update ordering bugs that break accounting assumptions, allowing money to disappear: the user expects to receive a loan while the protocol expects the collateral to remain locked, but the reality is that the loan is issued and the collateral is returned to the user in the same transaction.
summary: Currently the borrow function is at risk of cross-contract reentrancy. Consider the following scenario: (1) ImpermaxV3Borrowable.borrow with borrowAmount > 0 with an NFTLP collateral that is enough to cover the borrow. (2) Callback impermaxV3Borrow is called before tokenId's borrow balance is updated. At this point in time, the account's borrowed is 0. (3) Call ImpermaxV3Collateral.redeem with percentage=1e18 to get back the NFTLP. This is still in the context of the callback. (4) require(IBorrowable(borrowable0).borrowBalance(tokenId) = 0 and require(IBorrowable(borrowable1).borrowBalance(tokenId) = 0 should pass successfully as the account wasn't updated yet. (5) Back in ImpermaxV3Borrowable.borrow, canBorrow would be called, but the NFTLP position still has enough liquidity to cover the borrow and the getPositionData function would still return the proper values, even if Alice now holds the NFT instead of the ImpermaxV3Collateral contract. (6) Ultimately, Alice borrowed a non-zero amount but also holds the entirety of her collateral NFTLP.

title: C-01 | Missing Access Control In sendMessage Function
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access control flaw in the cross‑chain messaging function of the VaultCrossChainManager contract. The sendMessage routine is intended to forward messages to a counterpart contract on another blockchain, but it lacks any authentication checks, meaning that any external account or contract can invoke it directly. The root cause is the absence of modifiers such as onlyOwner, onlyTrusted, or a whitelist that would restrict callers to authorized vault contracts. Because the function accepts an arbitrary payload, an attacker can craft a malicious payload that, when delivered to the destination chain, triggers the remote contract to execute operations that were never intended to be exposed, such as withdrawing tokens from a vault, depositing counterfeit assets, or altering internal accounting state. Exploitation is straightforward: the attacker calls sendMessage with a payload that encodes a call to the remote contract’s privileged method, the message is relayed across the bridge, and the remote contract processes the call as if it originated from a trusted source. The impact can be severe, ranging from unauthorized fund transfers that empty user balances to the corruption of the protocol’s state, effectively compromising the integrity of the entire cross‑chain system. This condition can occur at any time the sendMessage function is invoked, because there is no conditional gate that limits who may send messages. All participants that rely on the cross‑chain bridge – including end‑users, vault operators, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected, as their assets may be moved without consent. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s public interface and identified that a function responsible for critical cross‑chain operations was exposed without any access restriction. The problem is subtle because the function’s name and purpose suggest a benign messaging role, so developers may assume it is safe to be public, and the malicious behavior only manifests when the remote contract processes the crafted payload, which may not be obvious during normal testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce strict access control on sendMessage, such as limiting calls to a set of whitelisted vault contracts, using role‑based permissions, or requiring cryptographic signatures that prove the payload originates from an authorized source. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model where only trusted components may initiate cross‑chain actions, thereby preventing arbitrary message injection and protecting user funds from unauthorized withdrawals or deposits.
summary: The VaultCrossChainManager contract implements the sendMessage which is used to send cross-chain messages. This function does not implement any type of access control and, therefore, any malicious user can craft arbitrary cross-chain payloads and transmit them causing the receiving chain’s contract logic to execute unverified operations. This could be easily exploited to perform unauthorized withdrawals or deposits.

title: C-02 | Some ProtocolVault Functions Do Not Validate Properly The PayloadType
content: The vulnerability resides in a vault contract that manages deposits and withdrawals through a generic function parameter called PayloadType. The contract does not verify that the supplied PayloadType matches the intended operation of the called function. Consequently, a caller can invoke the withdraw routine while passing a payload that is defined for deposits (LP_DEPOSIT or SP_DEPOSIT). The internal ledger interprets the payload as a deposit request and credits the caller with additional shares, even though no tokens are transferred into the vault. This mismatch creates unbacked shares on the accounting layer, effectively allowing a user to generate "free" deposits. The root cause is an absence of strict input validation: the withdraw function lacks a check that the payload belongs to the withdrawal enum (LP_WITHDRAW or SP_WITHDRAW), and the deposit function similarly does not restrict its payload to deposit types. An attacker can exploit the flaw by calling withdraw with a deposit payload, causing the ledger to increase the attacker’s balance without any corresponding token movement. The impact is severe: the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, share supply can be inflated arbitrarily, and honest participants may later find that the vault cannot honor withdrawals because the total shares exceed the actual token holdings. The condition under which this occurs is any execution of the withdraw function where the caller supplies an arbitrary PayloadType; there is no guard clause to reject mismatched types. All users of the vault, as well as the protocol that relies on the vault’s accounting, are affected because the inflated balances undermine trust and can lead to loss of funds for legitimate participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the function signatures and noticed that the enum argument was never compared against an allowed set. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the ledger update appears legitimate and no token transfer event is emitted, so external observers see a balance increase without any on‑chain transfer. To remediate, each entry point must enforce that only the appropriate PayloadType values are accepted: deposit functions should revert unless the payload is LP_DEPOSIT or SP_DEPOSIT, and withdraw functions should revert unless the payload is LP_WITHDRAW or SP_WITHDRAW. This aligns the on‑chain state with the intended business logic that deposits increase balances only when tokens are actually received and withdrawals decrease balances only when tokens are sent out. The bug belongs to the class of improper input validation leading to accounting inconsistencies, often manifested as “unbacked share creation” or “free minting” vulnerabilities. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is an unexpected increase in their vault share balance after calling withdraw, or a situation where the UI shows a higher balance but the actual token pool does not contain enough assets to satisfy future withdrawals. Users expect a withdraw to reduce their holdings, but the reality is that the balance may grow, violating the protocol’s financial guarantees.
summary: In the ProtocolVault contract, both the deposit and withdraw functions accept a PayloadType that is never validated against the function’s intended usage. As a result, a user could call the withdraw function but submit a payload indicating LP_DEPOSIT or SP_DEPOSIT. On the ledger side, this is interpreted as a deposit even though no tokens were transferred to the ProtocolVault, artificially increasing the user’s balance. This leads to unbacked shares on the ledger and allows users to perform “free” deposits.

title: C-03 | handleOpFromVault Function Does Not Scale Decimals
content: The vulnerability resides in the handleOpFromVault function of the ProtocolVaultLedger contract where the incoming operationData.amount is treated as a raw integer and is directly added to the ledger without any conversion based on the token's actual decimal places. The contract documentation states that assets and shares are stored with six‑decimal precision and assumes that the account token, typically USDC, always has six decimals. On several chains such as Oasys, BNB, OKX Chain, Sora, Kucoin Chain, Telos, Conflux and Bitgert, USDC is deployed with eighteen decimals. Because the function does not normalize the amount to the token's real decimals, the ledger either over‑counts or under‑counts the true token value. This mis‑scaling can cause user balances to appear correct on the front‑end while the internal accounting records are inflated or deflated, leading to situations where a user may receive no tokens on withdrawal, see a zero balance after a deposit, or where the protocol’s total asset accounting diverges from reality. The bug is triggered whenever an operation involving a token whose decimals differ from the hard‑coded six is processed, which includes deposits, withdrawals, or share calculations. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the arithmetic in handleOpFromVault and compared it against token metadata on the affected chains. The issue is subtle because token transfers succeed and UI values may still display the expected amount, masking the underlying ledger discrepancy until edge‑case operations expose the error. Exploitation is possible by an attacker who can supply operationData.amount for a token with mismatched decimals, causing the contract to credit or debit an incorrect amount and potentially extract value from the vault. The root cause is the assumption of a fixed decimal precision without querying the token contract for its decimals. The recommended remediation is to store each token’s decimal count on‑chain or query it at runtime and to normalize all incoming and outgoing amounts to a common internal precision before updating the ledger, thereby restoring correct accounting and preventing fund loss.
summary:
In the handleOpFromVault function, the ProtocolVaultLedger contract treats operationData.amount as a direct integer without adjusting for the underlying token’s decimals. Assets and shares are supposed to be stored with 6 decimals precision. As per the code comments, this accountToken will be USDC and USDC has 6 decimals in most of the chains. However USDC has 18 decimals instead of 6 on the following chains:
• Oasys
• BNB
• OKX Chain
• Sora
• Kucoin Chain
• Telos
• Conflux
• Bitgert
If accountToken has a different number of decimals than 6 the ProtocolVaultLedger contract calculations end up over-counting or under-counting actual token amounts which would totally break the accounting in the contract.

title: C-04 | State Variables Are Updated After A Failed Check
content: The vulnerability is that the contract performs a validation check for a withdrawal request but, when the check fails, it only emits an event and returns from the internal _checkWithdraw function without reverting the transaction. Because the calling function continues execution after this early return, subsequent code that updates accounting variables such as frozenShares is still executed. This means that even though the user does not have enough shares to withdraw, the contract records the request as if it were partially processed, inflating frozenShares or moving other state forward. The root cause is the misuse of a non‑reverting guard (emit + return) instead of a require/revert pattern, allowing control flow to fall through to code that assumes the check succeeded. An attacker can trigger the condition by deliberately requesting a withdrawal larger than their balance, causing the contract to emit the failure event but still increment frozenShares. Over time, the frozenShares counter can become out of sync with actual share holdings, leading to accounting mismatches, denial of legitimate withdrawals, or potential loss of funds if later logic relies on the inflated counter to calculate payouts. The issue manifests whenever a withdrawal request exceeds the caller’s share balance; it affects any user of the vault, the protocol’s overall liquidity, and any downstream contracts that depend on correct share accounting. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the control flow of the withdrawal path and noticed that the early‑return branch did not halt execution. The bug can be subtle because the transaction does not revert, so callers see a successful transaction receipt and may not notice that their shares were not actually withdrawn, while the internal state has been altered. To remediate, the guard should revert the transaction on a failed check, or the calling function must explicitly abort further processing when the check fails, ensuring that state‑changing operations such as updating frozenShares are only performed after a successful validation. In generic terms, this is a “post‑validation state update after a failed condition” or “missing revert after guard” class of bug, which violates the invariant that accounting state must only be modified for valid operations. From a user perspective, a withdrawal attempt that should be rejected results in a transaction that appears successful, but the user receives no tokens and may later find their share balance reduced or frozen unexpectedly.
summary: In the ProtocolVaultLedger contract, the _checkWithdraw function merely emits an event and returns early if a user attempts to withdraw more shares than they hold, instead of reverting the entire transaction. Because control flow proceeds after this early return, the contract continues to update its state variables (e.g., incrementing frozenShares or proceeding with other post-withdraw steps) even when the user’s withdrawal request is invalid.

title: C-05 | Initial DoS State Contract Multiple Divisions By Zero
content: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero denial‑of‑service condition that appears in the ProtocolVaultLedger contract when a strategy fund has not yet issued any shares. The contract stores the total number of shares for each strategy in a field that is initialised to zero. During the end‑of‑period settlement functions – specifically settleMainAndStrategyFunds and updateStrategyFundAssets – the code calculates the High Water Mark (HWM) by multiplying the fund assets after fee by a constant and dividing by totalShares. Because the implementation does not check whether totalShares is zero, the first execution of these functions triggers a revert due to a division by zero. This situation occurs exactly at the beginning of a strategy’s lifecycle, before any participant has minted shares, and therefore any attempt to settle the main vault or update the strategy’s asset accounting will fail. The impact is that the ledger cannot progress past the initial period, effectively locking the protocol’s accounting state and preventing operators from finalising periods, distributing rewards, or advancing to subsequent cycles. Users and protocol operators see symptoms such as “settlement failed”, “no funds are updated”, or “the vault appears stuck with zero balances”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the mathematical assumptions of the settlement logic and identified that the totalShares variable could be zero at deployment. It is hard to notice because the failure only manifests on the very first settlement call; if tests mint shares before invoking the functions, the bug remains hidden. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of arithmetic‑error DoS vulnerabilities where unchecked assumptions about non‑zero denominators cause contract execution to revert. To remediate, the contract should include explicit handling for the zero‑share case: skip or defer HWM calculation and any other division‑based formulas until at least one share exists, or provide a fallback value that does not cause a revert. This change restores the expected lifecycle where the first settlement can succeed, allowing the protocol to correctly record assets, calculate rewards, and move forward without locking funds.
summary: In the ProtocolVaultLedger contract, when a strategy fund has not yet minted any shares, strategyFundTokenInfo[strategyProviderId][USDC_HASH].totalShares remains zero, leading to a guaranteed division by zero during future certain end-of-period operations. In settleMainAndStrategyFunds, the code invokes _calculateHWM to update the High Water Mark, which executes the line hwm = strategyFundToken.fundAssetsAfterFee * 10 * priceDecimal / totalShares reverting because totalShares is zero. A similar issue appears in updateStrategyFundAssets if fundShares (i.e., strategyFundToken.totalShares) is zero, again causing a division-by-zero revert. As a result, the very first call to these functions in the ProtocolVaultLedger contract will always fail, blocking any attempt to settle or update strategy fund assets when no shares are yet in circulation. This breaks the normal lifecycle flow for the initial period, preventing operators from correctly finalizing and advancing the ledger state.

title: C-06 | rebalanceMint May Corrupt Ledger State
content: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain accounting inconsistency that can cause tokens to disappear during a rebalanceMint operation. The ledger coordinates a burn on the source chain and a mint on the destination chain by sending a permissionless message to messageTransmitterContract.receiveMessage. The design assumes that the Vault contract will be the first caller of receiveMessage, so that the ledger can interpret the outcome correctly: a successful call results in a rebalanceMintFinish that increases the destination balance, while a failure triggers a failed rebalanceMintFinish that restores the source balance from frozen tokens. Because receiveMessage has no access control, any external actor can invoke it before the Vault does. When an attacker (or any user) calls receiveMessage with the same nonce that the Vault intends to use, the nonce is consumed and the call succeeds, minting the tokens on the destination chain. However, the ledger receives the message from an unexpected sender and treats the mint as failed, leaving the source balance reduced and the destination balance unchanged. This mismatch leads to a loss of funds that appears to the user as a reduction of the source balance with no corresponding credit on the other chain. The issue occurs only while a rebalanceMint is in progress and before the authorized Vault processes the message, making it exploitable in a narrow time window. It affects any user attempting to move tokens across chains, the protocol’s cross‑chain bridge, and any role that relies on accurate accounting of minted and burned tokens. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the rebalance flow, where the lack of authentication on receiveMessage was identified as a logical oversight. It can be hard to notice because the mint transaction itself succeeds and emits the expected events, yet the ledger’s internal state diverges, resulting in silent fund loss without an explicit error. To remediate, the receiveMessage function should enforce that only the designated Vault (or a trusted forwarder) can invoke it, or it should verify the origin of the message before updating the ledger. Additionally, the ledger should handle a reused nonce gracefully by catching the revert and sending a successful rebalanceMintFinish, ensuring the state remains consistent even if the call order is disrupted. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of unauthorized state‑transition attacks caused by missing access control on a critical cross‑chain message handler, leading to accounting corruption and potential token loss.
summary:
The ledger can perform rebalanceBurn and rebalanceMint of tokens. This effectively burns the tokens on one chain and mints them on another one by using Circle's tokenManager. The flow is as follows:
1. Ledger.executeRebalanceBurn(). This will deduct the burnt amount from the chain's balance in VaultManager and will add it to the frozenBalances in case the burn fails.
2. A cross chain message is sent to Vault.rebalanceBurn().
3. Vault.rebalanceBurn() calls tokenMessengerContract.depositForBurn()
4. If the call fails, we send a failed rebalanceBurnFinish message to the ledger, to increase the chain's balance back from the frozen tokens.
5. If the call succeeds, the tokens are burnt from the vault and, event is emitted and a successful rebalanceBurnFinish message is sent to reduce the frozen tokens.
6. Once enough attestations confirm the message, it can be executed on the destination chain by calling messageTransmitterContract.receiveMessage().
7. If the receive is successful, the tokens are minted and a successful rebalanceMintFinish is sent to the Ledger to increase the balance of the destination chain.
8. Otherwise, if the receive fails, a failed rebalanceMintFinish will be sent to the Ledger.
The problem with this flow is that messageTransmitterContract.receiveMessage() is permissionless. If anyone calls it before the Vault, the message's nonce will be consumed and even though the mint is successful, the Vault will treat it as failed. In result, the tokens will be deducted from the source chain, but won't be credited to the destination chain, leading to loss of funds.

title: C-07 | Compilation Error Due To Naming Mismatch
content: The vulnerability is a compilation‑time type mismatch caused by a naming inconsistency between two related contracts. In the EventTypes.Withdraw2Contract struct defined in the orderly‑contract‑evm repository, the field that should identify the withdrawal period is named clientId and is declared as a uint256. The cross‑chain manager contract in the orderly‑evm‑cross‑chain repository, specifically the VaultCrossChainManagerUpgradeable.receiveMessage function, assumes that the same struct contains a field called periodId and attempts to read it. Because the struct does not contain a periodId member, the Solidity compiler raises a TypeError, preventing the contract from compiling and being deployed. The root cause is a lack of synchronization of the data model across repositories after a refactor that renamed clientId to periodId without updating all dependent code. Exploitation is straightforward: any attempt to compile or upgrade the cross‑chain manager will fail, halting deployment pipelines and rendering the cross‑chain withdrawal functionality inoperable. The impact is that the protocol cannot process cross‑chain withdrawals, potentially leaving user funds locked in the vault and breaking the expected user experience where a withdrawal request should be fulfilled. This condition occurs whenever the cross‑chain manager contract is built or upgraded, affecting developers, auditors, and ultimately end‑users who rely on the withdrawal feature. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a full compilation of the repository, where the auditor observed a TypeError in the receiveMessage function. Because the error is a compile‑time problem, it may be missed if developers only run unit tests that mock the struct or if they compile only a subset of contracts, making it harder to notice until a full build is attempted. The fix is to align the struct definition and its usage: either rename the field back to periodId in the original contract, add a periodId alias, or update the cross‑chain manager to read clientId instead of periodId. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of interface‑mismatch or data‑model inconsistency bugs, where two components that share a contract interface diverge, leading to type errors and broken business logic. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that withdrawal requests appear to be accepted by the UI but never result in any funds being transferred, and the backend logs show compilation failures. Users expect their cross‑chain withdrawal to succeed, but the contract cannot even be deployed, so the reality is that the operation is impossible until the naming mismatch is resolved. The failure violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that each withdrawal message contains a valid period identifier, causing the accounting flow to break and potentially leaving balances unchanged while the system reports a successful request.
summary: EventTypes.Withdraw2Contract struct in the orderly-contract-evm repo has a uint256 clientId parameter, which is used instead of periodId. However, the orderly-evm-cross-chain repo attempts to read periodId from this struct in the VaultCrossChainManagerUpgradeable.receiveMessage function, causing a TypeError compilation error.

title: C-01 | Inﬂation Exploit
content: The vulnerability is an inflation exploit that arises from a publicly accessible raw burn function in the LeveragedToken contract. When the contract is freshly deployed and has zero totalSupply, the first user can mint leveraged tokens at an exchange rate of 1 by depositing sUSD. Because the burn function only destroys the caller’s leveraged tokens and does not call the internal _withdrawMargin routine, the caller can burn all but one of the newly minted tokens, reducing totalSupply from the deposited amount to a single token while leaving the underlying margin unchanged. This mismatch causes the exchangeRate (totalValue / totalSupply) to inflate dramatically; the single remaining token now represents the full margin. Subsequent users who try to mint with any amount lower than the original deposit receive zero new tokens, or their transaction reverts due to the inflated rate, effectively allowing the attacker’s lone token to absorb any new deposits. When the attacker later calls redeemFor, they can withdraw far more sUSD than they originally supplied, while other depositors lose their funds. The attack can be carried out immediately after deployment, requires only a call to mint followed by a call to burn, and exploits the contract’s accounting assumption that totalSupply and margin move together. Users see the symptom of “deposit reverts” or “receiving no leveraged tokens” even though they have supplied sUSD, and the attacker sees a single token that can be redeemed for a huge amount, violating the intended one‑to‑one relationship between deposited margin and token supply. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between mint, burn, and redeem functions; it is subtle because the exchangeRate calculation itself appears correct, but the supply manipulation is not obvious from the UI. This class of bug is a supply‑manipulation or inflation attack, where reducing token supply without adjusting the underlying asset value inflates the price and enables fund extraction. The recommended mitigation is to remove the public burn function or to modify it so that burning proportionally withdraws margin, thereby preserving the invariant that totalSupply reflects the amount of underlying collateral.
summary:
When the LeveragedToken contract has no existing supply (right after its deployment) a new minter operates on an initial exchange rate of 1 for the ﬁrst deposit. Under normal conditions, once tokens are minted, a user must call redeemFor to withdraw margin. However, the contract also provides a raw burn function that simply destroys the user’s leveraged tokens without adjusting or withdrawing margin from the underlying Synthetix position. A malicious ﬁrst minter can exploit this by:
• Minting a large amount: Suppose the user deposits 100000 sUSD into a brand-new LeveragedToken. He receives 100000 leveraged tokens (exchange rate = 1).
• Burning all the leveraged tokens except one: The user calls burn(leverageTokenBalance - 1). This reduces the totalSupply drastically (e.g., from 100000 down to 1), but the contract margin remains the same (it does not call _withdrawMargin).
• As a result, exchangeRate inﬂates sharply (totalValue remains 100000, but totalSupply is only 1).
• This single remaining token now has a massively increased claim on the LeveragedToken’s margin.
• If a new user attempts to mint with an amount lower than the malicious user’s original deposit (e.g., just 10000 sUSD), the exchange rate calculates the new minted tokens at the already‐inﬂated ratio. The ﬁrst minter’s single token “absorbs” the new deposit, growing their share of the margin.
• The new minter performs the sUSD deposit but does not receive any leveraged token (totalSupply remains 1). This leads to a scenario where the malicious user can redeem their one leveraged token later for a higher amount than the original 100000 sUSD at the expense of other depositors.
• In a situation where future users set slippage, their deposits will always revert if its lower than the initial 100000 sUSD as, due to rounding, they would receive 0 leveraged tokens in exchange for their sUSD.

title: C-01 | Proﬁtable Self Liquidations
content: The vulnerability is an economic incentive flaw that allows a user to generate profit by performing a self‑liquidation after depositing an amount of collateral that is far smaller than the reward paid by the liquidateMarginOnly() function. The root cause is the absence of any validation that the deposited collateral (or the collateral remaining after a withdrawal) is at least equal to the maximum possible reward that the liquidation routine can distribute. Because the contract does not enforce this invariant, an attacker can deposit a single wei, immediately invoke liquidateMarginOnly(), and receive a reward calculated on the market price of the underlying asset that far exceeds the tiny deposit. The exploitation flow is straightforward: the attacker calls the deposit function with a negligible amount, calls the liquidation function, receives the reward (for example 24.0608 sUSD in the reported scenario), and walks away with a net profit measured in dollars while the protocol’s reserves are reduced. The impact is a direct loss of funds from the protocol’s liquidity pool, erosion of trust, and the possibility of repeated profit extraction until the pool is drained. This condition occurs whenever the contract permits a deposit or a withdrawal without checking that the collateral left on‑chain can cover the highest possible liquidation reward; it is therefore exploitable by any participant with access to the deposit and liquidation functions. The affected parties are the protocol itself, its honest users, and any downstream contracts that rely on the market’s solvency. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by the Guardian team, which provided a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrates the profit calculation using current ETH prices. The flaw can be hard to notice because the liquidation function appears to be a legitimate risk‑management tool and the reward logic is not obviously tied to the size of the user’s collateral, so a small deposit does not raise an immediate red flag. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that the collateral amount supplied on deposit is greater than or equal to the maximum possible marginLiquidationOnly reward, and after any withdrawal it must verify that the remaining collateral still satisfies this condition. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of reward‑misalignment or missing‑collateral checks that enable profit extraction through self‑liquidation, violating the accounting assumption that rewards are only paid against sufficient backing collateral. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a tiny deposit followed by a large unexpected reward, or other users may notice their balances shrink unexpectedly after another participant performs a self‑liquidation, contradicting the expectation that depositing a small amount should not generate a sizable payout.
summary:
When a user deposits, there is no validation that the amount that they deposit is enough to cover the fee for liquidateMarginOnly(). This allows a user to deposit 1 wei, and liquidate themselves immediately to realize a proﬁt. Below are the calculations based off current ETH prices:
Cost of Deposit: 0.001633216 ETH
Cost of Liquidation: 0.001899712 ETH
Collateral Cost: 0.000000000000000001 ETH
Total Cost ETH: 0.003656128000000001 ETH
Total Cost USD: $12.4097 = 0.003656128000000001 ETH * $3,394.23
Reward sUSD: 24.0608
Proﬁt: $11.6511

title: C-02 | mergeAccount Abused For Proﬁt
content: The vulnerability resides in the mergeAccount function of the market contract. When a user attempts to merge two positions, the function calls sameSide to verify that the fromPosition and toPosition are on the same side. The sameSide implementation returns true if either position has a size of zero. Consequently, if the fromPosition has already been settled and its size is zero, the check incorrectly passes. After the check, the contract deletes the fromPosition in settleOrder and then copies the entry price from the fromPosition to the toPosition. Because the deleted fromPosition has a size of zero, its entry price is treated as zero, and the toPosition entry price is overwritten with zero. For a long position this makes the current market price appear as a positive profit instantly, allowing an attacker to create a zero‑size fromPosition, merge it with a funded long position and obtain artificial profit without any capital outlay. The bug is triggered only when mergeAccount is called with a fromPosition of zero size and a toPosition that is long (or short with opposite sign). It affects any user who can invoke mergeAccount, the protocol’s accounting, and ultimately the funds held in the market because the artificial profit can be withdrawn. The issue was discovered during a security audit where a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated that calling mergeAccount with an empty position yields a non‑zero PnL. The problem is subtle because the sameSide function appears to perform a legitimate side check, and a zero entry price may not be obvious in UI displays, making the exploit easy to miss. To remediate, the contract should reject merges where the fromPosition size is zero, either by reverting in mergeAccount or by adjusting sameSide to return false when any position size is zero, thereby preserving the original entry price and preventing the creation of profit from nothing. This class of bug falls under improper validation of input state and incorrect handling of zero‑value edge cases, which can lead to accounting violations and unauthorized profit extraction.
summary: When calling mergeAccount() the check to verify the size of the fromPositon and toPosition calls sameSide(). sameSide() will always return true if either size is 0. This will then set entry price to the toPosition to 0, since the fromPositon was deleted in settleOrder(). Now the toPosition instantly has a positive PnL if the position is a long.

title: C-01 | New Resolver Loses Bond After Council Reset
content: The vulnerability concerns the accounting of resolver bonds in a market contract. When a resolver stakes a bond through the sendResolverBondToMarket function, the contract stores the amount using a simple assignment (marketBond[_market].resolverBond = _amount). This overwrites any existing resolverBond value. Under normal operation only one resolver is expected, so the overwrite appears harmless. However, when a market is reset by the council (resetByCouncil), the previous resolver’s bond remains locked in the contract but is not immediately returned. If a new resolver then proposes a resolution and stakes a new bond, the assignment overwrites the previous bond amount with the new amount, effectively discarding the original bond value. Later, when the protocol penalises the original resolver and transfers the original bond to the disputor, the contract resets resolverBond to zero. Because the stored value now reflects only the new resolver’s bond, the zeroing operation also clears the new resolver’s stake, causing the new resolver to lose their bond. The root cause is the use of a single scalar field to track resolver bonds and the lack of incremental accounting for multiple bonds that can coexist during a reset. Exploitation occurs when an attacker (or any council member) triggers a market reset and then a new resolver stakes a bond; the subsequent penalty of the old resolver unintentionally confiscates the new resolver’s funds. The impact is a loss of funds for honest resolvers, a reduction of trust in the market’s economic guarantees, and potential financial damage to participants who expect their bond to be safely held. The issue manifests only after a council‑initiated reset followed by a new resolution proposal, and it affects any resolver who stakes after such a reset as well as the overall protocol’s bond‑backing mechanism. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Guardian, which provided a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the bond disappearing after the reset sequence. It is difficult to notice because the contract’s logic assumes a single active bond, so the overwriting behaviour does not raise an error and appears to work in typical scenarios. To remediate, the contract should store resolver bonds incrementally (e.g., using += when a new bond is added) and decrement the stored amount when bonds are withdrawn or refunded, ensuring that each bond is accounted for separately and that the penalty of one resolver does not erase the stake of another. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that each resolver’s bond is independently protected and refundable according to the market’s rules.
summary:
In the sendResolverBondToMarket function, the resolver bond is currently stored using:
marketBond[_market].resolverBond = _amount;
This approach overwrites any existing resolver bond, which is generally acceptable as only one
resolution is expected.
However, an issue arises when a market status is resetByCouncil. Here’s the problematic sequence:
1. Reset State: The council votes to reset the market, leaving the previous resolver's bond intact but
not immediately returned.
2. New Proposal: A new resolver proposes a resolution, adding their bond via
sendResolverBondToMarket.
3. Bond Overwrite: The resolverBond value is overwritten with the new bond, effectively discarding
the previous bond value.
4. Loss of Funds: When the previous bond is sent to the disputor (to punish original resolver), the
resolverBond is reset to zero, causing the new resolver to lose their bond.

title: C-01 | Anyone Can Trigger Limit Orders
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized execution path in the limit‑order module where the public executeOrder function can be called by any address without any access control or state validation. The root cause is that the function does not verify that the supplied tickBeforeSwap and tickAfterSwap parameters correspond to the actual price ticks of the underlying pool at the moment of execution. Because these tick values are used to decide whether a limit order has been filled, a malicious actor can supply arbitrary values that make the contract believe the order price condition was met even though the market price never reached the limit. An attacker can therefore trigger the order settlement logic at any time, causing the contract to debit or credit balances based on a false fill. This leads to accounting inconsistencies: users may see their order marked as filled while the expected token transfer never occurred, resulting in missing or incorrect balances, and the overall protocol loses the guarantee that limit orders are only executed at the specified price. The issue manifests whenever a user creates a limit order and relies on the executeOrder function to be called only by the authorized LimitOrderHook contract; however, because the function is external and lacks modifiers, any external account can invoke it. The affected parties include all users placing limit orders, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream contracts that assume correct order settlement. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the function signature and noted the absence of any require statements checking caller identity or pool state consistency. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because the contract may still appear to work when honest actors call the function, and the incorrect accounting may only surface after a malicious call or during balance reconciliation. To remediate, the function should be restricted to calls from the designated LimitOrderHook contract using an access‑control modifier, and it should also validate that the tick values match the current pool state before proceeding with settlement. Conceptually, this is an access‑control and state‑validation bug that allows unauthorized users to manipulate order execution logic, breaking the business rule that limit orders execute only when market conditions satisfy the user‑specified price threshold.
summary:
The executeOrder function is external with no validation performed on the tickBeforeSwap and tickAfterSwap values to ensure that they align with the pool state.
As a result a malicious actor can trigger limit orders when they are not actually ﬁlled causing accounting issues within the system and of course defeating the purpose of a limit order.

title: C-02 | Position Liquidity Unaltered
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the limit‑order hook where the cancelOrder routine fails to adjust the totalLiquidity field of a position after an order is removed. The root cause is the absence of any state‑update logic comparable to the _updateUserPosition function, so the contract continues to record the original liquidity amount even though a portion has been burned for the cancelling user. An attacker or any participant can trigger the flaw simply by calling cancelOrder for an order that lies within a specific tick range. Because the position’s recorded liquidity is now higher than the actual amount, any subsequent swap that tries to execute orders in that range will invoke a callback that attempts to burn more liquidity than the position holds. The callback reverts, causing the swap to fail and effectively denying service to all users who wish to trade past that tick. From a user’s point of view the cancellation appears successful, but later trades return generic “insufficient liquidity” or revert errors, balances remain unchanged and no further swaps can be performed, giving the impression that funds have disappeared or the pool is frozen. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that can halt trading, prevent fee accrual and potentially lock user capital behind a non‑functional pool. The issue manifests whenever cancelOrder is executed, regardless of who initiates it, and affects every liquidity provider and trader interacting with the affected pool. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the behaviour of cancelOrder with the expected accounting updates performed elsewhere in the contract. The bug is hard to notice because the cancel operation itself does not revert and seems to succeed, while the inconsistency only surfaces later when a swap is attempted. The problem belongs to the class of liquidity‑accounting bugs where resource counters are not kept in sync, violating the invariant that totalLiquidity must always equal the sum of active order amounts. To remediate the issue the cancelOrder function should be extended to decrement the position’s totalLiquidity by the exact amount of liquidity that is burned for the cancelling user, mirroring the logic used in _updateUserPosition, thereby restoring the correct accounting invariant and preventing the DoS scenario.
summary:
In the cancelOrder function there is no logic to reduce the totalLiquidity amount stored on the position such as in the _updateUserPosition function.
As a result, as soon as one user cancels an order in a given range, all other users will be unable to be executed and swaps in the pool will be DoS’d past that tick as the callback reverts due to attempting to burn more liquidity than exists in the position.

title: C-03 | Range Orders Arbitraged
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running price manipulation flaw in the Gamma Uniswap V4 limit‑order contract that creates range orders based on the pool price at the moment the transaction is submitted, but does not verify that the price remains stable until the transaction is mined. The root cause is the reliance on a rounded tick derived from the current pool price without any slippage or tick‑range protection, allowing an attacker to change the pool price between submission and execution. An attacker can submit a zero‑input swap with an extremely low sqrtPriceLimit, pushing the pool price far below the market price just before the user’s range‑order transaction is included in a block. When the user’s transaction finally executes, the contract creates liquidity at this artificially low price, and the attacker can immediately buy that liquidity at a highly advantageous rate, extracting profit from the user. This results in the user receiving far fewer tokens than expected, sometimes seeing their balance drop to near zero after a seemingly successful limit order, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that liquidity is provided at market price are violated. The issue occurs whenever a user submits a range‑order transaction while there is little or no liquidity below the current price, creating an opportunity for a front‑runner to manipulate the price in the same block. All users of the Gamma limit‑order feature are affected, as are the protocol’s reputation and overall trustworthiness. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s order‑creation logic, where the auditor noted that the price used for range creation is taken from a mutable on‑chain state without any guardrails, making the problem subtle and easy to miss because the transaction itself does not revert and the price deviation is only visible after execution. To remediate, the contract should allow callers to specify a minimum and maximum acceptable tick (or a slippage tolerance) and reject the order if the pool price moves outside this range before execution, thereby preventing the attacker from forcing an unfavorable price and preserving the intended economic behavior of the limit order.
summary:
The creation of range orders starts from the current pool price using a rounded tick. However the current pool rounded tick at the time in which the user decides to send their range may be significantly different then the current pool price when their order creation transaction is recorded in a block.
The Uniswap V4 pool that is used for Gamma limit orders is distinct from other Uniswap V4 liquidity sources, therefore it is entirely possible that there is little or no liquidity below the current market price when a limit order creation transaction is submitted to the mempool by a user.
A malicious actor can therefore swap with 0 input amount and a sqrtPriceLimit set to an extremely low price to move the pool price very low directly before a user’s range is created.
After the user’s orders are created, liquidity will now be available in the pool at a very low price for the provided token. The malicious actor can now buy up this provided liquidity from the user at a very advantageous price to net a proﬁt.

title: C-04 | Limit Orders Missed Due
content: The vulnerability is an order‑matching logic error in the function that searches for overlapping positions when processing zeroForOne limit orders. The routine stops iterating as soon as it encounters a position whose top tick is greater than the current pool price, assuming that all subsequent positions are also unexecutable. Because the internal list of positions is sorted by the lower (bottom) tick rather than by the upper (top) tick, a later position can have a lower top tick that still overlaps the current price. Consequently, executable orders that appear later in the list are silently ignored. This happens when the pool price moves upward past the top tick of an early position while a later position with a lower top tick remains valid, as illustrated by a sorted list where the first entry has a top tick of 300 and the third entry has a top tick of 300 as well, but a pool price of 320 causes the loop to break before reaching the third entry. Users who placed limit orders expecting a fill at that price see no execution, their order remains pending, and their funds appear to be stuck, violating the expectation that a limit order will be filled when the market reaches the specified tick. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept script reproducing the missed execution scenario. It is hard to notice because the early‑break condition looks like an optimisation and typical test cases may not include the specific ordering of ticks that triggers the bug. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect early termination in sorted data structures” and breaks the accounting assumption that the matching engine will consider every order whose price range overlaps the current pool price. To fix the problem the matching logic should not rely solely on the bottom‑tick ordering; a common mitigation is to maintain a bitmap or a mapping that records which ticks are end ticks for any order, allowing the engine to correctly identify all positions that end at or before the current price, or to iterate over the full list without premature termination. Implementing such a data structure ensures that every executable limit order is discovered and processed, restoring correct fund flow and user expectations.
summary:
In the _ﬁndOverlappingPositions function the search for executable orders is halted as soon as a position is encountered which has an end tick after the resulting pool price and is therefore unexecutable.
However, for zeroForOne limit orders, since the positionTickRangeList is sorted by the bottom tick this results in orders often being skipped when they are in fact executable.
Consider the following sorted positionTickRangeList.
0: Position(lower: 60, 300)
1: Position(lower: 120, 360)
2: Position(lower: 180, 300)
When the pool price swaps to tick 320 the loop in the _ﬁndOverlappingPositions function will break because the order in the ﬁrst index has a top tick which is above the resulting pool price. However the subsequent order in index 2 should have been included in the positionsId list and executed.

title: C-05 | Wrongful Liquidity Burn
content: The vulnerability is a wrongful liquidity burn that occurs when a limit order that has already been executed is later cancelled. The contract’s cancellation routine checks only whether the claimable principal of the position is non‑zero before proceeding. After a position is executed the claimable principal is reset to zero, so the condition is never true and the function falls through to the cancellation logic even though the position is no longer active. As a result the contract treats the already‑executed position as if it were still open and proceeds to burn the entire liquidity associated with that tick range. This can be exploited by an attacker who first creates a limit order, lets a swap move the price past the order’s tick range so the order is executed and its liquidity is marked as burned, then moves the price back and creates a new order at the same tick range. The attacker then calls the cancel function on the original order, which erroneously burns the liquidity of the newly created order as well. The impact is a permanent loss of funds for the second user, because the liquidity that should have been available for their order disappears without compensation. Additionally, any subsequent swaps that try to interact with the affected tick range will revert, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the whole pool around those ticks. The issue manifests only when a cancellation is attempted after execution and when the price returns to a range where new orders are placed at the same ticks. All users who place limit orders in that range, as well as the protocol’s overall liquidity and swap functionality, are affected. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that simulated the described sequence of swaps and cancellations. It is subtle because the check for a non‑zero claimable principal looks reasonable at first glance, masking the fact that the position’s active flag is the true indicator of whether the order has been executed.
