When a new lien is created, we check that collateralStateHash != bytes32("ACTIVE_AUCTION") to ensure that the collateral is able to accept a new lien. However, calling listForSaleOnSeaport does not set the collateralStateHash, so it doesn't stop us from taking new liens. As a result, a user can deposit collateral and then, in one transaction:
• List the asset for sale on Seaport for 1 wei.
• Take the maximum possible loans against the asset.
• Buy the asset on Seaport for 1 wei.
The 1 wei will not be sufficient to pay back the lenders, and the user will be left with the collateral as well as the loans (minus 1 wei).

title: validateStack allows any stack to be used with collateral with no liens
content: The vulnerability is an improper validation of the collateral state in the validateStack modifier. The modifier is intended to ensure that the stack supplied by a caller matches the stored stateHash for a given collateral. However, when the stored stateHash is zero – which is the case for collateral that has not yet had any lien attached – the modifier skips the hash comparison and accepts any arbitrary stack. This logical gap allows an attacker to present a fabricated stack containing lien identifiers that do not actually exist or that belong to other parties. By calling functions such as createLien, makePayment, or buyoutLien with a crafted stack, the attacker can cause the protocol to record liens that were never created, force the system to mint or burn lien tokens arbitrarily, and manipulate the storage of public vault contracts that are designated as payees. The impact is that collateral owners may suddenly see additional debt recorded against their assets, payments may be applied to nonexistent liens leaving real debt untouched, and the overall accounting of the protocol can be corrupted, potentially leading to loss of funds, denial-of-service, and erosion of trust in the system. The condition occurs only for collateral whose stateHash has not been initialized; any function that relies on validateStack for authorization therefore becomes exploitable. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the intended invariant (stack must reflect the true lien state) with the actual code logic. Because a zero hash is a legitimate value for an empty state, the bug can be subtle and may not surface in normal testing where only collaterals with existing liens are exercised. To remediate, the modifier should explicitly reject non-empty stacks when the stored stateHash is zero, and the contract should define a distinct error code for this empty-state case. This restores the invariant that a stack can only be accepted when it faithfully represents the on-chain lien state, preventing unauthorized lien creation, unexpected debt, and storage manipulation.
summary:
The validateStack modifier is used to confirm that a stack entered by a user matches the stateHash in storage. However, the function reverts under the following conditions:
```solidity
if (stateHash != bytes32(0) && keccak256(abi.encode(stack)) != stateHash) {
    revert InvalidState(InvalidStates.INVALID_HASH);
}
```
The result is that any collateral with stateHash == bytes32(0) (which is all collateral without any liens taken against it yet) will accept any provided stack as valid. This can be used in a number of harmful ways. Examples of vulnerable endpoints are:
• createLien: If we create the first lien but pass a stack with other liens, those liens will automatically be included in the stack going forward, which means that the collateral holder will owe money they didn't receive.
• makePayment: If we make a payment on behalf of a collateral with no liens, but include a stack with many liens (all owed to me), the result will be that the collateral will be left with the remaining liens continuing to be owed
• buyoutLien: Anyone can call buyoutLien(...) and provide parameters that are spoofed but satisfy some constraints so that the call would not revert. This is currently possible due to the issue in this context. As a consequence the caller can
  – _mint any unminted liens which can DoS the system.
  – _burn lienIds that they don't have the right to remove.
  – manipulate any public vault's storage (if it has been set as a payee for a lien) through its handleBuyoutLien. It seems like this endpoint might have been meant to be a restricted endpoint that only registered vaults can call into. And the caller/user is supposed to only call into here from VaultImplementation.buyoutLien.

title: A borrower can list their collateral on Seaport and receive almost all the listing price without paying back their liens
content: During the collateral listing flow on Seaport, the contract function listForSaleOnSeaport does not initialise the internal auctionData structure. When the Seaport order is matched, the ClearingHouse fallback function is invoked with an empty auction stack (stack.length == 0). The repayment loop that normally distributes the sale proceeds to the lending vaults is therefore skipped, and the only payment that is executed is the transfer of the listing price to the caller (the borrower). After the transfer, the collateral token is burned via settleAuction, but the lien tokens that represent the outstanding loans remain unchanged and no repayment is recorded in the vaults. As a result, a borrower can borrow funds against collateral, list that same collateral for sale, have the order fulfilled, receive almost the full sale price, and walk away with both the borrowed amount and the sale proceeds while the protocol’s vaults lose the expected repayment. The bug occurs only when a borrower initiates a listing; liquidation by a designated liquidator follows a different code path that correctly updates the auction stack and repays the vaults. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the listing and liquidation flows and noticed that the auction stack was never set for borrower‑initiated listings. Because the contract still burns the collateral token, the missing repayment is not obvious from the token balances, making the problem hard to detect in routine testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of payment‑distribution logic errors where uninitialised state leads to funds being sent to an unintended recipient (address(0) for the liquidator) and legitimate creditors not receiving their due. Users see the expected sale proceeds, but the protocol’s accounting shows a sudden disappearance of collateral without any corresponding loan repayment, violating the fundamental invariant that every sale must at least cover the outstanding lien. The recommended fix is to treat borrower listings the same as liquidator auctions: populate the auctionData and stack before calling the fallback, ensure the liquidator address is correctly set, and execute the repayment loop so that vault balances are updated before the collateral is burned. Separating the listing and liquidation logic and enforcing a single, well‑defined payment path will close the leakage.
summary:
When the collateral is listed on SeaPort by the borrower using listForSaleOnSeaport, s.auctionData is not populated and thus, if that order gets fulfilled/matched and ClearingHouse's fallback function gets called since stack.length is 0, this loop will not run and no payment is sent to the lending vaults. The rest of the payment is sent to the borrower. And the collateral token and its related data gets burnt/deleted by calling settleAuction. The lien tokens and the vaults remain untouched as though nothing has happened. So basically a borrower can:
1. Take/borrow liens by offering a collateral.
2. List their collateral on SeaPort through the listForSaleOnSeaport endpoint.
3. Once/if the SeaPort order fulfills/matches, the borrower would be paid the listing price minus the amount sent to the liquidator (address(0) in this case, which should be corrected).
4. Collateral token/data gets burnt/deleted.
5. Lien token data remains and the loans are not paid back to the vaults.
And so the borrower could end up with all the loans they have taken plus the listing price from the SeaPort order. Note that when a user lists their own collateral on Seaport, it seems that we intentionally do not kick off the auction process:
• Liens are continued.
• Collateral state hash is unchanged.
• liquidator isn't set.
• Vaults aren't updated.
• Withdraw proxies aren't set, etc.
Related issue 88.

title: Phony signatures can be used to forge any strategy
content: The contract contains a signature validation flaw in the _validateCommitment() routine that is intended to ensure that a Merkle root representing a strategy is authorized by either the contract owner (strategist) or a designated delegate. The code recovers the signer address from an ECDSA signature using ecrecover and then checks the recovered address with the condition recovered != owner() && recovered != s.delegate && recovered != address(0). Because the three checks are combined with logical AND, the overall expression evaluates to true whenever the recovered address equals address(0). In Solidity, ecrecover returns address(0) when the supplied signature is malformed or deliberately crafted to be invalid. Consequently, an attacker can submit a “phony” signature that forces ecrecover to return address(0), causing the condition to pass and the contract to treat the signature as valid. This logical mistake allows any borrower to provide an arbitrary Merkle root, bypass the intended authorization, and have the commitment accepted by the vault. The vulnerability can be exploited by constructing a signature with zeroed v, r, s values or otherwise invalid parameters, submitting it together with a chosen Merkle root, and invoking the function that triggers _validateCommitment(). Once the check is bypassed, the attacker can execute a strategy that was never approved, potentially moving or draining funds that should be protected by the strategist’s consent. The issue manifests whenever the contract processes a commitment and relies on the flawed condition; it does not depend on specific state values beyond the presence of a signature. All participants who rely on the integrity of the strategy approval process—borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the trust model is broken and funds may be misallocated. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit (Spearbit) that examined the signature verification logic and identified the incorrect use of logical operators. It can be difficult to notice because the code appears to check three distinct authorized parties, and developers may assume that address(0) is automatically rejected, overlooking that the && combination actually permits the zero address case. The proper fix is to reject any recovered address that is not the owner nor the delegate, and also explicitly reject address(0). This can be expressed by separating the zero‑address check from the authorized‑signer check, for example by using (recovered != owner() && recovered != s.delegate) || recovered == address(0) and then reverting, or by writing a clearer require that recovered is one of the allowed addresses and is not zero. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of authorization bypasses caused by malformed logical conditions, leading to forged signatures, unauthorized strategy execution, and potential loss of funds.
summary:
In _validateCommitment(), we check that the merkle root of the strategy has been signed by the strategist or delegate. After the signer is recovered, the following check is performed to validate the signature:
```solidity
recovered != owner() && recovered != s.delegate && recovered != address(0)
```
This check seems to be miswritten, so that any time recovered == address(0), the check passes. When ecrecover is used to check the signed data, it returns address(0) in the situation that a phony signature is submitted. See this example for how this can be done. The result is that any borrower can pass in any merkle root they'd like, sign it in a way that causes address(0) to return from ecrecover, and have their commitment validated.

title: Inflating redemption request and DoS in the vault
content: The vulnerability is an inflation bug in the redemption workflow of a vault contract. When a user calls requestRedeem, the function checks that the caller owns enough shares but it does not validate the operator address supplied as a parameter. Because the operator field is unchecked, an attacker can submit multiple redemption requests using different arbitrary operator addresses while still referencing the same owner and share balance. Each request adds its share amount to the global redemption accumulator req.totalRedemption, and the accumulator is later used in the liquidate routine to increase req.totalClaimableRedemption. By repeatedly inflating req.totalRedemption beyond the actual totalAssets held by the vault, the calculation in totalAccountedAssets becomes negative (totalAssets minus an oversized claimable redemption). This negative value propagates to the sharePrice view function, which then reverts on every call. Since sharePrice is a core primitive for deposit, mint, withdraw and redeem, the entire protocol becomes effectively denied‑of‑service: users cannot deposit new funds, cannot withdraw existing balances, and redemption attempts fail with a revert. The issue manifests only after enough malicious redemption requests have been queued, making it easy to miss during casual testing because normal operation with a single request works correctly. It was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the redemption path and noticed the missing validation of the operator argument. The bug violates the accounting assumption that the sum of claimable redemptions can never exceed the vault’s assets, breaking the invariant that sharePrice must be a positive number. From a user’s perspective, a normal UI would show a successful redemption request, but later the interface would display errors such as “transaction reverted” or “share price calculation failed,” and deposits or withdrawals would appear to do nothing. The expected behavior – a smooth redemption and continued ability to interact with the vault – is replaced by a situation where funds appear stuck and operations are blocked. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that the operator address is either the owner itself or a whitelisted entity, and it should ensure that each owner can have at most one pending redemption request that does not exceed their share balance. Additionally, the accounting logic should guard against req.totalClaimableRedemption ever exceeding totalAssets, for example by capping the accumulator or by performing a safe subtraction that reverts with a clear error when the invariant would be violated. Implementing these checks restores the invariant that totalAccountedAssets remains non‑negative, allowing sharePrice to compute correctly and preventing the denial‑of‑service condition.
summary: In requestRedeem , the function ensures that the shares requested for redemption are not greater than the owner's share balance. However, the operator parameter is not validated. This allows users to inflate the req.totalRedemption value by repeatedly submitting redemption requests with different operator addresses. The req.totalRedemption can be inflated to be larger than totalAssets . function requestRedeem( uint256 shares, address operator, address owner ) public nonReentrant { if (owner != msg.sender || shares == 0 || balanceOf(owner) < shares) revert Unauthorized(); This inflation of totalRedemption subsequently leads to an increase in pendingRedemption during the liquidate function call by the keeper, which in turn inflates req.totalClaimableRedemption uint256 pendingRedemption = totalPendingRedemptionRequest(); req.totalClaimableRedemption += pendingRedemption; The inflated req.totalClaimableRedemption disrupts the sharePrice() function, causing it to consistently revert. This is problematic as critical operations like deposit, mint, withdraw, and redeem rely on the sharePrice function. function sharePrice() public view virtual returns (uint256) { uint256 supply = totalAccountedSupply(); return supply == 0 ? weiPerShare : totalAccountedAssets().mulDiv( // eg. e6 weiPerShare ** 2, // 1e8*2 supply * weiPerAsset ); // eg. (1e6+1e8+1e8)-(1e8+1e6) The sharePrice function reverts because the totalAccountedAssets calculation returns a negative value due to totalAssets being smaller than the inflated req. totalClaimableRedemption . This calculation error results in a DoS for the entire protocol. function totalAccountedAssets() public view returns (uint256) { return totalAssets() - req.totalClaimableRedemption.mulDiv( last.sharePrice * weiPerAsset, weiPerShare ** 2 ); // eg. (1e8+1e8+1e6)-(1e8+1e8) = 1e6

title: Wrong usage of mapping target in `cancelRedeemRequest`
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect use of a mapping that stores redeem request data, combinedwith a missing allowance check, which together allow an attacker to cancel another user’s redeem request and cause the contract to burn a portion of the victim’s token shares. The contract keeps redeem requests in a mapping indexed by the operator address (the caller that initiates the request) instead of the owner address (the token holder). When cancelRedeemRequest is invoked, the function first checks that either the caller is the owner or the operator, but it does not verify that the operator has been granted allowance over the owner’s tokens. Because the mapping is keyed by operator, an attacker can supply his own address as the operator argument while specifying a target user as the owner. The authorization check passes because msg.sender equals the supplied operator, and the function retrieves the request data that actually belongs to the attacker’s own request. It then calculates an opportunity‑cost burn based on the difference between the current share price and the price stored in the request. Since the request’s share price is lower than the current price, the contract burns the computed excess shares from the owner’s balance, effectively destroying the victim’s funds. This can be exploited whenever a user has an outstanding redeem request and the share price has increased since the request was created. The impact is a loss of token value for the affected user, a discrepancy in the protocol’s accounting, and a breach of the expectation that only the request owner or an authorized operator can modify the request. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the logic of redeem‑related functions and identified the mismatched mapping key and the absence of an allowance verification step. The bug is subtle because the UI may simply show that the redeem request was cancelled without indicating that shares were burned, making it hard for users to notice that their balance has decreased unexpectedly. To remediate, the contract should store and retrieve redeem requests using the owner’s address as the mapping key (e.g., req.byOperator[owner]) and must enforce that any operator acting on behalf of an owner has a sufficient allowance or explicit permission before allowing a burn. The same correction applies to requestRedeem and the internal _withdraw function, which currently suffer from the same mapping misuse. By aligning the data structure with the intended ownership model and adding proper allowance checks, the protocol can prevent unauthorized share burns and preserve the integrity of user balances.

title: AxiomV2GnosisHashiAmbHeaderVerifier does not whitelist yaru.adapters()
content: The vulnerability is a missing whitelist check for the oracle adapters used in cross-chain message verification in AxiomV2GnosisHashiAmbHeaderVerifier. The onlyFromL1Broadcaster modifier calls _checkL1Broadcaster() which verifies that msg.sender equals the yaru contract, that yaru.chainId() matches the expected source chain, and that yaru.sender() equals the L1 broadcaster address. These three conditions are necessary but insufficient because the function does not validate the list returned by yaru.adapters(), which enumerates the oracle adapters that attest to the legitimacy of the cross-chain payload. As a result any contract that can be presented as an adapter is accepted as a trusted oracle. An attacker can deploy a malicious oracle contract, register it as an adapter (or exploit a mutable adapters list if the protocol allows) and then craft a fake cross-chain call to updateLatestPmmr(). The call passes the existing checks, so the contract stores the attacker-chosen PMMR value. This enables arbitrary state manipulation, potentially breaking the accounting of the protocol, causing users to see incorrect proof-of-membership roots, loss of funds, or inability to withdraw. This issue manifests whenever a cross-chain update is performed through the onlyFromL1Broadcaster path, i.e., during normal L1-to-L2 broadcasts. All participants that rely on the integrity of the PMMR – the protocol itself, liquidity providers, and end-users – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, which noted that the adapters list was never compared against a known whitelist. Because the existing checks appear to enforce the correct broadcaster, the omission is subtle and may not be noticed during functional testing, especially if the adapters list is not exercised directly. To remediate, the contract should explicitly compare yaru.adapters() with the expected adapter(s), for example by requiring that the length of the adapters array equals one and that the sole element matches the hard-coded ambAdapter address. This restores the intended trust boundary that only the designated oracle may validate cross-chain messages. In user-facing terms, a user may expect a valid refund or balance update after a cross-chain operation but instead receives an unexpected zero or a mismatched proof, indicating that the PMMR was overwritten by a malicious message. The bug belongs to the class of missing authorization/whitelist checks, where a critical external component is not properly constrained, leading to arbitrary state injection.
summary:
The _checkL1Broadcaster() function within the onlyFromL1Broadcaster() modifier intends to check that the cross-chain call to updateLatestPmmr() originated from the L1 broadcaster. It does so by throwing the NotBroadcaster() error in the following scenarios:
• msg.sender != address(yaru)
• yaru.chainId() != SOURCE_CHAIN_ID
• yaru.sender() != L1_BROADCASTER
While these existing checks are indeed necessary, there's an essential check missing for yaru.adapters(). This function returns the list of oracles that are confirming the legitimacy of the cross-chain message, and without verifying this value, any oracle can be used. As a result, an attacker can validate fake cross-chain messages using their own malicious contracts, which allows them to store arbitrary PMMRs in the system.

title: Front-end owner can steal all bets balance
content: The vulnerability is an improper reward‑tracking flaw in the Azuro betting protocol that allows a front‑end operator to repeatedly withdraw the fee that is supposed to be collected once per bet. When a user places a bet through a UI owned by a front‑end address, the contract records that address in the bet data and later permits the address to call withdrawFrontFee to claim a small percentage of the bet amount as a front‑running fee. The withdrawFrontFee function sets a flag round.frontRewarded[msg.sender]=true with the intention of preventing the same address from claiming the fee again, but the contract never checks this flag before allowing another withdrawal. Moreover, the internal view function _viewFrontFee, which calculates the amount that can be withdrawn, does not subtract already claimed rewards. Consequently, an attacker who controls the front‑end can call withdrawFrontFee in a loop, each time receiving the full fee amount calculated from the current contract balance, until the contract’s bet token balance is exhausted. This can happen under any normal operation of the contract because the missing check is unconditional and does not depend on special inputs. The impact is that the front‑end owner can effectively steal all accumulated fees and potentially drain the entire pool of bet tokens, leaving regular bettors without expected refunds or winnings. Users experience symptoms such as their balances remaining unchanged after a win, refunds missing, or the UI showing a successful bet while the contract’s token balance suddenly drops to zero. The protocol’s accounting assumptions – that each fee is collected only once per round – are violated, breaking the economic model and undermining trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and noticed that the frontRewarded flag was never consulted. It is subtle because the code appears to set a protection flag, giving a false sense of safety, and the view function’s omission is not obvious without tracing the execution path. The correct mitigation is to modify _viewFrontFee (or the withdrawFrontFee entry point) to first verify whether round.frontRewarded[msg.sender] is already true and, if so, return zero, thereby preventing any further fee extraction by the same address. In broader terms, this is a classic double‑spend or re‑entrancy‑like flaw where state intended to guard against repeated claims is not enforced, leading to unauthorized repeated withdrawals.
summary:
The Azuro protocol allows any front-end owner to add his address in each bet placed through his UI. In SuperExpress , this address will be able to withdraw a fee amount that is taken from each bet, some small percentage. The problem is that the withdrawFrontFee method, from where this happens, is flawed - it can be called multiple times in a loop until there is no more bet token balance in the contract.
The flaw is that even though the method does this:
round.frontRewarded[msg.sender] = true;
which is an attempt at stopping the front-end owner from claiming his rewards again, this is not checked anywhere. The _viewFrontFee method should account for already claimed "front" rewards, but it doesn't.

title: Value of leaf argument when calling addReserve is hardcoded incorrectly
content: The vulnerability resides in the payout resolution logic of the BetExpress contract, specifically in the call to the liquidity pool’s addReserve function. The function expects three parameters: the amount of liquidity to add, the amount to withdraw, and a leaf identifier that selects a particular node in the LiquidityTree where the reserve should be applied. In the current implementation the leaf argument is hard‑coded to zero (lp.addReserve(fullPayout‑amount,fullPayout‑payout,0)). Because the tree indexes start at one, a leaf value of zero never matches a valid node. Consequently the liquidity that should be returned to the pool after a bet is settled is never credited, leaving the funds effectively locked in the contract. This occurs each time resolvePayout is executed, regardless of the bet’s outcome, and affects every participant whose bet triggers the function. The root cause is a design flaw: resolvePayout processes all conditions together and does not propagate the correct leaf identifier for each condition, resulting in an incorrect constant being supplied. An attacker can exploit this by forcing the contract to resolve payouts repeatedly, causing the liquidity pool to lose access to its own funds, which may lead to reduced liquidity, failed future bets, or even a denial‑of‑service scenario where the pool cannot honor withdrawals. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a successful payout, yet the underlying balance of the liquidity pool does not increase, leading to confusion when subsequent bets cannot be placed or when expected refunds are missing. The issue is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the incorrect leaf simply results in a no‑op on the tree, making the bug hard to detect without deep inspection of the tree indexing logic. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter hard‑coding” or “invalid state transition due to wrong identifier”, which violates the accounting assumption that every resolved bet must restore the exact amount of liquidity it consumed. To remediate, the resolvePayout routine must be refactored so that it iterates over each betting condition, determines the appropriate leaf index for that condition, and passes the correct leaf value to addReserve. This redesign ensures that liquidity is correctly returned to the corresponding node in the LiquidityTree, restoring the intended financial invariants of the protocol.
summary:
In BetExpress::resolvePayout we can see the following code:
uint128 reward = lp.addReserve(
fullPayout - amount,
fullPayout - payout,
where the last argument is 0 sent as a value for the leaf parameter. Since the leafs counting begins at 1, this will always be wrong and the liquidity won't be returned to the LiquidityTree.

title: Protocol fees from NFT mints can't be claimed in BatonLaunchpad
content: The vulnerability consists of a locked‑funds condition in the BatonLaunchpad contract that receives protocol fees during NFT minting. When a user calls the Nft::mint function, the contract calculates the required payment as the NFT price multiplied by the quantity plus a protocol fee. If the fee is non‑zero, the mint function forwards that amount to the BatonLaunchpad contract using a safe ETH transfer. BatonLaunchpad implements a payable receive() function, which correctly accepts the incoming ether, but the contract does not provide any external or internal method that allows the contract owner or any authorized party to move the received ether out of the contract. Consequently, the protocol fee becomes permanently trapped in the contract’s balance. The root cause is the absence of a withdrawal mechanism – the contract’s design assumes that receiving ether is sufficient, overlooking the need for a function to claim or forward the collected fees. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the contract; the vulnerability is triggered automatically whenever a mint transaction includes a protocol fee greater than zero. The impact is that the protocol’s revenue model is broken: fees that should be available to the launchpad for operational costs, treasury funding, or distribution remain inaccessible, effectively disappearing from the protocol’s accounting. Users see no direct symptom, but the protocol’s owners notice that expected fee balances never materialize, leading to a shortfall in funds. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of ether between contracts and identified that BatonLaunchpad’s receive function had no counterpart for withdrawing ether. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error when receiving ether, giving the impression that the transfer succeeded, while the subsequent lack of a withdrawal path is hidden in the contract’s interface. To remediate, the contract should be extended with a controlled withdrawal function, typically restricted to the contract owner or a governance role, that allows the accumulated ETH balance to be transferred out safely. This change restores the intended business logic that protocol fees are collectible and prevents the unintended accounting break where funds become irretrievable.

title: Reentrancy allows any user allowed even one free HoneyJar mint to mint the max supply for himself for free
content: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw in the claim function of the HoneyBox contract. The function is supposed to let a player claim a free HoneyJar NFT after the contract checks eligibility through the gatekeeper. However, the implementation calls _mintHoneyJarForBear, which internally invokes honeyJar.batchMint. That batchMint uses safeMint, which performs an external call to the recipient address. Because the contract updates the claimed mapping and calls gatekeeper.addClaimed only after the external call returns, an attacker who controls the recipient contract can re‑enter the claim function during that external call. By re‑entering before the accounting state is updated, the attacker can repeatedly satisfy the eligibility check and mint additional HoneyJar NFTs until the global maxHoneyJar limit is reached. This allows a malicious user to obtain the entire supply of HoneyJar NFTs without paying any fee, effectively becoming the sole winner of the game and breaking the intended distribution logic. The issue occurs whenever a legitimate claim is processed and the recipient is a contract capable of executing code on receipt of the NFT. It affects all participants of the HoneyBox game, the protocol’s token economics, and any users expecting a fair free‑mint mechanism. The bug was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the order of operations and the unsafe external call pattern. It is hard to notice because the external call is hidden inside a library function (batchMint) that appears to be a simple minting helper, and the contract otherwise respects gate limits, giving a false sense of safety. The root cause is a violation of the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: state changes (updating claimed counters and gatekeeper bookkeeping) are performed after the external call, allowing the contract’s invariants to be bypassed. To remediate, the claim function should be rewritten so that all state updates occur before any external call, or a nonReentrant guard should be applied. Additionally, the minting helper should avoid calling untrusted contracts directly or should use a pull‑payment model. Fixing the issue restores the intended accounting guarantees, prevents free‑mint abuse, and ensures that users receive the correct number of NFTs according to the protocol’s rules.
summary: The claim method in HoneyBox (from its NatSpec) "Allows a player to claim free HoneyJar based on eligibility". Let's look at this part of its code: _canMintHoneyJar //(bundleId_, numClaim); // Validating here because numClaims can change // If for some reason this fails, GG no honeyJar for you _mintHoneyJarForBear(msg.sender, bundleId_, numClaim); claimed[bundleId_] += numClaim; // Can be combined with "claim" call above, but keeping separate to separate // view + modification on gatekeeper gatekeeper.addClaimed(bundleId_, gateId, numClaim, proof); Where you update the claimed mapping and account for the claim in the Gatekeeper contract after you actually do the minting itself. The problem is that the _mintHoneyJarForBear method calls honeyJar::batchMint , that uses safeMint , which does an unsafe external call to the mint recipient. This call can reenter the claim method while the claimed accounting was still not done and actually claim all of the HoneyJar NFTs until mintConfig.maxHoneyJar is hit, which will most likely make him the winner of the game so he will get all of the NFTs in it as well, paying nothing. What makes it worse as well is that even though the claim method has protection because it accepts a gateId argument, and the gates themselves have a maxClaimable property, this is also broken since the gatekeeper::addClaimed call is also done after the unsafe external call, so multiple invariants can be broken here.

title: Anyone can mint all NFTs through the public mint before it has even started
content: The vulnerability is an uninitialized bundle check that allows the public mint functions mekHoneyJarWithERC20 and mekHoneyJarWithETH to be called before any bundle has been added. Both functions contain a guard that reverts when slumberParties[bundleId_].publicMintTime is greater than the current block timestamp, assuming that a non‑zero timestamp indicates an active mint window. When no bundles exist the mapping returns default values, so publicMintTime is zero. Because zero is not greater than the current timestamp, the guard does not revert and the subsequent _canMintHoneyJar logic also sees default values that satisfy its internal limits. An attacker can therefore pass a bundleId of 0, bypass the time restriction, and invoke the mint routine to create the maximum number of HoneyJar NFTs defined in the mint configuration. This can be done at any time before the first legitimate bundle is registered, effectively front‑running the game and draining the entire NFT supply. The impact is that anyone can obtain NFTs for free, breaking the intended scarcity model, causing loss of revenue for the protocol and unfair distribution to users. The issue affects all participants of the protocol, including legitimate users who expect the mint to be closed until the publicMintTime is reached, and it compromises the economic assumptions of the project. The bug was discovered during a manual security review that examined the control flow of the mint functions and noticed that the existence of a bundle was never verified. Because the check relies on a comparison rather than an explicit non‑zero validation, the problem can be subtle and may not be evident from the UI, which typically disables the mint button until the public mint opens. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to reject minting, yet a transaction with bundleId 0 succeeds and the user receives NFTs unexpectedly, violating the expectation that “mint is not open”. The vulnerability belongs to the class of uninitialized‑state or default‑value bypass bugs, where missing validation of a struct’s initialization allows default values to satisfy security checks. The recommended mitigation is to add an explicit revert in _canMintHoneyJar (or in the public mint functions) when slumberParties[bundleId_].publicMintTime equals zero, thereby ensuring that only bundles that have been properly initialized can be used for minting.
summary: Both the mekHoneyJarWithERC20 and mekHoneyJarWithETH methods are ways for the players to mint HoneyJar NFTs, but they should work only when general mint is open, as shown in this check that is present in both methods: if (slumberParties[bundleId_].publicMintTime > block.timestamp) revert GeneralMintNotOpen(bundleId_); The problem is that anyone can call both methods anytime before the first bundle was added. If there were no bundles, this means that if a user supplied bundleId_ == 0 to either method, all of the values in the slumberParties[bundleId_] mapping will have a default value, passing all of the checks in the methods and in the _canMintHoneyJar method. This essentially means anyone can front-run the games and mint the maximum available HoneyJar configured in the mintConfig .

title: Re-requesting randomness from VRF is a security anti-pattern
content: The vulnerability consists of an anti‑pattern where the contract exposes a function, forceHoneyJarSearch, that can be called to issue a new request for randomness from Chainlink VRF. This design violates the recommended VRF usage guidelines, which state that re‑requesting randomness is easily observable on‑chain and should be avoided because the VRF service provider can withhold the fulfillment of a pending request until a later request that is more favorable to them is submitted. The root cause is that the contract does not enforce a single‑use randomness request lifecycle and instead allows arbitrary callers to trigger additional VRF requests after an initial one has been made. An attacker, or a malicious VRF operator, can exploit this by deliberately delaying the original randomness response and waiting for the contract to issue a new request that aligns with the attacker’s desired outcome. By doing so, the attacker can bias the random value that the protocol ultimately uses, undermining the fairness of any game, lottery, or allocation mechanism that depends on unbiased randomness. The impact is that users who expect a fair random result may receive a manipulated outcome, potentially leading to loss of funds, unfair advantage, or erosion of trust in the protocol. The condition under which the issue manifests is any time the forceHoneyJarSearch function is invoked – either by a legitimate user or a malicious actor – after an initial VRF request has been sent but before it is fulfilled. All participants who rely on the randomness, including end‑users, token holders, and the protocol itself, are affected because the randomness may no longer be unpredictable. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s behavior against the official VRF best‑practice documentation. It can be hard to notice because the contract still receives a random number eventually, so the UI may appear to work normally, while the underlying randomness may have been subtly steered. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a game round may finish with an unexpected result, or a reward may be allocated in a way that seems unfair, even though the interface shows no error. The issue belongs to the class of “VRF re‑request abuse” bugs, where the contract’s logic permits multiple randomness requests that can be leveraged to influence the final random output. To remediate the problem the contract should eliminate the forceHoneyJarSearch function entirely, enforce a single request per randomness need, and follow the standard pattern of requesting VRF once and using the callback only once, thereby preventing any opportunity for the provider to withhold or manipulate the fulfillment.
summary: The forceHoneyJarSearch method is used to "kick off another VRF request", as mentioned in its NatSpec. This goes against the security standards in using VRF, as stated in the docs: Re-requesting randomness is easily detectable on-chain and should be avoided for use cases that want to be considered as using VRFv2 correctly. Basically, the service provider can withhold a VRF fulfillment until a new request that is favorable for them comes.

title: State is not properly updated on L2, leading to stuck prize NFTs
content: The vulnerability originates from a cross‑chain state inconsistency between the Layer 1 (L1) contract and its counterpart on Layer 2 (L2). When the addToParty function is called on L1, it correctly pushes new sleeper NFT identifiers into the party.sleepoors array stored on L1, but it fails to emit or forward a cross‑chain message that would update the same array on L2. As a result, the L2 party.sleepoors array retains its previous length, while the L1 view shows a larger number of sleepers. Subsequent calls to wakeSleeper on L2 perform a validation that compares the number of already used sleepers (party.numUsed) with the length of the party.sleepoors array on L2. Because the length on L2 is stale, the condition party.numUsed == party.sleepoors.length becomes true prematurely, causing the function to revert with PartyAlreadyWoke even though there are still unclaimed sleeper NFTs. This bug can be exploited unintentionally by any user who adds new sleepers after the contract is deployed: they will be unable to claim the associated prize NFTs because the contract believes the party is already fully woken. The impact is that prize NFTs become effectively locked; users see no reward, balances remain unchanged, and the protocol’s incentive mechanism breaks. The issue manifests only when the cross‑chain update is required – i.e., after addToParty is executed on L1 and a subsequent wakeSleeper is attempted on L2. It affects all participants who rely on the wakeSleeper function, including token holders, the protocol’s reward distribution logic, and any external services that display party state based on L1 data. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that examined the flow of cross‑chain messages and identified that addToParty does not forward the necessary state change. It is hard to notice because the L1 state appears correct and the UI may show the expected number of sleepers, while the L2 contract silently rejects claims. The appropriate remediation is to ensure that addToParty sends a reliable cross‑chain message that updates the party.sleepoors array on L2, or to redesign the validation logic to rely on a synchronized source of truth, thereby restoring consistency between layers and allowing users to successfully claim their prize NFTs.
summary: The addToParty method in HibernationDen does not send a cross-chain message, even though it pushes sleepers into the party.sleepoors array on L1. Since the array won't be updated on L2, now all the calculations and validations that are done based on the party.sleepoors.length value will be incorrect. This essentially means that the sleeper NFTs will be stuck as in wakeSleeper there is the following check: if (party.numUsed == party.sleepoors.length) revert PartyAlreadyWoke(bundleId_); Which means that even though there are actually let's say 10 sleepers (they were 7, but then 3 were added), when numUsed is 7 then no more sleepers would be claimable - the wakeSleeper call will revert will PartyAlreadyWoke .

title: Anyone can burn any NFT in the HoneyJarPortal
content: The vulnerability resides in the HoneyJarPortal contract where the internal _debitFrom method is used to burn a HoneyJar NFT. The method is invoked indirectly through the ONFT721Core sendFrom function, which calls _send and then _debitFrom without any access‑control verification that the caller actually owns the token being burned. Although the code contains a conditional if (_from != _msgSender()) revert OwnerNotCaller(); the _from parameter is never consulted in the burning logic, making the check ineffective. As a result any address can call sendFrom with an arbitrary tokenId and cause the contract to destroy the corresponding NFT, regardless of who holds it. The exploit can be performed simply by submitting a transaction that triggers the burn path; no special privileges, approvals, or prior ownership checks are required. When the burn succeeds the token is removed from the owner's balance, the UI shows the token missing, and the owner's NFT balance may drop to zero, leading to a loss of the asset. This issue affects all holders of HoneyJar NFTs and undermines the trust model of the protocol because the fundamental accounting assumption that only the owner can destroy their token is violated. The flaw was discovered during a security review that examined the call chain of sendFrom and identified that the ownership check was redundant. It can be hard to notice because the presence of a revert statement gives the impression that an access control mechanism exists, yet the actual burn operation does not reference the _from argument. To remediate the problem the contract should verify that the caller is the current owner or an approved operator of the token before invoking the burn logic, for example by comparing _msgSender() with the result of ownerOf(tokenId) or by using the standard ERC‑721 _isApprovedOrOwner check. Replacing the ineffective condition with a proper ownership validation will prevent arbitrary burning and restore the intended security guarantees.
summary: The _debitFrom method in HoneyJarPortal allows burning of any HoneyJar NFT, given its ID. This method is freely callable through ONFT721Core 's sendFrom method, which calls _send which calls the _debitFrom method without an access control check. This results in the ability for anyone to burn any HoneyJar NFT, no matter who holds it. There is the following check in the method: if (_from != _msgSender()) revert OwnerNotCaller(); which shows an access control intention, but is actually redundant as the _from argument is not used in the burning process.

title: Anyone can steal all HoneyJar NFTs in HoneyJarPortal and exploit its allowances
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked source address in the internal _debitFrom function of the HoneyJarPortal contract. The function is intended to debit an NFT from a given address by calling safeTransferFrom, which already checks that the caller is either the owner or an approved operator of the token. However, the function does not verify that the _from parameter matches the address that initiated the call (msg.sender). Because the public sendFrom method in ONFT721Core forwards the caller’s arguments directly to _debitFrom, an attacker can invoke sendFrom and supply the HoneyJarPortal contract’s own address as the _from argument while providing his own address as the destination. The safeTransferFrom call then succeeds because the portal is either the owner of the NFT or an approved spender, allowing the NFT to be transferred out of the portal to the attacker. The same logic also works for any NFT that the portal is merely approved to transfer, enabling theft of assets that the portal does not own. The flaw occurs whenever _debitFrom is executed without an explicit ownership check, i.e., any time a user calls sendFrom on a token that uses HoneyJarPortal as the bridge. The impact is the complete loss of NFTs held by the portal, effectively draining the contract’s holdings and any approved tokens, which may represent significant value. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the internal logic of the debit function and noticed the missing verification step. It is subtle because the safeTransferFrom call appears to provide sufficient protection, leading developers to assume that no additional checks are required. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the caller is the actual owner of the token or that the _from address equals msg.sender before performing the transfer, or restrict the function to be callable only by trusted internal components. This class of bug is an authorization bypass or unchecked external input leading to asset misappropriation, commonly referred to as an “allowance abuse” or “unrestricted transfer” vulnerability. From a user’s perspective, NFTs that were previously displayed in their wallet may suddenly disappear, balances may show zero, and attempts to withdraw or transfer assets may fail because the assets have already been moved to an attacker’s address. The discrepancy between the expected behavior (the portal should only move tokens that the caller owns) and the actual behavior (any caller can move any token the portal controls) violates the fundamental accounting assumptions of the protocol.
summary: The _debitFrom function in HoneyJarPortal is exploitable, as it looks like this: function _debitFrom (address _from, uint16, bytes memory, uint _tokenId) internal override { honeyJar.safeTransferFrom(_from, address (this), _tokenId); // Performs the owner & approval checks Since there is no check for the _from argument, anyone can call the function (through the sendFrom method in ONFT721Core ) and pass the address of HoneyJarPortal as the _from argument and his address as the _toAddress argument in the sendFrom method and essentially steal every NFT that is owned by the HoneyJarPortal . It can also steal NFTs that HoneyJarPortal does not own, but is an approved spender of, since the safeTransferFrom method will complete successfully.

title: Unvalidated ExecutionPayload.Timestamp can halt chain
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked ExecutionPayload.Timestamp field that is accepted by the consensus layer during the cometBFT ProcessProposal request. The root cause is that the beacon‑kit implementation never validates the timestamp against the current wall‑clock time or the minimum slot interval; it only relies on the execution client’s check that the new timestamp is greater than the parent block’s timestamp. Because of this omission a malicious proposer can embed an arbitrarily large future timestamp, for example the maximum unsigned 64‑bit value, into a BeaconBlock. The block will satisfy the execution client’s minimal check, pass the consensus process, and be committed to the chain with the extreme timestamp. Once the chain’s head carries such a value, any subsequent block must have a timestamp greater than it, which is impossible because timestamps are bounded by the system clock. Consequently the protocol becomes unable to propose new blocks, the chain halts, and all dependent services—such as time‑based events, fee calculations, and third‑party applications that rely on accurate block timestamps—stop functioning. This condition affects every participant in the network: validators cannot produce blocks, delegators cannot earn rewards, users see no progress in their wallets, and dapps that query the current time receive nonsensical values. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the beacon‑kit codebase, where the absence of a validation step in consensus/pkg/cometbft/service/abci.go was noted. The problem is subtle because the timestamp appears syntactically correct and the block passes all other consensus checks, so no immediate error is raised and the chain appears healthy until the next proposal attempt fails. To remediate, the ExecutionPayload.Timestamp should be compared with the timestamp supplied in the ProcessProposalRequest and enforced to be greater than the previous block’s timestamp but less than the current cometBFT time plus the minimum slot duration. This requires exposing the relevant fields to a common validation routine and adding the appropriate bounds check before the block is accepted. Implementing this fix restores the invariant that timestamps are a reliable indicator of execution time, prevents a proposer from freezing the network, and aligns the protocol with its intended time‑based security guarantees.
summary:
The Timestamp field in ExecutionPayload at consensus-types/pkg/types/payload.go#L60 is never
validated during a cometBFT ProcessProposal() request.
A malicious proposer could propose a BeaconBlock containing an ExecutionPayload.Timestamp in the future
(perhaps MaxUint64). The execution client will only check that the timestamp is after the timestamp in the parent
header, as seen in the implementation in go-ethereum at consensus/beacon/consensus.go#L243-L245. Since
beacon-kit does not validate the timestamp, the proposed block would pass consensus and set the timestamp to
MaxUint64. When proposing new blocks, it would be impossible to propose a block with a timestamp greater than
MaxUint64, and the chain will halt.
In the general case too, timestamps must be a somewhat reliable indicator of the actual time the ExecutionPayload
gets executed, due to events, blocks, and other third-party applications that rely on accurate timestamps from the
chain.

title: Validator deposits not verified against deposit contract
content: During the state‑transition phase of Beacon‑Kit, the function that applies a validator deposit does not check that the deposit originated from the official deposit contract on the execution layer. The code simply reads the deposit data that appears in the BeaconBlock and creates or updates a validator entry, but it never cross‑references the Deposit event logs emitted by the execution payload. Because of this missing verification step, a block proposer can craft a BeaconBlock that contains arbitrary deposit entries – for example, a deposit that credits a new validator with the required stake or inflates the balance of an existing validator – without actually sending any ETH to the deposit contract. When the block is finalized, the state‑transition logic processes these fake deposits as if they were genuine, adding validators to the registry or increasing balances for free. The impact is severe: the consensus set can be manipulated, validator economics are broken, and the protocol may mint funds out of thin air, undermining trust in the network. This condition occurs every time a BeaconBlock is processed in ProcessProposal, specifically when applyDeposit is called, and it affects all participants – validators, delegators, and users – because the altered validator set is accepted by the network. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Beacon‑Kit codebase, where the auditor traced the flow of validator updates and noticed that no step validates the deposits against the execution layer’s Deposit events. The bug is subtle because the block appears syntactically correct and the state transition does not raise any errors; the missing cross‑layer consistency check is easy to overlook. Conceptually, the problem belongs to the class of missing authentication or integrity checks for external data, a trust‑boundary violation where data from one layer is accepted without proof of origin. From a user’s point of view the symptoms may include new validators appearing with no associated deposit transaction, existing validator balances suddenly increasing, or rewards being issued without any prior stake – effectively “funds disappear” from the system or “unearned rewards” appear. An attacker can exploit the flaw by: (1) building a block that includes fake deposit entries, (2) signing and broadcasting the block, (3) having the network finalize the block, and (4) watching the state transition accept the deposits and update the validator set, thereby gaining free stake or control over new validators. The recommended mitigation is to retrieve the Deposit events from the execution layer (for example via the ReadDeposits RPC call) and compare each deposit listed in the BeaconBlock against those events before applying them. Any mismatch should cause the block to be rejected, aligning the implementation with the intent of EIP‑6110 and restoring the required cross‑layer verification.
summary:
During the state-transition period, the function applyDeposit at state-transition/pkg/core/state_processor_staking.go#L103 exists to validate a deposit and then apply the deposit to an updated validator set.
However, it does not verify that the deposit came from the deposit contract. In fact, there is no verification that the
deposits in the BeaconBlock correlate with anything from the ExecutionPayload or the node state.
Here is the full chain of where the validator updates come from:
• ProcessBeaconBlock() calls executeStateTransition(): beacon/blockchain/process.go#L66.
• executeStateTransition() calls Transition(): beacon/blockchain/process.go#L108.
• Transition() grabs the validatorUpdates from ProcessSlots(): state-transition/pkg/core/state_processor.go#L172.
• ProcessSlots() grabs updates from processEpoch(): state-transition/pkg/core/state_processor.go#L214.
• processEpoch() returns processSyncCommitteeUpdates: state-transition/pkg/core/state_processor.go#L344.
• Finally, processSyncCommitteeUpdates() grabs the new validators from st.GetValidatorsByEffectiveBalance(): state-transition/pkg/core/state_processor_committee.go#L34.
• The validators inside of st.GetValidatorsByEffectiveBalance() were committed to this BeaconState
during the previous slot's FinalizeBlock() in the processOperations() ! processDeposits() !
processDeposit() ! applyDeposit() ! createValidator() ! addValidatorToRegistry() at state-transition/pkg/core/state_processor_staking.go#L200.
Note that the validators in the BeaconState (st variable) are never validated against the Deposit contract event
logs. There is one location where deposits are fetched directly from the ExecutionPayload in fetchAndStoreDeposits() at execution/pkg/deposit/sync.go#L75. However, these fetched deposits seem to only ever be used to
build a new proposal at beacon/validator/block_builder.go#L286-L289 and are never used to validate.
If the block passes the proposal, then once it is finalized, it will execute the same code in the state-transition
and grab the validator updates at beacon/blockchain/process.go#L66. This means that a proposer could craft
arbitrary deposits in the BeaconBlock without changing anything in the ExecutionPayload, increasing validator
balances or creating new validators for free.
There is currently an EIP, EIP-6110, that changes validator deposits on Ethereum to be included in the ExecutionPayload by utilizing emitted Deposit events. The current deposit implementation on Beacon-Kit is very similar to this EIP but does not implement the execution layer side (because Beacon-Kit is not an EL client).
The current Beacon-Kit deposit contract applies deposits by emitting the Deposit event. After applying the ExecutionPayload during the state transition, the deposits in the BeaconBlock need to be validated against the events emitted in the ExecutionPayload. EIP-6110 suggests performing this validation by including the Deposit event
log receipts in the actual ExecutionPayload as a new field deposit_receipts, which is validated by the EL client to correspond with Deposit events. However, Beacon-Kit is not at liberty to make such changes as it does not
include an implementation of the EL.

title: Winner can withdraw deposit after winning
content: The vulnerability consists of an early‑withdraw flaw in the lottery deposit contract. Buyers purchase a ticket by depositing ether and become eligible participants when the seller calls startLottery. After the seller initiates winner selection, the contract requests a random number from the VRF. When the VRF callback fulfillRandomWords stores the randomness, the contract is still in a state where the seller has not yet called selectWinners to finalize the winner set. Because the buyerWithdraw function is only gated by a generic "whenLotteryNotActive" check, a participant who can determine that they are a winner – for example by observing the VRF fulfillment event – can call buyerWithdraw before the seller finalises the winner list. The contract does not exclude withdrawn participants from the subsequent winner selection, so the same buyer can later be recorded as a winner and receive the NFT without having paid the required deposit. This creates a situation where the seller receives no payment, the protocol tax is never collected, and the buyer ends up with both the NFT and the original ether, effectively making funds disappear from the protocol’s perspective. The issue occurs only in the narrow time window between randomness fulfillment and the seller’s selectWinners call, which can be hard to notice because the withdrawal function appears legitimate for losing participants and the window may be short. It was discovered during a security audit that added a targeted test reproducing the sequence: startLottery, initiateSelectWinner, mock VRF response, buyerWithdraw, then seller selectWinners and sellerWithdraw. The test showed that the winner’s balance remained unchanged while the contract still marked them as a winner, and the seller’s balance stayed at zero. The bug violates the core business logic that a winner must pay the deposit before receiving the NFT, breaking the accounting assumption that total deposits equal total payouts plus protocol tax. To remediate, the contract should restrict buyerWithdraw to a state where the lottery has fully ended and winners have been selected, or explicitly remove participants who have withdrawn from the eligible winner pool before the final selection. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce a withdrawal guard that only permits refunds after the lottery is closed, thereby preserving the intended payment flow and preventing the double‑benefit scenario.
summary: The lotteries in this protocol work in such a way that ticket buyers compete to have a chance to buy an NFT for the deposit they've provided. The proceeds from these NFTs can then be collected by the seller minus a protocol tax. In Deposit.sol buyers buy tickets, then when the seller is satisfied with the amount of buyers, they start the lottery by calling startLottery followed by initiateSelectWinner. This will request randomness from the VRF. Once randomness is returned the seller calls selectWinners where the winners will be selected using the randomness provided. The issue is that during the time between that the randomness is fulfilled in fulfillRandomWords and the seller calls selectWinners the buyer will know if they've won and can withdraw their deposit. Since the buyer is already added to the eligibleParticipants from when startLottery was called. They would still be able to win. Hence the buyer would get the NFT without paying.

title: Winner can mint any number of NFTs using reentry
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the winner‑minting function of the auction contract. The function first verifies that the caller is a winner and that the caller has not already minted an NFT, then it calls an external ERC‑1155 minting contract and only after that call marks the caller as having minted by setting a flag. Because the external contract invokes the receiver’s onERC1155Received callback, a malicious winner that is itself a contract can re‑enter the minting function before the flag is updated, bypassing the “already minted” check and calling the function repeatedly. This allows the attacker to mint an arbitrary number of NFTs, breaking the protocol’s assumption that each winner receives exactly one token. The issue occurs whenever the winner is a contract capable of handling ERC‑1155 callbacks and the external mint function is invoked after the state change, violating the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. The impact is that the scarcity model of the lottery is destroyed, the total supply inflates unexpectedly, and funds allocated for the lottery may be drained, leaving honest participants with fewer or no rewards. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by CD Security, which crafted a test contract that re‑entered the mint function through the ERC‑1155 receipt hook. It is hard to notice because the re‑entrancy happens inside a standard callback that many developers assume to be safe, and the state update appears after the external call, giving a false sense of protection. The proper mitigation is to move the state update (marking the caller as having minted) before the external call, or to employ a re‑entrancy guard or a non‑re‑enterable minting mechanism. This class of bug is known as a post‑call state‑update re‑entrancy or external‑call‑after‑effects vulnerability. From a user perspective, a winner may see that they receive many more NFTs than expected, while other users may notice that the total supply suddenly spikes and their chance of receiving a token drops to zero, violating the expected one‑per‑winner accounting logic.

title: User can bypass reroll & request randomness until win
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the lottery contract that allows any participant to invoke the public requestRandomness function without paying the required reroll fee. The contract’s deposit function correctly triggers a single VRF request and the roll function enforces a fee for additional attempts, but the separate requestRandomness function is exposed without any access control modifiers such as onlySeller. Because the function directly calls the internal _requestRandomness and emits the RandomRequested event, a user can call it repeatedly after the initial deposit or even after the first randomness has been fulfilled. Each call generates a new random number that is stored in rolledNumbers and immediately processed by _fulfillRandomness, which checks the number against the winning value. By looping calls until the extracted number matches the winning number, the attacker can win the lottery without ever paying the reroll fee. The impact is that the economic model of the lottery is broken: the protocol loses expected fee revenue, the fairness of the game is compromised, and other honest participants may be denied a chance to win because the attacker can keep trying for free. The condition occurs whenever the contract is deployed with the unprotected requestRandomness function and the lottery is in a started state. Any address that has purchased a ticket can exploit it, so all users of the lottery are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor wrote a test that called requestRandomness multiple times after a successful mock fulfillment and observed that the rolledNumbers value changed without any fee being deducted. The bug is subtle because the function name and its internal call resemble the legitimate internal request used by the contract, and there is no visible modifier that would raise suspicion in the UI. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that they can keep “rolling” without any cost and eventually receive a winning ticket, which contradicts the expectation that each additional roll costs a fee. The class of bug is an improper access control or authorization flaw that permits privileged actions to be performed by any caller. To remediate, the requestRandomness function should be restricted to the contract owner or seller (e.g., by adding an onlySeller modifier) or removed entirely, and the contract should ensure that any additional randomness request after the initial deposit requires the appropriate fee payment.

title: Scaling of underlyingTokenPrice will leave funds stuck in protocol
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect decimal scaling applied to the price of the underlying token inside the SwapFacility contract. The _getTokenPrices function multiplies the latest answer from a Chainlink oracle by 1e12, assuming the oracle returns a value with 0 decimals. In reality, the USDC/USD feed used by the protocol returns a price with 8 decimals. By multiplying an 8‑decimal value with 1e12, the resulting underlyingTokenPrice is inflated by four extra decimal places (effectively 1e12 times larger than intended). This inflated price is later divided by billyTokenPrice, which is also expressed with 8 decimals, so the division yields an outAmount that is orders of magnitude larger than the actual token balance available in the contract. When the _swap method attempts to transfer this exaggerated amount, the transfer fails and the transaction reverts because the SwapFacility contract does not hold sufficient tokens. As a consequence, the BloomPool contract, which relies on successful swaps to progress through its lifecycle, becomes stuck: all user deposits remain locked in the pool, but no further phases can be executed and users cannot withdraw their funds. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of price handling and identified the mismatched decimal scaling. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to perform a simple multiplication, and the error only manifests when the swap logic is exercised with real token balances, leading to a revert rather than an obvious overflow. The bug belongs to the class of decimal‑misalignment or unit‑conversion errors, where inconsistent precision between external data sources and internal calculations breaks accounting assumptions. From a user’s perspective, a deposit is accepted, but later attempts to claim a refund or receive swapped tokens result in a transaction that reverts, leaving the UI showing no tokens received and balances appearing unchanged. The protocol’s business logic assumes that price feeds share the same decimal precision, an assumption violated by the extra scaling. To remediate, the contract should stop scaling the oracle price by 1e12, or explicitly normalize both price feeds to a common decimal base before performing arithmetic, ensuring that the calculated outAmount reflects the true amount of tokens that can be transferred.
summary:
The _getTokenPrices method in SwapFacility has the following code:
```solidity
underlyingTokenPrice = uint256(IOracle(underlyingTokenOracle).latestAnswer()) * 1e12;
```
This scaling by 1e12 is an error, because most oracle price feeds in Chainlink (and more specifically, the one that is expected to be used, USDC/USD) return an 8 decimals number. Since this underlyingTokenPrice value will be divided by the billyTokenPrice value which again is in 8 decimals, this will result in a calculation error and overinflation of the outAmount in the _swap method.
Since the SwapFacility contract won't be holding so many tokens in its balance, the calls to swap will always revert, leaving the BloomPool contract in a stuck state - with all deposited funds in it but without an ability to continue further through its phases.

title: Any referrer can steal others scores
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the BunniHub.deposit function forwards a caller‑supplied referrer identifier to the BunniToken._mint routine, which inherits the ERC20Referrer logic. In ERC20Referrer the referrer field is stored together with the token balance and is overwritten on every mint operation without any check that the caller is authorized to change it or that the recipient’s existing referrer should remain unchanged. Consequently any user can invoke hub.deposit on behalf of another address, specify an arbitrary referrer value, and cause the contract to mint tokens for the victim while simultaneously overwriting the victim’s stored referrer score with the attacker‑chosen referrer. An attacker can therefore deposit a negligible amount of tokens (dust) for a victim, pay only a few wei, and steal the victim’s accumulated referral score, which is reflected in the BunniToken.scoreOf mapping. The impact is a loss of referral rewards for honest participants and a distortion of the incentive accounting that the protocol relies on; the token balances themselves remain correct, so the bug is subtle and may only be observed as a sudden drop of a user’s referral score to zero or an unexpected increase for another referrer. The issue manifests whenever deposit is called with a referrer argument that does not belong to the recipient, and because the contract does not enforce any access control or immutability on the referrer field, it can be triggered repeatedly with minimal cost. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the referral integration, where the auditor noticed that the _mint implementation stores the referrer together with the balance and does not guard against arbitrary overwrites. The problem is hard to notice because normal token operations succeed and UI components typically display only balances, not referral scores, so a user may only see their referral points disappear without an obvious on‑chain error. To remediate, the protocol should either make the referrer immutable after the first assignment, restrict the ability to set a referrer to the token holder themselves, or separate the referral bookkeeping from the minting path so that a caller cannot arbitrarily replace another user’s referrer. This class of bug falls under improper access control and mutable state abuse, often referred to as a referrer hijacking or score overwrite vulnerability, which violates the business logic that referral scores should only increase through legitimate referrals and never be transferred without explicit consent.

title: Fund loss because of wrong amAmm Fee Amount
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the fee handling logic of a swap hook that integrates an automated market maker (amAMM) manager. When the hook is active, the function that prepares a swap calculates three values: the total swap fee, the portion of that fee that should be sent to the amAMM manager (amAmmFeeAmount), and the portion that belongs to the hook itself (hookFeesAmount). The code initially assigns the entire swap fee to amAmmFeeAmount, then subtracts the hook fee from the swap fee variable, but it never updates amAmmFeeAmount to reflect this subtraction. As a result, amAmmFeeAmount continues to include the hook fee, and when the hook later distributes a portion of the hook fee to referrers, that same amount is also still counted as part of amAmmFeeAmount. This double‑counting means the protocol does not retain the intended swap fee; instead the hook fee is inadvertently credited to the amAMM manager, and the referrer reward is effectively spent twice – once to the referrer and once to the amAMM manager. The bug manifests only when the amAMM manager flag is enabled, so any swap that uses the BunniHook with amAMM active will suffer the loss. Users experience symptoms such as missing fee accruals, zero or unexpectedly low referral rewards, and overall reduction of protocol revenue, which may appear as “funds disappear” or “my balance stays at zero” after a swap. The issue was discovered during a manual security review of the BunniHook contract, where the auditor noticed that the variable representing the amAMM fee was never adjusted after the hook fee was deducted. It can be hard to spot because the code appears to correctly compute the hook fee and the referrer reward, but the subtle state mutation omission only becomes evident when tracing the flow of fee amounts across multiple internal calls. To fix the problem, the fee calculation should be corrected so that amAmmFeeAmount is set to the swap fee minus the hook fee (or minus the referrer reward, depending on the intended accounting model). This ensures that the amAMM manager receives only the net fee that excludes the hook’s share, preventing double spending and preserving the protocol’s intended revenue model. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fee‑misallocation or double‑spend accounting bugs, where incorrect state updates lead to unintended fund transfers and break business logic assumptions about fee distribution.

title: Fulfiller can arbitrate the rebalancing process interacting with BunniHub
content: The vulnerability is an inconsistency window in the FloodPlain.fulfillOrder rebalance flow that allows a malicious fulfiller to exploit the BunniHub contract. When an order is fulfilled, the contract first calls the pre‑hook of BunniHub, which transfers tokenIn out of the pool and updates the pool’s tokenIn balance. Immediately afterwards the contract calls sourceConsideration on the fulfiller, which can invoke arbitrary code while the pool’s tokenOut balance has not yet been updated and the internal timestamps (lastSwapTimestamp, lastSurgeTimestamp) are still stale. Because BunniHub does not lock its state between the pre‑hook and the post‑hook, the fulfiller can interact with BunniHub during this transient inconsistent state, for example by depositing liquidity before the tokenOut credit is recorded. This lets the fulfiller mint more Bunni shares than the amount of tokenOut that will actually be credited, effectively arbitraging the temporary discrepancy. The issue occurs whenever a fulfiller that is either whitelisted or the current amAMM manager calls the two‑parameter version of fulfillOrder; the manager may be untrusted. The impact is that the protocol can lose value: extra shares are created out of thin air, pool accounting becomes incorrect, and users may see their expected share allocation distorted or funds disappear from the pool. The problem is subtle because the rebalance steps are executed in a single external transaction and appear atomic, so the inconsistent state is not obvious from the UI; users only notice that the pool’s share price is off or that they receive more shares than expected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that traced the call flow and identified that BunniHub functions are callable from the fulfiller during the pre‑hook phase. The difficulty in detection stems from the fact that the contract uses non‑reentrant modifiers only on the outer fulfillOrder function, not on the internal BunniHub hooks.
