This results in unauthorized withdrawals, reduction or complete depletion of the victim’s share balance, and loss of the underlying assets. The flaw manifests whenever a non‑owner calls withdraw or redeem; there is no conditional branch that checks msg.sender against the owner or validates an allowance mapping. Consequently, any user of a vault deployed from ERC4626i is potentially exposed, including token holders, liquidity providers, and any protocol that relies on the vault for asset management. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a proof‑of‑concept test attempted to redeem tokens on behalf of another address and observed that the transaction succeeded and transferred the underlying tokens to the caller. The bug can be hard to notice because the function signatures and overall flow resemble the standard ERC4626 implementation, and developers may assume that the inherited access control is present without reviewing the overridden logic. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are stark: a user expects to receive a certain amount of underlying tokens after calling redeem, but receives zero, while the attacker’s balance increases; the victim’s share balance may drop to zero without any explicit approval transaction. This violates the fundamental accounting assumption that only the share owner or an approved spender may burn shares. The appropriate remediation is to introduce an allowance check similar to the one used in the original solmate ERC4626 contract: if msg.sender is not the owner, the contract must read the allowance[owner][msg.sender] value, ensure it is sufficient, and decrement it (unless it is set to the maximum value). This restores the intended access control and prevents unauthorized share burning. The class of bug can be described as a missing authorization check in token accounting functions, analogous to an ERC20 transferFrom implementation that fails to verify allowances before moving tokens.
summary: The withdraw and redeem functions in ERC4626i don‘t have a critical permissions check, which could allow an attacker to burn shares on behalf of an owner without their consent, stealing the underlying assets. This means that any user calling these functions can potentially affect the share balance of any other user, leading to unauthorized withdrawals or redeems.

title: Plugins can be maliciously overridden by colliding signatures
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the proxy stores plugins: a public mapping links each 4‑byte function selector to a plugin contract address. When a new plugin is installed, the installPlugin routine retrieves the list of selectors provided by the plugin and writes the plugin address into the mapping for every selector without checking whether a selector is already associated with another plugin. Consequently, a malicious actor can craft a seemingly harmless plugin that deliberately includes a selector already used by a legitimate plugin. During installation the new plugin overwrites the existing entry, so any subsequent call that matches the colliding selector is dispatched to the attacker‑controlled plugin instead of the intended one. This hijacks the control flow of the proxy mid‑execution, allowing the attacker to bypass the original plugin’s protection logic and execute arbitrary code under the proxy’s authority. In practice, the issue manifests when a protocol such as Sablier relies on a specific plugin hook (for example onStreamCanceled) to forward refunds to the rightful owner. If an attacker installs a plugin that declares the same selector, the refund is redirected to the attacker’s address, and the attacker may also gain the ability to cancel other streams and steal additional funds. The bug occurs whenever plugins are added without a collision check, affecting any user or contract that interacts with the proxy and expects the original plugin behavior, including stream participants, token holders, and protocol administrators. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the plugin installation logic and identified the lack of a selector‑collision guard. The problem is subtle because the mapping update looks innocuous and the overridden plugin may appear identical in name or purpose, making the malicious behavior hard to detect without tracing the actual execution path. To remediate, the installPlugin function should verify that each selector is unassigned before writing a new entry, rejecting any attempt to register a selector that already maps to a plugin. This preventive measure restores the invariant that each selector uniquely identifies a single plugin, preserving the intended accounting and refund logic of the system and preventing unauthorized redirection of funds.

title: Any token with large volume ﬂash minting capability can be stolen
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow/overflow chain that originates from an unchecked subtraction used to compute the amount a user can withdraw from a streaming payment contract. The contract assumes that the total streamed amount never decreases, so the withdrawn amount is always less than or equal to the streamed amount. However, a separate mathematical flaw causes the streamed amount calculation to produce a smaller value at a later timestamp when the exponentiation of a decreasing percentage is applied. Because the subtraction is performed inside an unchecked block, the contract does not revert when the streamed amount becomes lower than the previously recorded withdrawn amount. The subtraction therefore underflows, wrapping around to the maximum unsigned 128‑bit integer. This inflated withdrawable amount passes the contract’s internal checks, and when the withdrawn field is later increased by the same maximum value, another unchecked addition overflows, resetting the withdrawn counter to a low value that still satisfies the deposit‑withdrawn invariant. An attacker can trigger this sequence by creating a stream that will hit the buggy timestamp, withdrawing the maximum possible amount just before the bug manifests, and then using a flash‑minted token supply (up to type(uint128).max) to inflate the contract’s balance. The attacker then calls withdraw with the wrapped‑around amount, causing the contract to transfer the entire token balance to the attacker. The impact is a total loss of the token held by the contract, rendering all other streams unusable and effectively stealing all funds. The exploit can only be carried out against tokens that permit flash minting of the full uint128 range, a condition that may become common as new tokens are deployed. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that the streamed amount decreased as block.timestamp increased, contradicting the protocol’s core invariant. The problem is hard to notice because the unchecked block masks the underflow, and the decreasing streamed amount is a subtle numerical edge case rather than an obvious logic error. To remediate, the underlying exponentiation bug must be fixed so that streamed amounts are monotonic, and unchecked arithmetic should be removed or replaced with safe‑math checks around critical state updates, ensuring that any overflow or underflow reverts the transaction and preserves the intended invariants.

title: potCreator has a way to always win a round
content: The vulnerability is a predictability flaw in the on‑chain randomness used to select a round winner. When the contract calls entropy.request the current sequenceNumber becomes publicly known. Because the random number that will later be produced by entropy.reveal is derived deterministically from this sequenceNumber, the potCreator can calculate the exact winnerIndex before the rotateLiquidity function is executed. Armed with this knowledge the potCreator can insert an address it controls at the calculated index in the participants array, guaranteeing that its address is selected as the winner. This issue arises from the use of a deterministic entropy source that is observable by any participant, including the contract owner, and therefore does not provide true unpredictability. Exploitation follows a simple flow: (1) entropy.request is called, (2) sequenceNumber is read, (3) the future random number is derived, (4) the winnerIndex is computed, (5) the potCreator adds its own address at that index, and (6) rotateLiquidity distributes the reward to the attacker. The impact is that the potCreator can consistently capture the round reward, depriving legitimate participants of their expected payouts and breaking the economic fairness of the protocol. The condition for the exploit is that the attacker controls the potCreator role and can act between the request and the rotateLiquidity call. All users who join a round are affected because the reward may be siphoned away, leading to missing balances, zero refunds, or unexpected loss of funds. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the randomness generation logic and identified that the sequenceNumber is exposed before the random value is needed. The problem is subtle because the contract appears to use a random function, yet the randomness is fully predictable to an insider, making the issue easy to miss in functional testing. To remediate, the contract should replace the deterministic entropy source with a truly unpredictable one, such as block.prevrandao on OP‑compatible chains, or adopt a commit‑reveal scheme or an external verifiable random function (VRF) that prevents any party from calculating the outcome before the finalization step. By ensuring the random number cannot be known in advance, the protocol can restore its intended fairness and prevent the potCreator from always winning a round.
summary: Once entropy.request() is called and sequenceNumber is known, potCreator knows the random number that will be generated through entropy.reveal(). Thus, potCreator can predict winnerIndex before calling rotateLiquidity(). This information can be exploited by potCreator by inserting an address it control at that specific index in participants array.

title: Permanent failure to bridge wrapped ERC721 using Bridge::sendERC721UsingNative function
content: The vulnerability resides in the Bridge contract function that bridges ERC721 tokens across chains using LayerZero. The function is intended to handle both the original (unwrapped) NFT and its wrapped counterpart, but due to an implementation mistake the payload that is sent to the destination chain is built with the address of the original asset even when the caller supplies a wrapped ERC721 address. Consequently the bridge attempts to read metadata such as tokenURI from the original contract on the target chain, a contract that does not exist there. The call reverts, the transaction fails and the NFT remains locked inside the source bridge contract. This condition occurs whenever a user tries to bridge a wrapped ERC721 (WERC721) with Bridge::sendERC721UsingNative, regardless of the source or destination network, and it does not affect bridging of the native asset. The root cause is the incorrect selection of the current‑chain address and origin address inside the internal _getPayload and _getPayloadMessage helpers, which treat the wrapped token as if it were the original token. Exploitation is straightforward: a user initiates a bridge of a wrapped NFT, the transaction reverts, and the NFT is permanently unavailable on both chains because the bridge contract never releases it. From the user’s perspective the UI shows the NFT disappearing from their wallet, the balance becomes zero, and no receipt of the token appears on the destination chain, contrary to the expectation that the NFT would be transferred. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a Foundry test reproduced a revert with a message indicating that the original contract does not exist on the active fork. The bug is subtle because the same function works for original NFTs, so the failure only appears for wrapped assets, making it easy to overlook. The problem belongs to the class of cross‑chain address‑mapping bugs that cause asset lock due to incorrect payload construction. The recommended remediation is to modify the payload generation logic so that when a wrapped ERC721 is supplied the bridge uses the wrapped address for the current chain and the stored origin address for the source chain, as shown in the provided code snippet. This change ensures that the correct contract is referenced on the destination chain, allowing the token metadata call to succeed and the NFT to be released, thereby restoring the intended bridging functionality.
summary: The sendERC721UsingNative function of Bridge.sol bridges ERC721 NFTs between multiple supported networks using Layerzero's message bridge. This function helps to bridge both the original asset (the unwrapped asset) and the wrapped asset. However, due to an implementation error, this function works only for the original asset and locks the wrapped asset on the bridged chain, unable to bridge it. This failure to bridge would permanently lock the original NFT in the source bridge contract.

title: LayerZeroAdapter::executeMessages could lead to irrecoverable state
content: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the message that is selected for execution and the element that is removed from the pending‑message array inside the LayerZeroAdapter executeMessages function. When a cross‑chain message cannot be delivered to the Bridge contract, it is stored in an internal array called s_pendingMessagesToExecute. The executeMessages function receives a limitToExecute parameter that tells it how many pending messages to process. The implementation iterates over the array from the beginning but uses the native pop() operation, which always removes the last element of the array. As a result, the function may execute the first stored payload while popping the last one, leaving the originally intended payload still in storage but no longer reachable. This inconsistency creates an irrecoverable state: the pending message that should have been processed is lost, and any NFT that was supposed to be transferred remains locked in the bridge contract. The bug manifests only when there are multiple pending messages and the caller limits the number of executions, which is a common pattern when processing batches. Users who bridge NFTs experience a situation where the bridge transaction reverts on the second attempt, the expected NFT never arrives, and the balance appears unchanged, effectively “funds disappear”. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reproducing the scenario with a test that sent two NFTs across chains and called executeMessages twice; the second call attempted to transfer the same NFT ID again and reverted because the pending queue had been corrupted. The problem is hard to notice because the first call succeeds, giving the impression that the system works, while the hidden state inconsistency only surfaces on subsequent calls. The root cause is the misuse of the pop() operation on an array that is being iterated from the front, leading to a mismatch between execution order and storage mutation. To fix the issue, the contract should either process messages from the last index (so that pop removes the element that was just executed) or, more robustly, assign a unique nonce to each pending message and retrieve them by that identifier, eliminating reliance on array order altogether. This class of bug falls under improper handling of mutable data structures during batch processing, which can cause permanent asset lockup and violates the bridge’s accounting guarantees that every deposited NFT must be eventually released to its owner.
summary: The executeMessages function executes stored payloads in LayerZeroAdapter.sol Upon receiving a cross-chain message, the LayerZeroAdapter.sol tries to deliver it to the Bridge.sol contract. Any failure would result in storing the payload in the intermediary storage variable named s_pendingMessagesToExecute. After storage, the executeMessages function tries to redeliver them to the Bridge.sol contract later. This function accepts a limitToExecute_ parameter specifying the number of pending messages to execute. For example, if there are two messages stored in the s_pendingMessagesToExecute variable, specifying one will execute one of them. However, the implementation has a flaw. The function executes a different message but pops a different one from the s_pendingMessagesToExecute storage variable, leading to an irrecoverable state. The impact of this issue will lead to permanent locking of NFTs in the bridge contract, which in turn would lead to loss of user funds.

title: Anyone can call adjustMechRequesterBalances
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized state‑modification flaw in the balance‑tracking contract. The function that updates the internal accounting for both requesters and mechanics, adjustMechRequesterBalances, does not verify that the caller is the designated marketplace contract. Because the function lacks an access‑control check, any external address can invoke it with arbitrary arguments. When called, the function directly writes to the mappings that store requester balances (mapRequesterBalances) and mechanic balances (mapMechBalances). An attacker can therefore credit their own address in the mechanic balance mapping while simultaneously debiting the legitimate requester’s balance, effectively draining funds from the contract. This issue manifests whenever the function is invoked, regardless of the caller’s role, and it can be triggered by a simple transaction from any externally owned account. Users of the protocol are affected because their deposited tokens may disappear without any on‑chain indication other than a sudden zero balance; the UI would show a missing or reduced balance, contradicting the expectation that only the marketplace can settle payments. The flaw was discovered during a targeted audit that compared the access‑control patterns of similar functions (checkAndRecordDeliveryRates and finalizeDeliveryRates) and identified the missing marketplace‑only guard. It is easy to miss because the function’s signature appears benign and the contract’s public interface does not expose any explicit permission checks, leading reviewers to assume the same restrictions apply as in the other functions. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of missing‑access‑control or unauthorized state‑change vulnerabilities, where critical accounting logic can be manipulated by any actor. To remediate, the function should include a check that reverts unless msg.sender equals the stored marketplace address, thereby restoring the intended invariant that only the marketplace can adjust balances. After the fix, attempts to call the function from unauthorized accounts will be rejected, preserving the integrity of the accounting and preventing funds from disappearing unexpectedly.
summary: Unlike checkAndRecordDeliveryRates and finalizeDeliveryRates, adjustMechRequesterBalances is missing the check to make sure only the mechMarketplace can call this endpoint. Anyone can call this endpoint with arbitrary parameters and can manipulate all the mapRequesterBalances and mapMechBalances and thus drain all funds from this contract.

title: Withdrawing collateral and fees and bypassing trust safety mechanism
content: The vulnerability originates from an incomplete verification of Gnosis Safe proxy contracts used as beneficiaries for collateral and fee withdrawals. The protocol’s safety mechanism is intended to require two distinct parties – the project creator (sourcer) and a protocol‑controlled trustee – to approve any token transfer by checking that the beneficiary is a trusted Safe with exactly two owners and that the protocol trustee is one of those owners. The implementation only compares the runtime codehash of the proxy contract against the known Safe Proxy v1.3.0 hash, but it never confirms that the underlying singleton address pointed to by the proxy is the legitimate Gnosis Safe singleton. An attacker can therefore deploy a custom Safe contract whose singleton address is malicious yet still produces the expected proxy codehash. By overriding the owner‑enumeration and ownership‑check functions, the malicious singleton can report a fabricated owner list that includes the protocol trustee and always return true for the trustee’s ownership query, satisfying the two‑signatory requirement without the real trustee’s consent. When a user initiates a withdrawal (for example, claiming collateral after project success), the protocol’s check mistakenly believes the beneficiary Safe is trustworthy and proceeds with the token transfer. Consequently, the attacker can execute the withdrawal unilaterally, causing the beneficiary’s balance to drop to zero while the user sees no refund or reward. This flaw is triggered whenever a beneficiary address is a proxy that points to a non‑approved singleton, which can be crafted by any party with contract deployment capabilities. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the trust‑validation logic and identified that the singleton address was never validated, allowing a proof‑of‑concept malicious Safe to bypass the checks. The problem is subtle because the proxy’s bytecode matches the expected hash, giving the false impression that the contract is safe, and the owner‑related functions appear to behave correctly from the outside. To remediate, the contract should read the singleton address stored in the proxy’s first storage slot and compare it against a whitelist of known legitimate Safe singleton contracts before performing any owner or threshold checks. This additional verification ensures that only genuine Gnosis Safe instances can satisfy the two‑owner requirement, restoring the intended security guarantees and preventing unauthorized fund extraction. The bug belongs to the class of “proxy‑singleton mismatch” or “trusted‑contract impersonation” vulnerabilities, where a proxy’s appearance is trusted while its underlying implementation is malicious, leading to accounting violations and loss of funds.

title: Centrifuge router can perform untrusted actions on behalf of open vaults
content: The vulnerability originates from the Centrifuge router contract allowing it to act as an endorsed operator for any vault that has been opened with the public open() function. When open() is called, the router is added to the vault's isOperator mapping for the caller, which means the router can invoke privileged vault methods such as requestDeposit and requestRedeem on behalf of the vault owner without further checks. The router’s requestDeposit implementation accepts an arbitrary owner address and a controller address supplied by the caller, but it only verifies that the caller is the router itself (through the protected modifier) and does not confirm that the supplied owner matches the transaction initiator or the router’s own address. Consequently, any user who holds an approval for the vault can trigger the router to call requestDeposit or requestRedeem with a controller that they control. This enables an attacker to deposit assets on behalf of a victim while directing the resulting tranche tokens to an address they control, or to redeem tranche tokens from the victim’s balance to an attacker‑controlled controller. The impact is that funds can be moved out of a user’s vault without their consent, leading to unexpected zero balances, missing tranche tokens, or loss of deposited assets. The issue manifests whenever a vault has been opened (open() called) and the router is listed as an endorsed operator, which is the default behavior for permissionless claiming. It is difficult to notice because the router is intended to be a helper contract and the open() function is public, so developers may assume that only the vault owner can initiate deposits or redemptions. The root cause is the lack of ownership validation in the router’s requestDeposit and requestRedeem functions, relying on the isOperator mapping that trusts the router for any owner. To remediate, the router should enforce that the owner argument equals the transaction initiator or the router’s own address, for example by adding require(owner == _initiator() || owner == address(this), "CentrifugeRouter/invalid-owner");. Additionally, the intended usage of open() should be documented so that users only enable it when necessary, preserving the accounting guarantees of the vault and preventing unauthorized fund movements.

title: Attacker can drain all ETH from IPSeed due to re-configuring tokenId
content: The vulnerability is a re‑initialisation flaw in the token metadata handling of the IPSeed contract. The contract’s spawn function allows a creator to set the metadata for a tokenId only if the stored projectId string is empty. Because the existence check relies on the length of the projectId field rather than the ERC1155 totalSupply, a token whose projectId is the empty string can be configured multiple times. An attacker can first call spawn with an empty projectId and supply a curve address together with zero curve parameters, which makes the price calculation return zero. The attacker then mints an arbitrary amount of that tokenId at no cost. Afterwards the attacker calls spawn again with the same tokenId but now provides a legitimate curve and non‑zero parameters, overwriting the previously stored metadata. The contract now believes the token has a proper pricing curve, allowing the attacker to sell the previously minted tokens at market price and drain the entire ETH balance of the IPSeed contract. This issue occurs whenever a token is created with an empty projectId, which any user can do, and it affects the protocol’s economic integrity, the funds of all participants and the reputation of the platform. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of the spawn function and noticed that the existence guard does not prevent re‑configuration. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific warning when metadata is overwritten, and the UI may simply show the token as existing with updated attributes, giving the impression that nothing abnormal happened. The impact is that an attacker can mint unlimited free tokens and sell them, effectively stealing all ETH held by the contract. To remediate the issue the contract should make token metadata immutable after the first successful spawn, for example by requiring a non‑empty projectId, adding a boolean flag that blocks further configuration, or by using a proper existence check based on totalSupply rather than a mutable string field. This class of bug is known as a mutable initialization or re‑initialisation vulnerability, where critical parameters can be changed after deployment, breaking the intended accounting guarantees and allowing fund‑draining attacks.

title: Attacker can drain all ETH from IPSeed due to malicious IIPSeedCurve implementation
content: The vulnerability originates from the ability of a token creator to supply an arbitrary implementation of the IIPSeedCurve interface when spawning a new IPSeed token. The spawn function stores the supplied curve contract address directly in the token metadata without any validation or whitelist checks. Later, the contract relies on this external curve to compute both buy and sell prices through getBuyPrice and getSellPrice calls. Because the curve contract is fully trusted, a malicious implementation can return a zero price for purchases and an arbitrarily high price for sales. An attacker can therefore deploy a curve that reports a zero cost to acquire tokens, allowing users (or the attacker) to mint tokens for free, and then when those tokens are sold the curve reports an inflated gross amount. The protocol fee and sourcer fee are calculated on the inflated gross, resulting in a net payout that drains the ETH balance of the IPSeed contract. This exploit can be triggered whenever a user is allowed to specify a custom curve, which is the case for every call to spawn. The impact is the complete loss of ETH held by the contract, affecting all token holders, the protocol’s revenue model, and any parties that expected to receive a fair price. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the spawn function and the price‑calculation flow, noting that the contract trusts an external price oracle without restrictions. The problem is subtle because the price functions are external and may appear to work correctly for normal inputs; however, a malicious curve can silently manipulate pricing logic, leading to a situation where users see tokens minted for free and later observe the contract balance dropping to zero or receiving unexpectedly large payouts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal minting operation, but the balance displayed after a sell may be either zero (if the contract has been drained) or unexpectedly high, contradicting the expectation that the sell price reflects market value. This class of bug falls under untrusted external contract dependency or price‑oracle manipulation. To remediate, the protocol should restrict curve implementations to a vetted whitelist, enforce interface invariants, or move pricing logic into the core contract where it can be audited and bounded, thereby preventing arbitrary price manipulation.

title: OrderBook Denial of Service leveraging blacklistable tokens like USDC
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in an on‑chain order book that stores orders for each price level in a fixed‑size cyclic buffer (approximately 32,000 slots). When the buffer reaches its maximum capacity, the implementation overwrites the oldest (stale) order with a new one. Finalising a stale order requires transferring the quote token to the order owner as part of the claim process. If the quote token implements a blacklist (as USDC does) and the owner of the stale order NFT is an address that is blocked by that token, the transfer reverts and the stale order cannot be finalised. Because the contract cannot complete the replacement of the stale order, the buffer slot remains occupied and the system refuses to accept any new orders for that price index. The attack scenario is as follows: an attacker creates an order at a chosen price, then transfers the OrderNFT to a blacklisted address. When the cyclic buffer later wraps around and attempts to replace that order, the token transfer fails, leaving the order permanently unclaimable. Consequently, any subsequent attempt to place a new order at the same price point is rejected, effectively freezing that slice of the market. This condition is not immediately visible; it only manifests after the buffer has completed a full cycle, which can take many transactions, making the problem hard to notice. From a user perspective the UI may simply stop accepting orders for a particular price, showing no explicit error, while the user’s balance remains unchanged and no funds are transferred. The impact is a loss of functionality for market participants, potential manipulation of price levels, and the ability for an attacker to blackmail the DAO by demanding the release of the blocked address. The issue was discovered during a security audit when analysing additional impact and fixes for a previous finding, and a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated the failure using a mock USDC‑like token. The bug belongs to the class of resource‑exhaustion and state‑locking vulnerabilities caused by forced external calls that can revert. To remediate, the contract should avoid mandatory token transfers when overwriting stale orders, for example by decoupling order replacement from immediate asset delivery or by allowing the replacement to proceed even if the transfer fails, thereby preventing a single blocked order from halting the entire price bucket.
summary:
The issue was spotted while analysing additional impact and fix for 67
Proof of concept checked with the original audit commit: 28062f477f571b38fe4f8455170bd11094a71862 and the newest available commit from dev branch: 2ed4370b5de9cec5c455f5485358db194f093b01
Due to the architecture decision which implements orders queue as a cyclic buffer the OrderBook after reaching MAX_ORDERS (~32k) for a given price point, starts to overwrite stale orders. If an order was never claimed or it is broken, so it cannot be claimed, it is not possible to place a new order in a queue. This emerges due to a fact that it is not possible to finalize the stale order and deliver the underlying assets, what is done while placing a new and replacing a stale order.
Effectively this issue can be used to block the main functionality of the OrderBook, so placing new orders for a given price point. Only a single broken order per price-point is enough to lead to this condition. The issue will not be immediately visible as it requires the cyclic buffer to make a circle and encounter the broken order.
The proof of concept in SecurityAuditTests.sol attachment implements a simple scenario where a USDC-like mock token is used:
1. Mallory creates one ASK order at some price point (to sell X base tokens for Y quoteTokens).
2. Mallory transfers ownership of the OrderNFT token to an address which is blacklisted by quoteToken (e.g. USDC)
3. Orders queue implemented as a circular buffer over time overflows and starts replacing old orders.
4. When it is the time to replace the order the quoteToken is about to be transferred, but due to the blacklist the assets cannot be delivered.
5. At this point it is impossible to place new orders at this price index, unless the owner of the OrderNFT transfers it to somebody who can receive quoteToken.
Proof of concept result for the newest 2ed4370b5de9cec5c455f5485358db194f093b01 commit:
```
[25766] MockOrderBook::limitOrder(0x0000000000000000000000000000000000004444, 3, 0, 333333333333333334, 2, 0x)
[8128] OrderNFT::onBurn(false, 3, 0)
[1448] MockOrderBook::getOrder((false, 3, 0)) [staticcall]
←(1, 0, 0x00000000000000000000000000000000DeaDBeef)
emit Approval(owner: 0x00000000000000000000000000000000DeaDBeef, approved: 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000, tokenId: 20705239040371691362304267586831076357353326916511159665487572671397888)
emit Transfer(from: 0x00000000000000000000000000000000DeaDBeef, to: 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000, tokenId: 20705239040371691362304267586831076357353326916511159665487572671397888)
←()
emit ClaimOrder(claimer: 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000004444, user: 0x00000000000000000000000000000000DeaDBeef, rawAmount: 1, bountyAmount: 0, orderIndex: 0, priceIndex: 3, isBase: false)
[714] MockSimpleBlockableToken::transfer(0x00000000000000000000000000000000DeaDBeef, 10000)
←"blocked"
```
In real life all *-USDC and USDC-* pairs as well as other pairs where a single token implements a block list are affected. The issue is also appealing to the attacker as at any time if the attacker controls the blacklisted wallet address, he/she can transfer the unclaimable OrderNFT to a whitelisted address to claim his/her assets and to enable processing until the next broken order is placed in the cyclic buffer. It can be used either to manipulate the market by blocking certain types of orders per given price points or simply to blackmail the DAO to resume operations.

title: Overflow in SegmentedSegmentTree464
content: The vulnerability is an unsigned‑integer overflow in the first layer of a segmented segment tree that stores order‑book depth values as packed uint64 entries. The tree’s total() function aggregates the two groups of nodes by calling DirtyUint64.sumPackedUnsafe, which adds the packed values without performing any overflow check. When an update writes a value larger than half of the uint64 maximum into two distinct nodes of the same group, the sum of those packed values exceeds type(uint64).max and silently wraps around to zero because the addition is unchecked. This overflow is not caught by the existing overflow guard that only validates the difference added to each node during an update, nor by the final check that adds the two group totals, because both totals have already wrapped. The bug can be exploited by an attacker (or even an honest user) who submits large order amounts that trigger the overflow, causing the contract’s view of total depth to become incorrect – often zero – while the underlying node values remain high. As a result, the order‑book depth reporting, price‑impact calculations, and claim functions that rely on the total depth break for all participants; users may see no available liquidity, receive zero refunds, or be unable to settle positions. The condition occurs whenever the contract processes updates that push any group’s packed sum beyond the 64‑bit limit, which is feasible because the contract does not enforce a per‑group cap. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case updated two nodes with a value just above type(uint64).max/2, causing total() to return zero despite non‑zero inputs. The overflow is hard to notice because individual node values appear correct and no revert is emitted; only the aggregated total is wrong, leading to subtle accounting mismatches. To remediate, the implementation should replace sumPackedUnsafe with a checked addition routine (e.g., sumPackedSafe) and enforce that the combined sum of both groups never exceeds type(uint64).max, causing the transaction to revert if the limit would be breached. This change restores the invariant that the order‑book depth cannot overflow, preserving correct accounting and preventing users from experiencing missing depth or failed claims.

title: OrderNFT theft due to controlling future and past tokens of same order index
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the order book stores orders in a fixed‑size ring buffer and derives the OrderNFT identifier from the order index using a modulo operation (orderIndex % _MAX_ORDER). Because the same logical index repeats every _MAX_ORDER slots, the owner of an NFT for a given orderIndex also implicitly controls the NFTs whose indices are orderIndex + k*_MAX_ORDER. The contract does not clear token approvals when a new OrderNFT is minted; approvals are only cleared on burn. Consequently, an attacker can pre‑approve a future token ID that has not yet been minted, then wait for the order queue to wrap around and for a victim to receive that future token. When the victim mints the token, the stale approval remains, allowing the attacker to transfer the NFT from the victim and subsequently cancel the order to claim the underlying base tokens. This attack can be carried out whenever the order queue reaches its maximum size and starts reusing indices, which is a normal operating condition for a high‑throughput market. The impact is that an attacker can steal ownership of a legitimate order NFT, cancel the order, and extract the funds that belong to the original order creator, effectively causing loss of assets for users and undermining trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the mapping between order indices and NFT identifiers and noticed that approvals were not reset on mint. It is subtle because the token IDs appear distinct and the approval mechanism works as expected for already‑minted tokens, making the cross‑index relationship hard to spot without understanding the modulo indexing. To remediate, the contract should clear approvals during the onMint hook, enforce that an orderKey maps to an active, unburned token before allowing any operation, and reject requests that refer to indices outside the current valid window of the ring buffer. This eliminates the ability to pre‑approve future tokens and prevents an attacker from hijacking orders that reuse the same modulo index, restoring the intended ownership and accounting guarantees of the market.

title: OrderNFT theft due to ambiguous tokenId encoding/decoding scheme
content: The vulnerability is an ambiguity in the way a 256‑bit token identifier is decoded back into the logical order key that the contract uses to track ownership and approvals. The encodeId routine stores three fields – a bid flag, a price index and an order index – into a uint256 by packing them into fixed bit positions. The decodeId routine extracts those bits, interprets the first byte as a uint8, and then converts it to a boolean by checking whether the value equals 1. Because the function does not enforce that the extracted byte is either 0 or 1, any other non‑zero value is treated as false, meaning that many different raw tokenIds can map to the same OrderKey. An attacker can therefore craft an alternative tokenId that differs only in the high bits of the bid byte (for example by adding 1<<255) while still decoding to the same order key as the legitimate tokenId. The contract uses the decoded OrderKey to store approvals, so the attacker can approve the ambiguous tokenId to a second address, let the original owner transfer the NFT using the legitimate tokenId, and then transfer the same NFT from the victim to the attacker using the ambiguous tokenId. This attack is possible only for ASK limit orders where the bid flag is false, because flipping the high bit does not change the boolean result of the equality check. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that an order NFT that was transferred to a trusted party (for example a marketplace) later disappears from the user’s wallet, or that a third‑party address suddenly gains ownership without any explicit approval. The impact is the theft of the NFT representing the order, which may also allow the attacker to claim the underlying assets associated with the order. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors noticed that the decodeId function could return the same OrderKey for multiple distinct tokenIds. It is hard to notice because the tokenId looks valid and the contract’s events do not reveal the underlying decoding ambiguity. The proper mitigation is to validate that the extracted uint8 bid flag is strictly 0 or 1 before converting it to a boolean, thereby making the encode/decode pair bijective and preventing multiple tokenIds from mapping to the same logical order. In broader terms this is a classic case of non‑bijective encoding leading to authorization bypass, where ambiguous identifiers break the contract’s accounting assumptions about unique ownership.

title: C-1 Double-approval attack by malicious owner
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the multi‑signature wallet that allows a minority of owners to execute a transaction after the owner set has been changed. The contract keeps a numeric _approvalCount for each pending transaction and simply increments this counter whenever an owner calls approve(). When the owners are re‑configured through the configureOwners() function, the contract does not reset or recompute the stored approval counters. Consequently, approvals that were recorded under the previous owner list remain counted even though some of the approving addresses may no longer be owners. An attacker who controls at least one owner can exploit this by first creating a withdrawal transaction and approving it, then convincing the other owners to change their addresses (or adding/removing owners) via configureOwners(). After the change, the attacker can submit another approval for the same transaction; the stored counter now reflects two approvals – the original one and the new one – satisfying the required threshold (for example 2 out of 3) despite only one current owner having approved. The transaction can then be executed, allowing the attacker to move all funds out of the wallet. This issue manifests only when the wallet permits owner re‑configuration and does not clear pending approvals. Users see the expected multi‑sig protection disappear; a transaction that should require multiple distinct owners can be executed after a single owner’s second approval, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The problem is hard to notice because the UI typically shows the number of approvals as a positive integer and does not indicate that some approvals belong to former owners. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the approval bookkeeping logic. To remediate, the contract should not rely on a stale counter; instead it should recompute the set of valid approvals at execution time by iterating over the current owners and checking a per‑owner approval mapping, or it should reset all pending approval counters whenever the owner list changes. This aligns the approval state with the current governance rules and prevents a double‑approval attack that violates the intended multi‑signature security model.
summary:
Pending transactions have the _approvalCount counter.
The _approvalCount for each transaction is simply incremented by 1 each time an owner approves it.
However, when the owners are reconﬁgured using the configureOwners() function, the _approvalCount value for valid transactions remains positive. This can lead to a scenario where the minority of owners can execute a transaction.
• MultiSigWalletBase.sol#L345
• MultiSigWalletBase.sol#L370
For example, in a wallet requiring the 2/3 of approvals, a malicious owner can create a transaction to withdraw all funds and approve it. They can then claim their account has been hacked and ask the other owners to change their account address (using configureOwners()). After the address change, the malicious owner can approve the previously created transaction again reaching the minimum required approvals=2 and execute the transaction.

title: Codeup::claimCodeupERC20() may be forever DoSed by creating the Uniswap pool before it is called
content: The vulnerability resides in the claimCodeupERC20 function, which attempts to create a Uniswap V2 pair on‑chain by calling UniswapV2Factory.createPair. Uniswap pools can be instantiated even when the underlying token contracts have no liquidity or balances, and the factory will reject a second creation request for the same token pair by reverting. An attacker can therefore call the factory directly and create the pool before any legitimate user invokes claimCodeupERC20. When the legitimate claim is later executed, the internal call to createPair finds that the pair already exists and triggers a revert, causing the whole claim transaction to fail. This denial‑of‑service condition occurs whenever the pool is pre‑created, which can happen at any time after the contract deployment and before the first legitimate claim. The affected parties are token holders and any user trying to claim their Codeup ERC20 tokens; they experience a transaction that reverts, receive no tokens, and see their balances remain unchanged despite expecting a successful claim. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the claim logic and identified that the contract does not verify whether the pool already exists before attempting creation. The problem is subtle because creating a Uniswap pair without providing liquidity is a permitted operation on the factory, so the existence of a pool may not be obvious from the UI or from token balances. The bug belongs to the class of “improper external contract interaction” or “unchecked external state assumptions”, where a contract assumes a certain external resource (the Uniswap pair) does not exist and proceeds to create it, leading to a revert when that assumption is violated. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a claim button, the user clicks it, the transaction fails, and the balance stays at zero, contrary to the expectation that the claim would transfer tokens. To remediate, the contract should avoid calling createPair directly; instead it can rely on UniswapV2Router.addLiquidity, which creates the pool only if it does not exist, and then store the pool address by querying the factory with getPair after liquidity is added. This ensures the claim function does not attempt to recreate an existing pair and eliminates the denial‑of‑service vector.
summary: UP-C01 up::claimCodeupERC20() may be forever DoSed by creating the Uniswap pool before it is called Uniswap pools may be created without the underlying tokens existence, which means that up::claimCodeupERC20() is ever called, making it revert when UniswapV2Factory::createPair() is called as the pool has already been created.

title: tower.gameETHForWithdraw should be reduced pro-rata when there is not enough ETH
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the withdrawal and reinvestment logic of the contract that tracks pending gameETH for each user. The contract stores a value called tower.gameETHForWithdraw that represents the amount of gameETH a user is entitled to convert into native ETH. When a user calls up::withdraw() or Codeup::reinvest(), the implementation caps the actual ETH sent to the current contract balance, which is correct for preventing overdrafts. However, after the capped transfer the code unconditionally resets tower.gameETHForWithdraw to zero instead of reducing it proportionally to the amount that could actually be paid. The root cause is a missing pro‑rata reduction step: the state variable is cleared without accounting for the shortfall, so the user’s remaining entitlement is lost. An attacker or any user can exploit this by triggering a withdrawal when the contract’s ETH balance is insufficient, for example by submitting multiple withdrawal requests in quick succession. The first request may consume most of the balance, and the second request will receive only a fraction of the expected ETH, yet the contract will still set the user’s pending gameETH to zero, effectively burning the unfulfilled portion. The impact is loss of funds: users see their gameETH balance disappear, receive less ETH than expected, and cannot later claim the missing amount because the accounting entry has been erased. This condition occurs whenever the contract’s ETH reserve is lower than the aggregate withdrawal demand, which can happen due to normal usage patterns, malicious draining, or concurrency where two users withdraw simultaneously. All users who have a non‑zero tower.gameETHForWithdraw are affected, but the most severe loss is experienced by those whose withdrawals are processed after the balance becomes insufficient. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state updates in the withdraw and reinvest functions and noticed that the pending amount was always zeroed regardless of the actual payout. It is hard to notice because the contract still transfers some ETH, so the failure manifests only as a discrepancy between the displayed gameETH balance and the received ETH, which may be attributed to rounding or fee calculations. The bug belongs to the class of improper state handling or accounting bugs where a financial ledger is not updated consistently with the transferred value. To fix the issue, the contract should calculate the shortfall when the balance is insufficient, reduce tower.gameETHForWithdraw by the exact amount that could not be paid (using a pro‑rata formula rounded up), and only clear the entry when the full entitlement has been satisfied. This ensures that users retain the correct residual claim and can later withdraw the remaining funds once the contract’s balance is replenished. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing or zeroed gameETH balance after a withdrawal attempt, even though the UI may have shown a positive amount before the transaction. The expectation that “my gameETH will be fully converted to ETH” is violated, leading to “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error” scenarios that break the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary: UP-C02 tower.gameETHForWithdraw should be reduced pro-rata when there is not enough ETH up::withdraw() and Codeup::reinvest() cap the withdrawn amount to the available ETH balance, but always set the tower.gameETHForWithdraw to 0, which means that a user can have a significant amont of gameETH for withdraw, but due to the contract having low ETH balance, most of these funds could be lost. This is relevant because blockchains often have concurrency issues, which means, for example, 2 users trying to withdraw more than the contract balance at the same time could lead to one of them getting much less ETH than expected.

title: Total ETH, WETH and gameETH are not tracked which will lead to insolvency
content: The contract allows users to upgrade virtual towers and, in return, mints a proprietary token that represents a claim on future ETH withdrawals. However, the protocol does not keep any accounting of the total amount of native ETH, wrapped ETH (WETH) or the minted game‑specific token that backs those withdrawals. Because there is no state variable that records how much liquidity is actually available versus how much claimable token has been issued, the system can mint more claim tokens than the pool can ever honour. In practice a user can deposit a small amount of ETH, upgrade a tower, receive gameETH and later withdraw more ETH than they originally supplied, while the extra ETH is effectively funded by later users. As more participants join, early users continue to collect yields that exceed the pool’s balance, eventually exhausting all ETH and WETH. The problem is compounded by the fact that the contract provides no function for a user to redeem or withdraw their gameETH balance, even when they have fully upgraded their tower, and the commission mechanism locks the remaining WETH in a way that the last upgrader cannot recover it. The vulnerability was identified during a security audit that simulated user activity and observed that after only a few hours a single participant could claim more ETH than they deposited, demonstrating a clear path to insolvency. The issue is subtle because the contract appears to work correctly for the first few upgrades – yields are paid and no errors are thrown – but the missing accounting only manifests after the pool’s liquidity is depleted, making it hard to detect in short‑term testing. To remediate, the protocol should introduce explicit tracking of total ETH, WETH and gameETH balances, enforce that newly minted claim tokens never exceed the available liquidity, add a withdrawal mechanism for gameETH, and redesign the commission handling so that leftover WETH can be reclaimed by the protocol or its participants. By aligning the accounting model with the business logic that each token represents a real ETH claim, the protocol can prevent the situation where funds disappear, users receive zero or unexpected payouts, and the system becomes financially unsound.
summary: UP-C03 Total ETH, WETH and gameETH are not tracked which will lead to insolvency Users may upgrade their towers so they receive gameETH over time which can later be withdrawn for ETH. However, there is no actual tracking in either of the funds, which means that eventually once users stop entering the protocol, there will not be enough ETH to pay everyone for their yield. A poc was created showing that after just 16 hours a user receives more ETH as yield than their initial deposit when buying gameETH. Thus, initial users that upgrade their towers will just get all yield very quickly from new users, eventually making the protocol insolvent as everyone has yield to claim but nobody wants to deposit. Another related concern is that users have no option to withdraw their gameETH, even if they have for example upgraded their towers to the max level. It does not make sense to ever deposit more than the max cost to upgrade all builders. Lastly, the remaining weth balance will be impossible to withdraw because the last user that has upgraded their towers to the max builders will withdraw these funds and pay a commision to the pool in amountForPool, which will never be recovered.

title: Check for Staking liquidity in flip() does not account for other game contracts
content: The vulnerability is an over‑allocation of shared staking liquidity in a coin‑flip gambling contract. The flip() function verifies that the external Staking contract holds enough balance to pay the player’s reward, but the check only considers the amount locked by that particular game contract. Because the same Staking contract is used by multiple independent game contracts, the total amount locked across all games can exceed the actual token balance of the Staking contract. When this happens the contract will still claim that a win is payable, yet the Staking contract will be unable to transfer the promised reward. The root cause is a missing global accounting step: the contract does not aggregate the locked liquidity of every game that relies on the shared Staking pool before performing the balance check. An attacker can exploit the flaw by coordinating wins across several contracts, or by simply waiting until the cumulative locked amount surpasses the pool, then triggering a win in any of the contracts. The impact is that users who win may receive zero tokens, see their balance unchanged, or experience a reverted transaction, effectively losing the expected payout. This situation occurs only when more than one game contract is linked to the same Staking contract and the combined locked funds are greater than the Staking contract’s actual token holdings. All participants—players, the protocol operators, and any third‑party contracts that depend on the Staking pool—are affected because the protocol can no longer guarantee its advertised reward guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the liquidity checks in the flip() function and compared them against the global state of the Staking contract. It is hard to notice because each individual game contract passes its own check, giving a false sense of safety; the problem only becomes visible when the aggregate state is considered. To remediate, the flip() function (or a central manager) must query the Staking contract for the total amount of liquidity currently locked by *all* game contracts and ensure that the remaining free balance is sufficient to cover a potential win. Alternative mitigations include assigning a dedicated Staking pool per game, introducing a global reserve, or implementing a re‑entrancy‑safe accounting mechanism that updates a shared locked‑liquidity counter before each bet. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of shared‑resource accounting errors where per‑instance checks do not reflect the collective state, leading to reward‑payment failures and loss of user funds.
summary:
Flip.flip() checks that the Staking contract has enough funds to cover the player's reward in the case of a win. However, it is not taken into account that other game contracts might have also funds locked in the Staking contract. 
As a result, the total liquidity locked among all game contracts might exceed the total balance of the Staking contract, which would cause the Staking contract not to be able to cover all the rewards in the case of a win.

title: Bet amount remains locked in the Flip contract when player wins
content: The vulnerability consists of a logical accounting error in the coin‑flip betting contract that causes the original bet amount to remain permanently locked inside the contract whenever a player wins a round. The contract is designed to deduct a fee from the bet and forward the remainder to a staking contract that then pays the player. However, the implementation only transfers the fee portion (or a calculated manager fee) to the manager or staking contract and fails to release the rest of the bet amount from the Flip contract’s balance. As a result, after a winning game the player receives the expected payout from the staking contract, but the contract’s own token reserve is reduced by the unreleased portion of the bet. This occurs exclusively in the win‑path of the game logic; the lose‑path correctly transfers the full bet to the protocol. The root cause is an incomplete transfer statement that does not move the net payout (bet amount minus fee) out of the Flip contract, effectively locking those tokens forever. An attacker can exploit the bug simply by playing and winning repeatedly, causing the protocol’s token pool to shrink with each win while the attacker continues to receive payouts. Over time the protocol incurs a net loss equal to the bet amount minus the fee for every win, while it gains the full bet amount for every loss, making the economic model unsustainable. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the payout flow and token accounting. It can be hard to notice because the user interface shows a successful win and the player receives the expected tokens, masking the silent depletion of the contract’s balance. The bug violates basic accounting assumptions that all funds deposited by a player must either be transferred out or returned; instead, a portion is never accounted for. To remediate, the contract should ensure that after a win the full bet amount, less any applicable manager fee, is transferred out of the Flip contract (typically to the staking contract or directly to the player) so that no tokens remain locked. This aligns the token flow with the intended economic model and restores protocol sustainability.
summary:
When a game is completed and the player wins, a percentage of the bet amount (fee) is sent to the manager and/or the staking contract. But the rest of the bet amount remains locked forever. 
This means that for every game won, the protocol loses netPayout tokens, while for every game lost, the protocol gains betAmount tokens. 
Considering a scenario where the parameters are set to provide the maximum profitability for the protocol we would have the following: 
feePercentage = 10% 
managerWinFeePercentage = 0% 
liquidityEdge = 0% 
A player bets 100 tokens for 1 head out of 1 flip, so the chance of winning is 50%. 
If the player wins, Staking contract sends 190 tokens to the player, 10 tokens (fee) are transferred from Flip to Staking contract, and 90 tokens get locked in the Flip contract. The result for the protocol is a net loss of 180 tokens. 
If the player loses, the protocol gains 100 tokens from the player bet. 
As we can see, the protocol is not sustainable in the long term.

title: Pending payouts excluded from total balance cause incorrect share calculations
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch where pending payouts that failed to be transferred are stored in a pendingPayouts mapping but the contract continues to include the corresponding token amount in its total balance calculations. The root cause is that the protocol determines its total token holdings by calling IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) without subtracting the sum of pending payouts or the amount locked as liquidity for ongoing games. When a payout fails, the amount is recorded as a liability in pendingPayouts, yet the balance used for share valuation, totalOwed, lockLiquidity, finalizeStake and finalizeUnstake remains inflated. An attacker or any user can exploit this by triggering a payout failure (for example by causing the external call to revert) and then withdrawing shares based on the overstated pool balance. Because the share value is calculated on the inflated balance, the user can claim more tokens than are actually available, leaving the remaining shares under‑collateralised. The impact is that the pool can end up with fewer tokens than the total shares represent, causing share value to drop to zero for honest stakers, loss of funds, and the possibility for a malicious actor to drain the pool by repeatedly forcing payout failures and withdrawing inflated amounts. This condition occurs after a game completes and the transferPayout function returns false, and persists until the pending payouts are manually claimed or the contract is otherwise corrected. All stakers, winners, and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting error propagates to every function that relies on the total token balance. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the balance‑calculation logic and noticed that totalOwed could exceed the actual token balance when pending payouts exist. It is hard to notice because the ERC20 balanceOf view still reports the correct on‑chain token amount, masking the internal liability mismatch; the problem only surfaces when a payout failure happens, which may be a rare event. From a user perspective the symptoms are that a user may see their share value unchanged after a failed payout, can withdraw the full amount of tokens they expect, and later the pool shows a zero or negative backing for remaining shares, leading to unexpected zero balances or loss of value. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or liability‑exclusion vulnerabilities, similar to missing deductions for pending withdrawals. To remediate, the contract should track the total pending payout per token and subtract this amount (and optionally the lockedLiquidity representing ongoing game reserves) from the balance used in all share‑valuation calculations, ensuring that totalOwed never exceeds the actual token holdings and that share value accurately reflects the net assets after accounting for outstanding liabilities.
summary:
After each game completes, the protocol attempts to transfer the winner's payout through Staking.transferPayout(). If this transfer fails, the amount is stored in pendingPayouts to be claimed later. However, the contract continues to include these pending payouts in its balance calculations, which causes overestimation of the staking balance using in the calculation.
```solidity
function transferPayout(address token, address recipient, uint256 amount) external {
    //--- SNIPPED ---
    if (!callSucceeded) {
        pendingPayouts[token][recipient] += amount;
        emit TransferFailed(token, recipient, amount);
        return false;
    }
    //--- SNIPPED ---
}
```
The problem is from how the contract calculates total balance. It simply uses IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) without subtracting pendingPayouts. This inflated balance affects several critical functions: totalOwed(), lockLiquidity(), finalizeStake(), and finalizeUnstake().
Consider the following scenario:
Initial setup:
Alice has staked 1000 tokens (1000 shares)
Someone starts a game:
betAmount: 100 tokens
netPayout: 200 tokens (2:1 odds)
Protocol locks 200 tokens
The game ends, but winner's payout of 200 tokens fails to transfer:
Staking contract adds 200 tokens to pendingPayouts
Pool now holds 1100 tokens (original 1000 + 100 from betAmount)
200 tokens remain locked
Now, let's analyze the apparent token owned to Alice:
Alice's shares represent 1100 tokens (1000 shares × 1100 / 1000), but this does not account for the loss that has occurred (Alice's shares still appear to be worth 1:1)
Winner is owed 200 tokens
Total owed tokens: 1300 tokens, but the protocol only has 1100 tokens
For comparison, if the payout had gone through normally:
Pool would have 900 tokens (1000 - 200(netPayout) + 100(betAmount))
Alice's shares would correctly represent 900 tokens for maximum owed (1000 shares × 900 / 1000)
3. This has a cascading impact on the pool:
Alice withdraws 900 tokens, due to liquidity locks, but the incorrect calculation still propagates the effect.
Alice burns 900 shares, leaving 100 shares, which resulting in token balance of 200 (1100 - 900)
The winner claims their 200 tokens, depleting the token balance
As a result, the remaining 100 shares are no longer backed by any token balance
This leaves the pool in an loss state, as shares become worthless, and any new deposits would be immediately devalued. Furthermore, Alice could request to unstake her remaining shares and wait for new deposits, essentially stealing some of their stake.

title: Pending stake not accounted for in liquidity calculations
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the staking contract determines the amount of tokens that are considered available for share calculations and liquidity checks. The contract simply calls IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) to obtain the total token balance, assuming that every token held by the contract represents liquid, withdrawable liquidity. However, when a user calls requestStake, the contract immediately transfers the user’s tokens into its own balance but does not record the amount as a pending stake that is still awaiting finalisation. Because the pending amount is not excluded from the balance used in calculations, the contract over‑estimates the pool’s available liquidity. This over‑estimation propagates to several critical functions – share calculation during stake finalisation, the pro‑rata amount owed in finalizeUnstake, totalOwed, and lockLiquidity – all of which rely on the inflated balance. In practice, a user who requests a stake (for example Alice) sees her tokens transferred to the contract, but the contract still treats those tokens as part of the free pool. If another staker finalises an unstake before Alice’s stake is finalised, the contract will allocate the pending tokens to the withdrawing user. Consequently Alice may end up receiving zero tokens when she later finalises her own stake, even though she deposited tokens, effectively losing her funds. The issue occurs whenever requestStake is used and the pending amount is not tracked, which is true for every new stake request. All participants in the pool – existing stakers, new pending stakers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting invariants are broken and the pool can distribute more tokens than it should. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the token balance used in calculations with the logical state of pending deposits and identified the missing accounting entry. It is hard to notice because the contract’s balanceOf call returns a correct numeric value, and the code otherwise appears to follow standard share‑based accounting, so the discrepancy only surfaces under specific timing where a pending stake is overtaken by an unstake. The bug belongs to the class of liquidity‑miscalculation or accounting‑state‑inconsistency bugs, where pending deposits are not excluded from the pool’s available balance. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful stake request, but later the user receives no tokens back, sees a zero balance after finalising, or observes that the pool’s total liquidity suddenly drops without explanation. The expected behaviour – that a user’s deposited tokens are reserved until the stake is finalised – is violated, leading to funds disappearing and the protocol’s accounting breaking. The recommended remediation is to introduce a pending‑stake accounting variable, subtract pending amounts from the balance used in share and liquidity calculations, and update this variable when a stake is finalised so that the tokens become part of the genuine liquidity pool.

title: Lack of transferId Verification Allows an Attacker to Front-Run Bridge Transfers
content: The vulnerability is an integrity check omission in the bridge’s onReceive handler. The function extracts a transfer identifier from the extra data supplied by the caller but never validates that the identifier corresponds to the amount, token address, or originating chain that were originally locked on the source chain. Because the onlyBridgeRouter modifier only ensures that the caller is a BridgeRouter contract, an attacker can invoke the sendToHook entry point with arbitrary extraData and a minimal amount, causing the same transferId to be processed before the legitimate user’s message. When the malicious message is processed first, the contract marks the transferId as reconciled, and the subsequent honest transfer is rejected as already reconciled, leaving the user’s tokens effectively burned on the source chain while the attacker receives only the tiny amount they supplied. The issue manifests whenever a bridge router forwards a TransferToHook message that includes a user‑controlled extraData field and the destination contract does not cross‑check the amount, token address, or origin against the stored transferId. Any participant who relies on the bridge to move funds – end users, liquidity providers, or the protocol itself – can lose assets. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the reconciliation logic and noticed that the transferId is treated as an opaque value without any cryptographic binding to the transfer parameters. Because the contract simply checks a boolean flag, the problem is not obvious from the UI; users see their balance on the destination chain remain unchanged or become zero after a bridge transaction, with no error message indicating a replay. The bug belongs to the class of missing parameter validation / replayable identifier vulnerabilities, where an identifier can be reused with altered payloads. To remediate, the reconciliation routine must recompute the transferId from the amount, token address, origin chain, and any other relevant fields and compare it to the supplied identifier, and the router should also verify that the caller originates from the expected Connext Diamond on the source chain. Additionally, the token address supplied in the message should be validated against the expected canonical token. Implementing these checks prevents an attacker from front‑running a legitimate transfer and ensures that only the exact transfer that was locked can be reconciled.

title: Use of spot dex price when repay portal debt leads to sandwich attacks
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the NomadFacet contract calculates the amount of adopted assets required to repay a portal debt. When the _reconcileProcessPortal function is executed, it first calls _calculatePortalRepayment which determines totalRepayAmount based on the current spot price reported by an automated market maker (AMM). The subsequent call to AssetLogic.swapFromLocalAssetIfNeededForExactOut then performs a swap that aims for an exact output amount without enforcing any slippage protection. Because totalRepayAmount is derived directly from the AMM spot price, an attacker who can manipulate that price immediately before the repayment transaction can cause the contract to believe that a much smaller amount of adopted assets is sufficient. The attacker can front‑run the repayment, push the price down (or up) on the DEX, let the contract execute the swap at the manipulated price, and then back‑run to restore the market price, pocketing the difference. This sandwich attack can be repeated on any chain where the repayment logic is used, potentially draining millions of dollars from the protocol. The issue occurs whenever the portal repayment flow is triggered, affecting the protocol’s treasury and any users whose assets are used for the conversion. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditors noticed that totalRepayAmount is always smaller than the amount that would be obtained from the swap based on the spot price, meaning the swap never triggers a slippage revert even if the price is severely distorted. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the on‑chain logs show amounts that appear consistent with the manipulated price, making it easy to miss during normal testing. To remediate, the repayment calculation should not rely solely on a volatile spot price; instead it should use a price oracle with time‑weighted averaging, enforce explicit slippage limits on the swap, or compute the repayment using a worst‑case price bound. Adding these safeguards prevents an attacker from forcing the contract to accept an under‑priced swap and eliminates the economic incentive for sandwich attacks, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: swapOut allows overwrite of token balance
content: The vulnerability resides in the stable‑swap facet of the protocol where the public function swapExactOut (and its internal counterpart swapInternalOut) accepts two token addresses, assetIn and assetOut, without enforcing that they refer to different assets. Internally the function resolves each address to a token index and then calls a library routine swapOut that updates the pool’s internal balance array. The routine first copies the current balances into a temporary memory array, then writes the new balance for tokenIndexFrom, and finally writes the new balance for tokenIndexTo. When the two indexes are identical, the second write overwrites the first one, effectively applying the subtraction step after the addition step on the same balance entry. This results in a net reduction of the token’s recorded balance equal to the amount that was supposed to be transferred out, even though no actual token movement occurs. An attacker can therefore trigger a swap where assetIn equals assetOut, specify any positive amount, and cause the pool’s recorded balance for that token to decrease arbitrarily. Because the exchange rate calculation later reads the corrupted balance, the attacker can also manipulate the price curve to extract additional value from subsequent swaps. The flaw is a classic accounting‑logic error where a self‑overwrite of a state variable is not guarded against; it belongs to the class of “balance overwrite” or “self‑transfer accounting” bugs. The issue manifests whenever a user (or a malicious contract) calls swapExactOut with the same token for both input and output, which is allowed by the public interface. It was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditors noticed that the helper function getY contains a require‑statement preventing identical token indexes, but this check is never invoked from swapOut, leaving the path unprotected. The bug can be hard to spot because the code appears to handle swaps correctly and a same‑token swap might be assumed to be a no‑op, yet the sequential balance updates unintentionally create a loss. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the user’s token balance in the pool is reduced (e.g., a balance of 100 becomes 90 after a swap of 10 units with the same token), leading to symptoms such as “my funds disappeared” or “the pool balance is lower than expected”. The affected parties include any liquidity provider or trader interacting with the stable‑swap pool, as well as the protocol that relies on accurate accounting for its invariant. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce tokenIndexFrom != tokenIndexTo before performing the balance updates, either by re‑using the existing check from getY or by adding an explicit require statement in swapExactOut and swapInternalOut. Alternatively, the balance update logic could be rewritten to handle the equal‑index case without double‑writing. Applying the fix restores the invariant, prevents arbitrary balance reduction, and eliminates the avenue for value extraction.

title: Use of spot price in SponsorVault leads to sandwich attack.
content: The vulnerability resides in the SponsorVault contract that reimburses liquidity fees by swapping the native token for an adopted token using the on‑chain automated market maker (AMM) spot price. The contract calls a function that returns the amount of native token required to obtain a fixed amount of the adopted token, but it relies on the current spot price returned by the DEX.
