Because the spot price can be altered by external trades, an attacker can manipulate the price just before the sponsor’s reimbursement transaction, causing the getInGivenExpectedOut calculation to request far more native tokens than necessary. In a typical sandwich scenario the attacker first pushes the price of the native token down by executing a large trade, then the SponsorVault performs swapExactIn based on the depressed price, consuming an excessive amount of native tokens to purchase the promised adopted token amount. After the vault’s swap further depresses the price, the attacker buys back the native token at the new lower price, realizing a profit while the sponsor vault loses its native token balance, potentially draining it completely. This flaw occurs whenever the sponsor vault is funded with the native token and the reimbursement function is invoked, i.e., during any sponsored fee transfer. The affected parties are the sponsors who provide liquidity, the users expecting a fee rebate, and the protocol that relies on the vault’s balance to guarantee sponsorship. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee reimbursement flow and identified that the contract trusts a manipulable spot price instead of a reliable reference. The problem is subtle because the contract does not check for abnormal price deviations, so a normal‑looking swap may silently consume far more funds than intended, and the loss manifests only as a sudden drop in the vault’s native token balance. To remediate, the contract should obtain price data from a source that is resistant to short‑term manipulation, such as a trusted oracle or a time‑weighted average price (TWAP), compare it with the spot price, and either revert the transaction or use the oracle price when the two diverge beyond an acceptable threshold. This change restores the intended accounting logic that the sponsor vault should spend only the amount needed to cover the advertised fee, preserving sponsor funds and maintaining protocol integrity.

title: CRT-1 Anyone can perform any arbitrary calls on behalf of VoterProxy
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access control flaw in the deposit routine of the VoterProxy contract. The function accepts any caller, any ERC20 token address and any gauge address without verifying that the token is the one that the gauge expects or that the gauge is an authorized contract. Because the function forwards a call to the gauge’s deposit method, an attacker can craft calldata that causes the VoterProxy to execute arbitrary external calls on its behalf. This can be exploited by any external account to, for example, approve a malicious contract to spend the VoterProxy’s token balances, lock user funds in an incompatible gauge, or trigger withdrawals that send tokens to an address controlled by the attacker. The impact includes loss of user funds, violation of the protocol’s authorization model, and potential disruption of the voting/boosting mechanisms that rely on correct token‑gauge pairing. The condition occurs whenever a user or any actor invokes the deposit function; there is no restriction on the caller, token, or gauge, so the attack surface is always present. All participants that rely on VoterProxy – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because their assets can be moved or frozen without consent. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s external interfaces and identified missing whitelist checks and compatibility validation. Because the function appears to work correctly for legitimate use cases, the flaw can be hard to notice in normal operation; only when an unexpected token approval or a missing balance is observed does the problem become apparent. The proper mitigation is to introduce an explicit allow‑list of approved gauge contracts, enforce that the supplied token matches the gauge’s expected reward token, and add access control so that only authorized roles can invoke the deposit routine. In abstract terms the bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted external call” or “missing validation of input parameters” vulnerabilities that enable arbitrary contract interaction and token mis‑allocation. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may be that after a deposit transaction the user’s token balance in the VoterProxy becomes zero, approvals appear for unknown contracts, or funds that were supposed to be staked remain locked and cannot be withdrawn. The expectation that the contract will only interact with known gauges and tokens is violated, leading to funds disappearing or being redirected without the user’s consent.
summary: Function deposit in VoterProxy defined at VoterProxy.sol#L60 accepts call from anyone with any token and gauge, so anyone can craft calldata and make call on behalf of VoterProxy. That could lead to undesired behavior, e.g user's funds locked in contract or authorization violation. Also deposit can be called for gauge and token which are not compatible. Moreover for now anyone can allow spending tokens from contract balance for any third-party account by calling deposit for target token with evil gauge.

title: Malicious Users Can Steal All Staking Rewards From StakedCSX Due to a Logical Error
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the reward‑crediting routine of the StakedCSX contract. When the private function _claimToCredit is executed, it retrieves the pending reward amounts for each supported asset (WETH, USDC, USDT) via rewardOf and then adds those amounts to a per‑account credit mapping using the += operator. Because the credit mapping already contains the previously claimed reward, the addition effectively doubles the stored credit on every invocation. The function _claimToCredit is called from the _beforeTokenTransfer hook, which is triggered on any token transfer, including transfers of zero value. Consequently, a malicious user can repeatedly perform zero‑value transfers of the StakedCSX token, causing the credit for that account to double each time. Over a few iterations the credit grows exponentially, allowing the attacker to claim an amount far larger than their proportional share and ultimately drain all staking rewards from the contract. The impact is that the reward pool becomes empty, honest stakers receive no dividends, and the contract may become insolvent. The bug occurs whenever an account with a non‑zero balance initiates a transfer, even if the transferred amount is zero, because the hook does not check the transfer amount before calling _claimToCredit. The affected parties are all participants in the staking protocol, including token holders and the protocol itself, which loses the economic incentive mechanism. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that showed a user entitled to only one‑eighth of the rewards being able to claim the entire pool after a few zero‑value transfers. The problem is subtle because zero‑value transfers appear harmless in the UI and the credit values increase in a way that seems consistent with reward accrual, making the bug hard to notice without inspecting the internal accounting logic. The correct mitigation is to replace the addition assignment (+=) with a plain assignment (=) when writing the reward amounts to the credit mapping, ensuring that each credit entry reflects only the newly calculated reward rather than the sum of the old credit and the new reward. This change restores the intended accounting model where rewards are allocated proportionally and prevents any user from artificially inflating their claim.

title: Game fee handling is incorrect
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the contract calculates and distributes the game fee during the endGame routine. When the admin calls endGame, the function receives a list of participants together with their raw payout amounts (unsignedWinLossAmount). For each participant the contract adds a portion of the payout, computed as (unsignedWinLossAmount * takeRate) / 100, to a single state variable called gameFee. This variable is intended to hold the total fee collected from the whole game, but it is used inside the same loop to adjust each individual player's payout: the adjusted payout is calculated as unsignedWinLossAmount minus the current value of gameFee. Because gameFee is never reset for each iteration, it accumulates the fees of all previously processed participants. As a result, for the second, third, or any later participant the adjusted payout becomes smaller than intended, and when the accumulated fee exceeds that participant’s raw payout the subtraction underflows, causing the transaction to revert. In the worst case the function reverts part‑way through the loop, leaving the game in an unfinished state and preventing any user from receiving their funds. Even when the subtraction does not underflow, the fee is applied multiple times, leading to an incorrect distribution where winners receive less than they earned and the contract retains excess tokens. The issue is triggered only when endGame processes more than one winning participant or when a participant’s payout is relatively small compared to the total fee collected so far, which makes it easy to miss in simple single‑winner tests. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the fee‑handling logic and identified that the accumulator was not cleared between iterations. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or zero payout after a win, an unexpected reduction of the expected reward, or a complete inability to finalize the game and withdraw funds. This bug violates the core business rule that the fee should be taken once from the total pool, not repeatedly from each individual payout, breaking the accounting guarantees of the game. The conceptual fix is to separate fee accumulation from per‑player payout calculation: either compute each player’s fee in a temporary variable without mutating the shared accumulator, or defer the update of the global gameFee until after the loop has processed all participants, then distribute the net payouts accordingly. Implementing the fix restores the intended economic model, ensures that winners receive the correct net amount, and prevents the contract from reverting or mis‑allocating funds.
summary:
endGame function is called by the admin to finish the game. Admin provides a list of participants and their payouts and function loops through all of them. In case if user wins, then the game takes a fee from his reward. This fee is accumulated in the gameFee variable. It is increased with each new user and the real user's win is an unsignedWinLossAmount - gameFee.
uint256 gameTakeRate = takeRate[currentSession.gameType];
gameFee +=
(playerPayout.unsignedWinLossAmount * gameTakeRate) / 100;
uint256 adjustedPlayerPayout = playerPayout.unsignedW
gameFee is the variable that is used for the whole loop and is increased on each cycle. It is not reset for each new cycle. As a result adjustedPlayerPayout becomes incorrect and it may revert, when gameFee > unsignedWinLossAmount. Then the game will not be finalized and users will not be able to get back their funds.
Also, it is possible that the function will not revert, but gameFee and adjustedPlayerPayout will be wrong, which means incorrect payout distribution.

title: Winner's payout is incorrectly calculated
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic error in the winner payout logic of a betting game contract. When the game ends and a player has a payout greater than their original stake, the contract adds the full payout amount to the player’s stored balance instead of adding only the net gain (payout minus stake). The root cause is the use of the variable that represents the total amount the player should receive after the game, rather than the incremental winning amount, in the statement that updates the balance. This mistake occurs only in the branch that handles a winning player (payout > stake). As a result, the player’s existing stake, which is already part of their balance, is counted a second time, inflating the withdrawable amount. For example, with two participants each staking 1 ether, a winner who should end with 1.5 ether ends up with a recorded balance of 2.5 ether, allowing them to withdraw 1 ether more than intended. The impact is that winners can extract excess ether from the contract, draining funds that should belong to other participants and breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the end‑game accounting logic and identified the mismatch between expected and actual balance updates. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to credit the winner, but the subtle double‑counting of the stake does not raise an immediate error flag. The bug violates the fundamental business rule that a player’s balance after a win should equal the original stake plus the net profit, not the stake plus the total payout. To fix the problem, the contract should add only the difference between payout and stake (the net win) to the stored balance, ensuring that the player’s balance reflects the correct amount and that the contract’s total ether accounting remains consistent.

title: Incorrect logical check in endGame function
content: The vulnerability is a logical condition error in the endGame routine of a gaming smart contract. The function is supposed to iterate over all participants of a given game, identify those whose stored game identifier matches the identifier supplied to the call, and then execute payout logic and update the game status. Instead of checking for inequality, the code uses an equality comparison (==) and then continues to the next iteration when the hashes match. As a result, every player that actually belongs to the targeted game is skipped, so no balance adjustments, no token transfers, and no status change are performed. The transaction still returns a successful execution flag because no revert or require is triggered, making the failure silent. This bug manifests when any actor calls endGame with a valid gameId; the contract reports the game as ended while the internal state remains InProgress and all player funds stay locked in the contract. Affected parties include all players who have deposited funds for that game, as well as any downstream services that rely on correct payout accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual security review where the auditor inspected the control flow of the endGame function and noticed the inverted predicate. It can be hard to notice because the function does not emit an error, and external observers see only a successful transaction receipt, while the UI may still show the game as active and player balances unchanged. The bug belongs to the class of inverted logical checks or predicate errors, a common source of business‑logic failures where a condition is mistakenly negated. From a user perspective the symptoms are a missing refund, a balance that remains zero after the game should have finished, and a game status that never transitions from InProgress. The contract violates the fundamental accounting assumption that closing a game must release the locked funds to the rightful participants. The recommended remediation is to replace the equality operator with an inequality operator (or restructure the loop) so that players whose stored gameId differs from the supplied identifier are skipped, and the matching players are processed for payout and status update. After correcting the condition, the function will correctly adjust balances, emit the expected events, and set the game status to Completed, restoring the intended financial flow.
summary: The endGame function in the Game contract fails to function correctly due to an erroneous logical check. This function, intended to handle the payouts at the end of a game, incorrectly uses == instead of != when comparing the hash of the gameId provided with the gameId of each player. This results in the function skipping all players who are actually in the game it intends to end. Consequently, no player payouts or updates to game status are processed, and the transaction completes without performing any meaningful actions despite returning a successful execution state. This results in the players' funds staying locked in the contract as they cannot withdraw when the game status is InProgress.

title: C-1 Rebasing rewards will get stuck on the contract
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that occurs when the pool accepts rebasing tokens such as stETH. The contract stores each user’s balance in a mapping called stored_balances and uses this static value to validate withdrawals. Because rebasing tokens change their total supply automatically, the actual token balance held by the contract can increase after a reward distribution while stored_balances remains unchanged. When a user attempts to withdraw, the contract compares the requested amount with the stale stored_balances, the check fails and the transaction reverts. As a result the user’s deposited tokens, together with any accrued rewards, become permanently locked in the immutable pool contract. The issue was uncovered during the MixBytes audit by executing a test that simulated a token rebase and observing the revert on the balance‑validation lines in CurveStableSwapNG and CurveStableSwapMetaNG. The bug is subtle because rebasing events are external to the contract and do not produce obvious on‑chain errors; the UI may still display the correct share amount, leading users to believe a withdrawal should succeed. The impact is that funds disappear from the user’s perspective: the user expects to receive their tokens (including rewards) but receives a transaction failure and sees a zero balance returned. The affected parties are any depositor of rebasing assets in the pool, the protocol’s liquidity providers, and downstream applications that rely on the pool’s correctness. Because the contracts are not upgradeable, there is no mechanism to patch the logic, making the loss effectively unrecoverable. The root cause is the use of a static balance accounting model that does not incorporate the dynamic supply changes of rebasing tokens. To remediate, the contract should replace stored_balances with a share‑based accounting scheme or continuously adjust the stored value based on the token’s current rebasing factor, ensuring that withdrawal checks reflect the true token balance at the moment of execution.
summary:
The main problem here is that stored_balances does not account for rewards for rebaseable tokens (e.g. stETH):
CurveStableSwapNG.vy#L380
CurveStableSwapMetaNG.vy#L440
This leads to the situation where deposited tokens with accrued rewards cannot be removed from the contract because of the revert on the lines pointed above. The test scenario was sent to the client during the audit. This finding is classified as critical because pools' contracts do not allow upgrades, which means that users' tokens will get stuck on the contract and there will be no possibility to retrieve them.

title: C-2 getvirtualprice() can be manipulated
content: The vulnerability concerns the getVirtualPrice() function of Curve stable‑swap pools, which can be artificially inflated by sending tokens directly to the pool contract without using the official addLiquidity path. When an attacker transfers tokens straight to a base pool that is part of a meta‑pool, the internal balance accounting (the D value) increases because the pool now holds more assets, but the totalSupply of LP tokens remains unchanged. This mismatch causes the virtual price – a ratio of total pool value to LP token supply – to rise. The inflated virtual price can then be exploited: the attacker calls removeLiquidityOneCoin() on the meta‑pool, which, due to the higher virtual price of the underlying base‑pool LP token, requires fewer LP tokens to withdraw a given amount of the target coin. After extracting the desired coin, the attacker invokes exchangeReceived() on the base pool to reclaim the tokens that were originally donated in step one, effectively converting the artificial price increase into a net profit. The impact is severe because many protocols, including Curve itself, rely on the virtual price as an oracle for fee calculations, reward distribution, and risk assessments; a manipulated price can lead to incorrect accounting, loss of funds for honest participants, and erosion of trust in the system. The condition for exploitation is the ability to perform a direct ERC‑20 transfer to the pool, which the contract currently treats as a donation but still incorporates into its price calculation. This behavior is subtle and may go unnoticed because direct token transfers are a normal operation on ERC‑20 contracts and the virtual price appears higher rather than obviously broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test scenario demonstrated that a simple token donation followed by a strategic liquidity removal yielded a profit. To remediate, the design of exchangeReceived() and the balance‑querying functions should be revised so that unsolicited token transfers are either rejected, ignored for price calculations, or correctly reflected in totalSupply, thereby preventing the virtual price from being decoupled from the actual LP token economics. In broader terms, this is a class of oracle manipulation bug where an on‑chain price metric can be skewed by unaccounted token inflows, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that pool value and LP supply move together.
summary:
getvirtualprice() can be manipulated by directly transferring tokens to the pools. The thing is that directly transferred tokens can be skimmed via the exchange_received() function:
CurveStableSwapNG.vy#L1629
CurveStableSwapMetaNG.vy#L1610
One example of an attack that can make a profit for a hacker is:
1. Directly transfer one of the tokens to a basepool that was added to a metapool.
2. getvirtualprice() increases, because D increases and total_supply remains the same.
3. The hacker can call removeliquidityonecoin() in metapool. Due to the increased virtualprice of the basepool LP token, it will cost a lot less to remove coin[0] from meta_pool.
4. After this, the hacker can call exchangereceived in the basepool and return the deposited in (1) funds.
The test scenario was sent to the client during the audit.
This finding is classified as critical because many protocols rely on the virtual_price of the pool (even Curve relies on it), and manipulation of the virtual_price is very dangerous.

title: C-3 Read-only reentrancy in metapool with an old basepool
content: The vulnerability is a read‑only reentrancy flaw that appears when a Curve metapool is configured with an old base pool that does not implement a reentrancy lock on its getVirtualPrice function. The root cause is that the metapool contract calls getVirtualPrice on the base pool during a swap, and the old base pool allows the caller to re‑enter the metapool’s swap logic before the original call finishes. An attacker can therefore manipulate the virtual price of the base‑pool LP token by triggering a re‑entrant call that temporarily inflates the price, and then use that inflated price in the same swap to receive more of the second coin than the market rate would allow. This can be exploited by crafting a malicious contract that initiates a swap from a base‑pool LP token to the metapool’s second coin, intercepts the getVirtualPrice call, and during the re‑entrancy modifies the internal accounting of the base pool (for example by borrowing ETH or altering the pool’s balance) so that the virtual price returned is higher than the true value. The attacker then completes the original swap, which now uses the manipulated price, resulting in an over‑payment to the attacker and a loss of value for the honest participant. The impact is a direct loss of funds: users receive fewer tokens than expected, or the protocol loses value because swaps are executed at an artificially high rate. The condition required for the attack is the presence of an old base pool that uses ETH and lacks a reentrancy guard on getVirtualPrice; newer base pools include such a lock and are not vulnerable. Any user or liquidity provider interacting with a metapool that references such an old base pool can be affected, as can the protocol’s overall token reserves. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the Curve StableSwapNG contracts, where the auditors identified that the getVirtualPrice call could be re‑entered and that the virtual price could be increased without proper checks. The bug is subtle because the re‑entrancy occurs in a view‑only function, so typical re‑entrancy detection tools that focus on state‑changing calls may miss it, and the price manipulation may only be observable as an unexpected swap outcome rather than an outright transaction failure. To remediate the problem, the factory that registers base pools should reject pools that are paired with ETH or that do not implement a reentrancy lock on price‑oracle functions, and the metapool should enforce a non‑reentrant guard around getVirtualPrice calls. In broader terms, this is a class of price‑oracle manipulation via read‑only re‑entrancy, where an attacker exploits a missing lock to feed a falsified price into a financial calculation, breaking the accounting assumptions that token swaps are executed at fair market rates. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include receiving zero or far fewer tokens than expected after a swap, seeing balances that appear unchanged while the transaction succeeded, or noticing that the swap rate displayed in the UI does not match the market price. The expectation that a swap will exchange tokens at the current pool price is violated, leading to funds disappearing or being transferred at an unfair rate.
summary:
Old base pools cannot be added to CurveStableSwapFactory. Using an old base pool in meta_pool can lead to read-only reentrancy attacks because of the possible manipulation of the virtual price of a base pool LP token. There is a possible read-only reentrancy attack with a call to getvirtualprice in a metapool (At the line CurveStableSwapMetaNG.vy#L457). Virtual price can be incorrectly increased, and that rate can be used during a swap from base pool LP to the second coin in metapool. It will work with old base pools that use ETH (new ones have a reentrancy lock on the getvirtualprice function).
This issue has been assigned a CRITICAL severity level because working with old base pools that contain ETH will lead to rate manipulation and funds loss (exchanging tokens using manipulated prices).

title: C-1 An inﬂation attack allows for hard liquidations
content: The vulnerability is an inflation‑based manipulation that lets an attacker artificially raise the price of collateral shares in the TwoWayLending protocol and then trigger a hard liquidation of a seemingly healthy borrower. The root cause lies in two interacting design flaws: first, the protocol’s share price (the tick price returned by pcurrentdown) reacts to an oracle price increase with an amplification factor of roughly 3.3, meaning a modest 10 % oracle rise translates into a 33 % rise in the AMM price grid; second, the health() calculation that determines whether a loan is liquidatable ignores the dynamic fee component returned by limitpo, which can be very high immediately after a price swing and then decay after about 120 seconds. An attacker can exploit this by buying the victim’s collateral shares through the exchange() function, then directly transferring funds to the Controller to inflate the share price. Because the health() function does not account for the inflated tick price nor the temporary fee surge, the borrower’s health ratio is reported as negative even though the position remains solvent while fees are high. The attacker can then call liquidate() and seize the collateral at the inflated price, extracting profit without needing to reverse the trade. The impact is that users may lose collateral that should have been safe, leading to unexpected liquidation, loss of funds, and potential bad debt accumulation as the AMM price diverges from the true market price. The issue manifests whenever an oracle price moves upward and the attacker can quickly inflate the share price before the dynamic fee decays, which can happen in a single transaction or within a short time window. All borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting assumptions about collateral valuation and health checks are broken. The problem was discovered during a MixBytes audit that exercised the create_loan, exchange, and liquidation flows and observed that a small price increase could render health negative and enable a hard liquidation. The bug is subtle because the health ratio appears correct under normal conditions and the dynamic fee is hidden inside limitpo, making the discrepancy hard to notice without detailed testing. To remediate, the health() logic should incorporate the dynamic fee and use a more robust pricePerShare calculation that does not rely solely on balanceOf, and the protocol should prevent direct inflation of share price, for example by capping tick price movements relative to the oracle or by requiring a time‑weighted average price before allowing liquidation. This would close the inflation attack vector and align the accounting model with the intended economic guarantees of the lending platform.
summary:
In TwoWayLending, the share price can easily inﬂate through a direct transfer of funds to the Controller. This can be used to trigger hard liquidations:
1. A hacker buys the victim's collateral shares in the AMM using exchange().
2. The hacker inﬂates the collateral price per share (even a small increase of +1.1% may be sufﬁcient).
3. The victim's health becomes negative, and the hacker can liquidate it for proﬁt.
Multiple tests show that the attack have been forwarded to the client.
In order to understand why it works, we'll have to take two features of the protocol into consideration.
Feature 1: If the oracle price increases by N percent, then the price of the tick pcurrentdown() increases by ~3.3 times. That is, for example, if the price in the oracle increased by 10%, then the price grid in the AMM shifted not by 10%, but on average somewhere around 33%.
Feature 2: The AMM uses the limitpo() function which limits price surges and increases fees when the oracle price ﬂuctuates. For example, if the oracle price increases by 10% in a transaction (for example, from 1 to 1.1), then in the same transaction, limitpo() will return 1.1 (small ﬂuctuations are not thresholded), and the dynamic fee will be high. Over time, approximately after 120 seconds, the dynamic fee will drop to its minimum value.

title: C-1 Withdrawal of tokens from AMM
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized token withdrawal path in the controller contract that can invoke the AMM's withdraw function via a generic callback signature. The controller's liquidate_extended function accepts an arbitrary method identifier and calldata, and the audit discovered that passing the selector for withdraw(address,uint256) satisfies the internal callback checks. Because the controller does not restrict which AMM function can be called, an attacker can trigger liquidate_extended with the withdraw selector and an arbitrary amount, causing the AMM to transfer any amount of tokens to the attacker. This can be performed even when the attacker only initiates a partial liquidation, effectively allowing a full drain of the AMM's liquidity. The issue occurs whenever the controller's liquidate_extended is called with a crafted callback; it does not depend on any special state of the market. Users of the protocol are affected because their deposited tokens can be removed without consent, leading to loss of funds and a broken accounting model where the AMM's reserves no longer match the expected balances. The problem was identified during a manual code review of the controller's liquidation logic, where the lack of a whitelist for callback signatures was noted. Because the call appears to be a legitimate liquidation operation, the unexpected token movement may not raise immediate alarms, making the bug subtle. To remediate, the controller should enforce a strict whitelist of allowed callback signatures or require explicit approval for withdraw calls, ensuring that only intended functions can be executed during liquidation. This class of bug falls under unchecked external call delegation or improper access control on callback mechanisms, where an attacker can misuse a generic interface to execute privileged state‑changing functions.
summary:
Controller allows to call AMM via callback:
withdrawsig = get_method_id("withdraw(address,uint256)") # AMM
controller.liquidate_extended(user, 0, frac, True,
market_amm.address, withdrawsig, [])
AMM.vy#L728
```solidity
def withdraw(user: address, frac: uint256) -> uint256[2]:
```
This method is sufficient to fulfill all the necessary conditions for a callback (Controller.vy#L525).
Using liquidate_extended, a hacker has the ability to withdraw any amount from AMM. It is also
possible to make a complete liquidation through a partial one.
The test script was handed over to the customer.

title: C-2 Inflation attack on empty ticks
content: The vulnerability is an inflation attack that targets AMM ticks that are effectively empty, meaning they contain only a single wei‑sized share while holding an arbitrary amount of collateral. The root cause lies in the contract’s share‑minting formula, which performs integer division without safeguards against rounding to zero when the share supply is extremely low. Because the calculation multiplies the existing share amount by the deposited collateral and then divides by the current collateral, a tick that holds just one wei share will always mint only one wei share regardless of how much collateral is added, as the division truncates the fractional part. An attacker can exploit this by first ensuring a tick contains exactly one wei share and a modest amount of ETH (for example by using the AMM fee mechanism and then self‑liquidating 99 % of the position). The attacker then repeatedly calls a create_loan() followed by a repay() operation from a separate account; each iteration inflates the collateral by roughly 1.5 × while the share count remains unchanged due to the rounding error. By performing many such iterations the attacker can grow the collateral in the tick from a few wei to many ether while the share supply stays at one wei. When a legitimate user later submits a transaction that deposits a large amount of ETH into the same tick, the contract’s share‑minting logic again rounds down, granting the user only a single wei share instead of the proportional amount. The attacker then self‑liquidates their position, receiving half of the total collateral in the tick – a profit that can be several ether while their initial investment was much smaller. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome (receiving a proportional share of the pool and a corresponding increase in balance) is replaced by a symptom where the deposit appears to succeed but the user receives an almost zero share and sees no change in their effective ownership, while the pool’s total assets are drained. The attack occurs only when the tick is in the described low‑share state and when the attacker can front‑run victim transactions and execute many loan‑repay cycles, conditions that are realistic in a public mempool environment. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (MixBytes) that included functional testing of edge‑case tick states. It is hard to notice because the numbers involved are tiny (wei‑level shares) and the UI typically displays only aggregate balances, masking the fact that the share accounting is effectively broken. This flaw belongs to the class of rounding‑error and inflation bugs in liquidity‑pool accounting, where integer division leads to zero‑share minting and allows disproportionate extraction of collateral. To remediate, the protocol should prevent share issuance when the existing share supply is below a safe threshold, enforce a minimum share amount, or adopt virtual dead shares as suggested by OpenZeppelin, thereby ensuring that any deposit that adds collateral also creates a non‑trivial amount of shares and eliminating the rounding‑to‑zero condition.
summary:
Each AMM tick represents an empty vault, where shares are issued for collateral. A hacker can manipulate
a tick so that it contains just 1 wei share and any amount of collateral. For example, suppose the hacker
initially inflates the tick so that it contains 1 wei share and 1 ETH. Next, the hacker sees a victim's
transaction in the mempool, which is going to deposit 20 ETH into this tick. The hacker then needs to
inflate the tick to contain 1 wei share and 10 ETH + 1 wei right before the victim's transaction.
How many shares will the victim receive in this tick? The victim receives 1 wei share due to a rounding
error:
```solidity
1 wei share * 20 ETH / (10 ETH + 1 wei) = 1 wei share
```
Now there are 2 wei shares in total in this tick, one for the victim and one for the hacker.
The hacker then self-liquidates and receives 50% of the ether from the entire tick, which is 15 ETH, even
though they initially invested 10 ETH. The profit is +5 ETH.
How does the hacker inflate the collateral in the tick?
Step 1. Before the frontrunning, the hacker ensures that the tick contains 1 share and 100+ wei ETH. They
can do it using the AMM fee, performing exchange() back and forth. This is a heavy operation, plus there
may be fees if there are other positions before the hacker's ticks. Therefore, this must be done in advance.
After that the hacker self-liquidates 99% of their position, leaving one share. If there are no other positions
before the hacker, they only spend money on gas.
Step 2. Next, the hacker attacks themselves using an inflation attack. To do this, they perform
create_loan()+repay() 100 times from another account. Each pass inflates the collateral by 1.5
times.
How it works:
Suppose the tick currently contains 1 wei share and 106 wei collateral. The hacker deposits (106 * 2 - 1)
wei collateral into the tick. How many shares will be minted?
```solidity
1 wei share * (106 * 2 - 1) / 106 = 1 wei share
```
Only 1 wei share was minted due to a rounding error.
Now the tick has 2 wei shares and approximately 106 * 3 wei collateral.
What happens when the hacker performs a full repay? They get back approximately
```solidity
106 * 3 / 2 wei
```
The tick remains with approximately the same amount: 1 wei share and 106 * 3 / 2 wei collateral.
It can be seen that one pass of create_loan()+repay() does not change the number of shares but
increases the collateral by 1.5 times. 100 rounds can inflate the collateral from 106 wei to 42 ETH.
The test script was handed over to the customer.

title: Reentrancy in StEthHyperdrive.openShort
content: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw that appears in the short‑position opening flow of the StEthHyperdrive contract. When a user calls openShort, the contract internally invokes a private _deposit function that includes a refund step implemented as a low‑level .call to msg.sender. Because this external call is executed before the contract updates its internal accounting for short reserves (the reserves are only calculated but not yet written), a malicious caller can re‑enter the contract during the callback. By re‑entering, the attacker can invoke openShort again with the same reserve state, effectively splitting a single large short order into two smaller orders that each experience less price impact. After obtaining a more favorable execution price, the attacker immediately closes the combined short position, extracting a profit that comes directly from the pool’s liquidity. The issue manifests only when the short‑opening function is used and the caller is a contract capable of receiving the refund callback; honest users who open shorts see their expected position but may later notice that the pool balance has been drained, resulting in missing funds or reduced payouts. The root cause is the placement of an external call in the middle of a state‑changing operation, violating the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern and lacking any reentrancy guard. This ordering makes the bug subtle because the refund logic appears harmless and the contract otherwise updates reserves correctly, so static analysis may miss the re‑entrancy window. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the call flow and identified that the reserve updates were applied after the external call. Exploiting the bug requires the attacker to craft a contract that receives the refund, triggers a second openShort before the first call finishes, and then closes the position. The impact is critical: the attacker can siphon funds from the pool, undermining the protocol’s economic guarantees and potentially causing users to lose their deposited assets. To remediate, the refund should be moved to the end of the openShort execution after all reserve updates have been committed, or the contract should employ a reentrancy guard (e.g., a non‑reentrant modifier) on all public entry points. Applying the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern or consolidating the pause and reentrancy flags in a single storage slot can also mitigate the risk. In short, the bug is a reentrancy vulnerability caused by an external call placed between calculation and state mutation, allowing an attacker to manipulate pricing and drain pool funds.
summary:
The StethHyperdrive._deposit function contains refund logic which performs a .call to the msg.sender. When opening shorts, this _deposit with the callback happens in the middle of state updates which can be abused by an attacker. The _deposit happens after calculating the short reserves updates (_calculateOpenShort) but before applying these updates to the reserves. When the attacker receives the callback they can trade on the same curve with the same reserves a second time which allows them to get a better price execution (incurring less slippage) than a single large trade. In the proof of concept, the attacker opens half the short initially and half the short through reentrancy, and then immediately closes the total short amount for a profit, draining the pool funds.
