title: An attacker can force 0 shares to be minted for a liquidity provider
content: The vulnerability is a logic flaw that allows an attacker to cause a liquidity provider to receive zero LP shares when adding liquidity to a market that currently has no outstanding long positions. The root cause lies in two interacting pieces of code: first, the market’s internal update routine skips any share‑reserve adjustment when the current share reserve (denoted as z) is zero, deliberately avoiding a division‑by‑zero error; second, the MultiToken contract’s internal _mint function does not reject a mint request with an amount of zero, simply recording a zero balance increase and emitting a TransferSingle event. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a legitimate addLiquidity transaction, opening a maximal short position that drives the share reserve to zero before the victim’s call is processed. When the victim’s transaction executes, the _updateLiquidity step becomes a no‑op because shareReserves is zero, leaving the present value of the pool unchanged (endingPresentValue equals startingPresentValue). Consequently, the formula that computes the number of LP shares to mint evaluates to zero. The subsequent call to _mint therefore creates a zero‑amount LP token entry, which the contract permits. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the liquidity addition succeeded, but the LP balance remains unchanged or appears as a zero‑share token, leading to the expectation of a share that never materializes. The impact is that the provider’s deposited assets become locked in the pool without any corresponding ownership token, effectively losing the ability to withdraw the funds later. This condition occurs only when the market is in a state with no long positions and an attacker can manipulate the short side before the provider’s transaction. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between share‑reserve updates and token minting logic. It is subtle because the contract does not revert or throw an error on a zero‑mint, and the zero‑share reserve state may be rare in normal operation, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the mint function should reject zero‑amount mints, and the liquidity‑addition logic should enforce a non‑zero share reserve or include a minimum‑share check before calculating LP shares, thereby preventing the division‑by‑zero avoidance path from producing a zero‑share outcome. This class of bug falls under improper handling of edge‑case state (zero‑value invariants) combined with unchecked token minting, which can lead to silent loss of user funds and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that every deposited asset must be represented by a proportional ownership token.

title: Drain pool by sandwiching matured shorts
content: The vulnerability is a reserve‑manipulation attack that can be performed when short positions mature in a pool that uses a combined flat‑plus‑curve pricing model. In this design the amount of matured shorts is first converted 1‑to‑1 into a base amount and added to the share reserves, while the bond reserves are adjusted to keep the spot price unchanged. Because the same reserve variables are used for both the flat part (the direct conversion) and the curve part (the pricing function), the update of the reserves after maturity also influences the curve calculation. An attacker can exploit this coupling by sandwiching the reserve update: first they front‑run the checkpoint that applies the maturity by opening the maximum possible short position, which drives the share reserves close to zero. This extreme state amplifies the curvature of the pricing function and creates a large arbitrage window. When the checkpoint is then executed, the matured shorts increase the reserves, shifting the curve dramatically. The attacker immediately back‑runs by closing the short they opened, receiving a base amount far larger than the amount they supplied, often yielding returns of several hundred percent. The loss is borne by the liquidity providers, whose share reserves can be reduced by more than half, effectively draining a large portion of the pool’s value. The attack can be executed within a single transaction if the checkpoint has not yet been triggered, making it difficult to detect in real‑time. The root cause is the shared use of reserve variables for two distinct accounting models and the lack of safeguards that prevent the share reserve from approaching zero, combined with an overflow risk in the uint128 conversion used during the checkpoint update. This bug is hard to notice because the pool’s normal operation does involve reserve updates on maturity, and the extreme price movement only occurs under a very specific sequence of actions that may not be exercised in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the protocol should separate the accounting of flat‑model conversions from the curve‑model calculations, enforce invariants that keep share reserves above a safe minimum, limit the size of short positions relative to current reserves, and add explicit checks that prevent reserve manipulation before a checkpoint is applied. Conceptually, the fix is to ensure that maturity updates cannot be used to create arbitrage opportunities by isolating the two pricing mechanisms and protecting the curve from extreme reserve distortions. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after a seemingly normal short maturity, the pool’s share balance suddenly drops, liquidity providers see their token balances shrink dramatically, and the attacker walks away with a large amount of base tokens while other participants receive little or nothing. This constitutes a critical loss of funds and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: Unclaimed tokens locked in stats_token causing permanent fund loss
content: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch in the token‑sale contract. During the deposit phase the contract moves the full amount of tokens earmarked for the sale (sale_supply) from the authority’s wallet into an internal stats_token account. Later, when users invoke the claim function, the contract calculates each user’s payout using the ratio of tokens purchased to the total claimed_supply and then multiplies this ratio by the minimum of sale_supply and claimed_supply. Because claimed_supply is always less than or equal to sale_supply, the multiplier resolves to claimed_supply, meaning the payout formula effectively distributes only the portion of tokens that have already been marked as claimed. Any tokens that remain unclaimed – the difference between the original sale_supply and the final claimed_supply – stay locked inside the stats_token account because the claim logic never references the surplus and no withdrawal path is provided. This situation can occur whenever the sale does not fully exhaust the allocated token pool, for example if some participants never call claim or if the sale ends with unclaimed allocations. The protocol loses those surplus tokens permanently, reducing overall token supply and potentially affecting token economics. From a user’s perspective the contract behaves as expected for those who successfully claim – they receive the amount they purchased – but the protocol’s balance sheet shows a hidden pool of tokens that never reach any holder, contradicting the expectation that all deposited tokens will eventually be claimable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the token flow in deposit_token and claim_token functions and identified that the surplus is never transferred out. It is hard to notice because the visible user balances are correct and the stats_token account is not part of the public interface, so the locked tokens are not displayed in typical UI dashboards. To remediate, the contract should either (a) adjust the claim calculation to use the original sale_supply as the distribution base and then correctly account for any remainder, or (b) introduce an explicit function that allows the authority to withdraw the difference between sale_supply and claimed_supply after the claim period ends, ensuring that no tokens remain permanently stranded.
summary:
In the claim_token function, tokens are distributed to users based on the proportion of tokens they purchased relative to the total claimed_supply. If the claimed_supply is less than the sale_supply, users receive a proportional amount of claimed_supply rather than the full sale_supply.
This is reflected in the following code snippet:
let adjusted_tokens = (
(user_stats.tokens_purchased as f64 / token_stats.claimed_supply as f64)
* (token_stats.sale_supply.min(token_stats.claimed_supply) as f64))
as u64;
transfer(
CpiContext::new_with_signer(
ctx.accounts.token_program.to_account_info(),
Transfer {
from: ctx.accounts.stats_token.to_account_info(),
to: ctx.accounts.user_token.to_account_info(),
authority: ctx.accounts.stats.to_account_info(),
&[signer_seed],
adjusted_tokens,
Since the amount distributed from stats_token is less than the sale_supply originally transferred to the stats account in deposit_token, as shown below:
pub fn deposit_token_handler(ctx: Context<DepositToken>) -> Result<()> {
let token_stats = &mut ctx.accounts.token_stats;
transfer(
CpiContext::new(
ctx.accounts.token_program.to_account_info(),
Transfer {
from: ctx.accounts.authority_token.to_account_info(),
to: ctx.accounts.stats_token.to_account_info(),
authority: ctx.accounts.authority.to_account_info(),
token_stats.sale_supply,
This results in the difference between sale_supply and claimed_supply being locked indefinitely in the stats_token account, causing a permanent loss of funds for the protocol.

title: Tokens for deployment contribution can be stolen
content: During the Hyperdrive factory deployment, the DeployerCoordinator.initialize function accepts an address parameter _lp that is later used as the source address in a safeTransferFrom call inside _prepareInitialize. The contract assumes that the caller will pass its own address, but there is no check that _lp equals msg.sender. Consequently, any account that has previously approved the DeployerCoordinator to spend its tokens can be targeted: an attacker can invoke initialize with the victim’s address as _lp, causing ERC20.safeTransferFrom to move the victim’s contribution tokens into the newly created Hyperdrive instance. The attacker also controls the deployment parameters and can set the initial LP receiver to themselves, then immediately withdraw the LP shares, effectively stealing the victim’s contribution. This flaw occurs whenever a user grants an allowance to the DeployerCoordinator and does not revoke it before a malicious deployment is submitted. The vulnerability is an authorization bypass caused by unchecked external input, a classic case of improper access control over token transfers. From the user’s perspective the expected behavior is that their contribution is locked in a pool they control, but after the attack their token balance drops to zero and they receive no LP shares. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the initialization flow and noticed that the source address for the transfer is supplied by the caller rather than derived from msg.sender. Because the transfer is performed through a standard ERC20 safeTransferFrom, the loss of funds may not be immediately obvious in UI logs, making the bug hard to spot. The proper fix is to restrict the token transfer to msg.sender, remove the _lp parameter, or add an explicit require that _lp == msg.sender, ensuring that only the caller’s approved tokens can be moved.

title: C-1 Inﬂation attack on iToken
content: The vulnerability is an inflation‑type attack on the iToken contract that arises when the contract’s totalSupply is small or zero. Because the contract does not prevent external parties from sending the underlying asset directly to its address, an attacker can increase the contract’s underlying balance without a corresponding increase in iToken supply. This mismatch skews the internal exchange rate that is derived from the ratio of underlying balance to totalSupply. When users later call mint or redeemUnderlying, the contract performs integer division to compute the amount of iTokens to issue or the amount of underlying to return. The artificially inflated balance causes rounding errors that systematically favour the attacker and disadvantage honest users, resulting in a loss of a fraction of the underlying assets. The attack can be carried out at any time after deployment or after a large withdrawal when totalSupply is low, and it requires only a simple transfer of the underlying token to the iToken contract. Affected parties include all depositors and borrowers who interact with the iToken, because they may receive less underlying than expected when redeeming or may see their balances shrink unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, which identified that the accounting logic does not guard against unsolicited transfers and that the rounding logic can be manipulated. The problem is subtle because the contract’s balance appears higher, which may be interpreted as a healthy liquidity metric, while the exchange rate calculation silently incorporates the extra amount, leading to hidden loss. To remediate the flaw, the contract should either reject direct transfers of the underlying asset when totalSupply is below a safe threshold, enforce a minimum non‑zero totalSupply before allowing any minting or redemption, or adjust the accounting to explicitly account for any unexpected balance and use rounding methods that prevent systematic loss. In practice this means adding checks that prevent the contract from holding a non‑zero underlying balance without a proportional iToken supply, or redesigning the exchange‑rate computation to be robust against such inflation attacks. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a user who expects to receive the full amount of their deposited underlying after a redeem call may receive slightly less, or that their displayed iToken balance seems to disappear after a transaction, indicating a silent loss of funds due to the rounding discrepancy.
summary: Until iToken has sufﬁcient totalSupply, an attacker can manipulate the underlying/iToken exchange rate by directly transferring the underlying asset to the iToken smart contract. This leads to rounding issues in mint and redeemUnderlying causing a user to lose some amount of their underlying assets. Due to the possibility of permanent loss of user assets, such issues have a critical severity rating.

title: C-2 A detached reward distributor can be drained
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑distribution detachment flaw. When the contract owner calls the controller function that updates the address of the reward distributor, the previous distributor contract becomes detached from the controller. The controller stops recording any transfer or claim activity for that old distributor, but the old distributor still holds reward tokens that can be claimed through its public claim functions. Because the controller no longer enforces a single‑distributor invariant, an attacker can repeatedly fund the detached distributor (for example by calling a function that charges its balance) and then claim the accumulated rewards from arbitrary accounts, possibly using a flash‑loan to amplify the effect. This allows the attacker to drain the entire reward balance that was intended for the previous period. The issue manifests when the admin performs a migration of the reward logic without also migrating or disabling the old distributor, and it is hard to notice because the UI and the controller no longer reference the old contract, giving the impression that the rewards are no longer available. Users expecting a reward for a past period may see their claim return zero, while the attacker receives the tokens. The bug belongs to the class of “detached contract state leakage” or “inconsistent accounting after contract upgrade”. It violates the business assumption that only the currently registered distributor can hold claimable rewards. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit of the dForce Lending V2 protocol. To remediate, the protocol should either keep a single source of truth for reward distribution during migration (for example by migrating state instead of changing the address) or modify the controller to continue tracking balances for multiple distributors and to explicitly disable claims on any detached distributor.
summary: If admin decided to change the current reward distribution logic and set new one by using the Controller.sol#L548 function, the prev version is supposed to distribute rewards for the prev period. After detaching the reward distribution contract from the controller, transfers don't track by the controller any more and by abusing this issue an attacker can drain rewards from the old distributor by using cycles charge balance then claim from different accounts or a ﬂashloan attack.

title: C-1 Potential Old Data Processing
content: The vulnerability resides in the oracle data handling routine of a contract that receives price updates from an external oracle. The routine accepts a message and updates the stored price without verifying that the message is newer than the previously stored one. When a message execution runs out of gas, the transaction reverts but the message remains in the oracle's queue. A subsequent call to the handling function may then process that same reverted message because the contract does not compare timestamps. As a result the contract can overwrite a fresh price with an older, possibly outdated value. This stale price can be dramatically different from the current market rate, causing downstream calculations such as collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, or any protocol that relies on the price feed to be incorrect. Users may see their positions liquidated unexpectedly, balances appear reduced, or refunds fail because the system believes the collateral value has dropped. The issue manifests only when an out‑of‑gas revert occurs on a price update, which is a relatively rare but plausible condition in a high‑throughput environment. It affects any participant that depends on the oracle, including lenders, borrowers, and any integrated DeFi protocol that consumes the price. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that examined the control flow of the message‑handling function and noticed the absence of a freshness check. Because the contract silently accepts the data, the problem can be hard to notice; the price change may look legitimate on‑chain and the UI will simply display a new price without indicating that it is older than expected. The appropriate mitigation is to record the timestamp (or a monotonically increasing sequence number) of each incoming oracle message and reject any update whose timestamp is not greater than the currently stored one. Adding this simple freshness validation prevents old data from overwriting newer values and restores the integrity of price‑dependent logic. In broader terms the bug belongs to the class of stale‑data or replay vulnerabilities where a system fails to enforce that incoming state updates are newer than the current state, leading to incorrect accounting and potential financial loss.
summary:
An issue has been discovered within the handle function of the PushOracleReceiver contract. The
function is responsible for processing incoming oracle data messages. The issue arises due to the potential for
an old message to be processed if it was previously reverted due to an out of gas error. If this happens, the
oracle price will be updated, not with the most recent value, but with the old one, which could have potentially
significant negative consequences on liquidations and integrated protocols.
This issue is classified as Critical severity as it could induce misleading pricing information, which could lead
to inaccurate liquidation decisions or manipulation of integrated protocols.

title: C-2 Message Verification
content: The vulnerability is an access‑control bypass in the Interchain Security Module (ISM) where the verify function does not confirm that the caller of the Mailbox.process function is a trusted contract. Because the ISM trusts any caller, an attacker can invoke Mailbox.process with a crafted message from an arbitrary address, causing the Mailbox to accept and act on data that has not been authenticated. The root cause is the missing caller verification check and the presence of an allowAll flag that, when enabled, disables any source restriction, effectively opening a backdoor for any oracle or external entity to submit data. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary calls the ISM.verify function (or directly the Mailbox.process function if the ISM is used as a gate) from an untrusted address, passes a malicious payload, and the Mailbox processes it as if it were legitimate. This can lead to manipulation of cross‑chain messages, incorrect state updates, or execution of unintended logic in downstream protocols. The impact includes potential loss of funds, disruption of protocol operations, and violation of the trust model that assumes only authorized oracles can feed data. The condition under which it occurs is any situation where the ISM is used to gate messages for the Mailbox and the allowAll flag is set to true or the caller check is omitted; no special privileges are required. All participants that rely on the ISM for message integrity—users, validators, and integrated protocols—are affected because they may receive corrupted data or experience unexpected state changes. The issue was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, which identified the missing verification logic and the dangerous allowAll parameter as deviations from standard security patterns. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles and runs without errors, and the lack of a caller check does not produce obvious revert messages; only the downstream effects, such as unexpected balances or failed cross‑chain operations, reveal the problem. To remediate, the ISM.verify function should explicitly check that msg.sender equals the known Mailbox address (or another authorized contract) before accepting a message, and the allowAll flag should be removed or hard‑coded to false so that only whitelisted sources can submit data. In generic terms, this is an authorization bypass and whitelist‑override flaw that breaks the assumption that only trusted entities can influence protocol state, leading to data tampering and potential financial loss.
summary:
A critical security vulnerability has been identified within the verify function of the ISM (Interchain Security
Module) contract. The ISM doesn't verify the caller of the Mailbox process function, which could allow
untrusted addresses to pass an arbitrary message to the Mailbox, ultimately leading to potential manipulation
of the data that will be processed.
There is also a dangerous parameter allowAll, which may lead to anyone malicious submitting oracle data if
enabled.
This issue is classified as Critical because it could lead to manipulation of critical data processed by the
process function, which could result in unpredictable disruptions or severe losses in the integrated protocols.

title: C-1 Epoch Manipulation
content: The vulnerability is an epoch manipulation flaw in the deposit routine of a staking contract. The contract allows a caller to pass an epoch identifier when depositing tokens, but the implementation never records this identifier in the user’s staking wallet data structure. Because the epoch index is not persisted, the contract later determines the lock‑up period and unlock time from the epoch value supplied at deposit rather than from a trusted, immutable record. An attacker can therefore choose any epoch – for example, one that has a very short or already elapsed unlock time – and the contract will treat the deposit as if it belonged to that epoch. This enables the attacker to bypass the intended locking period, withdraw the staked assets immediately or far earlier than the protocol’s rules allow. The impact is a breach of the staking system’s fairness and economic guarantees: honest participants expect their funds to be locked for a defined duration, while the attacker can extract rewards or principal prematurely, potentially draining the pool or undermining confidence in the protocol. The flaw manifests whenever a user invokes the deposit function, because the missing assignment of epochIndex occurs unconditionally. All stakers, the protocol’s token economics, and any downstream reward distribution logic are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the state updates of the staking wallet and noticed that the epoch field was never written. It can be hard to notice because the function signature includes an epoch parameter, giving the impression that the value is used, yet no validation or storage occurs, so normal testing that only checks successful deposits may not reveal the premature unlock. To remediate, the contract should store the supplied epochIndex inside the StakingWallet struct at deposit time and later reference this stored value when calculating lock‑up duration and release timestamps. Additionally, the contract should enforce that the epoch cannot be altered after deposit and should validate that the chosen epoch is currently active or permissible. This correction restores the intended accounting model where each deposit is bound to a specific, immutable epoch, preventing users from gaming the system to obtain early withdrawals.
summary:
This issue has been identified in the deposit function of the Prestaking contract.
The epochIndex is not properly set or stored within the staking wallet structure. As a result, users can
manipulate the staking mechanism by selecting any epoch during deposit, allowing them to exploit epochs
with more favorable conditions, such as earlier unlock times. This can lead to users bypassing the intended
locking periods and gaining access to their staked tokens earlier than allowed, breaking the fairness of the
staking system.
The issue is classified as Critical severity because it allows users to bypass staking conditions, potentially
undermining the entire staking system.

title: Drained contract if holder fees were non zero and are zero now due to early return
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the reward‑distribution logic of a share‑based contract. The internal function that updates share rewards (_updateSharesReward) returns early whenever the calculated newRewards value is zero. While this early return correctly avoids updating the global rewardPerShareStored, it also skips the call to _updateHolderReward, which is responsible for synchronising each holder’s rewardPerSharePaid before any change to their share balance. The root cause is therefore a conditional shortcut that treats a zero‑reward situation as a no‑op for all state updates, ignoring the fact that a holder’s share balance may still be altered. When the contract owner reduces the holder fee percentage from a non‑zero value to zero, any holder who already has pending rewards can increase their share balance (for example by calling buyShares) while newRewards is zero. Because the early return prevents the holder’s rewardPerSharePaid from being refreshed, the contract still attributes the previously accrued fees to the holder. The holder can then call withdrawRewards and receive the full amount of the old fees, even though the protocol now advertises a zero fee. After claiming the inflated reward, the holder can sell the newly acquired shares, effectively draining the reward pool. This exploit occurs only when three conditions are met: (1) the holder fee was previously non‑zero, (2) the owner has set the fee to zero, and (3) the reward calculation for the current block yields zero newRewards. Any user who satisfies these conditions can trigger the bug, so both individual participants and the overall protocol are at risk. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, which traced the reward‑update flow and identified that the early return bypassed the holder‑specific update. The bug is subtle because the early return appears harmless when there are no new rewards, and typical tests may not cover the edge case where a share balance changes while newRewards is zero, allowing the stale accounting to go unnoticed. To remediate the problem, the contract should always invoke _updateHolderReward before any share balance modification, regardless of the newRewards value, and only skip the global rewardPerShareStored update when newRewards is zero. This ensures that each holder’s rewardPerSharePaid stays consistent with the current fee configuration and prevents the extraction of fees that should no longer exist. The flaw belongs to the class of “stale accounting state due to conditional early exit” bugs, where an optimization unintentionally leaves per‑user accounting out of sync with protocol parameters, leading to unexpected fund transfers and violation of the intended fee logic.
summary: _updateSharesReward() does an early return if the newRewards are 0. newRewards might be 0, but a user may still increase its shares balance, but due to the early return, its holderSharesReward[spaceId][holder].rewardPerSharePaid will not be updated. Thus, if a user had pending rewards to claim but the owner set holderFeePercent to 0, it could increase its balance by calling buyShares() without updating the pending rewards due to 0 newRewards, then claim rewards, getting much more in return and then selling the shares. Increase the amount bought in the poc to verify how the fees claimed via withdrawRewards() increase (when they should not as holder fees were set to 0).

title: C-1 Debug code in getPriceByExternal
content: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded return value left in the price‑retrieval routine of a betting protocol. The function that is supposed to query an external price oracle ends with an unconditional return of the constant 30_000e18 (and a zero second value). Because the function never forwards the oracle’s actual data, every settlement that relies on this price uses the same fixed figure. The root cause is debug or placeholder code that was not removed before deployment. An attacker can trigger the settlement logic with a known price, predict the outcome of the bet, and place opposing positions to guarantee a profit, since the protocol will calculate winnings based on the fabricated constant instead of the real market price. The impact is that users receive incorrect payouts: some may lose funds they should have won, while the attacker gains the difference. The bug manifests whenever the contract calls the price‑retrieval function, i.e., during every battle settlement, regardless of the external market conditions. All participants in the betting system are potentially affected, but the attacker benefits the most. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that inspected the oracle integration and noticed the final line returning a static value. Because the function signature appears legitimate and the constant value is large, the problem can be subtle and may not be obvious from high‑level testing that only checks that a price is returned. The bug violates the core accounting assumption that settlement amounts are derived from up‑to‑date oracle data, breaking the economic model of the protocol. To remediate, the constant return statement should be removed and the function must forward the actual price obtained from the external oracle, with appropriate checks for freshness and validity. After correction, settlements will reflect true market prices, restoring expected user behavior where a bettor receives a payout proportional to the real price rather than a fixed, erroneous amount.
summary:
The last instruction of the getPriceByExternal function will always return the same price (30_000e18).  
Oracle.sol#L43  
It leads to the incorrect settles of battles. An attacker can use this code issue for getting profit from bets.

title: C-2 Battle fishing attack
content: The vulnerability is an unprotected public function in the Arena contract that creates a new battle instance without performing any initialization or access‑control checks. Because the function can be called by any address, an attacker can invoke it directly and supply a malicious manager contract as the battle’s manager. The manager role is privileged: it is allowed to mint the protocol’s spear and shield tokens and to deposit those tokens into the battle’s liquidity pool. Once the attacker‑controlled manager has populated the pool with freshly minted tokens, regular users can trade those tokens for collateral, believing they are interacting with a legitimate battle. After the battle concludes, the attacker can call the battle’s withdrawal function to extract the collateral and the minted tokens, effectively draining assets from the pool. The flaw occurs whenever the public battle‑creation function is executed, which happens as part of the normal BattleInitializer workflow but is also reachable directly by external callers. All participants who trade in the battle – users, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the assets they expect to receive are either reduced or disappear entirely. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s call graph and identified that the battle‑creation entry point lacked any restriction on the caller or on the manager argument. It is easy to miss because the function appears to be a standard factory method and the code does not contain explicit require statements that would raise an alarm. To remediate, the contract should enforce strict access control on the battle‑creation function, ensuring that only authorized contracts (for example, the BattleInitializer) can invoke it, and that the manager address is validated against a whitelist or role‑based permission system. Additionally, the battle instance should be fully initialized within the factory call, preventing external actors from injecting arbitrary manager contracts. By applying proper access‑right modeling and initialization checks, the protocol can prevent the privilege escalation that currently enables token minting and unauthorized withdrawals, thereby protecting user funds and preserving the intended accounting logic of the arena system.
summary: The Arena smart contract contains a public Arena.sol#L67 function that creates a new battle without initializing. This function is used in the BattleInitializer's function BattleInitializer.sol#L14. It means that an attacker can create a new battle and binds it to a fake manager behind the scene. Using the manager privilege, the fake manager contract can mint spear and shield tokens and put them to the pool. A user will trade these tokens for collateral. At the end of the battle the attacker could withdraw assets using the Battle.sol#L271 function of the battle.

title: C-3 Multiple redemptions of position are possible
content: The vulnerability is a missing state transition in the redemption routine of a lending position. When a user calls the redeemObligation function the contract transfers the collateral token to the caller, but it never updates the internal status of the position to a terminal state such as ObligationRedeemed. Because the position remains marked as active, the same function can be invoked again with the same parameters, causing the contract to repeat the collateral transfer. The root cause is a logical oversight: the code that should mark the position as redeemed is absent or ineffective, leaving the position in a redeemable state indefinitely. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly invoking redeemObligation, each time receiving the same amount of collateral, effectively creating an unlimited drain of the token reserves. The impact is a potential loss of all collateral held by the protocol, which would affect all users who rely on the protocol for secure asset custody and could lead to a total collapse of the financial product. The condition under which the bug becomes exploitable is when no other protective mechanism blocks repeated calls; currently the issue is not exploitable because a separate flaw (referred to as issue M.5) prevents the function from being called more than once, but if that issue is fixed the redemption loop becomes active. The affected parties include any holder of positions that can be redeemed, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and downstream applications that assume a one‑time redemption. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit where the reviewers traced the state changes of a position and noticed that the status flag was never set after a successful redemption. The bug can be hard to notice because the function appears to work correctly on the first call, and typical unit tests may only cover a single redemption scenario, missing the repeated‑call case. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of state‑injection or double‑spend bugs where a contract fails to record that a critical operation has already occurred. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful redemption, but subsequent attempts would still credit the user with additional collateral, contradicting the expectation that a redemption empties the position. To remediate the issue the contract should update the position’s lifecycle flag to a redeemed state immediately after the collateral transfer and enforce a check that prevents further redemption calls on the same position. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that each position can be redeemed only once, thereby protecting the protocol’s funds and preserving trust in its financial guarantees.
summary: The redeemObligation function does not change the state of the position to ObligationRedeemed. This allows an attacker to call it multiple times, potentially gaining an unlimited amount of the collateral token. Currently, this issue is unexploitable because of issue M.5 (described below), however, it becomes relevant if issue M.5 is fixed.

title: C-4 Incorrect price calculation on more than two phases
content: The vulnerability resides in the price‑determination routine of the protocol, specifically the internal _getPrice function that computes the cost of a battle phase. The algorithm is intended to iterate through pricing phases, stop once the final phase is identified, and then apply a single adjustment factor (price *= decimalDiff) to align the price with the token’s decimal representation. Due to a typographical error, the loop does not break after the final phase is found, causing the adjustment statement to be executed repeatedly for each remaining iteration of the loop. As a result, the price variable is multiplied by decimalDiff multiple times, inflating the computed price far beyond the intended value. This is a classic loop‑exit bug that leads to an arithmetic over‑adjustment. The bug can be triggered whenever a battle involves more than two pricing phases; under those conditions the loop continues past the point where the correct price has already been calculated. An attacker or a regular user does not need to craft special input – simply initiating a battle that spans three or more phases will cause the contract to return an excessively high price. The inflated price is then used for battle resolution, meaning that participants may be charged far more than the protocol’s economic model expects, potentially draining funds or causing unfair loss of assets. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a battle cost that is dramatically larger than anticipated, or the transaction may revert due to insufficient funds, leading to a perception that “my funds disappear” or “the battle price is wrong”. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit by MixBytes, who noticed that the loop condition never forces an early exit after the final price is set, a subtle logical flaw that does not raise compiler warnings and can be missed in functional testing because the price still changes, just not correctly. Detecting the problem is difficult because the contract still produces a numeric result; only when the price is compared against expected values or when extreme over‑charging is observed does the bug become apparent. To remediate the issue the algorithm should be rewritten to ensure that once the final phase is identified the loop terminates, or the price adjustment should be performed exactly once outside the loop. In broader terms, the fix belongs to the class of “incorrect loop termination leading to arithmetic mis‑calculation”. Proper unit tests covering multi‑phase scenarios and static analysis rules that flag loops without explicit break statements after a condition are satisfied would help prevent recurrence. The vulnerability violates the protocol’s core accounting assumption that each battle’s price is a deterministic function of its phase count, breaking financial integrity and potentially eroding user trust.
summary:
In the _getPrice function, probably due to a mistype, the cycle is not exited after the determination of the final price. This may lead to several executions of the price *= decimalDiff code which renders the price significantly higher than it should be.  
As this issue may lead to an incorrect battle resolution, we assign the CRITICAL severity rating to it.

title: The auction can be bricked
content: The vulnerability is an auction bricking condition caused by the withdrawBid function allowing the current highest bidder to retrieve their funds without resetting the stored highestBid and highestBidder fields. In an English‑style auction the contract records the amount of the highest bid in a state variable and later the endAuction function transfers that amount to the owner. Because withdrawBid only clears the caller’s entry in the bids mapping and does not adjust the global highestBid, a bidder who is currently winning can call withdrawBid, receive the ether back, and leave auction.highestBid set to a value that is no longer backed by contract balance. When the owner later calls endAuction the contract attempts to send auction.highestBid to the owner; the call fails due to insufficient balance and the transaction reverts, leaving the auction active but impossible to finish. The issue can be exploited with a flash loan or any user who simply wishes to reclaim their ether, and it may also happen unintentionally if the leading bidder needs to withdraw for personal reasons and no higher bid arrives. The impact is that the auction cannot be concluded, the NFT remains locked, bidders cannot retrieve the item, and the owner cannot receive payment, effectively locking funds and breaking the business logic of a fair auction. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between bid withdrawal and auction finalisation; it is subtle because the withdraw function appears normal and does not emit any warning about affecting the highest bid. The problem belongs to the class of state‑invariant violations where a mutable accounting variable is not kept in sync with external transfers. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the auction still open, the highest bid amount displayed, but the contract balance is zero, leading to a situation where the auction ends but no one gets the NFT and the owner gets nothing. To remediate the issue the contract should either forbid withdrawal of the current highest bid, automatically reset highestBid and highestBidder when the highest bid is withdrawn, or lock the highest bid amount in escrow until the auction is successfully closed, ensuring that the invariant between highestBid and contract balance is always maintained.

title: The house fee cap mechanism is flawed
content: The vulnerability is a mismatched‑unit reward‑capping logic in the transferPlayerRewards function. The function calculates a player reward in MONT tokens (18‑decimal precision) and then compares it to _totalAmount, which represents USDT amount (6‑decimal precision). Because the two values are expressed in different token denominations, the direct comparison is meaningless; any reward that is numerically larger than the USDT amount is truncated to _totalAmount, which after the implicit decimal mismatch results in a severe under‑payment. The root cause is the absence of a scaling step that normalises both quantities to the same decimal base before the comparison. An attacker who can influence game outcomes does not gain additional profit from this bug, but honest players receive far less MONT than the protocol’s economic model promises, often seeing rewards that are near zero or completely missing. The impact is a breach of the expected reward distribution: users expect to receive a proportion of the house fee converted at the current MONT/USDT price, but in practice the cap forces the reward to be limited by a USDT value, causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective. This condition triggers whenever the calculated reward exceeds the USDT amount, which is common because MONT’s 18‑decimal representation makes the raw number much larger than the 6‑decimal USDT figure. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditor noticed that the comparison mixes two different tokens and that the UI displayed unexpectedly low or zero rewards. The issue is subtle because both variables are uint256, so the compiler does not warn, and the symptom only appears as an abnormal reward amount, which can be mistaken for a normal variance. To fix the problem the cap should either be removed or the _totalAmount value should be scaled to 18 decimals before the comparison, ensuring that both sides of the inequality are expressed in the same token unit. In broader terms this is a classic unit‑conversion or decimal‑precision bug that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions and breaks the guarantee that a player’s reward is at least the value dictated by the house fee conversion.

title: The entire kerosene supply can be drained by claiming rewards
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked reward‑calculation formula that multiplies the elapsed time, a global rewardsRate, the amount of liquidity a user stakes and the raw XP balance of a note. Because the XP values returned by dyadXP.balanceOfNote are extremely large – often exceeding the total token supply of 1 000 000 000 * 1e18 – the product can become astronomically high. The root cause is the absence of any scaling or normalization of the XP term before it participates in the multiplication, effectively treating XP as a raw integer rather than a fixed‑point value. An attacker can exploit this by staking a negligible amount of liquidity (as little as 1 wei) on a note that carries a huge XP balance, waiting any non‑zero time interval, and then calling the reward‑claim function. The contract will compute a reward that may be larger than the entire kerosene supply, allowing the attacker to drain almost all tokens from the protocol. The impact is a total loss of the token’s circulating supply, rendering the protocol economically unusable and leaving honest users with empty balances. This condition can be triggered whenever a note with large XP is staked, regardless of the amount of liquidity provided, and it can be repeated after each reward period. All participants – regular users, delegators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the token balance can be depleted without warning. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared realistic XP magnitudes with the reward formula and identified that the arithmetic would overflow the intended accounting model. It is hard to notice because the code appears to follow a simple linear reward model and the test suite may not include notes with extreme XP values, so the excessive reward amounts only become evident under edge‑case inputs. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic scaling errors or reward‑inflation vulnerabilities, where a large input is multiplied unchecked, breaking the accounting invariants of the system. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a sudden, massive increase in claimed rewards or, conversely, the protocol’s treasury would drop to zero, contradicting the expectation that a small stake yields a modest reward. To remediate the problem the XP term must be normalized, for example by dividing by 1e18 after multiplying rewardsRate and liquidity, or by applying fixed‑point arithmetic throughout the calculation, ensuring that the reward amount stays proportional to the actual economic parameters and cannot exceed the token supply.

title: Underlying tokens of UniV3 Liquidity Position are unchecked
content: The vulnerability resides in the staking function ofa Uniswap V3 liquidity staking contract that assumes the underlying assets of a deposited liquidity position are the specific stablecoins USDC and DYAD. The contract does not verify the token pair of the position before accepting it for staking. Because of this missing validation, a malicious actor can create a new Uniswap V3 pool using any two arbitrary ERC‑20 tokens, mint a large supply of those tokens, and then provide the resulting liquidity position to the staking contract. The contract treats the position as if it were composed of the expected USDC/DYAD pair and therefore allocates rewards based on the reported liquidity amount, which can be artificially inflated by the attacker’s custom token pool. This economic manipulation allows the attacker to earn an excessively large amount of staking rewards, draining the reward pool that legitimate users expect to share. The issue is discovered during a security audit when the reviewer noticed that the stake() method never checks the token addresses of the supplied position. It is hard to notice because the function signature and surrounding code appear normal, and the contract’s external behavior (accepting a position and emitting reward events) does not raise immediate red flags. The impact is that the protocol’s reward distribution model is broken, leading to loss of value for honest participants and potential reputational damage. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked token validation or whitelist bypass bugs, where assumptions about asset types are not enforced, resulting in accounting errors and reward calculation anomalies. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may be that some accounts receive unusually high reward amounts while others see their expected rewards shrink or disappear, contradicting the expectation that rewards are proportional to genuine USDC/DYAD liquidity. The fix is to add explicit verification inside stake() that the underlying token addresses of the supplied liquidity position match the allowed USDC and DYAD contracts, rejecting any position that does not meet this criterion, and optionally emitting a clear error message when the check fails.
summary: Within UniswapV3Staking.stake(), the underlying tokens of the staked UniV3 Liquidity Position are unchecked. This lets a malicious actor create a new UniV3 pool with their own arbitrary ERC20 tokens, where they mint themselves a large number of tokens. This causes the liquidity of their position in this pool to be extremely high, allowing them to earn an extremely large amount of rewards from staking this position.

title: Missing Asset Decimal Adjustment When Calculating TVL
content: The vulnerability originates from the way total value locked (TVL) is calculated in the VaultKerosene.sol contract. The implementation multiplies the raw token balance by the price reported by a Chainlink oracle and then divides only by the oracle’s decimal factor. It completely omits any adjustment for the token’s own decimal precision. Because different assets such as WBTC (8 decimals) and WETH (18 decimals) share the same oracle decimal setting, the same numeric price is applied to balances that are expressed in different scales. Consequently, the TVL for a low‑decimal asset is dramatically undervalued while the TVL for a high‑decimal asset is dramatically overvalued. For example, with both assets priced at 100 USD and the oracle returning 1e10, a balance of 1e8 WBTC yields a TVL of 1e10, whereas a balance of 1e18 WETH yields a TVL of 1e20, a difference of ten orders of magnitude. This mis‑scaling can be exploited by an attacker who deposits a low‑decimal asset, causing the protocol to believe the TVL is far smaller than it actually is, which may allow the attacker to mint an excessive amount of protocol tokens, withdraw more funds than entitled, or manipulate pricing mechanisms that rely on TVL. The impact is a breach of the accounting assumptions that TVL accurately reflects the value of all assets held, leading to incorrect token issuance, distorted user dashboards, and potential loss of funds for honest participants. The bug manifests whenever the TVL aggregation loop processes vaults that hold assets with differing decimal counts, which is a common scenario in multi‑asset protocols. Users may notice that the displayed total value seems unusually low for certain assets, that their expected share of rewards is missing, or that token prices appear inconsistent with market rates. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that compared the arithmetic of the TVL function against the known decimal specifications of the assets. It is hard to spot because the contract compiles and runs without reverting, and the TVL numbers may still be non‑zero, giving a false sense of correctness. The proper remediation is to incorporate the asset’s decimal factor into the calculation, typically by multiplying the intermediate result by a common scaling constant (e.g., 1e18) and then dividing by both the asset’s decimals and the oracle’s decimals. This ensures that all assets are normalized to the same base unit before aggregation, restoring accurate accounting and preventing the described exploitation scenario.

title: User can steal vault funds by sequencing deposit, rebase, and redeem
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in a vault that converts deposited ETH to internal shares using two separate price sources. When a user deposits, the contract first reads the current ETH/USD price from a Chainlink oracle to compute the USD value of the ETH, then it calculates the number of shares based on a stored totalDeposit figure that is only updated when the rebase() function is called. Because the stored totalDeposit is not synchronised with the latest oracle price, a depositor who acts before rebase() can obtain shares at a stale, lower price while the oracle already reflects a higher price. After the attacker’s deposit, calling rebase() inflates the stored totalDeposit by a percentage that corresponds to the price increase, effectively granting the attacker extra shares for free. When the attacker later redeems those shares, the withdrawal logic uses the current (higher) price to determine how much ETH to return, allowing the attacker to claim more ETH than the vault actually holds. This creates a solvency breach: the vault’s internal accounting shows more claimable ETH than the contract balance, leading to a situation where the vault can be drained completely, especially when the attacker leverages a large flash‑loan deposit to magnify the effect. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between deposit, rebase, and redeem functions and identified that the price used for share issuance and the price used for totalDeposit updates were out of sync. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to function correctly under normal price‑stable conditions; only when the oracle price moves between a deposit and a subsequent rebase does the discrepancy surface, making it hard to notice without targeted testing. To remediate, all functions that move value (deposit, withdraw, redeem) should reference the same stored ETH price, and rebase() should be invoked at the start of those functions to keep the price and totalDeposit aligned. Additionally, rebase() should early‑exit when the price has not changed instead of reverting, and a more robust design might involve queuing orders and processing them only after a confirmed price update from the oracle. The flaw belongs to the class of “price‑oracle desynchronisation” or “share‑minting misalignment” bugs, where inconsistent valuation sources enable an attacker to obtain more tokens or assets than they are entitled to, violating the protocol’s accounting invariants and leading to fund loss for honest users.
summary:
When a user deposits into the protocol, their msg.value is converted into a number of shares in two steps:
_eth2dyad() calculates the USD value of the ETH, based on the current oracle.
_deposit2Shares() calculates the number of shares they should receive for that USD value.

The issue lies in the fact that the USD-ETH conversion used for Step 1 is out of sync with Step 2. Specifically, Step 1 relies on the current Chainlink Oracle, while Step 2 relies on the saved totalDeposit value to account for moving prices, which requires rebase() being called.

The result is that, if a user deposits before rebase() is called, they capture the benefits of the higher exchange rate for their ETH. And when rebase() is called, they capture an additional appreciation of their shares.

This is a significant problem for two reasons.

Problem 1: The adjustment doesn't just give them more upside relative to other users. It actually breaks the vault accounting and can leave the protocol insolvent. This is because the withdrawal process is based on the current price of ETH, and the user in the above situation is entitled to more ETH than is actually in the vault.

For a simple example, you can walk through the math imagining they are the first depositor:
The initial price of ETH in the vault is 1000 USD/ETH
The price increases to 1100 USD/ETH, but rebase hasn't been called yet
Alice deposits 5 ETH, and receives 5500 shares as a result
At this point, totalDeposits also equals 5500
Rebase is called, and totalDeposits is increased by 10%, moving to 6050
Alice tries to withdraw her 5500 shares = 6050 DYAD = 5.5 ETH
The vault is insolvent, because there is only 5 ETH in it

Problem 2: More importantly, the appreciation from rebase() is a percentage, not a fixed value. The result is that, if the deposit() is very large (say, through a flash loan), a user is able to use the insolvency to withdraw the full holdings of the vault. See the Proof of Concept below for an example.

title: Wrong router is hardcoded and _transfer will be bricked
content: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded router address that points to a LeetSwapRouter contract while the surrounding code assumes the behaviour of a standard UniswapV2Router. The token contract implements the IUniswapV2Router02 interface and calls swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens and addLiquidityETH during a transfer. Because the address 0xfCD3842f85ed87ba2889b4D35893403796e67FF1 resolves to a router whose addLiquidityETH implementation works with wrapped Canto (wcanto) instead of the wrapped ETH (WETH) expected by UniswapV2Router, the call to addLiquidityETH attempts to deposit and transfer wcanto. When wcanto is not supplied, the internal calls to wcanto.deposit and wcanto.transfer fail, causing the addLiquidityETH call to revert. This revert propagates back to the token’s _transfer function, effectively bricking any transfer that relies on the router. The issue is triggered whenever a user initiates a token transfer that invokes the router functions, which includes normal token transfers, swaps, or liquidity provision. Affected parties are token holders, liquidity providers and any protocol component that depends on successful transfers. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the hard‑coded address against known router implementations and identified the mismatch in token handling. It is difficult to notice because the contract compiles against the standard IUniswapV2Router02 interface, so the compiler does not flag any type errors; the problem only manifests at runtime when the router’s internal logic diverges from the expected behaviour. The impact is that users may see their balances remain unchanged, receive zero ETH from a swap, or experience failed transactions, effectively freezing funds and breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a swap returns ETH. To remediate the issue the contract should either replace the hard‑coded address with the genuine UniswapV2Router address or refactor the code to correctly interact with the LeetSwapRouter, handling wcanto appropriately and ensuring that the expected token (WETH) is used throughout the liquidity‑addition flow.

The IUniswapV2Router02 interface is implemented and two of it's functions are called during a transfer -
swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens and addLiquidityETH. The problem

As you can see from the code snippet above the function works with wrapped Canto while the wrapped

title: Can steal all dNFTs and funds from contract by flash loaning deposits & liquidations
content: The contract implements a liquidation mechanism that triggers when the share of a deposited dNFT falls below a very small threshold (0.1% of total pool shares) and then requires the liquidator to deposit enough ETH so that the resulting share balance exceeds the same 0.1% threshold. This design creates a logical flaw: an attacker can artificially inflate the total pool size by depositing a massive amount of ETH, thereby reducing the relative share of any target dNFT to well below the threshold. After the pool is inflated, the attacker calls liquidate on the victim’s dNFT, which satisfies the first condition because the victim’s shares are now a tiny fraction of the enlarged pool. The attacker then adds a minimal amount of ETH to push the victim’s share just above the 0.1% limit, satisfying the second condition, and completes the liquidation. Because the internal accounting of balances is tied to the dNFT itself rather than to the original user, the liquidation transfers ownership of the dNFT to the attacker and allows the attacker to withdraw the large initial deposit, effectively draining the vault of all value associated with that dNFT. By iterating over all dNFTs sorted from lowest to highest balance, an attacker can repeat the process and exfiltrate every token and its underlying funds, provided sufficient capital is available – a requirement that can be met with flash‑loaned ETH. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit when the tester crafted a scenario that combined extreme deposits with the liquidation call and observed that ownership of a victim’s dNFT changed to the attacker and that the attacker could redeem the deposited ETH. The issue is subtle because the share‑based thresholds appear reasonable at a glance and the contract does not directly expose the pool size, making the manipulation non‑obvious during casual testing. The impact is severe: any user holding a dNFT with a small share can lose ownership of that token and all associated funds, and the protocol can lose the entire value locked in the vault. The bug belongs to the class of economic‑logic vulnerabilities where threshold‑based liquidation logic can be gamed by inflating the denominator of a ratio. To remediate, the liquidation logic must be redesigned to prevent manipulation of the total share denominator, for example by using absolute value checks, time‑locked or capped deposit amounts, or by requiring that the share ratio be evaluated against a snapshot that cannot be altered by a single large deposit. In short, the contract currently allows an attacker to deposit a huge amount, trigger liquidation of any dNFT, and withdraw the deposited funds, resulting in loss of ownership and disappearance of user balances.
summary:
When liquidate() is called for a given dNFT ID, there are two requirements:
The current shares of that ID must be less than 0.1% of the total shares in the pool
The shares after the liquidator's funds are deposited must by greater than 0.1% of the total shares in the pool

This can be exploited to steal any dNFT by depositing sufficient ETH to move the pool to greater than 1000x a given depositor, liquidating them and adding a small balance to push them over 0.1% of the pool, and withdrawing the initial deposit.

By sorting all dNFTs from lowest balance to highest, an attacker could perform this attack in such a way as to liquidate every dNFT, assuming sufficient funds (which would be easy to secure via Flash Loans).

Because internal balances are held by the dNFT rather than the user, this would also have the effect of moving the entire value of the vault to the attacker.

title: Using oracle provided price for deposits and redemptions allows user to steal funds
content: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on a single, instantly‑queried oracle price to compute the exchange rate for both deposits and redemptions. For a deposit the contract multiplies the amount of ETH by the oracle‑reported price of ETH and divides by 1e8, while for a redemption it multiplies the amount of DYAD by 1e8 and divides by the same oracle price. Because the oracle price can change between the moment a user submits a transaction and the moment the contract’s rebase function updates the internal accounting, an attacker who can anticipate the direction of the price movement – either by observing market price trends before the oracle updates or by watching pending oracle‑update transactions in the mempool – can front‑run the update. By depositing or withdrawing immediately before or after the price change, the attacker obtains a more favorable exchange rate, effectively receiving a larger share of the pool than their proportional contribution warrants. This share dilution can be repeated on each price update, gradually eroding the ownership of honest participants. The impact is a subtle but cumulative loss of value for all users who are not able to anticipate the price shift; from a user’s perspective the expected amount of DYAD on deposit or ETH on redemption may be slightly higher or lower than anticipated, and over time their percentage of the pool may shrink without an obvious on‑chain event. The condition for exploitation is the existence of a price‑sensitive oracle that is not protected by a delay, averaging mechanism, or withdrawal waiting period, combined with the attacker’s ability to observe or predict the price movement. The affected parties include every depositor, redeemer, and token holder of the pool, as well as the protocol’s overall fund integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the mathematical relationship between the oracle price and the share accounting and identified that the exchange rate is directly exposed to front‑running. It is difficult to notice because the per‑transaction profit is small and the share percentages change only marginally, making the loss appear as normal variance. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of oracle‑price‑timing or front‑running vulnerabilities where on‑chain logic uses a mutable external data point without safeguards. To remediate the problem the protocol must decouple deposit and redemption calculations from the instantaneous oracle price, for example by batching operations and applying a future exchange rate, using a time‑weighted average price, or enforcing a mandatory waiting period before withdrawals can be executed, thereby removing the attacker’s ability to profit from immediate price changes.

title: Verifying Beacon Chain Withdrawals Break After Deneb
content: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal verification routine of the EigenPod contract, specifically the BeaconChainProofs.verifyWithdrawal() function. The function assumes a fixed Merkle tree height of four levels when validating beacon chain withdrawal proofs. After the Ethereum Deneb upgrade, the ExecutionPayload structure gained two additional fields for blob data, expanding the tree from fifteen to seventeen fields and increasing its height to five levels. Because the verification logic still uses the pre‑Deneb constant, two distinct problems arise. First, any legitimate withdrawal proof generated after Deneb is incorrectly evaluated as invalid, preventing normal users from receiving the ETH they expect; from a user’s perspective a withdrawal transaction appears to succeed but the contract balance remains unchanged, leading to the symptom “my balance stays at zero after I request a withdrawal”. Second, the mismatch in tree height opens a second‑pre‑image attack: an attacker can craft a malicious intermediate node and present it as a leaf in the proof, causing the verification algorithm to accept a fabricated withdrawal that does not exist on the beacon chain. This enables the attacker to claim ETH that was never deposited, effectively stealing funds from the contract. The issue manifests only when withdrawals are processed after the Deneb fork; withdrawals that occurred before the upgrade continue to verify correctly because the older tree height matches the hard‑coded expectation. The bug was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime, which noted that the verification routine did not adapt to the protocol change. It can be difficult to notice because the contract still functions for pre‑Deneb withdrawals, and the failure mode appears as a simple “withdrawal not credited” problem rather than an obvious security flaw. To remediate, the verification code must be updated to detect the payload version or the presence of the new fields and compute the correct tree height dynamically, while preserving compatibility with older withdrawals. In conceptual terms, the fix requires replacing the constant tree‑height assumption with a version‑aware calculation and ensuring that proof validation correctly traverses the five‑level Merkle tree for post‑Deneb withdrawals, thereby eliminating both the denial‑of‑service effect for honest users and the second‑pre‑image attack surface.
summary:
The BeaconChainProofs.verifyWithdrawal() function does not support withdrawals that occur after the Ethereum Deneb upgrade, resulting in withdrawals being stuck or maliciously fabricated inside the EigenPod contract.
The Deneb upgrade adds two new fields to the ExecutionPayload container to account for blobs, increasing the number of fields from 15 to 17, which results in a tree height increase from 4 to 5. However, the BeaconChainProofs library assumes a constant tree height of 4, resulting in the following:
1. Valid withdrawal proofs that occur after Deneb are incorrectly verified to be invalid - normal users cannot withdraw their ETH from the EigenPod contract,
2. The BeaconChainProofs.verifyWithdrawal() function is now susceptible to a second pre-image attack where a malicious attacker can pose an intermediate node as a leaf to successfully verify withdrawals that don’t exist on the beacon chain.

title: C-1 Reentrancy Vulnerability in _claimWithdrawal Function
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the internal _claimWithdrawal function of the vault contract that handles user withdrawals. The function transfers ERC777 tokens to the caller before it updates the internal accounting that records the amount owed tothat caller. Because ERC777 tokens invoke a user‑defined tokensReceived hook during the transfer, a malicious contract can implement that hook to call back into _claimWithdrawal (or the public claimWithdrawal wrapper) before the original call finishes. Each re‑entered call sees the same un‑updated balance and can trigger another transfer, allowing the attacker to repeat the process until the vault’s token balance is exhausted. This flaw occurs only when the contract interacts with tokens that provide a callback, such as ERC777, and when the contract does not employ a reentrancy guard or the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. The impact is that an attacker can drain all assets from the vault, leaving legitimate users with empty balances, failed withdrawals, or zero token amounts returned by the UI. From a user’s perspective the expected behavior – I request a withdrawal and receive the exact amount I am owed – is violated; instead the user may see no tokens arrive, the displayed vault balance becomes zero, or subsequent withdrawal attempts revert because the funds are gone. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which identified the external call preceding state changes and recognized the special behavior of ERC777 token transfers. The bug can be hard to notice because most developers test with ERC20 tokens that do not execute callbacks, leading to a false sense of safety, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the balance is unexpectedly depleted. To remediate the problem the contract should either move the balance update before the external token transfer and/or apply a reentrancy guard such as the nonReentrant modifier, thereby ensuring that any recursive call is blocked. This class of vulnerability is commonly referred to as a reentrancy attack and is a fundamental violation of the contract’s accounting assumptions, where the invariant that the sum of user balances equals the contract’s token holdings no longer holds after exploitation.
summary:
A significant security issue has been located in the _claimWithdrawal function of the EnjoyoorsVaultWithdrawals contract.
The vulnerability is embedded within the potential for a reentrancy attack. This could occur with ERC777 tokens, due to their callback on transfer. In this scenario, a hacker could repetitively call the claimWithdrawal function until the contract is fully drained of its assets.
This issue deems Critical severity because a reentrancy attack can end up causing serious damage by draining funds from the contract. Particularly for a contract handling withdrawal functions, this vulnerability exposes the contract to a substantial risk of loss.

title: C-2 Stuck Rebase Rewards Due to Internal Balance Tracking
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the vault contract records each depositor's balance by storing a static amount in an internal mapping (userSupply[token][msg.sender] += amount). This approach assumes that the token balance remains constant after the deposit, which is true for standard ERC‑20 tokens but false for rebasing tokens such as stETH or aTokens that automatically increase the holder's balance when the underlying protocol distributes rewards or interest. Because the contract does not adjust the internal accounting when a rebasing token's total supply grows, any additional tokens that appear in the contract are not reflected in the recorded userSupply value. When a user later calls the withdrawal function, the contract limits the amount that can be transferred to the originally recorded deposit amount, effectively leaving the rebased portion permanently locked inside the vault. The issue can be triggered simply by depositing a rebasing token and then waiting for the token to rebase; no special malicious transaction is required. The impact is that users see their expected rewards disappear – they may notice that the balance displayed in the UI shows a higher token amount than the amount they are able to withdraw, or that after a rebase their withdrawal returns only the original deposit while the extra tokens remain inaccessible. This affects every user who deposits a rebasing token, the overall accounting of the protocol, and the trustworthiness of the vault because rewards that should be claimable become unrecoverable. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which identified that the internal balance tracking logic does not incorporate rebasing behavior. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the contract simply refuses to transfer the extra tokens, making the loss easy to overlook unless the auditor compares the contract's token balance with the internal accounting. To remediate the issue, the contract should adopt a share‑based accounting model where deposits are converted into proportional shares of the total pool, allowing withdrawals to be calculated from the current total balance and automatically including any rebased tokens. Alternatively, the contract could explicitly reject rebasing tokens or require users to wrap them into a non‑rebasing representation before deposit. In summary, the flaw belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting for rebasing assets” bugs, where static balance tracking collides with dynamic token supply, leading to locked funds, missing refunds, and a breach of the expected financial logic of the vault.
summary:
The issue is identified within the function _deposit of contract EnjoyoorsVaultDeposits.
The contract implements internal balance tracking through userSupply[token][msg.sender] += amount which does not account for rebasing tokens. Rebasing tokens (like stETH, aTokens) can increase their balance over time through protocol rewards or interest accrual. Since the contract tracks user balances internally and limits withdrawals to the tracked deposit amount, any additional tokens received from rebasing will become permanently locked in the contract.
The issue is classified as Critical severity because:
1. It leads to permanent loss of user rewards from rebasing tokens
2. There is no mechanism to recover these stuck tokens
3. The issue affects all users of rebasing tokens systematically
4. The locked rewards could potentially accumulate to significant amounts over time

title: C-1 Destruction of the EnsoWallet implementation contract
content: The vulnerability is that the implementation contract of a proxy‑based wallet can be destroyed by an attacker who calls the initialization function directly or becomes the authorized executor. The root cause is that the initialize function, which is intended to be called only once through the proxy during deployment, contains a call to SELFDESTRUCT that is not protected against external invocation. Because the contract does not restrict direct calls or verify the caller’s role before allowing the SELFDESTRUCT path, any external address can trigger the opcode or later be granted the EXECUTOR role, which also has permission to invoke SELFDESTRUCT. An attacker can therefore send a transaction directly to the implementation contract, causing the bytecode to be removed from the blockchain. Once the implementation is self‑destructed, the proxy’s fallback logic no longer has a valid target, so all wallet operations – deposits, withdrawals, token transfers – revert or become no‑ops. Users see their wallet UI showing no balance changes, withdrawals failing with “execution reverted”, or the entire interface becoming unresponsive. The impact is a complete loss of access to the wallet’s functionality; funds remain locked in the proxy’s storage but cannot be moved because the implementation logic that mediates calls is gone. In the worst case, if the attack occurs after the beacon contract has renounced its administration rights, there is no privileged entity that can redeploy or upgrade the implementation, leaving the funds permanently frozen.
