The condition for exploitation is the ability to send a transaction to the implementation address without going through the proxy, which is possible because the contract’s source does not include a modifier that blocks external calls to initialize. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s upgrade and initialization flow, where the auditor noticed that the initialize function contains a SELFDESTRUCT branch and that the EXECUTOR role can be set by any caller. The bug is subtle because SELFDESTRUCT is rarely used in upgradeable contracts, and the presence of the opcode does not affect normal proxy interactions, so testing through the proxy may not reveal the problem. To remediate, the initialize function should be protected with an onlyProxy or onlyConstructor guard, and the EXECUTOR role assignment should be restricted to a trusted admin. Additionally, the SELFDESTRUCT call should be removed or guarded behind a multi‑signature governance process, ensuring that the implementation contract cannot be destroyed by an arbitrary external address. This class of vulnerability falls under “unprotected self‑destruct in upgradeable contracts” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the implementation code remains immutable after deployment, breaking the guarantee that user funds can always be managed through the proxy.
summary:
An attacker can make a direct call (not via proxy) to EnsoWallet.sol#L24 and execute the SELFDESTRUCT
opcode or specify themself as EXECUTOR and gain the ability to execute SELFDESTRUCT later.
Consequently, the current implementation contract will be destroyed, and all users' wallet functionality will
be inaccessible until the core upgrade. The worst case occurs if an attack happens after
EnsoBeacon.renounceAdministration(), and all users' funds will be frozen.

title: C-2 Front-run attack on the deployment of EnsoWalletFactory
content: The vulnerability is a front‑run race condition that occurs during the two‑step deployment of the EnsoWalletFactory upgradeable proxy. The factory contract is first deployed as an implementation, and in a separate transaction the proxy is initialized and the owner is set at line 26 of the source file. Because these actions are not atomic, an attacker who can observe the pending deployment can submit a transaction that executes between the implementation deployment and the initialization, thereby claiming ownership of the proxy. Once the attacker becomes the owner, they can invoke the upgrade function to replace the legitimate factory implementation with a malicious version that contains backdoor logic, such as functions that allow the attacker to seize control of any wallet created by the factory. This exploitation path leads to the loss of user funds, unauthorized transfers, and a complete breach of the protocol’s trust model. The issue manifests only when the deployment process is split into multiple transactions, which is common in upgradeable proxy patterns that separate constructor logic from initializer calls. Users are affected because any wallet instantiated by the compromised factory may behave incorrectly, for example a user may expect a newly created wallet to hold their deposited assets but instead finds the balance empty or transferred to an unknown address. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the deployment flow and identified that ownership could be transferred to an arbitrary address before the intended initializer runs. Detecting the flaw is difficult because the contract appears functional after deployment; the malicious upgrade can be performed later without obvious on‑chain signals, and the backdoor may only be triggered when a user interacts with their wallet. To remediate the issue, the deployment and initialization steps should be combined into a single atomic transaction, or the proxy should enforce that only a pre‑defined admin (e.g., a multisig) can perform upgrades, and the ownership transfer logic should be protected against external calls during the construction phase. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “initialization race” or “ownership takeover during upgradeable proxy deployment” vulnerabilities, where improper sequencing of contract setup allows an attacker to hijack control and subvert the intended business logic of wallet creation and fund management.
summary:
An attacker can place their transactions between the deployment of the EnsoWalletFactory implementation
and EnsoWalletFactory.sol#L26 to specify themself as the contract owner and make an upgrade of the
EnsoWalletFactory to the modified one. The modified factory contract may implement backdoor
functionality to gain control of the deployed user wallets.

title: Malicious but registered Device Wallet can steal an eSIM Wallet
content: The vulnerability is an improper access‑control flaw in the Registry contract that allows any registered device wallet to reassign the ownership mapping of an eSIM wallet. The function updateDeviceWalletAssociatedWithESIMWallet is protected only by a modifier that checks the caller is a valid device wallet, but it does not verify that the caller is the current owner of the eSIM wallet or that the eSIM wallet is unlinked. Because the mapping is overwritten unconditionally, a malicious device wallet can call the function with the address of a victim’s eSIM wallet and cause the internal association to point to the attacker’s device. This can be exploited by first registering a device wallet, then invoking updateDeviceWalletAssociatedWithESIMWallet with the victim’s eSIM address; the contract updates isESIMWalletValid[_eSIMWalletAddress] to the attacker’s device address, emits an event, and effectively transfers control of the eSIM wallet. The impact is that the legitimate owner loses the ability to manage the eSIM wallet, may lose any funds or services tied to it, and the attacker gains full control. The condition under which it occurs is any call to the function by a device wallet that passes the isDeviceWalletValid check; there is no additional ownership check. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the function’s modifiers and the state changes. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to have a sensible guard (onlyDeviceWallet) and the mapping update looks innocuous, yet the missing owner verification creates a privilege‑escalation path. The bug belongs to the class of “missing authorization” or “improper access control” vulnerabilities, where a state variable is overwritten without confirming the caller’s right to do so. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that an eSIM wallet that was previously linked to their device suddenly appears to be linked to an unknown device, resulting in loss of control, possible zero balance, or inability to perform expected actions such as refunds or top‑ups. The expected behavior is that only the current device owner can change the association, but the reality is that any registered device can hijack the link. The recommended fix is to add an ownership check that requires the caller to be the current owner of the eSIM wallet or to allow the update only when the eSIM wallet is not already linked, for example by requiring isESIMWalletValid[_eSIMWalletAddress] == msg.sender before overwriting the mapping.

title: Frontrunning Attack Leading to Permanent ETH Loss in createAccount
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the DeviceWalletFactory.createAccount function that can cause a user’s prefunded ETH to become permanently locked in the factory contract. The function first checks whether a wallet already exists for a given device identifier and public key, and if it does, it returns the existing wallet address without performing any further logic. Only after this uniqueness check does the function attempt to deposit ETH that the caller sent together with the transaction. Because the existence check is performed before the deposit, an attacker who observes a victim’s transaction in the mempool can submit an identical createAccount call with a higher gas price, causing their transaction to be mined first. The attacker’s transaction creates the wallet (or registers the identifier) but does not send any ETH. When the victim’s transaction is processed second, the uniqueness check now finds the wallet already deployed, returns the attacker’s wallet address, and skips the deposit step. The ETH that the victim attached to the transaction remains in the factory contract because the code never forwards it to the newly created wallet and does not refund it. This results in a loss of funds for the victim while the attacker only pays the gas cost of their front‑run transaction. The issue occurs whenever a user tries to create a new DeviceWallet and simultaneously prefunds it, and the protocol relies on the assumption that the wallet creation and funding happen atomically. Users are affected because they receive a wallet address as expected, but the balance of that wallet stays at zero and the prefunded ETH disappears from their perspective, violating the business logic that a newly created wallet should contain the deposited amount. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s control flow, where the early return path was identified as bypassing the deposit logic. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it appears successful and the returned address matches the expected wallet, yet the funds are missing, which may only be observed later when checking the wallet balance. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or race‑condition vulnerabilities where state‑dependent early returns allow an attacker to manipulate the order of operations. To remediate, the contract should either revert the transaction when msg.value is sent and the wallet already exists, or explicitly refund the ETH before returning the existing address. Moving the uniqueness checks after the deposit, or adding a require that msg.value be zero when a wallet already exists, would also close the race window and prevent permanent loss of funds.

title: C-1 Missing validation of vesting wallets in
content: The vulnerability resides in the EscrowManager.createLock function, which aggregates token balances from a list of vesting wallet contracts without performing any validation on the wallet addresses themselves. The function only checks that each wallet’s beneficiary matches the caller, but it never verifies that the wallet address is whitelisted, unique, or even a legitimate vesting contract. As a result, an attacker can supply the same malicious vesting wallet multiple times in the vestingWallets array. The malicious wallet is crafted so that its transfer() function is a no‑op, meaning that when the loop calls m_vestingWallet.transfer(address(this)) no tokens are actually moved out of the wallet. Nevertheless, the loop adds the wallet’s token balance to the total lock amount on every iteration, effectively multiplying the reported balance by the number of times the wallet appears in the array. This artificial inflation of the lock amount translates directly into increased voting power within the DAO, because voting weight is derived from the locked token amount. The issue manifests whenever a user calls createLock with a duplicated or poisoned vesting wallet; it does not require any special conditions beyond the ability to deploy a custom vesting contract. All participants in the DAO, including token holders and governance processes, are affected because the inflated voting power can be used to sway proposals, potentially leading to governance takeover or misallocation of funds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the logic of createLock and noticed the absence of address validation. It can be hard to detect because the token balances reported by each wallet appear correct, and the transfer call does not revert, giving the impression that the operation succeeded. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms may include a situation where a user’s voting power seems disproportionately high compared to the visible token balance, or where a lock transaction reports a larger locked amount while the actual token balances remain unchanged. The root cause is a missing whitelist or uniqueness check for vesting wallet addresses, which is a classic example of an unchecked input leading to double‑counting or replay‑type attacks. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce validation of each vesting wallet address—such as by maintaining a whitelist of approved wallets, ensuring each address appears only once in the array, or using a factory pattern that only creates vetted wallets—thereby preventing the same contract from being counted multiple times and guaranteeing that the lock amount accurately reflects the true token holdings.

title: C-2 Incorrect checkpoint handling nullifies voting weights
content: The vulnerability resides in the checkpoint management logic of the EscrowManager contract, specifically in the internal _findCheckpoint function. When a new checkpoint is created in the same block as an existing one, the function treats the current timestamp as distinct and increments the per‑account checkpoint counter even though the timestamp has not changed. This results in the same token identifier being pushed again into the tokenIds array and the counter being increased, which creates a new checkpoint entry whose tokenIds array is empty. Because the _moveVotes routine later reads the checkpoint assuming a unique timestamp, it retrieves the current token list instead of the historical one, causing the old token list (m_oldTokenIds) to match the new checkpoint’s tokenIds. Consequently, the incremented checkpoint index points to a non‑existent array element, corrupting the vote‑tracking data structure. An attacker can exploit this by performing multiple lock or transfer operations that generate checkpoints within a single block – for example, sending a minimal amount of EYWA tokens to a target address several times in the same block. Each operation creates a duplicate timestamp checkpoint, ultimately overwriting the target’s voting power with an empty token set and reducing the reported votes to zero. From a user’s perspective the expected behavior is that locked tokens confer a proportional voting weight, yet after the attack the UI shows a vote count of zero despite the tokens still being locked. The issue is triggered only when the contract processes several state‑changing calls in the same block timestamp, a condition that is not obvious during normal operation and therefore easy to miss in testing. The bug belongs to the class of “checkpoint collision” or “duplicate‑timestamp state corruption” errors, where accounting assumptions about monotonic timestamps are violated. It was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, which reproduced the effect with a simple proof‑of‑concept that called createLock twice in the same block and observed the vote count drop to zero. To remediate the problem the contract should avoid incrementing the checkpoint counter when the new checkpoint’s timestamp equals the previous one, should not push a token identifier that already exists in the current checkpoint, and should adjust vote‑moving logic to correctly handle equal‑timestamp scenarios, thereby preserving the integrity of voting weights across all updates.
summary:
• https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowManager.sol#L869
A vulnerability has been identified in the _findCheckpoint method of the EscrowManager contract, where it incorrectly handles checkpoints that occur within the same block.timestamp. When the current timestamp equals the timestamp of the checkpoint [currentCheckpointNumber - 1], the same token is added to the tokenIds array, and s_checkpointsNumberByAccount is incremented by one. As a result, this creates a checkpoint with an empty tokenIds array.
When multiple checkpoints share the same timestamp, the method erroneously retrieves the current value instead of the correct historical value. This issue arises because s_checkpoints[account][m_checkpointsNumber - 1].timestamp == block.timestamp leads to improper retrieval logic.
The _moveVotes function (see EscrowManager.sol#L723) does not account for this condition, causing an error where m_oldTokenIds == s_checkpoint.tokenIds. This inconsistency leads to ++s_checkpointsNumberByAccount[to] pointing to a non-existent array element, effectively corrupting the vote tracking mechanism.
An attacker can exploit this vulnerability to nullify any user's votes by performing actions that create multiple checkpoints at the same block.timestamp. For instance, by transferring a minimal amount (e.g., 1 wei of EYWA tokens) to the target user's account multiple times within the same block, the attacker can reset the user's voting power to zero.

title: C-3 Duplicate voting via EscrowManager NFT transfers
content: The vulnerability is a duplicate‑voting flaw in the governance system that relies on an ERC‑721‑style voting NFT and the getPastVotes(account, timepoint) function to read the voting power of an address at a historic snapshot. The root cause is that the contract does not bind a specific tokenId to a proposal nor does it prevent the same voting power from being used by multiple accounts after the snapshot has been taken. Because getPastVotes returns the amount of voting power that an address owned at the snapshot timestamp, the value remains unchanged even if the underlying NFT is transferred afterwards. An attacker can therefore vote on a proposal, transfer the NFT to a second address, and let that address also cast a vote using the same historic voting power. By repeating the transfer to many addresses, the attacker can artificially inflate the total votes counted for a proposal, potentially causing a proposal to pass without holding the legitimate quorum. This issue manifests whenever a proposal’s voting period uses a snapshot that predates any token transfer and the system does not track whether a tokenId has already been used for that proposal. All token holders, the governance process, and any downstream actions that depend on proposal outcomes (such as fund allocation) are affected because the integrity of the vote tally is compromised. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when the auditors observed that after an NFT transfer the getPastVotes query returned the same non‑zero value for both the original owner and the new owner, demonstrating that the same voting power could be counted twice. The problem is subtle because the function behaves correctly for historical queries, the UI typically shows the correct individual voting power, and there is no explicit error; the double counting only becomes visible in the aggregated vote result, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that each voting NFT can be used at most once per proposal – for example by recording that a tokenId has voted and rejecting further votes from that token, or by locking the token for the duration of the voting period, or by computing voting power based on current ownership at the snapshot rather than per‑address historical balances. This class of bug is analogous to a double‑spend or replay attack on governance rights, where the same economic weight is spent multiple times. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a user can vote, then transfer the NFT and still see their voting power unchanged, while another user can also vote with the same power, leading to a proposal passing unexpectedly and the community’s expectations of one‑vote‑per‑token being violated.

title: C-4 Reentrancy in EscrowManager
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the EscrowManager contract that arises when the contract performs ERC721 operations that trigger external callbacks, such as safeTransferFrom and _safeMint, before its internal state has been fully updated. Because EscrowManager does not employ a reentrancy guard or the check‑effect‑interaction pattern, an attacker can supply a malicious contract as the ERC721 receiver. During the callback, the attacker can re‑enter EscrowManager functions like deboost, createLock or withdraw, causing the contract to execute state‑changing logic while the original call is still in progress. This re‑entrance can corrupt storage variables – for example, it can repeatedly transfer a boosting NFT back to the manager, reducing the recorded boost coverage to zero while other NFTs remain, which leads to an incorrect calculation of the lock amount and an artificial inflation of voting power. Similarly, invoking withdraw from within the _safeMint callback can alter the totalLocked amount before the lock creation finishes, distorting token emission calculations in downstream contracts. The impact is that users may see their voting power unexpectedly surge, boosting NFTs appear to disappear, or token emissions become unfairly high, effectively allowing an attacker to gain disproportionate influence or cause economic imbalances. The issue manifests whenever a function that mints or transfers an ERC721 token is called and the receiving address is a contract that can execute code, i.e., under any scenario where the safeTransferFrom or safeMint callbacks are triggered. All participants that rely on correct voting weight, boost accounting, or token emission – including token holders, delegators, and the protocol itself – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a security audit performed by MixBytes, which identified the missing reentrancy protection as a logical oversight rather than a simple coding mistake. Because the reentrancy occurs through standard ERC721 callbacks, it can be difficult to notice in normal testing; the contract appears to function correctly until a malicious receiver is used, at which point the state inconsistency becomes evident only through abnormal vote tallies or unexpected zero balances. To remediate the issue, the contract should be refactored to follow the check‑effect‑interaction pattern, applying state changes before external calls, and should incorporate a reentrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard) on all functions that involve ERC721 transfers or minting. Additionally, developers should avoid designs that rely on callbacks that can be controlled by untrusted contracts, or use safe internal minting mechanisms that do not invoke external code. By enforcing these safeguards, the protocol can prevent the reentrancy vector that currently enables boost manipulation and storage corruption.
summary:
OpenZeppelin ERC721 NFT implementations invoke the receiver whenever the safeTransferFrom() or safeMint() methods are called.
A hacker can exploit this mechanism by triggering a callback from EscrowManager during the execution of methods such as createLock() (when _safeMint() is invoked), deboost() (when safeTransferFrom() is invoked), and withdraw() (also when safeTransferFrom() is invoked), especially when the state of EscrowManager is inconsistent. This can corrupt storage variables or result in voting power gain.

title: C-1 An incorrect version calculation will lead to a token loss for a user
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of a token version inside the TokenVersionUtil library, specifically in the getTokenInfo function. The logic that determines the version number, which should be constrained to the range 10000 to 990000, produces values outside this range. Because the version is used to map a token to its collection, an out‑of‑range version causes the contract to reference a different collection than the one the user actually owns. As a result, a user who initiates a mint, transfer or any operation that queries token information may lose the token that belongs to the current collection and receive a token identifier that points to a collection that does not yet exist or is unrelated. This mismatch is not caught by the contract, so the user’s balance appears to drop to zero or the token disappears from their wallet, while the contract records a token from an invalid collection. The issue occurs whenever getTokenInfo is called with inputs that trigger the faulty arithmetic or boundary check, which can happen for certain token IDs or under specific state conditions. It was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who identified the mis‑calculation by reviewing the library code and reasoning about the expected version bounds. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; instead it silently returns an incorrect version, making the loss appear as a normal state change. The class of bug is an arithmetic or indexing error that violates the accounting assumption that each token version uniquely maps to an existing collection. To remediate, the version calculation should be rewritten to enforce the proper range, include explicit bounds checking, and ensure that the derived collection identifier is validated against existing collections before being returned. Proper testing of edge cases and integration of safe‑math libraries can prevent similar version‑mapping errors in the future.
summary:
A token version is calculated incorrectly (the version is in range [10000:990000]) which means that a user
will lose a token from the current collection and receive a token from another collection (which probably
hasn't existed yet).
TokenVersionUtil.sol#L23-L24

title: C-2 There are no checks that an athlete sent funds to the FantiumClaimingV1 contract
content: The contract implements a claim function that is supposed to distribute tokens to athletes after they have transferred a required amount of funds to the FantiumClaimingV1 contract. The vulnerability consists of the absence of any verification that the athlete actually sent the required tokens before the claim is processed. Because the state variable tracking the incoming payment (amountPaidIn) is never checked, the claim routine proceeds even when the payment flag is zero. An attacker can therefore invoke the claim for a distribution event that has not been funded, causing the contract to treat the request as valid and release tokens that belong to other distribution events or to the protocol’s pool. This flaw can be triggered at any time a user calls the claim function, especially when an athlete fails to send funds on schedule; the contract does not reject the claim, so malicious users can harvest unallocated tokens. The impact is the unauthorized transfer of assets, leading to loss of funds for legitimate athletes and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the claim logic, where the auditor noted that the require statement checking distributionEvents[_distributionEventId].amountPaidIn was missing. The bug is subtle because the function may still appear to work correctly when payments are made on time, masking the problem until a missing payment scenario occurs. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that the payment amount for the specific distribution event is non‑zero (or meets the expected threshold) before allowing any claim, effectively restoring the intended payment‑before‑claim invariant. This class of bug falls under unchecked state conditions or missing authorization checks, which violate the business rule that only funded athletes may receive payouts. From a user’s perspective, an athlete who expects to receive a refund after sending funds may see the contract allowing claims from unrelated parties, or a user may notice that tokens disappear from the pool without a legitimate claim, contradicting the expectation that only funded athletes can withdraw.
summary:
There are no checks that an athlete has sent tokens to the contract (amountPaidIn is not checked). So,
users from the collections that are not able to claim funds will be able to claim them from other
distributions. It can be extremely dangerous if some of the athletes do not send funds to the contract on
time.
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L405

title: C-3 An unlimited claim
content: An unlimited claim vulnerability exists in the claim function of the FantiumClaimingV1 contract. The function is supposed to record that a user has already claimed a reward by updating a mapping that tracks claimed status. However, the code uses the equality operator (==) instead of the assignment operator (=) when attempting to update the mapping. As a result, the mapping is never changed, so the contract believes the user has not claimed yet on every call. Any address that holds a qualifying NFT can invoke the claim function repeatedly, each time passing the superficial check and receiving the full payout. This allows an attacker to drain all funds that the contract holds for rewards. The bug manifests when a holder calls the claim function; the contract transfers the reward, but the internal record remains unchanged, leading to an infinite loop of claims. Users expect to receive a single reward and see their balance reduced accordingly, but instead the contract continues to dispense funds, eventually leaving the contract balance at zero. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which identified the incorrect operator in the mapping update. The problem is hard to notice because the surrounding code appears to perform a guard check, and typical unit tests may only verify a single claim, not repeated calls. The vulnerability belongs to the class of logic errors where state is not correctly mutated, often referred to as missing state update or incorrect operator. To remediate, the equality operator must be replaced with an assignment so that the mapping is updated after a successful claim, and additional safeguards such as re‑entrancy protection and proper access controls should be considered. Until fixed, the contract can lose all reward funds, harming NFT holders and the overall protocol integrity.
summary:
An unnecessary check was implemented instead of updating the mapping here:
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L456-L458
This allows an unlimited claim for a user, so anybody with an NFT could drain the contract.

title: C-4 A possible transfer of funds of another athlete
content: The contract allows a manager to close a distribution for an athlete. When closing, the code transfers the amount that the athlete has previously paid into the contract to the athlete's address. However, the function does not verify that the amountPaidIn field for the specific distribution event is non‑zero before performing the transfer. As a result, a manager can invoke the close operation for an athlete who has not yet transferred any funds, and the contract will still execute a transfer using the amountPaidIn value from a different distribution event that happens to be stored in the same mapping slot. This permits the manager to unintentionally or maliciously move the funds belonging to another athlete into the account of the athlete requesting closure. The bug originates from missing validation of the payment state, a classic unchecked‑state‑transition error. An attacker who controls the manager role can trigger the function with a crafted distributionEventId that points to a record where amountPaidIn is set, even though the target athlete has not contributed. The contract will then debit the original athlete’s balance and credit the wrong athlete, effectively stealing or misallocating funds. The impact is critical because it can lead to loss of funds for the original athlete, incorrect accounting, and erosion of trust in the protocol. The condition occurs whenever a manager calls the closeDistribution function without a prior check that the athlete has already funded the contract. The affected parties are the athletes whose funds are stored in the contract and any users relying on the protocol's accounting integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the state‑transition logic of the distribution closing routine. Because the function performs a transfer regardless of the payment flag, the problem may not be obvious during normal operation where most athletes follow the expected flow, making it easy to overlook. The proper fix is to add a require statement that ensures amountPaidIn is true (or non‑zero) before allowing the closure, thereby enforcing that only athletes who have actually transferred funds can be closed. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that a distribution may only be settled after the athlete has contributed, preventing accidental or malicious cross‑athlete fund movement. From a user’s perspective, an athlete may see an unexpected increase in their balance after closing, or another athlete may notice that their balance has been reduced without any action on their part, violating the expectation that closing only returns their own funds.
summary:
There is no check that an athlete has already transferred funds to the contract here:
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L624-L652
It means that the manager by mistake can transfer the funds of another athlete to the athlete that asked to
close their distribution.

title: Anyone can move EURS tokens that the user allowed FlorinTreasury to spend
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted token transfer flaw in the depositEUR function of the FlorinTreasury contract. The function accepts a user‑controlled address parameter called from and then calls SafeERC20Upgradeable.safeTransferFrom to move EURS tokens from that address into the treasury. Because the contract does not verify that the caller is the same as the from address, any external account can supply the address of a victim who has previously granted an allowance to FlorinTreasury and cause the contract to pull the specified amount of tokens. The root cause is the missing access control check that should restrict the source of the transfer to the transaction sender (msg.sender) or to a trusted caller such as the LoanVault contract. An attacker can exploit this by calling depositEUR directly, passing the victim’s address as the from argument and an amount up to the victim’s approved allowance. If the victim approved the maximum uint256 value, the attacker can drain the entire EURS balance of the victim. The exploit works whenever the contract is not paused, the victim has set any allowance for FlorinTreasury, and the attacker can submit a transaction to the network. Affected parties include any user who has approved FlorinTreasury to spend their EURS tokens, especially those who used an unlimited allowance, as well as the protocol that relies on the treasury to hold funds securely. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the public interface of the contract and noticed that the from argument was not validated. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to be intended for internal use by LoanVault, and the code does not emit any warning when called by an arbitrary address. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that EURS tokens disappear from their wallet after they see a transaction that they did not initiate; the UI may show a successful deposit but the user’s balance is reduced unexpectedly, violating the expectation that only the user can move their own tokens. This bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted token transfer” or “arbitrary from address” vulnerabilities, where a contract allows an attacker to specify an arbitrary source for a transfer without proper authorization. The recommended fix is to replace the from parameter with msg.sender, or to add a require statement that enforces msg.sender == from, and to restrict the function to be callable only by the LoanVault contract through an appropriate access control modifier. By ensuring that only the token holder or an authorized component can trigger the transfer, the protocol regains its intended accounting guarantees and prevents unauthorized draining of user funds.

title: Wrong tokensToCheck logic in BaseRouter enables attackers to steal funds
content: The vulnerability resides in the BaseRouter contract’s token‑tracking mechanism, which is intended to prevent assets from becoming permanently locked by checking that the router’s token balances are unchanged before and after a user‑initiated operation. The root cause is an incorrect implementation of the internal functions that maintain the list of tokens to be checked. When a new token is interacted with, the _addTokenToList routine mistakenly stores the token address at the first array slot (index 0) regardless of how many tokens have already been recorded. Consequently, the helper _isInTokenList returns 0 both when the token is actually present at the first position and when the token is absent from the list. The subsequent position calculation (uint256 position = index == 0 ? index : index + 1) therefore always resolves to 0, causing the router to treat any token as if it were already accounted for. This logic flaw allows an attacker to manipulate the tokensToCheck array: by waiting for a legitimate user’s withdraw approval, the attacker can trigger a withdrawal that sends the user’s assets to the BaseRouter, then immediately perform a deposit into a different vault. The deposit operation removes the just‑withdrawn asset from the tokensToCheck array because the router believes the token is already present at index 0. After the asset is removed from the tracking list, the router’s balance‑equality check no longer includes it, and the attacker can subsequently withdraw the same funds to their own address by depositing them back into a vault owned by the router and then pulling them out. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are subtle: a withdrawal appears to succeed, but the user’s balance in the affected vault drops to zero and no refund is received, leading to “funds disappear” or “my tokens are missing” messages in the UI. The issue is hard to notice because the contract still reports that the overall token balance before and after the operation matches, masking the fact that a specific token entry has been silently dropped from the internal list. The bug was uncovered during a manual security audit performed by ThreeSigma, which highlighted the mismatch between the intended accounting guarantees and the actual list‑management code. To remediate the problem the token‑list handling must be rewritten so that _addTokenToList correctly appends new tokens without overwriting the first slot, and _isInTokenList should return a distinct sentinel value (e.g., type(uint256).max) when the token is not found. The position calculation must be adjusted to differentiate between “found at index 0” and “not found”, and the tokensToCheck array should be kept in sync with every deposit and withdrawal operation. In broader terms the flaw belongs to the class of “incorrect sentinel handling in dynamic arrays” that can break invariant checks and enable asset‑theft attacks.
summary:
The BaseRouter implements a mechanism to prevent tokens from being stuck that checks the balance of the router before and after the actions and ensures it remains equal. Problem is, the _addTokenToList(...) function has a bug such that only the last token interacted with is added to the array at the first element (0). The _isInTokenList(...) function returns index 0 if the token is not in the array, so the position uint256 position = index == 0 ? index : index + 1; will always be 0. Attackers can use this to steal other users by waiting for withdraw approvals for the BaseRouter of other users and then use these approvals to withdraw to the BaseRouter, followed by a deposit action in another vault to remove the asset of the withdraw from the tokensToCheck array. The asset is then held by the BaseRouter, which can be retrieved in a following transaction by the attacker by
1) depositing the funds to the vault, where the receiver and owner are the BaseRouter.
2) withdrawing these funds to the attacker, where the receiver is the attacker and the owner the BaseRouter.
3) depositing another asset to another vault, removing the first asset from the tokensToCheck array.

title: Uniswap oracle manipulation to buy for a lower price
content: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on UniswapV2Router.getAmountsIn to determine how many units of a payment token are required to purchase a given amount of a reference token. This function reads the current on‑chain reserves of the Uniswap pair and returns a spot price that can be dramatically altered by a single large swap. Because the calculation is performed without any time‑weighted averaging or external validation, an attacker who can obtain a flash‑loan of the reference token can execute a three‑step attack in a single transaction. First, the attacker flash‑loans a large amount of the reference token and swaps it against the payment token on the same Uniswap pair, driving the reference token’s price down to near zero. Second, the attacker calls the TokenBox minting function, which uses the manipulated price from getAmountsIn, allowing the attacker to spend a tiny amount of payment token to acquire a TokenBox that is priced in the reference token. Third, the attacker returns the flash‑loaned reference token, leaving the protocol with a large amount of payment token that was paid for almost nothing. The impact is that the attacker can acquire valuable TokenBox assets for a fraction of their intended cost, effectively draining revenue from the protocol and breaking the economic assumptions of the token sale. The issue manifests whenever the minting function is invoked while the attacker can perform a flash‑loan and a large swap within the same block, meaning it is exploitable under normal market conditions for low‑liquidity pairs. Users of the protocol are affected because the price displayed in the UI may appear normal, yet the contract accepts an unexpectedly low payment, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual costs. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle usage pattern and identified the lack of a protective price‑averaging mechanism. It can be hard to notice because the price manipulation is transient and undone by the flash‑loan repayment, leaving no obvious on‑chain trace of the abnormal price. To remediate, the contract should replace the direct spot‑price query with a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) from the Uniswap pair, or preferably use a trusted external oracle such as Chainlink. Additional safeguards like slippage limits, minimum price thresholds, or restricting the use of flash‑loans for the reference token can further reduce the attack surface. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of oracle manipulation vulnerabilities where a contract trusts an on‑chain price feed that can be cheaply distorted, leading to under‑payment, loss of revenue, and violation of the protocol’s accounting logic.
summary:
uniswapV2Router.getAmountsIn() is used to calculate the amount of paymentToken required for the amount in referenceToken. This feed is easily manipulated by a large swap in Uniswap pairs. So the attacker can in one transaction:
1. Flashloan referenceToken
2. Sell this referenceToken in the Uniswap pair buying paymentToken. The price of referenceToken is decreased up to almost zero.
3. Paying using paymentToken to mint in TokenBox. The manipulated price will help to spend a very small amount of paymentToken to buy TokenBox priced in referenceToken
4. Return flashloaned referenceToken.

title: Mistake using primary price for customSaleWithPermit()
content: The vulnerability is a logical pricing error in the customSaleWithPermit function of the ToyBox contract. The function is intended to handle non‑primary sales that use a permit signature for token transfer, and it should calculate the payment amount based on the price stored in the saleStruct for that specific custom sale. However, the implementation mistakenly references the global variable that holds the primary sale price instead of the saleStruct.price field. This root‑cause stems from reusing the same price variable name that is appropriate for primary sales but not for custom sales, leading to a mismatch between the price displayed to the user and the price actually applied during execution. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug simply by invoking customSaleWithPermit with a valid permit; the contract will charge the primary sale price, which may be higher or lower than the intended custom price. The impact is that users signing permits may overpay or underpay, receiving an unexpected number of tokens or paying more ether than advertised. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to customSaleWithPermit for a non‑primary sale where the primary price differs from the custom sale price. Affected parties include buyers who rely on permit‑based purchases, the protocol’s revenue model, and any token holder whose balance may be altered incorrectly. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the logic of customSale and customSaleWithPermit and noticed the inconsistent price source. It can be hard to notice because the function signature and surrounding code look identical to the correct customSale implementation, and the UI may continue to show the intended custom price while the contract silently uses the wrong one. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a discrepancy between the expected payment (e.g., a discounted rate) and the actual amount deducted, often resulting in a smaller token allocation or an unexpected loss of funds. This violates the business logic that each sale must be priced according to its own parameters, breaking accounting assumptions about price per token. The recommended remediation is to replace the reference to the global price variable with saleStruct.price, mirroring the correct behavior of customSale, thereby ensuring that the price used for permit‑based purchases matches the custom sale configuration.

title: Liquidators seizing NFTs retain their interest index, allowing theft of funds from interest market
content: During a liquidation where an NFT is seized, the contract calls accrueInterest to update global interest variables but fails to update the per‑account interestIndex and interestAccrued for the borrower and the liquidator before the token transfer. As a result the liquidator receives the seized NFT while still holding the old interestIndex that was recorded years earlier when the attacker first supplied the same NFT. When the global supply index later increases, the liquidator can claim interest on the newly acquired NFT as if it had been supplied for the entire elapsed period. An attacker can prime an address by minting and immediately redeeming an NFT, thereby fixing its interestIndex to a low historical value, then later create a liquidatable position for another address and liquidate it, receiving the NFT with the stale index. The attacker then withdraws the accrued interest, converts it to USDC and drains the interest market. The vulnerability appears only when an NFT is used as collateral and the _seize function is executed; normal mint, borrow or redeem operations update indices correctly, so the bug is hidden from routine balance checks. Users may notice that after a liquidation the protocol’s USDC reserve shrinks unexpectedly while the liquidator’s USDC balance spikes, and borrowers may see their positions liquidated without a proportional loss of collateral value. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test reproducing the exploit over a simulated year, showing thousands of dollars of unearned interest can be extracted. The flaw belongs to the class of accounting checkpoint bugs where per‑account state is not synchronized with global state during asset transfers. To remediate, the contract should checkpoint both interestIndex and interestAccrued for the borrower and the liquidator before moving the seized NFT, using the same logic employed in the transferTokens function, thereby ensuring that the new holder starts with the current index and cannot claim retroactive interest.
summary:
When an NFT is used as collateral for a liquidated loan and is seized as collateral, the `_seize()` function performs the following logic:
call `accrueInterest()`, which updates the borrowIndex, supplyIndex, totalReserves, and accrualBlockNumber
round up the number of tokens seized to the nearest whole NFT
ensure the borrower is on the liquidator
move `accountTokens` from borrower to liquidator
While the `accrueInterest()` logic updates the global variables, the borrower or liquidator do not have their `interestAccrued` or `interesstIndex` values updated at this point. This has the consequence that the liquidator will end up with the additional seized tokens, but with their original `interestIndex`, allowing them to claim interest for these new tokens on the index increases since their `interestIndex`.
This exploit can be used maliciously to extract additional interest from the pool, potentially even putting the solvency of the interest market at risk. To understand why, consider the following scenario:
Alice the Attacker deposits a BAYC NFT and immediately withdraws is, which sets her supply `interestIndex` to the current value.
Years later, Bob deposits a BAYC NFT. He withdraws interest and acts like a typical user. Eventually, due to borrowed token appreciation (or BAYC depreciation) he ends up in a shortfall.
Alice can liquidate Bob's loan to claim his BAYC. At that point, she will have a BAYC deposited and an `interestIndex` that is multiple years old.
This will allow her to claim interest as if she had loaned that BAYC for years. That interest can be collected and immediately redeemed for USDC, which comes out of the interest market.
In an extreme case, a user could farm hundreds of addresses with old `interestIndex` values by minting and redeeming the same NFT through each of them. Later, they could create hundreds of liquidatable positions (using other wallets) and liquidate themselves to claim an unbounded amount of unearned interest.
In this case, it is likely that the amount of phony interest earned would outstrip the actual interest paid by such a substantial amount that the interest market could be drained of all its funds.

title: Logic Flaw in verify() Function in ChainlinkLightClient.sol Contract
content: The vulnerability resides in the verify function of the ChainlinkLightClient contract, which is intended to confirm that a query response is authentic by performing either a storage proof verification or an account proof verification depending on whether the queried account's storage root is already recorded in the approvedStorageRoots mapping. In practice the mapping is never populated because the code that should store the account.storageRoot after a successful account proof either never executes or writes to the wrong key, causing the condition that checks for an existing storage root to always evaluate as false. Consequently the branch that should perform the storage proof verification is never taken, and the function proceeds without validating the actual storage values. This logical omission allows malformed or malicious data to be accepted and subsequently forwarded by the Gateway contract to the UserContract, breaking the fundamental assumption that the data reflects the true on‑chain state. The impact is that downstream contracts may act on incorrect balances, state variables, or other critical information, potentially leading to loss of funds, incorrect business logic execution, or a breach of trust in the protocol. The flaw manifests whenever the Gateway invokes verify with a query whose storage root has not been pre‑registered, which is the normal case for most queries. All users, developers, and auditors relying on the light client’s attestations are affected because they receive data that appears verified but is actually unchecked. The issue was uncovered during a manual security review by Shiedify, who noted that the approvedStorageRoots mapping is never updated despite comments suggesting it should be. The problem is subtle because the function still returns a success flag and does not revert, making the missing verification easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract must correctly update the approvedStorageRoots mapping when an account proof succeeds and adjust the conditional logic to reference the storage root rather than the state root, ensuring that the storage proof is always verified when required. This correction restores the intended security guarantees and prevents the propagation of invalid data to user contracts.
summary:
The goal of this function is to validate the receipt of the query. There are two scenarios depending on if the account.storageRoot is stored in the approvedStorageRoots mapping:

1. When it is stored, the account proof verification is skipped and only the storage proof is verified.

2. When it is not stored in the approvedStorageRoots mapping, only the account proof is verified.

However, the storage root corresponding to the query is checked if it exists in the approvedStorageRoots mapping, but actually, this mapping is never updated, which results in Case-1 becoming inaccessible. This leads to omitting the storage proof verification check every time the Gateway.sol contract calls verify() function on the ChainlinkLightClient.sol contract. Without this check wrong data might be passed to the UserContract.sol through the Gateway.sol contract.

title: Protocol Misses Upgradability Mechanism, Hindering the Proper Implementation of The Custom Relayer
content: The vulnerability consists of two tightly coupled design flaws in the Gateway contract. First, the receiveQuery function is protected by the onlyGelatoRelayERC2771 modifier, which restricts calls to the single Gelato relayer address. This hard‑coded access control prevents any other relayer, including a future custom relayer that the protocol documentation promises, from submitting query responses. The root cause is the use of a static modifier that checks msg.sender against a fixed Gelato address, rather than a configurable whitelist or role‑based system. An attacker or developer who deploys a custom relayer will find that their transactions are reverted, leading to a situation where users submit queries but never receive a response, effectively making the service unusable for those users. The impact is a broken business assumption that the protocol can evolve its relayer infrastructure, and it may cause users to see no refunds, zero balances, or missing data in the UI. Second, the contract is deployed without any proxy or upgradeability pattern, making it immutable. Because the estimateFee function currently returns a constant zero and there is no setter to change the fee, the protocol cannot adjust pricing even after a custom relayer is introduced. The immutability stems from the absence of a UUPS or Transparent proxy and from the lack of any administrative function to modify fee state. Consequently, the fee logic is locked at zero, which can lead to under‑payment, over‑payment, or accounting mismatches, and it prevents future bug fixes or feature additions. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a non‑upgradeable contract with hard‑coded parameters. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Gateway.sol source, where the reviewer compared the on‑chain code with the protocol’s roadmap and noted the mismatch between the documented intention to support an independent relayer and the actual access restriction. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and works with the Gelato relayer, so a superficial test that only uses Gelato will not reveal the limitation. Only when a developer attempts to integrate a new relayer or when the protocol wishes to change the fee does the failure become apparent. To remediate, the contract should be refactored to use an upgradeable proxy pattern such as UUPS, allowing future logic changes without redeploying a new address. The onlyGelatoRelayERC2771 modifier should be replaced with a role‑based access control that can be updated by an admin, or the relayer address should be stored in a mutable variable with a setter function. Additionally, the fee calculation should be made configurable, with a setter that can be called by a governance or admin role, and the estimateFee function should return the stored fee rather than a constant zero. Implementing these changes restores alignment with the protocol’s roadmap, enables future extensions, and prevents the current denial‑of‑service scenario where users receive no response or see unexpected zero balances.

title: Attacker can manipulate the protocols AUM
content: The vulnerability stems from the protocol’s reliance on an off‑chain bot that writes the total assets under management (AUM) as an absolute value directly into the smart contract. Because the contract accepts the bot‑provided number without checking the current on‑chain balance, an attacker who monitors the mempool can front‑run the bot’s update transaction. In a typical scenario the protocol reports an AUM of 100 000 USD. An attacker deposits 20 000 USD, which temporarily reduces the reported AUM to 98 000 USD. The bot then submits a transaction that sets the contract’s AUM to the new absolute value of 98 000 USD. The attacker sees this pending transaction, submits a withdrawal of 4 000 USD before the bot’s transaction is mined, and the real on‑chain assets drop to 94 000 USD while the contract’s stored AUM remains 96 000 USD. When the bot’s transaction finally executes it overwrites the stored AUM with the stale value of 98 000 USD, creating a discrepancy of 4 000 USD between the contract’s view and the actual assets. By repeating this pattern for each AUM update the attacker can gradually widen the gap, causing the protocol to allocate fewer shares to honest users and to mis‑price withdrawals. The issue occurs whenever the bot performs an absolute AUM update, especially in periods of high deposit or withdrawal activity. All participants—depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting invariant that total shares represent the true value of the pool is broken. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the update logic and identified that the contract trusts an off‑chain source to set a critical economic variable without any on‑chain verification or differential update mechanism. The problem is subtle because the mismatch may start as a small percentage and only become noticeable after several iterations, making it easy to attribute to normal market fluctuations. To remediate, the contract should accept only incremental changes (e.g., “increase AUM by X” or “decrease AUM by Y”) or compute the new AUM from on‑chain balances directly, thereby preventing a stale absolute value from overwriting the correct state. Additionally, incorporating a commit‑reveal scheme, time‑locked updates, or oracle signatures can further mitigate front‑running risks and ensure that the protocol’s accounting remains aligned with the real assets.
summary:
In the new design, the AUM value will be set and updated by off-chain bot.
The issue is that the bot defines the absolute value of the AUM and the Fyde contract changes the current AUM based on the bot-provided value so the attacker can change the current AUM by front-running and causing the wrong AUM value when the bot's transaction executes. This is POC:
1. Suppose the current AUM is $100K and the attacker deposited $20K into the protocol.
2. The AUM decreases to $98K and the off-chain bot sends a transaction to update the AUM to $98K.
3. The attacker was watching the mempool and saw the AUM update transaction and front-run it and withdrew $4K from the protocol. Now the protocol AUM is $96K and the real AUM is $94K.
4. When the AUM update transaction executes the AUM would be set to $98K and the difference between protocol AUM and real AUM would be 98K - 94K = 4K.
5. So while in the beginning, the protocol's AUM had $2K difference(about 2%) in the end it has $4K(more than 4%) difference.
6. The attacker can perform this attack again and again for each AUM update and cause more differences between the protocol's AUM and real AUM. As their difference increases protocol would calculate fewer shares for the attacker when he withdraws tokens.
In fact, each user would have an incentive to withdraw before the AUM update transaction because AUM is getting decreased. So the protocol would be in an unstable situation and the difference between real AUM and the protocol's AUM would increase.

title: Incorrect reserve order in _swap()
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the GachaTickets contract reads liquidity reserves from a Uniswap V2 pair inside the internal _swap function. The code calls getReserves() and assigns the first returned value to wethReserve and the second to tokenReserve without checking the ordering of the tokens in the pair. Uniswap V2 defines a deterministic token order: token0 is the address with the lower numeric value and getReserves() always returns (reserve0, reserve1) corresponding to (token0, token1). Because the contract assumes that the payment token is always token0, the reserves can be swapped when the payment token is actually token1. This mismatch is the root cause of the bug. When the swapped reserves are fed into the amount‑out formula (uni.getAmountOut(cost, wethReserve, tokenReserve)), the calculated maximum token amount may be far from the true value. An attacker or even a normal user can trigger a swap that either returns too few tokens, causing a silent loss of funds for the lottery reward pool, or produces a min‑tokens requirement that is unrealistically high, causing the transaction to revert every time and effectively denying service to anyone trying to purchase tickets. The impact is observed as users receiving fewer tickets than expected, the reward pool shrinking without an obvious error, or purchases failing with no clear reason. The issue manifests whenever the _swap function is invoked with a token pair where the payment token is not the lower‑address token, which can happen for many ERC‑20 pairs. All participants who rely on correct ticket allocation – end users, the protocol’s reward mechanism, and any downstream contracts – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s reserve handling against the Uniswap V2 specification. It is difficult to notice because the swap may still succeed, merely delivering a reduced amount, and the contract does not emit an explicit warning when the reserve order is wrong. To remediate the problem, the contract should first read token0 from the pair, then retrieve reserve0 and reserve1, and finally assign wethReserve and tokenReserve based on whether token0 matches the payment token. Adding a check that both reserves are non‑zero and that the ordering matches the expected token pair eliminates the incorrect swap calculation and prevents the potential denial‑of‑service and silent fund loss scenarios.
summary:
In the GachaTickets::_swap function, reserves are retrieved from the UniswapV2Pair contract as follows:
```solidity
address pair = factory.getPair($.paymentToken, token);
(uint256 wethReserve, uint256 tokenReserve, ) = IUniswapV2Pair(pair).getReserves();
if (wethReserve == 0 || tokenReserve == 0) revert InvalidPair();
```
However, there is no validation to ensure that wethReserve and tokenReserve are correctly assigned based on the actual token pair order.
Uniswap V2 reserves must be retrieved in a consistent order:
(token0, token1) = (pair.token0(), pair.token1())
where getReserves() always returns (reserve0, reserve1), and token0 is always the smaller address.
Due to the above issue following consequences can occur:
Incorrect Swap Calculation:
If the wrong reserves are used in:
```solidity
uint256 maxTokens = uni.getAmountOut(cost, wethReserve, tokenReserve);
```
The function may return a wrong actualTokens value, leading to incorrect token amounts received.
Potential Denial of Service (DoS):
If the minTokens calculation is incorrect (is very high), a swap may always revert, making purchases impossible.
Silent Loss of Funds:
The protocol may receive fewer pool tokens than expected from the swap if the minToken (slippage parameter) is extremely less (than the correct value), thus reducing the lottery reward pool size.

title: Decreasing position size via leverage update can be abused to steal from diamond
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw that occurs when a trader reduces the size of an existing leveraged position by updating the leverage parameter. The contract calculates the profit associated with the reduced position and then calls handleTradePnl to settle the trade. The function compares the amount of collateral that will be sent to the trader (_collateralSentToTrader) with the amount of collateral that remains available in the protocol’s vault (the diamond) (_availableCollateralInDiamond). When the reduction creates a negative available collateral value – which happens when the closing fees are larger than the remaining collateral after the profit is realized – the condition _collateralSentToTrader > _availableCollateralInDiamond is true and the code sends the difference (_collateralSentToTrader - _availableCollateralInDiamond) to the trader. Because the negative _availableCollateralInDiamond is subtracted, the closing fee that should stay in the vault is added to the amount transferred to the trader. As a result, the trader receives not only the expected profit but also the closing fee, effectively stealing funds from the diamond. This can be repeated over many trades, slowly draining the protocol’s fee pool. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit, where the auditor noted a comment indicating that the branch would incorrectly send closing fees to the trader when the available collateral is negative. The bug is subtle because it only manifests under the specific condition of a negative vault balance, which may be rare and therefore easy to overlook during normal testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a trader receives more DAI than the calculated profit – for example expecting a 250 DAI profit but receiving 255 DAI, where the extra 5 DAI are the closing fees that should have remained in the vault. The protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated because fees that are meant to be retained for the system are incorrectly allocated to an individual user. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fee‑leakage bugs caused by incorrect handling of negative balances in settlement logic. To remediate the issue the contract should separate the fee amount from the profit settlement and always route closing fees to the vault, adding an explicit check that prevents the fee portion from being included in the transfer to the trader when the vault balance is negative.

title: disburseClaims() allows theft of unclaimed funds
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the FundingVault contract records the amount of tokens that can be claimed for each reward period. When the manager calls disburseClaims, the function overwrites the totalClaimable entry for the current period with the entire token balance held by the contract, without subtracting any rewards that were allocated to earlier periods but have not yet been claimed. This logical error means that tokens that belong to previous periods are mistakenly considered part of the new period’s pool. An attacker or any user who claims in the later period can therefore drain the pool, receiving more than their entitled share and leaving earlier claimants with insufficient balance. For example, if Alice is owed 1,000 tokens from period 2 and does not claim before period 3 begins, the manager’s call to disburseClaims will set totalClaimable[3] to the contract’s full balance (the 1,000 tokens from period 2 plus the new 500 tokens for period 3). Bob, who is only entitled to 100 tokens in period 3, can claim first and receive a large portion of the 1,500‑token pool, reducing the remaining balance so that Alice later receives little or nothing. The impact is a loss of funds for legitimate claimants, a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and a potential erosion of trust because users see their expected rewards disappear. The bug manifests whenever there are unclaimed rewards from a previous period and a new period is opened, and it is triggered by the manager’s disburseClaims call. It affects all token holders who rely on the claim mechanism, the protocol’s economic model, and any role that expects fair distribution of rewards. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the period‑tracking logic and noticed that the balance of the claim token was assigned directly to totalClaimable without considering pending claims. Because the contract’s public view functions still report a non‑zero balance, the misallocation can be subtle and may not be obvious from the UI, which typically shows that rewards are available but does not reveal that they belong to a different period. To remediate the problem, the contract should maintain a separate accounting entry for each period that records only the newly added claimable amount, or it should subtract any outstanding unclaimed balances from previous periods before assigning the totalClaimable value. In practice this means passing the amount of new rewards to disburseClaims and updating totalClaimable[_period] with that delta, rather than with the full contract balance, thereby preserving the integrity of earlier period allocations and preventing accidental or malicious theft of unclaimed funds.
summary:
The FundingVault's disburseClaims function incorrectly assigns all current contract token balances to the current period, without accounting for unclaimed rewards from previous periods. This allows funds allocated to previous periods to be claimed by users in the current period.
We can see that the FundingVault enables users to make claims for the previous period. The claimable amount is determined by the lesser value between _claimable and the current balance of the claimToken.
```solidity
function claim(uint256 _period) external override virtual lock {
    _claimable = GSMath.min(GammaSwapLibrary.balanceOf(claimToken, address(this)), _claimable);
    GammaSwapLibrary.safeTransfer(claimToken, _to, _claimable);
```
However, disburseClaims fails to track unclaimed amounts from previous periods. And it assigns the entire token balance to the current period without reservation for pending claims.
```solidity
function disburseClaims() external override virtual isManager {
    totalClaimable[_period] = GammaSwapLibrary.balanceOf
    //(claimToken, address(this)); // @audit Incorrectly assigns all current balan
```
Scenario:
In period 2, Alice is eligible to claim 1000 tokens but hasn't claimed yet.
Period 3 begins, and new claim amount worth 500 tokens are added.
disburseClaims is called, setting totalClaimable[3] = 1500 (1000 + 500).
Bob, who is eligible for only 100 tokens in period 3, claims first and receives more than his fair share from the total 1500 tokens.
When Alice tries to claim her 1000 tokens from period 2, insufficient funds remain. She may receive 0 if all the tokens are claimed in period 3.

title: Important Balancer fields can be overwritten by EndTime
content: The vulnerability isa packed‑storage overflow in Balancer ManagedPool contracts where the 32‑bit startTime and endTime values are written into a 32‑byte _miscData slot without properly masking excess bits. The insertUint32 helper clears only the 32‑bit region at the given offset but does not truncate the supplied value, so any bits above the 32‑bit boundary remain and spill into the neighboring fields that share the same slot. Because the slot also contains flags such as the "restrict LP" boolean, the swap‑enabled flag, fee‑start and fee‑end timestamps, and fee percentages, an oversized endTime can silently flip these bits. The overflow can be triggered by the manager through updateWeightsGradually or by the owner via enableTradingWithWeights when they pass a startTime or endTime larger than type(uint32).max. When this occurs the contract believes the pool is still respecting the original restrictions, but internally the restrict‑LP flag is cleared, allowing any address to join the pool, and fee parameters may be set to unintended values, potentially resulting in unauthorized participation, fee manipulation, or loss of funds. From a user perspective the UI may still display the expected start and end times while the pool suddenly accepts unrestricted joins or shows a zero swap fee, creating a mismatch between expected and actual behavior. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the bit‑packing logic of BasePool and identified that insertUint32 does not enforce a 32‑bit ceiling. It is difficult to notice because the overwritten bits are not directly exposed in the contract’s public getters and the packed representation masks the problem from casual observation. The correct mitigation is to upgrade to a ManagedPool version that validates the inputs against the uint32 range or to add explicit checks (startTime <= type(uint32).max and endTime <= type(uint32).max) before writing them, ensuring that only the intended 32 bits are stored and that adjacent flags remain untouched.

title: sweep function should prevent Treasury from withdrawing pool’s BPTs
content: The vulnerability resides in the privileged sweep() routine of the vault contract. Sweep() is intended to let the vault owner, referred to as the Treasury, recover stray ERC20 tokens that may have been accidentally sent to the vault. However, the implementation does not discriminate between arbitrary tokens and the pool’s own Balancer Pool Tokens (BPTs) that represent ownership of the underlying liquidity. Because there is no explicit check rejecting BPT addresses, the Treasury can invoke sweep() with the BPT contract address and transfer those tokens out of the vault. The root cause is a missing validation step that should prevent privileged functions from moving assets that are integral to the pool’s accounting. Exploitation is straightforward: after the pool’s initialDeposit() creates BPTs for the vault, the Treasury calls sweep(BPT_address, amount) and receives the BPTs. Since the vault’s withdraw() and finalize() flows already move the underlying assets without requiring the BPTs, the Treasury can bypass the normal time‑locked finalization window, ignore the validator’s allowance limits, and avoid paying the manager’s fee that would normally be deducted on the last withdrawal. Moreover, by swapping the manager contract and setting the swap fee to zero, the Treasury can sell the extracted BPTs on the market without incurring any swap fees, effectively doubling the extracted value. The impact is severe: pool participants see a reduction in the total value of the pool, their expected returns disappear, and the economic model of the protocol is broken because fees are not collected and the pool can be emptied without proper authorization. The condition under which this occurs is any situation where the Treasury holds the owner role and the sweep() function is callable; it does not depend on a specific transaction ordering beyond the existence of BPTs in the vault. All users who have deposited into the pool, as well as any downstream protocols that rely on the pool’s liquidity, are affected because the pool’s balance can be drained silently. The issue was discovered during a manual security review by Spearbit, who noted that the sweep logic lacked a token whitelist or blacklist. It is easy to miss because sweep() is a common utility function and BPTs appear as ordinary ERC20 tokens, so a casual glance may not reveal that moving them undermines the pool’s accounting guarantees. The recommended remediation is to add a check on the token parameter of sweep() that rejects the pool’s own BPT contract address, or to maintain an explicit list of tokens that are prohibited from being swept. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unauthorized asset extraction caused by insufficient validation of privileged token‑transfer functions, leading to a violation of the protocol’s financial invariants and user expectations that deposited funds remain locked until the defined finalization process completes.
summary:
The current sweep() implementation allows the vault owner (the Treasury) to sweep any token owned by the vault including BPTs (Balancer Pool Tokens) that have been minted by the Vault during the pool’s initialDeposit() function call.
The current vault implementation does not need those BPTs to withdraw funds because they are passed directly through the AssetManager flow via withdraw()/finalize().
Being able to withdraw BPTs would allow the Treasury to:
• Withdraw funds without respecting the time period between initiateFinalization() and finalize() calls.
• Withdraw funds without respecting Validator allowance() limits.
• Withdraw funds without paying the manager’s fee for the last withdraw().
• finalize the pool, withdrawing all funds and selling valueless BPTs on the market.
• Sell or rent out BPTs and withdraw() funds afterwards, thus doubling the funds.
Swap fees would not be paid because Treasury could call setManager(newManager), where the new manager is someone controlled by the Treasury, subsequently calling setSwapFee(0) to remove the swap fee, which would be applied during an exitPool() event.

title: CRT-1 Incorrect calculation of borrowed amount
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect aggregation of the amount borrowed by individual credit accounts within the Gearbox protocol. When a user opens a credit account and borrows assets, the contract updates a per‑account borrowed balance, but the logic that adds this amount to the global pool counter (totalBorrowed) does not apply the same increment for every borrow operation. As a result the sum of all credit‑account borrowed balances can be larger than the pool’s totalBorrowed value, creating a persistent mismatch. This mismatch originates from a faulty calculation in the CreditManager component, where the borrowed amount is either rounded, truncated, or omitted when updating the pool’s accounting state. An attacker or any participant can exploit the discrepancy because the pool uses totalBorrowed to compute liquidity‑provider (LP) shares, reward distribution, and collateral requirements. If the pool believes less capital has been borrowed than actually is, LPs are credited with a larger share of the pool than they are entitled to, and borrowers may appear to be under‑collateralised, potentially allowing premature withdrawals or inflated reward claims. The impact is therefore a distortion of accounting that can lead to loss of funds for honest LPs, over‑payment of incentives, and a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees. The condition manifests on every borrow transaction, especially when multiple accounts interact with the pool, and becomes more pronounced over time as the divergence grows. All participants who rely on accurate pool accounting – lenders, borrowers, and LP token holders – are affected.
