The check requires three conditions: the caller must be authorized, the calculated payoff must be strictly greater than zero, and the current block timestamp must fall within the exercise window defined as maturity through maturity plus a configurable duration. Consequently, if an option reaches maturity and either the holder does not exercise it, or the payoff calculation yields a non‑positive value, the unlock condition is never satisfied. The locked funds therefore remain forever marked as unavailable, effectively disappearing from the pool’s usable liquidity. This situation can be triggered simply by the passage of time or by creating out‑of‑the‑money options, and it does not raise an explicit error, making it easy to overlook during testing. The impact is severe: liquidity providers lose access to their capital, the pool cannot honor new trades, and the protocol’s economic model is broken because assets that should be recyclable stay frozen. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the option‑handling logic, where the auditor noticed that the state variable tracking locked tokens never receives a corresponding decrement outside the exercised path. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after an option’s expiry the UI shows no way to withdraw the deposited liquidity, balances appear unchanged, and funds seem to have vanished despite no transaction failure. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of resource deadlock or lockout due to missing release conditions. To remediate the problem the contract should implement a fallback unlock mechanism that releases the locked assets after the exercise window closes regardless of payoff, or allow any participant to trigger a liquidation of unexercised positions, thereby ensuring that liquidity is always eventually recoverable.

title: PLP transfer or balance updates do not update reward index
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑index staleness bug in the liquidity‑pool contract where the pending reward calculation relies on the user’s PLP token balance multiplied by the difference between the global rewards‑per‑LP accumulator and a per‑user reward index. The per‑user reward index (usrRwdIndexQ128) is only refreshed during three specific actions: the first deposit, a full exit, and an explicit claim. It is never updated when the PLP balance changes as a result of ordinary token transfers, partial liquidity withdrawals, or any other balance‑affecting operation. Because the calculation uses the current PLP balance but an outdated reward index, a user can artificially inflate the balance after the index was set, causing the contract to credit rewards based on a larger balance than entitled. An attacker can exploit this by moving a large amount of PLP tokens to an address they control after the last index update and before invoking the claim function; the pending reward function will then multiply the inflated balance by the stale index difference, yielding excess reward tokens. The impact is over‑allocation of rewards, draining the reward pool and effectively stealing value from other participants or the protocol treasury. This condition occurs whenever PLP tokens are transferred or partially withdrawn without a corresponding index update, affecting any holder who can perform such transfers, as well as the overall protocol’s accounting integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑distribution logic, where the limited update points for the reward index were noted as inconsistent with the many ways a balance can change. It can be hard to notice because the contract still allows legitimate reward claims and the over‑reward may appear as a normal high payout, masking the accounting error until the reward pool is unexpectedly depleted. From a user’s perspective the symptom is receiving more reward tokens than expected, or seeing the protocol’s reward balance shrink rapidly. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities where a dependent variable is not kept in sync with its source of truth. The correct mitigation is to ensure that the reward index is refreshed on every balance‑changing event, typically by adding a hook in the PLP token’s transfer and withdraw functions that updates usrRwdIndexQ128 for the involved addresses before the balance change is finalized, thereby keeping the reward calculation consistent with the actual holdings.

title: Incorrect index reset in Fenwick tree after full withdrawal
content: The vulnerability is an incomplete reset of the Fenwick tree data structure that tracks locked deposit amounts in a liquidity pool. When a user fully withdraws all of their funds, the contract marks the tree as dirty and overwrites only the indices that are visited by the update loop – typically the power‑of‑two positions (1,2,4,8,16,…). Indices that are not part of this sequence, such as 3,5,6 and other intermediate nodes, are left unchanged. Because the old values remain in those slots, any subsequent deposit adds the new amount to the stale value, causing the cumulative sum stored in the tree to be larger than the actual amount deposited. When the user later unlocks or removes liquidity, the contract calculates the withdrawable amount from the inflated tree entries, allowing the user to extract more tokens than they contributed and potentially siphon assets that belong to other liquidity providers. This flaw occurs specifically after a full withdrawal followed by a new deposit when the isDirty flag is true. It affects any participant who interacts with the pool, and an attacker can repeatedly trigger the pattern to repeatedly over‑withdraw. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the _updateLockData and Fenwicks._deposit functions, where the reset logic was examined and found to only touch a subset of tree nodes. The bug is hard to notice because the Fenwick tree is an internal accounting structure; normal balance queries may appear correct until the user performs multiple deposit‑withdraw cycles, at which point the over‑allocation becomes evident as unexpectedly large unlocked amounts or other users’ balances decreasing without a corresponding deposit. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that after depositing a small amount they can withdraw a much larger sum, or that the pool’s total liquidity shrinks unexpectedly. The class of bug is a partial state‑reset or residual data bug in a prefix‑sum data structure, similar to “dirty state not fully cleared”. To remediate, the contract should clear all entries of the Fenwick tree (or recompute it from scratch) whenever a full withdrawal occurs, ensuring that no stale values remain in any index before new deposits are recorded. Properly resetting the entire tree restores the accounting invariants and prevents unauthorized fund extraction.

title: delegate() permits unauthorized vote delegation
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized vote‑delegation flaw in the vePeg contract’s delegate() function. The function is meant to let the owner or an approved operator of a lock NFT transfer voting power from one lock (_from) to another (_to). However, the implementation forwards the call to an internal _delegate routine without any access‑control check, meaning that any address can invoke delegate() on any lock ID. This missing authorization check is the root cause. An attacker can simply call delegate(victimLockId, attackerLockId) and reassign the victim’s voting power to themselves or to a third party, effectively stealing votes. Additionally, because the contract tracks delegated checkpoints with a hard limit of 128 entries, a malicious actor can repeatedly delegate on behalf of the same lock to fill the checkpoint array, causing subsequent calls to _delegate (including lock_perpetually, unlock_perpetual, and delegateBySig) to hit the MAX_DELEGATES limit and revert. The impact includes loss of voting influence, potential manipulation of governance decisions, and a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate users cannot lock, unlock, or delegate their tokens. The bug manifests whenever delegate() is called; no special state or pre‑condition is required. All NFT lock owners, their operators, and any participants relying on the voting mechanism are affected, as are the protocol’s governance processes. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s public interface and noticed the absence of a require statement checking ownership or approval. It can be hard to notice because the function signature appears innocuous and the contract does not emit explicit events for unauthorized delegations; the symptoms may only surface as missing votes, unexpected revert messages, or an inability to perform lock‑related actions. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that their voting power is zero, that votes cannot be cast, or that attempts to lock or unlock fail with a checkpoint‑overflow error, contrary to the expectation that they retain full control over their delegated votes. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑authorization or insecure‑external‑call vulnerabilities. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check such as require(_isApprovedOrOwner(msg.sender, _from)) before invoking the internal delegation logic, thereby restricting delegation to the lock’s owner or an approved operator and preventing arbitrary third‑party reassignments. This conceptual fix restores the intended access control and eliminates the possibility of vote theft and checkpoint‑overflow denial of service.
summary:
The delegate() function in the vePeg contract is intended to delegate votes from an NFT (lock) to another NFT/lock (delegatee). However, the issue is that this function allows anyone to delegate on behalf of any lock (NFT) owner, which should not be the case. Delegation should only be allowed from the owner or operator of the lock:
```solidity
function delegate(uint256 _from, uint256 _to) public {
    return _delegate(_from, _to);
```
This results in the following risks:
Malicious actors can delegate votes on behalf of any lock (NFT) owner, thus stealing their votes.
Malicious actors can delegate votes on behalf of any owner to grief them, causing an increase in their checkpoints beyond the MAX_DELEGATES of 128, which leads to a DoS of all functions calling _delegate(), such as lock_perpetually(), unlock_perpetual(), and delegateBySig().

title: Redeem period is less than intended down to 0
content: The contract implements a cooldown‑then‑redeem flow for a staked token. After a user calls cooldown(), the contract records a timestamp and expects the user to wait COOLDOWN_SECONDS before calling redeem(). Once the cooldown period has elapsed, the user should be able to redeem within a further UNSTAKE_WINDOW seconds. The implementation, however, contains a logic error in the time‑window check. The code verifies that block.timestamp - cooldownStartTimestamp + COOLDOWN_SECONDS is not greater than UNSTAKE_WINDOW. Because COOLDOWN_SECONDS is added instead of subtracted, the effective redeemable period is reduced by twice the cooldown length. In the worst case the calculation can make the window zero, causing the redeem() call to revert immediately after the cooldown finishes. This bug is discovered during a security audit that examined the redemption logic. It is hard to notice because the condition looks syntactically correct and the off‑by‑two‑cooldown error only manifests as an unexpectedly short window, which may be attributed to network latency or user error. An affected user experiences a revert with the message StakedToken_UnstakeWindowFinished even though they have waited the full cooldown period and expect to be able to withdraw their funds. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style loss of access to staked assets; funds remain locked in the contract until the bug is fixed or an administrative escape hatch is provided. The issue belongs to the class of time‑window miscalculation bugs, where arithmetic on timestamps is performed incorrectly, leading to accounting violations. To remediate the problem the check should subtract COOLDOWN_SECONDS from the elapsed time, i.e., verify that block.timestamp - cooldownStartTimestamp - COOLDOWN_SECONDS is not greater than UNSTAKE_WINDOW. This restores the intended UNSTAKE_WINDOW duration and allows users to redeem their tokens as expected.

title: Multiple staking_states can be created for the same stake-mint, letting attackers steal rewards and principal
content: The contract allows the creation of multiple staking_state accounts for the same stake‑token mint because the staking_state PDA is derived from the mint and the pool authority. At the same time the user_staking_account PDA is derived only from the mint and the user’s public key, so the same user account is silently shared across every staking_state that uses that mint. When a user deposits tokens in one staking_state, the shared user_staking_account.staked_amount is increased globally, but each staking_state updates only its own total_staked value. An attacker can therefore open a second pool with a different authority, deposit a modest amount, and then claim rewards from the first pool. The first pool calculates rewards based on the inflated global staked_amount while its total_staked remains low, causing an over‑payment that drains the reward vault. In addition, the withdraw_stake instruction accepts an external vault address but never verifies that the vault belongs to the staking_state supplied in the call. By calling withdraw_stake on pool A while passing the vault of pool B, the attacker can move principal tokens from B’s vault into their own account, leaving pool A appearing correctly unstaked while pool B becomes insolvent. This bug manifests whenever two or more pools share the same stake token mint and an adversary can create a parallel pool. Honest participants experience symptoms such as receiving unexpectedly large reward payouts from a pool they never earned from, or seeing their pool balance drop to zero after a claim, effectively losing both rewards and principal. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PDA seed definitions and the reward/withdraw logic, where the mismatch between the keys used for staking_state and user_staking_account was identified as a missing isolation check. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit errors for the mismatch and the shared user account appears to work correctly in single‑pool scenarios. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper state isolation and missing validation of cross‑contract references, allowing cross‑pool fund leakage. To remediate, the user staking account should be bound to a specific staking_state by including the staking_state’s public key in the PDA seed list, ensuring a one‑to‑one relationship between a user position and a pool. This change prevents a single user account from being used to inflate stakes in unrelated pools and forces the withdraw function to operate only on the vault that belongs to the invoked staking_state, thereby protecting reward and principal integrity.
summary:
In IndexTokenStaking, the pool state (staking_state) is keyed by both the stake‑token mint and the pool authority, so anyone can initialize parallel pools that accept the same token but track rewards separately. By contrast, a user’s position (user_staking_account) is keyed only by the mint and the user’s key, so that a single PDA is silently shared across every staking_state built on the same token.
https://github.com/OpenDeltaLabs/index_token_staking_audit/blob/main/programs/index_token_staking/src/instructions/stake.rs#L61C9-L61C98:
```
// staking_state-specific
seeds = [STAKING_STATE_SEED, stake_token_mint.key().as_ref(),
authority.key().as_ref()],
]
https://github.com/OpenDeltaLabs/index_token_staking_audit/blob/main/programs/index_token_staking/src/instructions/stake.rs#L40:
// user position  (authority missing)
seeds = [USER_STAKING_ACCOUNT_SEED, stake_token_mint.key().as_ref(),
user.key().as_ref()],
]
```
Because deposits made in one staking_state increase user_staking_account.staked_amount for all staking_states while only the local total_staked is updated, an attacker can over‑state their stake in a victim staking_state, drain its reward vault, and make staking_states insolvent.
If two states share the same stake mint, an attacker is able to call unstake() in pool A (which internally uses the correct staking_state); then call withdraw_stake() but pass the vault of pool B.
Because withdraw_stake() does not verify that the supplied staking_state matches the vault it debits, the attacker successfully pulls tokens from B’s vault, leaving pool A insolvent for honest stakers.
#### Steps to Reproduce
Reward-vault drainage:
1. Alice initializes pool P₀ with authority = Alice.
2. Bob initializes pool P₁ with the same stake_token_mint but authority = Bob.
3. Bob stakes N tokens in P₁; user_staking_account.staked_amount becomes N.
4. Bob calls claim_rewards/withdraw_rewards on P₀. P₀ uses the bloated staked_amount with its smaller total_staked, over‑paying Bob.
Cross-pool principal theft / Insolvency
1. Attacker calls unstake in pool A; A’s staking_state is updated correctly.
2. Attacker calls withdraw_stake but supplies B’s vault and B-specific accounts.
3. Because withdraw_stake never checks that the vault matches the supplied staking_state, tokens are pulled from B’s vault.
4. Pool A now shows the position closed while pool B has lost funds, leaving honest stakers under-collateralised.

title: Missing _grantRole for GOVERNANCE_ROLE will prevent calling of onlyGovernor functions including upgrades
content: The vulnerability is an access‑control misconfiguration in the InfraredBERA suite of contracts where the privileged GOVERNANCE_ROLE is never assigned to any address during the contract’s initialization. The contracts inherit from UUPSUpgradeable and AccessControlUpgradeable, and the internal function _authorizeUpgrade is protected by the GOVERNANCE_ROLE, as are several protocol‑critical onlyGovernor functions such as setWithdrawalsEnabled, setFeeShareholders, setDepositSignature, setDepositor, setWithdrawor, setClaimor, setReceivor, setMaxVotingNum, whitelistNFT, killBribeVault, reviveBribeVault and setPayoutAmount. Because the role is not granted (the expected call to _grantRole(GOVERNANCE_ROLE,_admin) is missing), any transaction that tries to invoke these functions reverts with an access‑control error, and the contract cannot be upgraded through the UUPS proxy pattern. This situation can be exploited simply by attempting to call the protected functions; the calls will fail, preventing the protocol from performing essential actions such as enabling voluntary withdrawals, configuring deposit signatures for validators, managing bribe vault lifecycles, or setting the payout amount for bribe collections. The default payoutAmount remains zero, which unintentionally allows anyone to claim bribe tokens without cost, effectively draining the bribe pool. The impact is high because the protocol’s core governance mechanisms are disabled, users cannot withdraw their staked assets, deposits may be rejected, and the economic incentives built around bribes are broken. The issue manifests after deployment when the initialize function finishes without assigning the role, and it persists for the lifetime of the contract unless upgraded, which itself is impossible because the upgrade function is also gated by the missing role. All participants—governance participants, stakers, bribe claimers, and the protocol itself—are affected because expected functionality is unavailable and funds may be lost or unclaimable. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit; unit tests passed because the test harness explicitly granted the role, masking the problem in a production setting. The bug is hard to notice because the contracts compile and deploy without errors, and the missing role does not surface until a privileged call is attempted, which may not be exercised in early testing. To remediate, the initialize routine of each contract should include a call to _grantRole(GOVERNANCE_ROLE,_admin) or an equivalent mechanism that ensures the governance address receives the required role before any onlyGovernor function can be used, thereby restoring proper access control and upgradeability. In abstract terms, this is a classic case of an uninitialized privileged role leading to a denial‑of‑service for governance functions and unintended economic behavior.
summary:
All InfraredBERA related contracts derive from UUPSUpgradeable and AccessControlUpgradeable where _authorizeUpgrade is restricted to the GOVERNANCE_ROLE. InfraredBERA also has several protocol-critical onlyGovernor functions of setWithdrawalsEnabled(), setFeeShareholders(), setDepositSignature(), setDepositor(), setWithdrawor(), setClaimor(), setReceivor(). However, the GOVERNANCE_ROLE is not granted to any privileged address during initialization, as done in Infrared.sol via _grantRole(GOVERNANCE_ROLE, _admin). This is the case in Voter.sol, which prevents upgrading it and calling onlyGovernor functions of setMaxVotingNum(), whitelistNFT(), killBribeVault() and reviveBribeVault(). This is also the case in BribeCollector.sol, which prevents upgrading it and calling onlyGovernor function of setPayoutAmount(). Related unit tests succeed because this role is granted during their setup. Impact Explanation: High, because several protocol-critical functions can never be called, for example:
1. setWithdrawalsEnabled() cannot be called to enable voluntary withdrawals in future.
2. setDepositSignature() cannot be called to set valid deposit signatures for validators, which will prevent InfraredBERADepositor deposits from executing and effectively preventing liquid staking to function.
3. Voter bribe vaults cannot be killed or revived.
4. BribeCollector.setPayoutAmount() cannot be called to set payoutAmount, which allows anyone to claim all bribe tokens for free (because default payoutAmount is 0).
5. None of these contracts can be upgraded in future.

title: Adversary can lock tokens forever for any HoneyLocker
content: The vulnerability resides in the onlyOwnerOrMigratingVault modifier that protects the depositAndLock function of the HoneyLocker contract. The modifier attempts to restrict access to the contract owner or a designated migration vault by checking two conditions: msg.sender != owner() and owner() != Ownable(msg.sender).owner(). Because the second check calls an external contract (msg.sender) that implements an owner() function, an attacker can deploy a malicious contract whose owner() function simply returns the current owner address of the HoneyLocker. When the attacker invokes depositAndLock through this malicious contract, the second condition evaluates to false, allowing the call to bypass the intended restriction. Consequently, the attacker can call depositAndLock with an arbitrarily large _expiration timestamp, effectively setting the lock period to a value that will never be reached. The legitimate owner then loses the ability to withdraw the locked tokens because the expiration condition will never become true. This issue manifests whenever a non‑owner caller can supply a contract that mimics the owner interface, which is possible because the modifier does not verify the authenticity of the external owner() call. The impact is severe: funds become permanently inaccessible to the rightful owner, breaking the core accounting assumption that locked tokens will eventually become withdrawable. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that examined the access‑control logic of the modifier and identified the unsafe external call pattern. It can be hard to notice because the code superficially appears to enforce owner‑only access, yet the indirect call to an untrusted contract creates an implicit trust boundary violation. To remediate, the contract should replace the indirect owner() comparison with a direct, immutable whitelist of authorized callers (e.g., a dedicated migration vault address set by the owner) or use a more robust access‑control pattern such as OpenZeppelin’s Ownable with explicit role checks, eliminating any external contract calls in the modifier. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after depositing tokens, the UI shows a positive balance but the withdraw button remains disabled forever, and the user receives no tokens when attempting to claim them, contrary to the expectation that tokens will unlock after the specified period. This class of bug is an access‑control bypass caused by unsafe delegation to external contracts, leading to a permanent lock of assets.

title: Using underlying as the input amount instead of normalized balances
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the token transfer routine handles amounts in a non‑rebasing ERC20 token that inherits a reward‑token implementation. The contract’s private _transfer function accepts an amount expressed in the underlying asset, then converts this amount to a normalized representation by dividing with the current supplyFactor. Because the token is non‑rebasing, the supplyFactor can change after interest is accrued, but the function does not trigger an accrue‑interest step before performing the division. Consequently the conversion may use a stale supplyFactor, producing an amountNormalized that does not correspond to the true underlying value the sender intended to move. In addition, the ERC20 balanceOf view now returns the internal _normalizedBalances rather than the user‑visible underlying balances. Integrators that read balanceOf and then pass that value as the amount argument to transfer therefore supply an already‑normalized number to a function that expects an underlying amount, causing a double conversion. The net effect is that the transferred normalized amount can be smaller or larger than expected, leading to user balances that appear to lose or gain tokens incorrectly, refunds that are missing, or situations where a transfer emits a non‑zero Transfer event but the recipient’s visible balance remains unchanged. This bug manifests whenever a transfer is executed after the supplyFactor has been updated by interest accrual, and it affects all token holders, third‑party contracts that rely on balanceOf for accounting, and any UI that displays the underlying token amount. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the token’s accounting logic, where the mismatch between the expected and actual balance changes was observed. It can be hard to notice because the Transfer event logs the normalized amount, while front‑ends typically display the underlying amount, masking the discrepancy until a user compares on‑chain balances with expected values. The appropriate remediation is to redesign the transfer interface so that it accepts a normalized amount directly, or alternatively to ensure that interest is accrued and the supplyFactor refreshed before any conversion, and to align the balanceOf view with the representation used by external callers. By doing so the contract will preserve the invariant that the sum of all normalized balances multiplied by the current supplyFactor equals the total underlying supply, preventing funds from disappearing or being transferred in the wrong proportion and restoring correct accounting semantics.

title: Mint decimal manipulation through MintCloseAuthority leads to inflation of ld2sd_rate
content: The vulnerability is a decimal manipulation flaw that allows an initializer who controls the MintCloseAuthority extension of a Solana token mint to change the mint’s declared decimal precision after the mint has been created. The root cause is that the ONFT program stores the local‑to‑shared decimal rate (ld2sd_rate) based on the mint’s decimals at the moment of initialization and never updates it, while the mint itself can be closed and re‑initialized with a different decimal value when a close authority is present. An attacker can therefore create a mint with a high decimal count (for example 18), let the ONFT program compute an ld2sd_rate of 1e12 assuming six shared decimals, then close the mint and reopen it at the same address with a lower decimal count (for example 6). Because the program continues to treat the mint as if it still has 18 decimals, all subsequent token calculations use an inflated conversion factor. This mismatch leads to erroneous accounting: legitimate transfers may be classified as dust and removed, cross‑chain transfers can be over‑credited, and arbitrage opportunities arise when the attacker switches between ONFT configurations that use different rates. The exploit can be carried out whenever the mint is created with the MintCloseAuthority extension and the close authority is controlled by the attacker, the mint supply is still zero, and the ONFT configuration does not re‑validate the mint’s decimal precision after a close/re‑open cycle. Users experience symptoms such as receiving zero tokens when a transfer is expected, seeing their balances disappear after a dust‑removal step, or observing unexpectedly large amounts arriving from another chain. The issue is difficult to notice because the decimal value is not displayed in most user interfaces and the program’s internal rate appears correct, so the mis‑calculation only manifests in edge‑case operations. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the initialization logic of the ONFT contract and identified that the MintCloseAuthority extension permits mutable token metadata. To remediate the problem, the protocol should forbid the MintCloseAuthority extension on any mint used by ONFT, enforce that the close authority is set to None at creation, and add an explicit check in the InitOFT instruction that validates the mint’s extensions and ensures the stored decimal count cannot be altered after initialization. This restores the invariant that the ld2sd_rate reflects the true token precision, preventing inflation of conversion rates and the associated financial exploits.
summary:
The ld2sd_rate (local-to-shared decimal rate) can be manipulated by the initializer through the exploitation of the MintCloseAuthority extension in the Solana program. This manipulation is possible because the initializer has control over the mint’s decimal value, which can be changed after the mint’s creation, leading to critical discrepancies in token accounting and potential financial exploits.
The process to execute this exploit is as follows:
1. The admin creates a mint with an initial decimal value of 18 using the MintCloseAuthority extension, assigning the close authority to an address they control.
2. The admin uses the mint in the InitONFT, resulting in 1e12 as a value of the ld2sd_rate (assuming 6 shared decimals).
3. With the mint supply still at 0, the admin then uses the close authority to close the mint account.
4. After the mint is closed, the admin can reinitialize a new mint at the same address, but this time with a reduced decimal value, such as 6.
This manipulation of decimal values causes the ld2sd_rate to become inflated, as the program (ONFT) will still treat the mint as though it has 18 decimals while it actually operates with only 6 decimals. This mismatch leads to erroneous token calculations and can be used for various financial exploits.
Example Exploits:
• Legitimate transfers treated as dust:
Assume a token with a value of $1, where 1 token equals 1e6 units (decimal of 6). An admin or attacker can send 100,000 tokens (with a total value of $1,000,000). Using the manipulated ld2sd_rate, the program with an inflated rate of 1e12, causing the whole amount 1e11 (100 billion units) to dust due to remove_dust, meaning the tokens will not be sent as intended.
• Cross-chain Manipulation:
The attacker can initialize another ONFT_config with a different token escrow account, using the manipulated ld2sd_rate to transfer tokens from another chain (e.g., Ethereum) to Solana. The inflated rate on Solana causes the amount received to be much higher than intended. Once the tokens are transferred, the attacker switches the peer to the new ONFT_config using the correct (lower) rate and transfers the tokens back to the original chain, gaining an arbitrage-like advantage due to the discrepancy in the rates between the ONFT_config accounts.

```solidity
pub struct InitAdapterONft<'info> {
    [account(mut)]
    pub payer: Signer<'info>,
    [account(
        init,
        payer = payer,
        space = 8 + ONftConfig::INIT_SPACE,
        seeds = [ONft_SEED, token_escrow.key().as_ref()],
        bump
    )]
    pub ONft_config: Account<'info, ONftConfig>,
    [account(
        init,
        payer = payer,
        space = 8 + LzReceiveTypesAccounts::INIT_SPACE,
        seeds = [LZ_RECEIVE_TYPES_SEED, &ONft_config.key().as_ref()],
        bump
    )]
    pub lz_receive_types_accounts: Account<'info, LzReceiveTypesAccounts>,
    [account(mint::token_program = token_program)]
    pub token_mint: InterfaceAccount<'info, Mint>,
    [account(
        init,
        payer = payer,
        token::authority = ONft_config,
        token::mint = token_mint,
        token::token_program = token_program,
    )]
    pub token_escrow: InterfaceAccount<'info, TokenAccount>,
    pub token_program: Interface<'info, TokenInterface>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}

impl InitAdapterONft<_> {
    pub fn apply(ctx: &mut Context<InitAdapterONft>, params: &InitAdapterONftParams) -> Result<()> {
        ctx.accounts.ONft_config.bump = ctx.bumps.ONft_config;
        ctx.accounts.ONft_config.token_mint = ctx.accounts.token_mint.key();
        ctx.accounts.ONft_config.ext = ONftConfigExt::Adapter(ctx.accounts.token_escrow.key());
        ctx.accounts.ONft_config.token_program = ctx.accounts.token_program.key();
        ctx.accounts.lz_receive_types_accounts.ONft_config = ctx.accounts.ONft_config.key();
        ctx.accounts.lz_receive_types_accounts.token_mint = ctx.accounts.token_mint.key();
        let oapp_signer = ctx.accounts.ONft_config.key();
        ctx.accounts.ONft_config.init(
            params.endpoint_program,
            params.admin,

            ctx.accounts.token_mint.decimals,
            ctx.remaining_accounts,
            oapp_signer,
        )
    }
```

title: CRT-1 Impossible withdraw for smart contract
content: The vulnerability originates from the way StakingRewardsV3 handles NFT deposits. The contract accepts NFTs via the ERC721 safeTransferFrom function, which triggers a callback to the recipient contract's onERC721Received method. If the depositing contract does not implement this callback, the safe transfer succeeds only because the staking contract does not enforce the interface, but later when the user attempts to call withdraw the internal logic expects the token to have been received through the safe transfer flow. Because the onERC721Received hook is missing, the withdraw function encounters a revert condition and the NFT becomes permanently locked in the staking contract. This situation can be reproduced whenever a smart contract that lacks the ERC721Receiver interface deposits an NFT into StakingRewardsV3. From the user’s perspective the deposit transaction may appear to have succeeded – the UI shows a confirmation and an event is emitted – yet when the user later tries to retrieve the NFT, the transaction fails with a generic revert, leaving the balance displayed as zero or unchanged. The impact is severe: the staked NFT cannot be reclaimed, effectively removing the asset from the user’s control, which justifies the critical severity rating. The issue was identified during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the contract’s reliance on safeTransferFrom without a corresponding onERC721Received implementation creates an implicit requirement that is not documented for callers. The bug is subtle because the failure only manifests on withdrawal, not at deposit time, making it easy to miss during functional testing. To remediate the problem the staking contract should either enforce that callers implement ERC721Receiver, or, as recommended, replace the safeTransferFrom call with a plain transferFrom call that does not require a callback. This change removes the hidden dependency on onERC721Received and ensures that any contract, regardless of its interface, can safely deposit and later withdraw NFTs without risking a permanent lock.
summary:
If any smart contract deposits NFT to StakingRewardsV3 it must have onERC721Received() function or withdraw() will always revert:
StakingRewardsV3-1.sol#L256

title: CRT-2 Incorrect update of totalLiquidity
content: The vulnerability is an incorrectaccounting of the pool’s totalLiquidity variable in the staking rewards contract. The root cause lies in the update modifier that adjusts totalLiquidity unconditionally, even when the caller does not hold the required NFT that represents a stake. When a user executes the sequence deposit() → withdraw() → getReward(), the contract reduces the user’s balance but still increments totalLiquidity during the withdraw step, leaving the global liquidity figure higher than the actual amount of tokens locked. Because reward distribution is calculated as a function of totalLiquidity, the inflated figure skews the reward formula, allowing the attacker to receive a larger share of rewards than entitled or causing other participants to receive less. The exploit can be carried out by any participant who can deposit, immediately withdraw, and then claim rewards, thereby manipulating the accounting state before the reward calculation runs. The impact is a distortion of the reward economics: users may see unexpectedly high rewards, the protocol’s reward pool can be drained faster than intended, and overall trust in the staking mechanism is compromised. This condition occurs only when the contract’s update logic does not verify NFT ownership before adjusting totalLiquidity, which is triggered by the specific call order described. All stakers, the protocol’s token economics, and any downstream applications that rely on accurate reward numbers are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined state‑transition flows and identified that the totalLiquidity variable was not being guarded by the expected ownership check. Because totalLiquidity is an internal bookkeeping variable, the bug does not manifest as a direct UI error; instead, users notice that the reward amount they receive does not match the expected proportion, or that the reward pool depletes unusually fast, making the problem subtle and easy to miss. The recommended remediation is to revise the update modifier so that totalLiquidity is modified only when the contract actually holds the NFT representing a stake, or to recompute totalLiquidity after a withdraw before any reward calculation. In broader terms, this is a classic accounting‑state inconsistency bug where a global pool metric is updated without proper validation, leading to reward misallocation and potential fund loss.
summary:
If user calls deposit() -> withdraw() -> getReward() then contract will incorrectly calculate totalLiquidity which will lead to incorrect calculations of rewards for users:
StakingRewardsV3-1.sol#L342

title: Credentials can be manipulated
content: The vulnerability originates from unsafe downcasting of several numeric parameters in the credential creation flow. When KeyringCoreV2::createCredential() prepares data for RsaVerifyOptimized::verifyAuthMessage() it truncates a 24‑bit policy identifier, two 32‑bit timestamps (epoch and epochExp) and a 168‑bit cost value to smaller integer types without performing any overflow checks. The RSA verification only sees the truncated values, so a malicious signer can craft a signature for a small epoch or expiry while actually submitting the same variable with the high bits set to one. Because the downcast does not revert, the signature verification succeeds, but the original, larger values are stored in the internal credential mapping. As a result an attacker can inflate the expiry timestamp far beyond the intended limit (up to a 64‑bit range) or set the epoch to an arbitrarily large number, effectively making the credential permanent. This manipulation is invisible to users: the UI may still display a valid credential, but the underlying policy never expires, allowing continued privileged actions such as unlimited trading or access. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the type conversions and noticed that the Solidity compiler does not automatically guard against overflow on explicit casts. It is subtle because the signature appears valid and the contract does not emit any warning about the oversized fields, making the bug hard to notice without a deep review of the casting logic. The impact is critical because it breaks the fundamental accounting assumption that timestamps bound the lifetime of a credential, leading to potential loss of control over privileged functions and indefinite access to resources. To remediate, every downcast should be replaced with OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library, which reverts on overflow, and the authentication scheme should incorporate a nonce or similar replay‑prevention mechanism tied to the epoch argument, ensuring that only the exact values signed are accepted and stored.
summary: KeyringCoreV2::createCredential() downcasts several variables, uint24(policyId), uint32(epoch), uint32(epochExp), uint168(cost) when sending them to RsaVerifyOptimized::verifyAuthMessage(), where they are encoded to a signature. Downcasting does not revert so if a key signs a message with a certain variable smaller than the casting that is being made, attackers can send this variable but with higher upper bits set to 1, such that the encoded message is still the same but the variable that is sent to KeyringCoreV2Base::_createCredential() is actually much bigger. One example of an abuse is an attacker setting a much bigger epochExp, which is downcasted to the much lower value to sign, but sets the expiry of its _entityData[policyId][tradingAddress].exp to a value very far away in the future (up to uint64). Another example is an attacker setting epoch to a much larger value such that it can set the credentials forever.

title: C-1 Bypassing KYC in KintoWallet
content: The vulnerability is a KYC‑bypass flaw in the KintoWallet contract that stems from the way the _validateSignature and resetSigners functions verify identity. Only the first owner (owner[0]) is checked against the KintoID registry, while the remaining owners are never validated. Because a wallet can be configured with a multi‑signature policy such as 2‑of‑3, an attacker who can obtain a legitimate KintoID for a single address can create a wallet, then replace the signer set so that the KYC‑verified address occupies the first slot and the attacker’s own externally owned accounts fill the other slots. The contract then treats any transaction that gathers two valid signatures – which the attacker can provide using their own accounts – as authorized, even though the majority of signers have no KYC verification. This can be exploited by first acquiring a KintoID through a stolen or fabricated identity, deploying a wallet, and subsequently calling resetSigners to set a 2/3 policy with the KYC‑verified address as owner[0] and the attacker’s EOAs as owner[1] and owner[2]. Once the policy is in place, the attacker can execute withdrawals, transfers, or any privileged operation without triggering further KYC checks, effectively bypassing the platform’s anti‑money‑laundering controls. The impact includes unauthorized control of user funds, potential loss of assets, erosion of trust in the KYC process, and regulatory non‑compliance. The issue manifests whenever a wallet is created with more than one owner and the signature policy allows a subset of owners to approve actions, combined with the ability to modify the owner list after creation. All users of KintoWallet, the protocol operators, and any entity relying on KYC assurances are affected because the contract’s accounting assumptions – that every signer has passed KYC – are violated. The flaw was discovered during a security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the validation logic only references the first owner, making the bypass subtle and easy to miss in functional testing that focuses on the happy path. From a user’s perspective the wallet UI may display a KYC‑verified owner, leading the user to expect that all transactions are fully vetted, yet the wallet may allow transfers that appear to come from a verified source while actually being signed by unverified accounts, resulting in unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce KYC verification for every owner that participates in a signature, either by checking each signer against the KintoID registry during validation or by restricting the signer set to only KYC‑approved addresses. This change restores the intended security model where all parties involved in authorising a transaction are known and compliant, preventing the described bypass and aligning the implementation with the platform’s compliance requirements.
summary:
• KintoWallet.sol#L204
A KintoWallet can have from one to three owners and have different signer policies. _validateSignature() and resetSigners() check KintoID only for the owner[0], which allows setting up a KintoWallet in such a way that it can be used by a user without a KintoID. To do this, a hacker first obtains a KintoID and KintoWallet. This is done either through a fake or stolen ID, or by stealing someone else's private key. Next, the hacker sets a 2/3 signature scheme in the KintoWallet and sets owner[0] to a person who has passed KYC and is not connected to the hacker. For example, they set Vitalik Buterin's account as owner[0]. The owner[1] and owner[2] accounts are the hacker's regular EOAs (Externally Owned Accounts) without KintoID. Now, the KintoWallet is in no way tied to the original account that created it, and the revocation or invalidation of the original owner's KintoID does not affect it. The hacker can use the KintoWallet, as they own 2/3 of the signatures, and the _validateSignature() function checks the KYC of only the first owner, who, in our example, is Vitalik Buterin.

title: C-2 Malicious bundler can steal funds from SponsorPaymaster
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked reward mechanism in the SponsorPaymaster that allows a malicious bundler to drain the sponsor’s funds by submitting a user operation with arbitrarily high gas parameters, such as an extremely large preVerificationGas value. The root cause is the absence of validation or caps on the gas‑related fields (preVerificationGas, verificationGasLimit, callGasLimit, maxFeePerGas, etc.) that the paymaster uses to calculate the compensation it must transfer to the bundler’s beneficiary when entryPoint.handleOps() is executed. Because the paymaster trusts the values supplied by the caller, a malicious actor can craft a user operation where preVerificationGas is set to a value equivalent to dozens of ether; the paymaster then deducts that amount from its balance and sends it to the attacker’s address. This can be exploited in a single transaction: the attacker, acting as the bundler, calls handleOps() with the inflated user operation, causing the sponsor’s ETH reserve to be transferred to the attacker’s wallet. The impact is a complete loss of the sponsor’s funds, leaving users without the expected sponsored service and breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol that sponsors will reliably cover gas costs. The condition for exploitation is that the SponsorPaymaster is used and that any address is allowed to invoke handleOps() with user operations containing unchecked gas parameters. The affected parties include the sponsor who funds the paymaster, any users relying on sponsored transactions, and the overall protocol that depends on the integrity of its paymaster model. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the handling of user operation fields and identified that the contract does not enforce any upper bounds or beneficiary restrictions. It is hard to notice because normal usage with realistic gas values behaves correctly; only when extreme values are supplied does the loss become apparent, a scenario often omitted from standard testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce reasonable maximums on all gas‑related fields, validate that the caller of handleOps() is a trusted bundler, and require that the beneficiary address matches a predefined wallet. Alternatively, the architecture could be changed so that users themselves pay for execution rather than relying on a sponsor, eliminating the incentive for a bundler to inflate rewards. This class of bug falls under unchecked external input leading to economic overflow or reward manipulation, where a contract’s accounting logic can be subverted by providing malicious parameters, resulting in funds disappearing from the sponsor’s balance.
summary:
• SponsorPaymaster.sol#L156
A hacker can drain the SponsorPaymaster in just one transaction. This can be achieved by executing a userOp with an extremely high gas parameters. As an example, we provided a test where a hacker sets preVerificationGas value to 99 ETH. This value is deducted from the SponsorPaymaster and sent to the hacker who runs handleOps().

title: Status
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution component of the protocol, which assumes that the contract’s token balance can only increase over time. A mapping that records the total amount of fees already accounted for, called _accountedFees, is only ever written with the current balance during the checkpoint function. The checkpoint routine reads the contract’s token balance, computes the difference between the current balance and the previously recorded amount, adds that delta to the epoch‑specific fee total, and then overwrites _accountedFees with the new balance. This logic works while deposits are the only operation that changes the balance. However, when a user claims rewards, the contract transfers tokens out, reducing the balance, but the claim implementation does not adjust _accountedFees to reflect the withdrawn amount. Consequently, the next call to checkpoint observes a balance that is lower than the stored _accountedFees value. The subtraction balance - _accountedFees therefore underflows, causing a revert in Solidity versions that check for underflows. The revert propagates to any function that invokes checkpoint, including claimLiquidation on the lending side and buy/sell on the trading side. As a result, users are unable to claim liquidations, cannot buy or sell NFTs through the protocol, and the overall system may become unusable until the bug is fixed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting flow of fee distribution and noticed that the mapping was never decreased after withdrawals. It is subtle because normal operation with only deposits never triggers the underflow, making the bug easy to miss in tests that do not simulate reward claims. The impact is critical: it blocks core user actions and can lead to loss of confidence in the protocol. To remediate, the claim routine should update the _accountedFees mapping before transferring tokens out, decreasing the stored amount by the claimed value, or the checkpoint logic should be rewritten to safely handle decreasing balances, for example by using a checked subtraction or by recording deltas based on actual token transfers rather than assuming monotonic growth. This class of bug is an accounting underflow caused by an invariant violation in fee accounting, where the contract’s internal state no longer matches the external token balance, breaking the business logic that rewards are always distributable.

title: Numerators are off by one
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation of the scaling factors (numerators) that determine how much donation a user must provide in order to claim ZRO tokens. During contract construction the code computes each numerator as 1 * 10 ** (decimals‑1) for USDC and USDT pools and as nativePrice * 10 ** (18‑1) for the native pool. The subtraction of one from the exponent reduces the intended power of ten by one, meaning the resulting numerator is ten times smaller than the protocol’s specification. Because the required donation amount is derived from these numerators, the contract accepts a donation that is only one‑tenth of the amount that should be required. An attacker can therefore submit the minimal donation, receive the full amount of ZRO tokens, and effectively claim ten times more tokens than intended. This flaw manifests whenever the constructor receives a non‑zero address for any of the Stargate pool parameters, which is the normal deployment scenario. All users who interact with the claim function are affected: they see a lower donation requirement, the protocol suffers from token inflation, and token holders see their holdings de‑valued. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the comment “@audit this is off by a factor of 10”. It is subtle because the numbers still look like valid token amounts; the error is a single exponent adjustment that does not trigger a compile‑time warning, making it easy to overlook during testing. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a donation field that accepts a small amount (for example 0.1 USDC) while the user expects to pay the full amount (1 USDC) and receives a disproportionately large token allocation, leading to confusion or suspicion that the protocol is broken or malicious. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic scaling errors, specifically off‑by‑one exponent mistakes that break accounting assumptions. To remediate the issue the contract should compute the numerators using the full decimal precision, i.e., replace 10 ** (decimals‑1) with 10 ** decimals and 10 ** (18‑1) with 10 ** 18, thereby restoring the correct donation‑to‑reward ratio and preventing unintended token over‑issuance.

title: Remote donations are stuck
content: The RemoteDonate contract enables users to donate assets on non‑Ethereum chains and forwards those donations to a designated receiver on Ethereum using a Stargate cross‑chain transfer. For native‑currency donations (e.g., ETH), the contract expects the caller to provide the LayerZero (LZ) messaging fee via msg.value while the actual donation amount is taken from the contract’s balance. The vulnerability arises because the code assigns donationAmount = address(this).balance, which already includes the msg.value intended for the LZ fee. When the contract later calls IOFT(stargate).send{value: msg.value + donationAmountNative} the total value sent exceeds the contract’s current balance, causing the external call to revert. Consequently, every attempt to withdraw a native‑currency donation fails, leaving the donated funds permanently locked in the contract. This bug manifests only during the withdrawDonation function when the selected currency is Native and a Stargate endpoint is configured; token‑based withdrawals (USDC, USDT) are unaffected because they do not involve msg.value. The affected parties are donors who expect their contributions to be transferred, the donationReceiver who never receives the funds, and the protocol that loses credibility. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the incorrect balance calculation. It can be difficult to notice because the contract’s balance appears sufficient before the call, and no explicit error message indicates an overdraw; the transaction simply reverts. The root cause is an accounting error: the fee and the donation are summed together instead of being treated as separate amounts, leading to an insufficient‑balance condition. To remediate, the contract should compute the donation amount as address(this).balance minus msg.value (or otherwise isolate the fee) before invoking the cross‑chain send, ensuring that the total value transferred never exceeds the contract’s actual holdings. This class of bug is a mis‑accounted fund transfer or insufficient‑balance error, common in cross‑chain protocols where fees must be deducted from the pool of user funds. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “withdrawal failed” message, the donation appears to remain in the contract, and the expected receipt on Ethereum never arrives, violating the business logic that a donation should be moved atomically to the receiver.

title: CRT-1 Possibility of taking burned shares
content: The vulnerability resides in the profit‑distribution logic that handles shares that have been burned in the Lido staking protocol. When a user or contract burns stETH shares, the protocol records the amount of burned tokens and later, during the execution of the processLidoOracleReport routine, it calculates a profit share that should be allocated to the remaining holders. Because the implementation does not enforce any upper bound on the amount of burned tokens that can be considered for profit calculation, an attacker can submit a transaction that burns a large number of shares and then front‑run the oracle‑report transaction in the same block. By doing so, the attacker causes the profit‑allocation formula to treat the freshly burned shares as if they were still eligible for reward, and the contract subsequently transfers the calculated profit to the attacker’s address. This exploitation does not require the attacker to have held the shares before the burn; the profit is derived solely from the manipulated accounting state. The impact is that the attacker can siphon a portion of the rewards that should have been distributed to legitimate stETH holders, effectively reducing the overall returns for all participants and potentially draining the pool of profit that is meant for burned‑share holders. The condition for the exploit is the ability to control transaction ordering, i.e., to front‑run the oracle‑report call, which is feasible for miners, bots, or any entity with sufficient gas price leverage. All users of the Lido protocol who rely on accurate reward distribution are affected, as the bug undermines the accounting assumptions that burned shares do not generate profit. The issue was uncovered by the MixBytes audit team through a combination of static analysis and manual testing, which produced a proof‑of‑concept that demonstrated the profit‑stealing flow. The bug is subtle because the normal reward distribution appears unchanged for most users; only the portion that should have been allocated to burned shares disappears, making it difficult to detect without detailed accounting checks. To remediate the problem, the contract should introduce a strict limit on the amount of burned tokens that can be considered in a single profit‑distribution cycle, or redesign the accounting so that burned shares are excluded from the profit calculation entirely. Additionally, reordering state updates to occur before profit distribution, or adding a commit‑reveal scheme for burns, would mitigate the front‑run vector. Implementing these safeguards restores the intended economic model where burned shares do not generate unexpected profit and protects user funds from being illicitly captured.
summary:
With attack it is possible to take burned shares profit even without taking shares before processLidoOracleReport() execution.
SelfOwnedStETHBurner.sol#L252
This exploit shows how the attack is done:
https://gist.github.com/georgiypetrov/22c0649058a97102e2fd97a1c619a3b3
If this is a front-run attack, then it will be the most convenient for the attacker.

title: CRT-1 Possible underflow
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that can occur in the stake ledger management of the Lido KSM protocol. When a ledger’s total stake is dramatically reduced by a rebalance operation, the recorded stake value becomes very small. If, shortly after this reduction, the ledger is subjected to a large slash – for example because a validator misbehaves – the contract subtracts the slash amount from the already‑low stake without first verifying that the stake is sufficient. Because the subtraction is performed with unchecked arithmetic, the result wraps around to a very large unsigned integer instead of reverting. This underflow corrupts the internal accounting of the affected ledger, causing its recorded balance to appear astronomically high while the actual staked amount is near zero. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include a sudden loss of expected rewards, a balance that shows zero or an unexpectedly huge number, and the inability to withdraw the correct amount of tokens. The impact is critical: the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, which can lead to over‑issuance of shares, loss of funds for delegators, and a breach of trust in the staking service. The condition under which the bug manifests is a specific sequence – a rebalance that shrinks a ledger’s stake followed by a slash that exceeds the remaining stake. It affects any delegator whose stake is routed through the impacted ledger, as well as the protocol itself because the total supply of staking tokens may become inconsistent with the recorded ledger totals. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by MixBytes, which identified the unchecked subtraction in the slash handling code (Lido.sol line 608). The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not revert on underflow, and the resulting large number may only be detected later when aggregate accounting checks fail or when users experience unexpected balance anomalies. To remediate the problem the slash logic should be redesigned so that the penalty is distributed proportionally across all ledgers, ensuring that no single ledger can be forced into a negative balance. Additionally, safe‑math checks or explicit require statements should be added to guarantee that the slash amount never exceeds the ledger’s current stake, thereby preventing the underflow from occurring.
summary: If a ledger's stake dramatically decreases due to rebalance and after that the ledger receives a huge slash, then underflow can occur: Lido.sol#L608

title: CRT-2 Possible overflow on cast to uint
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked conversion from a signed integer to an unsigned integer that can cause an arithmetic overflow when the signed value is negative. In the staking logic of the contract, a variable representing the change in stake (newStake) is calculated as a signed integer. The code then casts this signed value directly to an unsigned type without verifying that the value is non‑negative. If newStake becomes negative – for example due to an under‑flow in a prior subtraction or an unexpected input – the cast wraps the negative number to a very large unsigned integer. This overflow can be exploited by an attacker who crafts a transaction that forces newStake to be negative, causing the contract to record an absurdly large stake amount. The inflated stake may bypass limits, distort accounting, allow the attacker to claim excessive rewards, or cause other invariants to fail, potentially leading to loss of funds or a denial‑of‑service condition for honest users. The issue manifests during the execution of the stake‑update function (line 730 in Lido.sol) whenever the signed‑to‑unsigned conversion occurs. Any user interacting with the staking interface, as well as the protocol itself, can be affected because the protocol’s balance sheet may become inconsistent, showing balances that are far larger than the actual deposited amounts. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, where the auditors identified that the cast does not include a sign check and therefore may overflow. The problem is subtle because Solidity’s built‑in overflow checks only apply to arithmetic operations, not to type casts, so the conversion silently produces a large value without reverting. From a user’s perspective the symptom can appear as a sudden, unexplained increase in their recorded stake, or conversely as a missing or zero balance when they try to withdraw, because the protocol’s internal accounting no longer matches reality. The root cause is the lack of validation that newStake is non‑negative before casting. To remediate, the code should explicitly verify that the signed value is greater than or equal to zero before converting it to an unsigned type, or use a safe‑casting library that reverts on negative inputs. This change restores the intended business logic that stake changes must be non‑negative and prevents the overflow from breaking accounting assumptions.
summary: If newStake is a negative number, then overflow can occur: Lido.sol#L730

title: An attacker can freeze all incoming deposits and brick the oracle members' reporting system with only 1 wei
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that allows an attacker to lock all future deposits and prevent the oracle reporting mechanism from reaching a quorum by injecting a single wei into the River contract before any legitimate user deposit occurs. The root cause is the contract’s share‑minting logic, which assumes that the total asset balance will be zero on the first legitimate deposit and therefore mints an initial amount of shares in a special branch. This branch is skipped when the asset balance is non‑zero, and the subsequent calculation of shares to mint divides the underlying asset value by the old total asset balance while multiplying by the current total supply. Because the total supply is still zero at that point, the computed share amount is zero, resulting in the user receiving no shares despite the contract’s balance increasing. The problem propagates: every following deposit also yields zero shares, the internal accounting (Shares.get or totalSupply) never advances, and when an oracle member finally attempts to report beacon data, the earnings handler checks that totalSupply is non‑zero before proceeding. Since totalSupply remains zero, the contract reverts with a ZeroMintedShares error, aborting the quorum formation and any reward distribution. This attack can be performed by an adversary who force‑sends 1 wei via selfdestruct or a similar low‑value transfer, timing the transaction to precede the first legitimate deposit by monitoring the mempool and front‑running. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that a deposit succeeded, but the user’s share balance stays at zero, rewards never accrue, and withdrawals may become impossible because the protocol believes no shares exist. The issue is difficult to notice because the contract does not reject the deposit; it simply mints zero shares, which can be mistaken for a normal zero‑balance state. The bug belongs to the class of initialization‑state manipulation where an invariant that should only be true on a pristine contract is broken by a minimal external balance, leading to a division‑by‑zero‑avoidance path that never restores the invariant. The discovery was made during a security audit that examined the minting flow and the earnings callback, revealing that the early‑deposit branch is bypassed when the asset balance is artificially non‑zero. To remediate, the contract should decouple share minting from the asset‑balance‑zero check, enforce a minimum non‑zero totalSupply before allowing earnings processing, and protect the initial state from external balance manipulation, for example by requiring that the first deposit be performed by a privileged initializer or by rejecting unexpected low‑value forced transfers before the protocol is fully initialized.
summary: An attacker can brick/lock all deposited user funds and also prevent oracle members to come to a quorum when there is an earning to be distributed as rewards. Consider the following scenario: 1. The attacker force sends 1 wei to the River contract using, e.g., selfdestruct. The attacker has to make sure to perform this transaction before any other users deposit their funds in the contract. The attacker can look at the mempool and also front-run the initial user deposit. Now the b = _assetBalance() > 0, is at least 1 wei. 2. Now an allowed user tries to deposit funds into the River protocol. The call eventually ends up in _mintShares(o, x) and in the 1st line oldTotalAssetBalance = _assetBalance() - x, _assetBalance() represents the updated River balance after taking into account the x deposit as well by the user. So _assetBalance() is now b + x + ... and oldTotalAssetBalance = b + ... where the ... includes beacon balance sum, deposited amounts for validators in queue, ... (which is probably 0 by now). Therefore, oldTotalAssetBalance > 0 means that the following if block is skipped: if (oldTotalAssetBalance == 0) { _mintRawShares(_owner, _underlyingAssetValue); return _underlyingAssetValue; } And goes directly to the else block for the 1st allowed user deposit: else { uint256 sharesToMint = (_underlyingAssetValue * _totalSupply()) / oldTotalAssetBalance; _mintRawShares(_owner, sharesToMint); return sharesToMint; } But since shares have not been minted yet _totalSupply() == 0, and therefore sharesToMint == 0. So we mint 0 shares for the user and return 0. Note that _assetBalance() keeps increasing, but _totalSupply() or Shares.get() remains 0. 3. Now the next allowed users deposit funds and just like step 2. River would mint them 0 shares, _assetBalance() increases but _totalSupply() or Shares.get() remains 0. Note that _totalSupply() or Shares.get() remains 0 until the oracle members come to a quorum for the beacon balance sum and number of validators for a voting frame. Then the last oracle member who calls the reportBeacon to trigger the quorum causes a call to _pushToRiver which in turn calls river.setBeaconData. Now in setBeaconData if we have accumulated interest then _onEarnings is called. The 1st few lines of _onEarnings are: uint256 currentTotalSupply = _totalSupply(); if (currentTotalSupply == 0) { revert ZeroMintedShares(); } But _totalSupply() is still 0 so revert ZeroMintedShares() is called and the revert bubbles up the stack of call to reportBeacon, which means that the last oracle member that can trigger a quorum will have its call to reportBeacon reverted. Therefore, no quorums will ever be made which has some earnings and the River protocol will stay unaware of its deposited validators on the beacon change. Any possible path to _mintRawShares (which could cause Shares.get() to increase) is also blocked and _totalSupply() would stay at 0. So even after validators, oracle members, etc.. become active, when an allowed user deposits they would receive 0 shares. Note, that an attacker can turn this into a DoS attack for the River Protocol, since redeployment alone would not solve this issue. The attacker can monitor the mempool and always try to be 1st person to force deposit 1 wei into the River deployed contract.

title: Operators._hasFundableKeys returns true for operators that do not have fundable keys
content: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that determines whether an operator has fundable keys. The function incorrectly uses the operator’s stopped counter as part of its eligibility test. As a result, an operator whose funded keys count equals its stopped count – meaning all keys have already been funded and the operator has effectively exited – is still reported as having fundable keys. Consequently, the operator is added to the array returned by the public getAllFundable function. This array is later consumed by the pickNextValidators routine, which selects the next validator and delegates user ETH to it. When the only operators in the list are those that have no remaining keys, pickNextValidators receives an empty candidate set and either returns no validator or causes a revert. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition for the Alluvial staking workflow: delegators see no validator selected, their staking transactions fail or appear to do nothing, and the protocol cannot accept new stake. The issue affects any user or contract that attempts to delegate ETH through the staking interface, as well as the protocol’s ability to maintain active validators. It was discovered during a security audit that exercised the operator selection logic with edge‑case data where funded equals stopped and funded equals the minimum of limit and keys. The bug is subtle because the function returns true, giving the impression that the operator is eligible, yet no downstream error is emitted until the selection step, making the failure appear as an empty list rather than an explicit exception. The proper fix is to redesign the eligibility check so that it returns true only when the operator is active and the number of funded keys is strictly less than the number of keys that can still be funded, removing any reliance on the stopped counter. By aligning the check with the intended business rule – that an operator must have at least one unfunded key – the protocol regains its ability to select validators and prevents the DOS scenario where funds cannot be delegated.
summary: Because _hasFundableKeys uses operator.stopped in the check, an operator without fundable keys be validated and return true. Scenario: Op1 has • keys = 10 • limit = 10 • funded = 10 • stopped = 10 This means that all the keys got funded, but also "exited". Because of how _hasFundableKeys is made, when you call _hasFundableKeys(op1) it will return true even if the operator does not have keys available to be funded. By returning true, the operator gets wrongly included in getAllFundable returned array. That function is critical because it is the one used by pickNextValidators that picks the next validator to be selected and stake delegate user ETH. Because of this issue in _hasFundableKeys also the issue OperatorsRegistry._getNextValidatorsFromActiveOperators can DOS Alluvial staking if there's an operator with funded==stopped and funded == min(limit, keys) can happen DOSing the contract that will always make pickNextValidators return empty. Check Appendix for a test case to reproduce this issue.

title: OperatorsRegistry._getNextValidatorsFromActiveOperators can DOS Alluvial staking if there's an operator with funded==stopped and funded == min(limit, keys)
content: The vulnerability resides in the validator selection routine of the Alluvial staking contract, specifically the private function that gathers the next set of validators from the pool of active operators. The routine iterates over all operators and chooses the one with the smallest difference between its funded and stopped counters, assuming that this metric reflects the number of validators that can still be funded. However, when an operator has its funded counter equal to its stopped counter, the difference becomes zero. Because zero is lower than any positive difference, the loop mistakenly selects this operator even though it has no remaining fundable keys – its funded amount already equals the minimum of its limit and its total keys. After the selection, the code computes the number of available keys by subtracting the funded amount from the smaller of the operator’s key count and its limit. For the operator with funded equal to stopped, this calculation yields zero, causing the function to return two empty byte arrays and abort the pick‑next‑validator process. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: any user who deposits ETH for staking receives no validator assignment, the UI may show an empty validator list or a message that no validators are available, and the deposited funds remain idle in the contract. This situation can affect all participants of the Alluvial protocol, including regular stakers, operator owners, and the protocol’s revenue model, because the staking pipeline is effectively halted despite the presence of other operators that still have fundable validators. The issue was uncovered during a security audit performed by Spearbit, which highlighted that the selection logic incorrectly incorporates the stopped attribute instead of focusing solely on active operators with fundable keys. The bug is subtle because the loop appears to implement a reasonable “minimum‑difference” heuristic, yet it fails to filter out operators that are already fully funded or stopped, making the problem easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate the flaw, the selection algorithm should be rewritten to ignore the stopped counter when evaluating fundable capacity, and it should explicitly prioritize operators that have a positive number of remaining keys (i.e., where funded is less than the minimum of limit and keys). By ensuring that only operators with actual fundable validators are considered, the function will return a non‑empty validator set and restore the staking flow, preventing the denial‑of‑service condition.
summary: This issue is also related to OperatorsRegistry._getNextValidatorsFromActiveOperators should not consider stopped when picking a validator. Consider a scenario where we have Op at index 0 name op1 active true limit 10 funded 10 stopped 10 keys 10 Op at index 1 name op2 active true limit 10 funded 0 stopped 0 keys 10 In this case, • Op1 got all 10 keys funded and exited. Because it has keys=10 and limit=10 it means that it has no more keys to get funded again. • Op2 instead has still 10 approved keys to be funded. Because of how the selection of the picked validator works uint256 selectedOperatorIndex = 0; for (uint256 idx = 1; idx < operators.length;) { if ( operators[idx].funded - operators[idx].stopped < operators[selectedOperatorIndex].funded - operators[selectedOperatorIndex].stopped ) { selectedOperatorIndex = idx; } unchecked { ++idx; } } When the function finds an operator with funded == stopped it will pick that operator because 0 < operators[selectedOperatorIndex].funded - operators[selectedOperatorIndex].stopped. After the loop ends, selectedOperatorIndex will be the index of an operator that has no more validators to be funded (for this scenario). Because of this, the following code uint256 selectedOperatorAvailableKeys = Uint256Lib.min( operators[selectedOperatorIndex].keys, operators[selectedOperatorIndex].limit ) - operators[selectedOperatorIndex].funded; when executed on Op1 it will set selectedOperatorAvailableKeys = 0 and as a result, the function will return return (new bytes[](0), new bytes[](0));. In this scenario when stopped==funded and there are no keys available to be funded (funded == min(limit, keys)) the function will always return an empty result, breaking the pickNextValidators mechanism that won't be able to stake user's deposited ETH anymore even if there are operators with fundable validators. Check the Appendix for a test case to reproduce this issue.

title: _pickNextValidatorsToExitFromActiveOperators uses the wrong index to query stopped validator count for operators
content: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that selects the next validators to exit from active operators. The function builds a temporary in‑memory list of cached operator structures, but this list is filtered: operators that have no exitable keys are omitted, which means the order of the cached array does not match the order of the permanent operator array stored in contract state.
