BasicVault::_redeem() is inconsistent as it burns newAmount, the value returned from the
hook, but pushes a request to the redeem queue with amount. As hook::reportRedeem()
will cap the amount to redeem to the current load, the last user to withdraw may specify a
huge amount to redeem, which will be capped to the remaining load, burning the capped
newAmount shares, but pushing a request with the huge amount.

title: Creating a pair while the token is in the initial sale phase
content: The vulnerability originates from the refund mechanism that is executed after a token purchase during the final phase of the initial sale. When a buyer sends more ETH than the remaining token supply, the contract calculates the maximum number of tokens that can be delivered, refunds the excess ETH, and performs the refund with a low‑level call to msg.sender. Because this external call is made before the contract checks the liquidity goal and creates the token/WETH pair, a malicious contract can exploit the receive callback to execute arbitrary logic. In the callback the attacker creates a liquidity pair on a router, approves the router to spend tokens, adds liquidity with a small amount of AVAX, and then transfers a large amount of the bonding token back to the sale contract. This sequence disables the liquidityGoalReached condition for subsequent calls, causing the later _createPair transaction to fail. As a result the sale contract is left in a state where the collected ETH and minted tokens remain locked in the initial‑sale phase, preventing the intended liquidity provisioning and effectively trapping user funds. From a user’s perspective the purchase may appear to succeed but the expected token balance is either zero or lower than anticipated, and the refund may be missing or the transaction may revert unexpectedly when the sale cap is reached. The issue is hard to notice because developers often assume that the refund recipient is an externally owned account and that a simple call cannot affect contract state. The root cause is a violation of the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: state‑changing operations (such as updating the liquidity‑goal flag or creating the pair) are performed after an external call, allowing re‑entrancy‑like manipulation. The flaw can be mitigated by moving the refund after the liquidity‑goal check and pair creation, by using a pull‑payment model for refunds, by restricting refunds to EOAs, or by applying a re‑entrancy guard that ensures no state can be altered during the external call.

title: Creating a token with a poisoned router
content: The vulnerability originates from a token factory function that allows the caller to supply an arbitrary router address when deploying a new bonding ERC20 token. The deployBondingERC20Token function does not perform any validation or whitelist check on the _router parameter, and it simply stores the provided address in the newly created token contract. Because the router address is later used to route token‑sale payments and swaps, a malicious actor can pass a contract that pretends to be a legitimate DEX router but actually forwards or drains all incoming ETH to an attacker‑controlled address. This flaw can be exploited by any user who can invoke the factory, which is typically unrestricted, to create a token whose sales are wired to a “poisoned” router. When a buyer sends ETH to purchase the token, the malicious router intercepts the payment, causing the buyer’s ETH balance to decrease while the expected token allocation may still be recorded, or the transaction may revert silently, leaving the buyer with no tokens and no refund. The impact is a loss of funds for token purchasers and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions, as the treasury or token sale mechanism no longer receives the intended revenue. The issue manifests whenever the factory is used to launch a new token without a prior check that the router address matches a known, trusted DEX deployment (for example, the official Uniswap or Trader Joe router contracts). Users experience symptoms such as “my ETH vanished after buying a token”, “the token sale returned zero ETH”, or “my balance shows zero after a purchase”. The problem was identified during a manual security review that highlighted the lack of input sanitisation for critical external contract references. It is difficult to notice because the router address is just an ordinary parameter; the UI may display a familiar name while the underlying address is malicious, and there is no on‑chain event indicating a mismatch. To remediate, the factory should enforce a whitelist of approved router contracts, compare the supplied address against the official router addresses published by the DEX, or hard‑code the router address in the factory so that users cannot supply a custom one. Additionally, the token constructor could verify that the router implements the expected interface and that calls to it behave as intended before accepting it as a payment conduit. By ensuring that only trusted router contracts are used, the protocol can prevent the theft of ETH during token sales and preserve the intended economic flow.

title: Blocking the initial liquidity seed with a 1 wei donation
content: The vulnerability is an initial‑liquidity blocking flaw that allows an attacker to prevent the protocol from creating a Uniswap pair for the bonding token after the sale phase. The root cause is that the contract that adds liquidity assumes both token reserves are zero when a pair does not yet exist, and it uses the router’s _addLiquidity logic which calls UniswapV2Library.quote only when at least one reserve is non‑zero. By pre‑creating an empty TOK/WETH pair and sending a single wei of WETH, the attacker makes one reserve non‑zero while the other remains zero. When the router later calls sync, the pair reports a non‑zero reserve, causing the addLiquidity function to invoke quote. Quote requires both reserves to be greater than zero, so it reverts with INSUFFICIENT_LIQUIDITY. This revert stops the router from minting LP tokens, leaving the bonding tokens and the collected ETH trapped in the contract. The exploit can be carried out during the initial sale, before the protocol attempts to add liquidity, and it affects any user expecting to receive LP tokens or to have their contribution reflected in a market. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidity‑initialisation code, where the auditor noticed that the router’s addLiquidity path does not handle a pair with a single‑sided reserve. It is subtle because a one‑wei donation appears harmless and does not affect price calculations, yet it changes the reserve state enough to trigger a failure path that is not exercised in normal testing. The impact is that the protocol cannot bootstrap its market, causing funds to be locked and users to see no LP tokens, zero balances, or missing refunds. The fix is to avoid relying on the router’s addLiquidity for the first liquidity provision and instead interact directly with the pair contract: create the pair if needed, deposit the native token, transfer both assets to the pair, and call mint, thereby bypassing the quote check that fails when one reserve is empty. This ensures that the initial liquidity can be added even when one side has a minimal amount, preserving the intended accounting and preventing funds from disappearing.

title: The verifyUser method is flawed and it will not work Molly_report.md
content: The contract implements a verifyUser function that attempts to grant a boolean flag isVerified to the caller after checking an ECDSA signature. The function builds a hash of the supplied data, prefixes it with the Ethereum signed‑message prefix using ECDSA.toEthSignedMessageHash, and then recovers the signer address from the provided signature. It compares the recovered address against a signer variable that is set only once in the constructor and never updated. Because the signer cannot be changed after deployment, any signature that does not originate from that fixed address will cause the require statement to revert with \"Invalid signature\". Consequently, legitimate users who are supposed to be verified with a different authority cannot succeed, and the function may be effectively unusable if the stored signer does not match the intended verifier. Even if the signer issue were corrected, the verification logic does not bind the signed message to the caller’s address or to a unique nonce. An attacker observing a pending transaction in the mempool can copy the exact _data and _signature values, submit a competing transaction with a higher gas price, and become verified before the original user’s transaction is mined. This replay‑or front‑running vulnerability allows any party with access to a valid signature to impersonate the original signer and obtain verified status, breaking the intended access‑control model. The function also imports an outdated version of OpenZeppelin’s ECDSA utilities; the toEthSignedMessageHash helper has been moved to the MessageHashUtils library in recent releases, meaning the contract may be missing security patches and could behave unexpectedly if the older implementation is deprecated. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that an account may appear verified without the user having performed the expected signing step, or conversely a legitimate user may receive the \"Invalid signature\" error despite providing a correct signature. The impact includes unauthorized privilege escalation, potential loss of trust in the protocol’s identity checks, and denial of service for genuine participants. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the signature verification flow and identified the immutable signer, lack of caller binding, and outdated library usage. The bug is subtle because the code superficially appears to perform a standard signature check, yet it fails to enforce a one‑to‑one relationship between a signature and the caller, and the immutable signer constraint is not obvious without reviewing the constructor. To remediate the problem the contract should either make the signer address updatable through a secure governance mechanism or store a mapping of authorized signers per user. The signed message should incorporate msg.sender and a per‑user nonce or timestamp so that each signature is unique to the caller and cannot be replayed. Updating the OpenZeppelin imports to the latest version and using MessageHashUtils for the hash prefix will ensure the code benefits from recent security improvements. By tightening the signature binding and allowing proper signer management, the verification process will correctly reflect the intended identity model and prevent front‑running or unauthorized verification.
summary:
There are several problems with the verifyUser function:
```solidity
function verifyUser(bytes memory _data, bytes memory _signature)
external {
    bytes32 _hash = ECDSA.toEthSignedMessageHash(keccak256(_data));
    require(
        ECDSA.recover(_hash, _signature) == signer,
        "Invalid signature"
    );
    isVerified[msg.sender] = true;
```
- The first is the use of ECDSA.verify method to validate the signature.
```solidity
require(
    ECDSA.recover(_hash, _signature) == signer,
    "Invalid signature"
);
```
to change it. The signer is set in the constructor by calling the internal _setSigner function and there is
no way to call it again and change it to another signer:
```solidity
constructor() ERC20("Molly", "MOLY") {
```
This will lead to the require statement always reverting and returning "Invalid signature".
- The second problem is that even if the above problem is fixed, anyone can front run the call with the
same input parameters and be verified. For example, user Bob calls the function with valid bytes
memory _data, bytes memory _signature parameters which will pass the require statement
and he will become verified. However, while the call is in the mempool, malicious user Alice sees the
transaction and calls the function with the same input parameters as Bob but with higher gas price.
This will result in Alice being a verified user even if she is not supposed to be.
- The third problem is that the function calls the ECDSA.toEthSignedMessageHash method.
However, in the latest OpenZeppelin version of the libraries, the toEthSignedMessageHash
method is part of the MessageHashUtils library which should be imported as well, as it is best
security practice to use the latest versions of OZ libraries as they are constantly updated and
optimized.

title: Users will not be able to claim tokens during AngelSale and PrivateSale
content: The vulnerability is a missing initialization of the Merkle tree roots that are used to verify token claim eligibility for AngelSale and PrivateSale participants. The contract declares two public variables, merkleRoot and privateMerkleRoot, but never assigns them a non‑zero value either in the constructor or through a setter function. As a result, both variables retain the default value bytes32(0). When a user calls claimAngelSale or claimPrivateSale, the function builds a leaf from the caller address and the claimed amount and then calls MerkleProof.verify with the supplied proof and the stored root. Because the stored root is zero, the verification always fails, causing the transaction to revert with the error message "Invalid proof!" even if the off‑chain proof is correct. This denial‑of‑service condition prevents any legitimate participant from receiving the tokens they purchased, breaking the core business logic that token allocations must be claimable after the sale. The issue manifests whenever a claim is attempted after deployment, affecting all AngelSale and PrivateSale users, as well as the protocol that relies on successful distribution for its token economics. It was discovered during a manual code audit that inspected the claim functions and noticed the absence of any setter or constructor assignment for the Merkle roots. The problem can be hard to notice because the claim functions appear syntactically correct and the revert message suggests an invalid proof rather than a configuration error. To remediate, the contract should initialise merkleRoot and privateMerkleRoot with the correct values at deployment or provide an access‑controlled function to set them before claims are allowed, and the claim logic should include a check that the root is non‑zero before attempting verification. This class of bug is a configuration‑or‑initialisation flaw that leads to a functional lockout of user funds, effectively making the allocated tokens disappear from the user’s perspective despite being held by the contract.

title: Funds may be stolen by calling onMoreFlashLoan() directly
content: An unauthorized external call vulnerability exists in the flash‑loan strategy contract. The function onMoreFlashLoan is intended to be invoked only by the market contract that coordinates flash‑loan cycles. However, the implementation does not contain any check of msg.sender, so any address can call the function directly. When called, the function releases the collateral that was previously locked for the flash‑loan operation to the caller without verifying that the caller is the legitimate market. An attacker can therefore trigger the function, receive the locked collateral, and the original borrower loses the assets. The bug manifests when a malicious actor sends a transaction that calls onMoreFlashLoan with arbitrary parameters; no prerequisite flash‑loan execution is required. The impact is a loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, because the protocol assumes that only the market can move collateral after a flash‑loan. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of flash‑loan related functions and noticed the missing require statement. Because the function name suggests internal use, the lack of an explicit access‑control modifier can be easy to overlook, especially if the function does not emit distinctive events. The vulnerability belongs to the class of missing access‑control or unauthorized external call bugs, which break the trust model of the contract. From a user perspective the symptom is that collateral disappears from their balance, or a refund that should be returned after a flash‑loan is missing, leading to a zero or reduced balance. The fix is to add a validation that the caller equals the market address (for example, using a require statement) or to restrict the function with an onlyMarket modifier, thereby ensuring that only the designated market contract can trigger the collateral release logic.
summary:
```solidity
LoopStrategy::onMoreFlashLoan() does not validate that the caller is the market, which allows attackers to steal collateral by calling it directly.
```

title: Malicious path can be passed to redeem/withdraw() allowing an attacker to draing the strategy
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted token swap path in the redeem/withdraw functions of a LoopStrategy contract. Because the contract does not validate that the path used for swapping sells and buys the same underlying token, an attacker can supply a malicious path that includes a reentrant token. When the withdraw call initiates a swap through this token, the token’s callback can re‑enter the strategy contract during the swap execution. The re‑entrancy occurs after the contract has already burned the caller’s shares but before the assets have been transferred out. By re‑entering, the attacker can deposit additional assets into the strategy while the withdrawal is still in progress, receiving inflated shares because the share accounting assumes no intermediate deposits. After the swap completes, the attacker redeems the artificially inflated shares for a larger amount of assets than originally deposited, effectively draining the strategy’s funds. This flaw manifests whenever redeem/withdraw is called with an arbitrary path that contains a token capable of invoking external code (for example, ERC777, ERC1363, or a custom token with a callback). The affected parties are the protocol that relies on the strategy for yield, any users who have deposited assets, and the vault that aggregates the strategy’s balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, which noted the missing path validation and the potential for re‑entrancy through a token swap. It can be hard to notice because the path parameter looks innocuous and the share‑burn‑then‑withdraw sequence appears correct on the surface, while the re‑entrancy side‑channel silently inflates share values. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted external call leading to re‑entrancy and accounting distortion”. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal withdrawal request, but after execution the user’s balance may be reduced to zero while the attacker’s balance increases dramatically, violating the expectation that a withdrawal returns exactly the deposited amount. To remediate, the contract should restrict the swap path to a whitelist that only contains the expected token pair, enforce that the input and output tokens are identical, and add a re‑entrancy guard or move the share‑burn operation after the asset transfer so that external calls cannot manipulate the accounting state during withdrawal.

title: Side effects of LTV = 0 assets: Morpho's users will not be able to withdraw (collateral and "pure" supply), borrow and liquidate
content: The vulnerability originates from the interaction between Morpho’s integration with Aave V3 and Aave’s loan‑to‑value (LTV) configuration for aTokens. When an aToken is configured with LTV = 0, Aave enforces additional safety checks that prevent any operation which would treat that token as collateral while the user has an outstanding borrow position. Morpho’s contracts assume that any supplied aToken can be freely withdrawn, transferred or marked as non‑collateral, regardless of its LTV value. Because Morpho holds the aToken in its internal wallet and does not provide a mechanism to unset the collateral flag for LTV‑zero assets, any attempt by a user to withdraw their supplied balance, move the token, or change its collateral status triggers Aave’s internal revert logic. Consequently, users of Morpho are unable to withdraw both collateral and “pure” supply, cannot open new borrow positions, cannot be liquidated, and may even fail to claim rewards if the reward token is an aToken with LTV = 0. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal balance, but when the withdraw or borrow button is pressed the transaction reverts silently, leaving the balance unchanged or showing an error message. The impact is that funds become effectively locked in the protocol and the core lending‑borrowing workflow is broken, which is especially severe for a protocol that advertises seamless supply‑borrow cycles. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by Spearbit, which highlighted that the edge case of LTV‑zero assets was not covered by Morpho’s collateral management logic. It is difficult to notice because the same aToken behaves correctly while its LTV is non‑zero, and the failure only appears after a governance change or market addition that sets LTV to zero, a situation that may not be exercised in routine testing. To remediate the problem Morpho should avoid creating markets for aTokens that have LTV = 0, or promptly pause and unwind any existing markets that become LTV‑zero. The unwind procedure must empty user balances, leave only a minimal collateral amount (e.g., one wei) to keep the reserve healthy, and set the reserve as non‑collateral to prevent further reverts. By ensuring that no aToken with zero LTV remains listed as an active market, Morpho can restore the expected withdraw, borrow, liquidation and reward‑claim functionality.
summary:
When an AToken has LTV = 0, Aave restricts the usage of some operations. In particular, if the user owns at least one AToken as collateral that has LTV = 0, operations could revert.
1) Withdraw: if the asset withdrawn is collateral, the user is borrowing something, the operation will revert if the withdrawn collateral is an AToken with LTV > 0.
2) Transfer: if the from is using the asset as collateral, is borrowing something and the asset transferred is an AToken with LTV > 0 the operation will revert.
3) Set the reserve of an AToken as not collateral: if the AToken you are trying to set as non-collateral is an AToken with LTV > 0 the operation will revert.
Note that all those checks are done on top of the "normal" checks that would usually prevent an operation, depending on the operation itself (like, for example, an HF check).
While a "normal" Aave user could simply withdraw, transfer or set that asset as non-collateral, Morpho, with the current implementation, cannot do it. Because of the impossibility to remove from the Morpho wallet the "poisoned AToken", part of the Morpho mechanics will break.
• Morpho's users could not be able to withdraw both collateral and "pure" supply
• Morpho's users could not be able to borrow
• Morpho's users could not be able to liquidate
• Morpho's users could not be able to claim rewards via claimRewards if one of those rewards is an AToken with LTV > 0

title: Morpho is vulnerable to attackers sending LTV = 0 collateral tokens, supply/supplyCollateral, borrow and liquidate operations could stop working
content: The vulnerability is a collateral‑handling flaw that arises when Morpho interacts with Aave V3 and receives an aToken whose loan‑to‑value (LTV) parameter is set to zero. Aave treats any aToken deposited as collateral, but it also blocks a set of operations—withdraw, transfer, and the ability to mark the asset as non‑collateral—whenever the underlying aToken has LTV = 0. Morpho’s internal logic assumes that any token it holds can be withdrawn or transferred without additional checks, so when a zero‑LTV aToken is inadvertently added to Morpho’s wallet, every subsequent call that tries to move or modify that token reverts. An attacker can exploit this by supplying an underlying asset that maps to a zero‑LTV aToken and transferring it to the Morpho contract. Because the victim does not own that asset, Morpho automatically registers it as collateral; the protocol then cannot remove the “poisoned” token, causing supply, borrow, liquidation and reward‑claim functions to fail. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that withdrawals return no funds, borrowing attempts are rejected, liquidation transactions revert, and reward claims yield zero even though the user is entitled to rewards. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on core financial operations for any user of the affected Morpho market, effectively freezing assets and preventing normal protocol usage. The issue occurs only when a zero‑LTV aToken becomes part of Morpho’s collateral set, which can happen at any time an attacker is able to transfer such a token to the contract. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit by Spearbit, where the auditors traced the Aave collateral checks and identified the missing validation for zero‑LTV assets. It is hard to notice because zero‑LTV assets are uncommon and the reverts happen only in edge‑case paths that are not exercised in typical testing. To remediate the problem Morpho should add explicit validation that rejects or safely isolates zero‑LTV aTokens as collateral, allow the DAO to mark such assets as non‑collateral, and provide a controlled withdrawal or transfer mechanism that does not rely on Aave’s blocked operations. In broader terms the bug belongs to the class of “collateral‑state inconsistency” or “asset‑poisoning” vulnerabilities where a protocol’s assumptions about asset properties are violated, leading to unexpected reverts and loss of functionality.
summary:
When an AToken has LTV = 0, Aave restricts the usage of some operations. In particular, if the user owns at least one AToken as collateral that has LTV = 0, these operations could revert
1) Withdraw: if the asset withdrawn is collateral, the user is borrowing something, the operation will revert if the withdrawn collateral is an AToken with LTV > 0
2) Transfer: if the from is using the asset as collateral, is borrowing something and the asset transferred is an AToken with LTV > 0 the operation will revert
3) Set the reserve of an AToken as not collateral: if the AToken you are trying to set as non-collateral is an AToken with LTV > 0 the operation will revert
Note that all those checks are done on top of the "normal" checks that would usually prevent an operation, depending on the operation itself (like, for example, an HF check).
In the attack scenario, the bad actor could simply supply an underlying that is associated with an LTV = 0 AToken and transfer it to the Morpho contract. If the victim does not own any balance of the asset, it will be set as collateral and the victim will suffer from all the side effects previously explained.
While a "normal" Aave user could simply withdraw, transfer or set that asset as non-collateral, Morpho, with the current implementation, cannot do it. Because of the impossibility to remove from the Morpho wallet the "poisoned AToken", part of the Morpho mechanics will break.
• Morpho's users could not be able to withdraw both collateral and "pure" supply.
• Morpho's users could not be able to borrow.
• Morpho's users could not be able to liquidate.
• Morpho's users could not be able to claim rewards via claimRewards if one of those rewards is an AToken with LTV > 0.

title: Morpho is not correctly handling the asset price in _getAssetPrice when isInEMode == true but priceSource is addres(0)
content: The vulnerability resides in the internal price‑retrieval routine used by Morpho when a user is operating in e‑mode. The function _getAssetPrice receives a flag indicating e‑mode participation, a reference to the Aave oracle, and an address that should point to the e‑mode specific price source. The current implementation first checks the e‑mode flag and, if true, unconditionally queries the oracle with the supplied priceSource address. When the e‑mode price source has not been configured, the address is the zero address. Because the code does not verify that priceSource is non‑zero before invoking oracle.getAssetPrice, the call is forwarded to the oracle with address(0). Depending on the oracle’s internal fallback logic, this may return a zero price, a price from a generic fallback oracle, or cause the call to revert if the fallback oracle does not support the asset. Consequently, Morpho diverges from Aave’s reference behavior, where the underlying asset price is always used when no explicit e‑mode oracle is set. The root cause is a missing validation of the priceSource parameter, leading to an unintended oracle selection path. An attacker or a misconfigured user can trigger the faulty path simply by being in e‑mode while the protocol’s e‑mode oracle is unset. The exploit consists of initiating any operation that relies on asset pricing—such as liquidation, collateral withdrawal, or borrowing—while the flag is true. The oracle will then supply an incorrect price (often zero) or revert, causing the price computation to fail. The impact includes transaction reverts that break liquidations, prevent borrowers from withdrawing collateral, or allow borrowers to avoid liquidation because the protocol perceives their health factor as higher than it actually is. Users experience symptoms like “price computation error”, unexpected transaction failures, or seeing their collateral locked with no apparent reason. The issue is discovered during a security audit that compared Morpho’s logic with Aave’s official implementation and identified the discrepancy. It is hard to notice because a zero address may still yield a fallback price, making the bug subtle until a failure occurs in a critical operation. The appropriate remediation is to guard the e‑mode price retrieval: only use the e‑mode price when both isInEMode is true and priceSource is a valid non‑zero address; otherwise fall back to the underlying asset price. This class of bug falls under improper validation of external address parameters leading to incorrect oracle selection and price miscalculation, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that asset prices must be deterministic and consistent across all operations.

title: Isolated assets are treated as collateral in Morpho
content: The vulnerability consists of Morpho incorrectly marking assets that are designated as isolated on the Aave v3 protocol as usable collateral within Morpho’s own accounting. In Aave, isolated assets are subject to strict isolation mode: a borrower may supply such an asset as collateral only if no other non‑isolated assets are already being used as collateral, and borrowing against it is limited by a per‑asset debt ceiling. Morpho’s supplyCollateral function assumes that any successful call to the Aave pool’s supplyToPool method automatically registers the supplied token as collateral on Aave. When a user supplies an isolated asset while already having other collateral, Aave accepts the supply for yield generation but deliberately does not set the asset as collateral. Morpho, however, records the asset as collateral and permits the user to borrow any other token against it, bypassing the isolation ceiling. This mismatch can be exploited by a malicious borrower who first supplies an isolated token together with other collateral, then initiates a borrow against the isolated token through Morpho. Because Aave does not recognise the isolated token as collateral, the Morpho‑Aave position’s health factor is calculated without the protective isolation constraints, potentially dropping below safe levels and triggering liquidation on Aave while the borrowed funds remain in Morpho. The impact is that funds supplied by honest users may be liquidated without warning, and the protocol may suffer loss of capital due to under‑collateralised loans. The issue manifests whenever a supplyCollateral transaction involves an isolated asset while the user already has non‑isolated collateral, a scenario that can occur in normal user flows. All participants who interact with Morpho’s supplyCollateral feature and use isolated assets are affected, including lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that compared Morphi’s internal collateral bookkeeping with Aave’s isolation mode specifications, revealing the inconsistency. It is subtle because the transaction succeeds on Aave and the UI shows a normal supply, so users do not see an error, while the internal state diverges silently. To remediate, Morpho should either reject isolated assets in supplyCollateral calls when the user already has other collateral, or verify after each supplyToPool call that the asset is indeed registered as collateral on Aave before allowing any borrowing against it. Conceptually, this is a cross‑protocol state‑synchronisation bug where one contract assumes another’s state transition without explicit confirmation, leading to a violation of the isolated‑asset collateral model and breaking the accounting invariants that guarantee that borrowed value is always backed by sufficient collateral.
summary:
Aave-v3 introduced isolation assets and isolation mode for users:
"Borrowers supplying an isolated asset as collateral cannot supply other assets as collateral (though they can still supply to capture yield). Only stablecoins that have been permitted by Aave governance to be borrowable in isolation the mode can be borrowed by users utilizing isolated collateral up to a specified debt ceiling."
The Morpho contract is intended not to be in isolation mode to avoid its restrictions. Supplying an isolated asset to Aave while there are already other (non-isolated) assets set as collateral will simply supply the asset to earn yield without setting it as collateral. However, Morpho will still set these isolated assets as collateral for the supplying user. Morpho users can borrow any asset against them which should not be possible:
• Isolated assets are by definition riskier when used as collateral and should only allow borrowing up to a specific debt ceiling.
• The borrows are not backed on Aave as the isolated asset is not treated as collateral there, lowering the Morpho Aave position's health factor and putting the system at risk of liquidation on Aave.

title: Wrong P2P exchange rate calculation
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect arithmetic ordering in the calculation of the peer‑to‑peer (P2P) exchange rate used by the protocol. Instead of scaling the delta by the pool index and then dividing by the P2P rate, the implementation first divides the delta by the pool index and multiplies by the P2P rate. This reversal of multiplication and division produces a share of the delta that is off by a factor of the pool index squared over the P2P rate squared, leading to systematically wrong P2P rates whenever a supply or borrow delta is present. The root cause is a simple but critical mistake in the formula: the operations .rayDiv(_poolIndex).rayMul(_p2pRate) were used where .rayMul(_poolIndex).rayDiv(_p2pRate) is required. Because the rates are used throughout all markets to determine how much a lender receives or a borrower pays, the error propagates to every transaction that involves a non‑zero delta. An attacker can exploit this by creating or triggering large deltas, causing the protocol to quote overly favorable rates to the attacker while other participants receive less favorable terms, effectively extracting value from the system. The impact is that users may see lower returns on supplied assets, higher costs on borrowed assets, or outright loss of expected profit, which from a UI perspective appears as “my balance didn’t increase”, “my repayment cost is higher than advertised”, or “the exchange rate shown is wrong”. The bug manifests only when the delta variables are non‑zero, i.e., during normal market activity, making it hard to notice because the rates still look plausible and no transaction reverts. It was discovered during a formal security audit (Spearbit) by reviewing the mathematical expressions used for rate computation. The issue violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the P2P rate accurately reflects the proportion of the delta between pool and peer participants. To remediate, the formula must be reordered so that the delta is first multiplied by the pool index and then divided by the P2P rate, and the resulting share must be adjusted accordingly, as shown in the recommended code snippet. This correction restores the intended economic behavior and prevents mispricing attacks.
summary: _p2pDelta is divided by _poolIndex and multiplied by _p2pRate, nevertheless it should have been multiplied by _poolIndex and divided by _p2pRate to compute the correct share of the delta. This leads to wrong P2P rates throughout all markets if supply / borrow delta is involved.

title: MatchingEngineForAave is using the wrong totalSupply in updateBorrowers
content: The vulnerability resides in the MatchingEngineForAave contract where the function that updates borrower reward allocations queries the total supply of the wrong token. Instead of reading the scaled total supply of the variable debt token that represents the amount actually borrowed, the code uses the address of the AToken (the interest‑bearing token) and calls its scaledTotalSupply. Because the AToken total supply reflects the total amount deposited, not the total debt, the reward calculation is based on an inflated or otherwise incorrect figure. This mismatch occurs whenever the updateBorrowers routine is executed, which is the core point where the protocol distributes incentive tokens to borrowers. As a result, users may receive reward amounts that do not correspond to their real borrowing position – for example, a user who has borrowed a small amount could be granted rewards proportional to the entire pool’s deposit balance. The impact is economic: the protocol’s reward pool can be drained or its accounting become inconsistent, undermining the incentive model and potentially harming other participants. The bug is subtle because the reward token balances still change in a plausible direction, making the error hard to spot without inspecting which token’s supply is used. It was uncovered during a formal security audit performed by Spearbit, which identified the logical flaw in the token address selection. To remediate the issue, the contract should retrieve the variable debt token address from the lending pool’s reserve data and then query its scaledTotalSupply, ensuring that reward distribution aligns with the actual debt outstanding. This correction restores proper accounting, prevents over‑allocation of rewards, and aligns the system with its intended business logic of rewarding borrowers proportionally to their debt.
summary: _poolTokenAddress is referencing AToken so the totalStaked would be the total supply of the AToken. In this case, the totalStaked should reference the total supply of the DebtToken, otherwise the user would be rewarded for a wrong amount of reward.

title: RewardsManagerAave does not verify token addresses
content: The vulnerability resides in the public function that accrues unclaimed rewards for a user in the Morpho‑Aave integration. The function accepts an arbitrary list of token addresses and, for each address, determines whether the token is a variable‑debt token (vToken) or, by default, treats it as the corresponding aToken. This logic omits any verification that the supplied address is actually an aToken; consequently a stable‑debt token (sToken) can be passed. Because the reward index for an sToken is never initialized in the Morpho reward accounting, the contract calculates a reward delta using the user’s supply balance against a zero or stale index, which results in an artificially large reward amount. An attacker can exploit this by first supplying a large amount of the underlying asset for which an sToken reward is defined, then invoking accrueUserUnclaimedRewards with the sToken address, causing the contract to credit the attacker with unearned rewards. The attacker can immediately claim those rewards through the PositionManager.claimRewards function and withdraw the originally supplied tokens, all within a single transaction. The impact is a theft of unclaimed rewards from every position that holds the affected asset, effectively draining the incentive pool and reducing the expected earnings of honest users. The flaw manifests whenever the public accrueUserUnclaimedRewards function is called with a token address that is not the variable‑debt token, because the code assumes any other token must be the aToken. All users of the Morpho protocol who hold positions in the affected reserve are potential victims, while any external actor who can call the function can act as the attacker. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, where the logical assumption about token types was identified as missing validation. It can be difficult to notice because the function does not revert on unexpected token addresses and the reward calculations appear correct for supported tokens, so the loss of rewards may only be observed after the attacker has already withdrawn them. The recommended remediation is to explicitly verify that each asset address is either the aToken or the variable‑debt token of the reserve, rejecting any other address with a clear error. This input validation prevents the reward calculation from being performed on unsupported token types and restores the integrity of the reward accounting. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that rewards that should have been accrued remain at zero or disappear after a claim, contrary to the expectation that supplying assets generates proportional rewards. The bug belongs to the class of improper input validation and asset‑type confusion, where unchecked token addresses enable manipulation of accounting formulas and lead to unauthorized reward extraction.
summary:
Aave has 3 different types of tokens: aToken, stable debt token and variable debt token (a/s/vToken). Aave’s incentive controller can define rewards for all of them but Morpho never uses a stable-rate borrows token (sToken). The public accrueUserUnclaimedRewards function allows passing arbitrary token addresses for which to accrue user rewards. Current code assumes that if the token is not the variable debt token, then it must be the aToken, and uses the user’s supply balance for the reward calculation as follows:
```solidity
uint256 stakedByUser = reserve.variableDebtTokenAddress == asset
    ? positionsManager.borrowBalanceInOf(reserve.aTokenAddress, _user).onPool
    : positionsManager.supplyBalanceInOf(reserve.aTokenAddress, _user).onPool;
```
An attacker can accrue rewards by passing in an sToken address and steal from the contract, i.e:
• Attacker supplies a large amount of tokens for which sToken rewards are defined.
• The aToken reward index is updated to the latest index but the sToken index is not initialized.
• Attacker calls accrueUserUnclaimedRewards([sToken]), which will compute the difference between the current Aave reward index and user’s sToken index, then multiply it by their supply balance.
• The user accumulated rewards in userUnclaimedRewards[user] can be withdrawn by calling PositionManager.claimRewards([sToken, ...]).
• Attacker withdraws their supplied tokens again.
The abovementioned steps can be performed in one single transaction to steal unclaimed rewards from all Morpho positions.

title: Wrong token transfer in executeWithdrawal()
content: During a withdrawal request the contract's executeWithdrawal function is supposed to transfer the user's deposited DAI or sDAI token. Instead the implementation uses a low‑level call with a value field that sends native Ether equal to the stored amount. Because the contract never receives Ether, the call always reverts, triggering the error handling path and leaving the withdrawal marked as unexecuted. As a result the user's token balance remains recorded in the contract's internal mapping but cannot be retrieved, effectively locking the funds. The bug originates from a copy‑paste or misunderstanding of the token transfer mechanism, treating an ERC‑20 token amount as if it were an Ether amount. An attacker does not need to be malicious; any legitimate user invoking executeWithdrawal will experience a failed transfer and loss of access to their tokens. The impact is that users see no tokens arrive in their wallet, the UI may show a successful withdrawal event while the actual asset never moves, and the protocol's accounting becomes inconsistent because the internal ledger still credits the user while the external token balance is unchanged. The condition occurs whenever the strategyExecutor calls executeWithdrawal, which is the only authorized caller, so the bug is triggered in normal operation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended token transfer logic with the actual low‑level call. It can be hard to notice because the function emits a WithdrawalCompleted event, giving the impression of success, and the revert path only surfaces when the call fails, which may be masked by the contract not holding Ether. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect asset transfer or misuse of value field for token transfers. To fix the issue the function should invoke the ERC‑20 token's transfer (or safeTransfer) method with the stored token address and amount, and remove the value‑based call. Proper checks should ensure the contract holds the token balance before attempting the transfer, and events should be emitted only after a successful token transfer.

title: Incorrect reward calculation due to decimal handling
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic mis‑handling of token decimals in the reward calculation function. The function computes a user’s asset balance by multiplying the ERC20 token balance with a conversion factor that already returns a value expressed with 18 decimal places, but it fails to scale the result back down, effectively leaving an extra factor of 1e18 in the numerator. This root cause originates from treating a value that is already in wei‑scale as if it were a plain integer, and then using it directly in a subtraction that determines the reward amount. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug simply by calling the view function or by triggering a deposit that reads the inflated reward value; the contract will report a reward that is up to 1e18 times larger than the true amount. The impact is that the reported reward inflates the share price used by downstream deposit contracts, causing early depositors to receive fewer shares than they should while later depositors are charged an artificially high price. Consequently, early participants gain an unfair financial advantage and later participants may lose value, effectively stealing value from them. The condition for the bug to manifest is when the computed assetBalance exceeds the net strategy balance, which is the typical case for a profitable strategy. All users who interact with the reward‑distribution logic, as well as the protocol’s overall accounting, are affected because the inflated rewards break the fundamental accounting invariant that total shares must represent the underlying assets. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted an unexpected multiplication by a conversion function without a corresponding division, a pattern that is easy to miss because the code compiles and the function is view‑only, giving a false sense of safety. From a user perspective the symptoms are confusing: a depositor sees a dramatically higher reward amount, the UI may display a huge “pending reward” number, yet the actual token balance does not increase accordingly; later users may notice that their deposited amount yields fewer shares than advertised, or that the protocol’s share price appears unusually high. The bug belongs to the class of decimal‑handling or scaling errors, where mismatched units cause arithmetic overflow or under‑flow in financial calculations. To remediate the issue the conversion result should be divided by 1e18 (or the multiplication should be performed with properly scaled values) before it is used in the reward subtraction, thereby restoring correct unit consistency and preventing reward inflation.

title: Inaccurate share price due to lack of withdrawal tracking
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the deposit contracts that manage ETH and stable‑coin shares. When a user withdraws funds the contracts do not update the withdrawal counters (ethWithdrawn / stableWithdrawn) nor the total amount of minted shares (nETHMinted, nUSDMinted). Because the share price is calculated from the expression (total assets = ethDeposited - ethWithdrawn + rewardsClaimed) divided by the total minted shares, the omission causes the withdrawn amount to remain counted as part of the pool. Consequently the share price is artificially lowered after a withdrawal, so later depositors receive a larger number of shares for the same amount of ETH, and when they later redeem those shares they obtain more ETH than they should. The root cause is a missing state update in the withdrawal routine: the contract burns the appropriate number of shares and increments the withdrawn amount, but the code only records the withdrawal request and never adjusts the global counters. This can be exploited by a malicious or even honest user who simply withdraws and then allows other users to deposit; the subsequent users will be over‑compensated, effectively stealing rewards that belong to the original withdrawer. The impact is a breach of the fundamental invariant that total shares represent an exact proportion of total assets, leading to misallocation of rewards, potential loss of funds for the protocol, and confusing user experiences such as receiving more ETH than deposited or seeing their balance disappear while the share price still reflects the withdrawn amount. The bug manifests whenever a withdrawal is processed, affecting all participants in the pool, especially later depositors. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the share‑price update function and noticed that ethWithdrawn and nETHMinted were never modified in the withdrawal path. The issue is hard to notice because the share‑price variable updates normally and no explicit error is emitted; the discrepancy only becomes apparent after several deposit‑withdraw cycles. To remediate, the withdrawal logic must be extended to increment ethWithdrawn (or stableWithdrawn) by the withdrawn amount and decrement the corresponding minted‑share counter by the number of shares being burned. Additionally, care must be taken to handle integer‑division precision to avoid leftover dust in the share accounting. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of ledger‑state‑inconsistency or missing‑state‑update vulnerabilities, where a contract’s internal accounting diverges from the actual token balances, violating business logic that assumes accurate proportional ownership of pooled assets.
summary:
The DepositETH and DepositUSD contracts fail to update the withdrawal counters (ethWithdrawn / stableWithdrawn) and shares (nETHMinted, nUSDMinted) when processing withdrawals. This leads to incorrect accounting because the share price will be calculated by including the portion of withdrawn funds in the total balance.
```solidity
function _updateSharePrice(uint256 _rewardsEarned) internal {
    rewardsClaimed += _rewardsEarned;
    uint256 totalEthBalance = (ethDeposited - ethWithdrawn + rewardsClaimed);
    if(nETHMinted == 0){
        sharePrice = BASE_POINT;
    } else {
        sharePrice = (nETHMinted) * BASE_POINT / (ethDeposited - ethWithdrawn + rewardsClaimed);
    }
    emit SharePriceUpdated(sharePrice);
}
```
This can lead to incorrect share price calculations, causing new depositors to receive fewer rewards, as the shares include withdrawn funds from the account of a previous withdrawer.
Let's consider this scenario:
Initial State:
sharePrice = 1e18
All balances = 0 ETH
Alice Deposits 1 ETH:
Gets 1e18 shares
ethDeposited = 1e18
nETHMinted = 1e18
System Earns 0.05 ETH Reward:
rewardsClaimed = 5e16 (0.05 ETH)
totalEthBalance = 1.05 ETH
sharePrice updates = 1e18 * 1e18 / 1.05 ETH = ~0.952e18
Alice Withdraws Everything:
Withdraws ~1.05 ETH (original + rewards)
But shares and ethWithdrawn not updated
sharePrice calculation still includes withdrawn amount
Carol Deposits 1 ETH:
Gets 0.952e18 shares: nETHShares = 1e18 * 0.952e18 / 1e18 = 0.952e18
nETHMinted += 0.952e18 = 1.952e18
ethDeposited += 1e18 = 2e18
CAROL_SHARES = 0.952e18
System Earns Another 0.05 ETH Reward:
rewardEarned = 5e16 (0.05 ETH)
rewardClaimed += 5e16 = 1e17
totalEthBalance = ethDeposited - ethWithdrawn + rewardClaimed
totalEthBalance = 2e18 - 0 + 1e17 = 2.1e18
New sharePrice = 1.952e18 * 1e18 / 2.1e18 = 0.929e18
Carol Claims Withdrawal:
withdrawAmount = 0.952e18 * 1e18 / 0.929e18 = 1.024e18
Carol receives 1.024 ETH for her 1 ETH deposit, even though she should have received all rewards because she held all available shares.

title: Protocol assets can be stolen through sandwich attacks
content: The Capsule contract allows users to swap assets and manage liquidity through functions that query the current pool state on‑chain to calculate a slippage bound. The vulnerability arises because the contract determines the minimum acceptable amount (expectedAmount) using the pool’s instantaneous price and then enforces a slippage check based on that same on‑chain value. An attacker can observe a pending transaction that calls a swap such as tradeCRVtoWETH, then submit a large front‑run transaction that deliberately skews the pool’s price, causing the contract’s on‑chain price query to return a much lower expected amount. When the victim’s transaction executes, it receives far fewer WETH than anticipated, satisfying the flawed slippage check because the lower bound was already manipulated. Immediately after the victim’s trade, the attacker can execute a back‑run transaction that restores the pool price, completing a classic sandwich attack. This sequence results in the protocol losing assets: the user receives less output than expected, sometimes effectively zero, and the attacker profits from the price differential. The issue occurs whenever the contract calls pool methods such as add_liquidity, remove_liquidity_one_coin, calc_withdraw_one_coin, or calc_token_amount and relies on on‑chain calculations for slippage tolerance. It affects any user interacting with the Capsule contract, the protocol’s overall asset pool, and any role that depends on accurate accounting of swaps and liquidity operations. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the slippage logic and identified that the on‑chain price can be manipulated within the same transaction. The problem is subtle because the contract includes explicit slippage checks, giving a false sense of safety, and the price manipulation happens atomically, making it hard to detect from transaction logs alone. To remediate, the contract should stop performing on‑chain price queries for slippage limits and instead require callers to supply an off‑chain calculated minimum amount (e.g., a minAmountReceived parameter) that cannot be altered by a malicious front‑runner. This moves the trust to an external price oracle or off‑chain calculation and eliminates the attack surface where an attacker can influence the price used for the slippage check. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of price‑manipulation or sandwich‑attack vulnerabilities caused by reliance on mutable on‑chain state for critical economic checks, leading to unexpected loss of funds and violation of the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary:
The Capsule contract is currently vulnerable to sandwich attack in many
places. Every place which does a swap or provides/removes liquidity is done in
a manner that is vulnerable. While the code has slippage checks, they are
flawed. Take for example the tradeCRVtoWETH method, here is how a swap is
done:
uint256 expectedAmount = curvePoolWETHCRV.get_dy(2, 1, crvBal); // Estimate WETH received for CRV:WETH exchange
// Exchange CRV for WETH within the slippage limit
curvePoolWETHCRV.exchange(2, 1, crvBal, expectedAmount * LPslippageNum / LPslippageDen);
The problem is that if an attacker sees you calling tradeCRVtoWETH he can
imbalance the pool with a very big front-run transaction, which will give you a
much smaller expectedAmount, and then after you do the swap he will execute
a back-run transaction putting the price back to normal, essentially
sandwiching your bad trade and profiting your loss. This is a problem in all
methods that have an underlying call to add_liquidity,
remove_liquidity_one_coin, calc_withdraw_one_coin and
calc_token_amount.

title: Polygon chain reorgs will often change game results
content: The vulnerability is that the contract uses a fixed confirmation count of 3 when requesting randomness from Chainlink VRF. Polygon frequently experiences chain reorganizations deeper than three blocks, meaning that the block containing the VRF request can be replaced after the randomness has been delivered. Because the contract trusts the randomness as final after only three confirmations, a reorg can cause the VRF output to change, which in turn changes the winner of the lootbox game. This happens whenever a reorg depth exceeds the configured confirmation threshold, which on Polygon can be as high as 156 blocks in extreme cases and more than five times per day with depth greater than three. Users are affected because they see a winning item displayed in the UI, but after the reorg the recorded winner is different or the reward is not transferred, leading to missing balances or zero‑value loot. The audit discovered the issue by analysing the README that targets Polygon and by measuring recent reorg statistics, revealing that the chosen confirmation value is insufficient for the network’s finality characteristics. The problem is hard to notice because the randomness appears correct at the moment of receipt and the UI does not indicate that the underlying block may be reverted, so the discrepancy only becomes visible later when the reward is not delivered. The root cause is an under‑estimation of the required finality margin for the randomness source, a classic case of insufficient confirmation depth leading to reorg‑sensitive logic. To remediate, the contract should increase the REQUEST_CONFIRMATIONS parameter to a value that exceeds the observed maximum reorg depth on Polygon, such as 60 confirmations, thereby ensuring that the randomness is settled on a block that is highly unlikely to be reorganized. This adjustment restores the guarantee that the random outcome is immutable, aligns with the business rule that a lootbox result must be final, and prevents the loss of user trust and potential financial loss.
summary:
The REQUEST_CONFIRMATION constant in VRFv2Consumer is set to 3. This value
is used to tell the Chainlink VRF service how much blocks do you want to wait
at a minimum before receiving randomness. The reason this value was added is
because of chain reorganizations - when this event happens, blocks and
transactions get reorganized and they change. This is a serious problem in this
application as it is expected to be launched on Polygon (mentioned in
README.md), but as we can see here there are more than 5 block
reorganizations a day with depth that is more than 3 blocks. In this article we
can even see a recent event where there was a 156 block depth chain reorg on
Polygon. This means that it is possible that often the winner of a lootbox game
to be changed since when your transaction for requesting randomness from
VRF is moved to a different block then the randomness will change as well.

title: reduceOnly limit order update does not take into account that a new amm may be selected, which may lead to loss of funds
content: The vulnerability is a state‑management flaw in the limit‑order update routine of a perpetual AMM protocol. When a trader modifies a limit order through the internal function that updates the order, the code does not correctly handle the situation where the order is reassigned to a different AMM while the reduceOnly flag is true or changes state. The root cause is that the update logic only considers the reduceOnly flag transition but ignores the possibility that the AMM identifier stored with the order may also change, resulting in the order remaining linked to the old AMM or being removed from the wrong AMM. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit this by submitting a limit‑order update that switches the AMM and toggles the reduceOnly flag from true to false (or keeps it true). In that scenario the contract removes the order from the newly selected AMM instead of the original one, leaving the previously locked WETH in the contract without an associated order. Consequently the trader’s balance is reduced because the protocol pulls WETH to satisfy the order, but the order is later deleted, so the funds become inaccessible and appear to disappear. The impact is loss of user funds, broken accounting, and a mismatch between the UI (which may still display the order) and the on‑chain state (where the funds are locked with no order to claim). This condition occurs only during a limit‑order update where the AMM reference changes while reduceOnly is true or transitions from true to false, affecting any user who relies on reduceOnly protection for their positions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, who noted that the update routine does not link the order to the new AMM nor correctly unlink it from the previous AMM. Because the bug does not emit an explicit error and the UI may still show the order, it can be hard to notice until funds are missing. The appropriate remediation is to redesign the update logic so that it always re‑associates the order with the currently selected AMM and removes the order from the previously associated AMM, handling all combinations of reduceOnly flag changes. In generic terms this is a cross‑entity reference inconsistency or improper state synchronization bug, where the contract’s internal bookkeeping of order‑to‑AMM relationships is out of sync with user expectations, violating the protocol’s accounting invariants and leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds.
summary:
On a limit order update, in _updateLimitOrder(), changing amm is not being taken into account. The following scenarios are possible:
- if reduceOnly remains false, no problem
- if reduceOnly goes from false to true, no problem
- if reduceOnly remains true, it won't link the reduceOnly order in the new amm B, nor remove it from amm A
- if reduceOnly goes from true to false, it will remove the linked order from the new amm B, instead of the old amm A. This seems the worst scenario, as updating the limit order from false to true will pull weth from the trader, but this order may be deleted if the trader closes its position on amm A, losing the funds.

title: Anyone can re-mint a token that was burned by the owner
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized re‑mint of an NFT that has been burned by its owner. The contract uses a _beforeTokenTransfer hook that only permits token transfers (including minting) when the caller is the designated beacon contract, unless the token is marked as locked. By default new tokens are locked, so the hook blocks any non‑beacon caller from creating or moving a token. However, the burn function allows the owner to destroy a token regardless of its lock status and, when the token is unlocked, it calls the internal _burn routine without resetting the lock flag. After the burn, the token no longer exists on‑chain but its lock state remains unlocked. Because the hook checks the lock flag to decide whether to enforce the beacon restriction, an unlocked, non‑existent token bypasses the check, allowing any address to invoke a mint operation for the same token identifier. An attacker can therefore call the minting function (or any transfer that creates the token) and obtain ownership of a token ID that the original owner thought was permanently destroyed. The impact is a breach of the uniqueness guarantee of the NFT collection: unauthorized parties can recreate burned tokens, potentially usurping value, confusing marketplaces, and breaking accounting assumptions that a burned token is permanently removed. The issue manifests only when a token is burned while unlocked; locked tokens remain protected because the hook still rejects non‑beacon callers. Users, token owners, and any downstream applications that rely on the immutability of burned NFTs are affected. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the lock‑state logic and the burn routine, noting that the lock flag was never restored after a burn of an unlocked token. It can be hard to notice because the contract appears to enforce a strict beacon‑only minting policy, and the default locked state gives a false sense of safety for non‑existent tokens. To remediate, the burn function should explicitly reset the token’s lock status to locked (or another safe default) after destroying an unlocked token, or the _beforeTokenTransfer hook should enforce the beacon restriction regardless of the lock flag for tokens that do not currently exist. This ensures that once a token is burned, it cannot be recreated by arbitrary callers, preserving the intended scarcity and ownership model.

title: NFTR-1 | Two Names For One Token
content: The vulnerability is a stale‑mapping bug in the name‑to‑token registry of the NFT marketplace. When a name is transferred to an NFT that already has an assigned name, the contract updates the tokenByName mapping for the incoming name but fails to clear the entry that previously pointed to the target NFT’s original name. As a result the same token identifier becomes reachable through two distinct names. This occurs because the transfer logic does not invoke the releaseTokenByName routine that would deregister the old name, leaving the old mapping entry untouched. An attacker or any user can exploit the flaw by moving a name onto a token that already owns a different name; after the transfer both names resolve to the same token address. Consequently a buyer who pays for a specific name (for example "Bob") may receive a different NFT that carries the other name ("Alice"), leading to a mismatch between expected and actual assets. The impact includes user confusion, potential loss of funds if the buyer assumes they own the purchased name, and a breach of the marketplace’s accounting guarantees that each name uniquely identifies a single token. The condition is triggered whenever the name‑transfer function is called on a token that already has a name, without first clearing the previous name entry. All participants who rely on name uniqueness – token owners, marketplace users, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state‑transition logic of the name registry and identified that the old name entry was never removed. It can be hard to notice because the UI may still display both names as owned by the same address, and no explicit error is emitted; the duplicate mapping silently violates the one‑name‑one‑token invariant. To remediate, the contract should always deregister the existing name of the target token before assigning a new one, for example by calling releaseTokenByName, and should enforce a check that prevents a token from being associated with more than one name at any time. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a stale reference or duplicate identifier vulnerability, where outdated entries remain in a lookup table, breaking the integrity of the system’s naming and ownership model. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after purchasing a name they receive an NFT with a different name, or they see two names pointing to the same token, contrary to the expectation that each name uniquely maps to a distinct NFT.
summary:
Names could be transferred to an NFT with an existing name but the tokenByName mapping still contains the overwritten name pointing to the NFT. As a result, two different names may point to the same NFT. Consider the following scenario:  
1) Alice owns an NFT with name “Alice”  
2) Bob owns an NFT with name “Bob”  
3) Name “Alice” is transferred to Bob’s NFT  
4) tokenByName is updated to reflect that “Alice” points to Bob’s NFT.  
5) tokenByName still has an entry for name “Bob” also pointing to Bob’s NFT.  
6) It now appears that Bob is now the owner of both names “Bob” and “Alice”.  
7) A user purchases name “Bob” but ends up receiving name “Alice” upon transfer.

title: NMKT-1 | No Bids Can Be Entered
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the marketplace contract attempts to place the first bid. The contract stores the current highest bid in a struct that contains a collection address and a tokenId. When no bids have been entered, these fields contain their default values: the collection address is address(0) and the tokenId is 0. The contract unconditionally calls an external function getOwner(collection, tokenId) to verify the ownership of the existing bid. Because address(0) does not implement the ERC‑721 interface, the call to ownerOf reverts, causing the entire bid‑placement transaction to fail. As a result, no user can ever submit the initial bid, effectively locking the marketplace and preventing any trading activity. The root cause is the assumption that an existing bid always exists and the lack of a guard that bypasses the ownership check when the stored collection address is zero. The issue was discovered during an audit when the tester attempted to submit a bid on a freshly deployed contract and observed an immediate revert without any explicit error message. It can be hard to notice because default struct values are often considered harmless, yet the external call to a non‑existent contract triggers a low‑level failure. The impact is critical: users cannot place bids, funds that might have been deposited for bidding remain unusable, and the protocol’s core functionality is broken, violating the business logic that a marketplace must accept the first offer. To remediate, the contract should detect the empty‑bid state (e.g., collection == address(0)) and skip the ownership verification, or initialize the bid struct with a sentinel that is explicitly handled, ensuring that the first bid can be recorded without invoking a call on a zero address.
summary: Initially, when no bids have been entered, the existing bid will have default values – address(0) as the collection and 0 for the tokenId. The zero address does not have function ownerOf, so the call to getOwner will revert. As a result, no bids can be entered.

title: CRT-1 Reward sniffing
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑sniffing flaw in the staking contract that allows an attacker to inflate the amount of rewards they can claim by repeatedly depositing and withdrawing tokens within the same execution context. The root cause is that the contract’s reward accounting is performed on a cumulative token balance without protecting the withdrawAll routine from concurrent deposit operations. Because the contract does not enforce a deposit‑disabled state or a re‑entrancy guard when a user calls withdrawAll, a malicious participant can interleave a series of small deposits followed immediately by withdrawals, thereby shifting the internal accounting of total staked tokens and the share of rewards attributed to each participant. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling depositTokens and withdrawAll (or withdrawAll after each deposit) in a tight loop, as demonstrated in the Python emulation where user2 performs 100 deposit‑withdraw cycles while user1 holds a large stake. The manipulated accounting causes the contract to allocate a larger portion of the reward pool to the attacker, effectively “sniffing” rewards that should belong to honest stakers. The impact is a loss of legitimate rewards for other participants and a potential drain of the reward pool, undermining the economic guarantees of the staking protocol. The issue manifests when deposits are enabled and the withdrawAll function is invoked; it can be triggered by any address that can call depositTokens and withdrawAll in rapid succession. All stakers, the protocol’s reward distribution mechanism, and any users relying on fair reward allocation are affected. The flaw was discovered during a MixBytes audit through systematic testing that simulated repeated deposit‑withdraw cycles and observed an unexpected error when a legitimate user later attempted to withdraw, indicating that the reward state had become inconsistent. The problem is subtle because normal usage patterns involve infrequent deposits and withdrawals, so the accounting discrepancy is not obvious during routine operation. To remediate the issue, the contract should either require that deposits be disabled before a withdrawAll call, introduce a re‑entrancy lock around the withdrawAll logic, or redesign the reward calculation to use a snapshot of the total stake taken before any state‑changing operations, ensuring that reward shares cannot be manipulated by rapid deposit‑withdraw sequences. This class of bug falls under improper accounting and missing state‑transition checks, which can lead to reward theft and broken financial invariants in staking systems.
summary:
User can deposit-withdraw tokens several times (at the same transaction), causing reward sniffing.
The emulation of this behavior is presented below:
```python
def main():
    deployer = accounts[0]
    workerOwner = accounts[1]
    escrow = deployer.deploy(StakingEscrowMock)
    escrow.setAllTokens(9000)
    token = deployer.deploy(EasyToken, 1000_000)
    stacking = deployer.deploy(PoolingStakingContractV2)
    workerFraction = 1
    stacking.initialize(workerFraction, token, escrow, workerOwner, {'from': deployer})
    stacking.enableDeposit({'from': deployer})
```

title: Attack to force the project into the exodusMode
content: The vulnerability allows a malicious actor to force the Nume protocol into a permanent exodus mode by exploiting the way ETH (or ERC20) deposits are settled and withdrawn. The root cause is that the contract assumes a successful transfer of funds to the caller during the withdrawal settlement, but it does not verify that the receiving address can actually accept the transfer. When a malicious contract deliberately reverts on receiving ETH, the owner’s attempt to settle the withdrawal fails. Because the protocol’s challenge mechanism sets the flag isInExodusMode to true after a 14‑day waiting period without any additional validation, the failed settlement triggers the challengeUserWithdrawal function, which flips the flag permanently. Once isInExodusMode is true, the enforceExodusMode guard blocks normal deposit and withdrawal functions, effectively putting the system into a mass‑exit state where no new deposits are accepted and forced withdrawals are enabled without proper request handling. This condition can also be reproduced with blacklisted ERC20 tokens such as USDC, where a token transfer that reverts leads to the same flag being set. The impact is severe: the protocol’s core business logic is broken, users cannot make new deposits, pending withdrawals cannot be processed, and the project may be forced to shut down or require a full contract upgrade to reset the flag. The issue manifests when a deposit is made from a contract that is programmed to revert on receipt of funds, the owner attempts to settle the withdrawal within the 14‑day window, and the challenge period expires. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the settlement flow and the exodus‑mode transition logic. The bug is hard to notice because the revert occurs only on a malicious contract, and normal user accounts that accept ETH do not trigger the failure, making the problem appear only under adversarial conditions. To remediate, the withdrawal logic should be changed to a pull‑based pattern where the contract records the amount owed to each user in a mapping and lets users withdraw themselves, eliminating the need for the contract to push ETH to an arbitrary address. Additionally, the exodus‑mode flag should be protected by stricter checks, possibly requiring a multi‑signature or governance vote to activate, and a mechanism to reset the flag after a proper resolution. This class of bug falls under improper handling of external calls and unsafe state transitions that enable denial‑of‑service and forced protocol shutdown.
summary:
The attack flow:
1. Deposit ETH from a malicious smart contract A, which reverts when receiving ETH
2. Await for the deposit settlement to Nume network
3. call submitWithdrawalRequest()
4. the owner has 14 days to withdraw via notarizeSettlement()
5. the owner tries to settle the withdrawal but it fails - a malicious smart contract A intentionally reverts not receiving ETH
6. The attacker waits 14 days
7. The attacker calls challengeUserWithdrawal() => ns.isInExodusMode = true;
As a result, the check enforceExodusMode will not pass in core Nume functions - enabling a Mass exit scenario for the project, which means no new deposits and force withdrawals enabled (with no withdrawal requests on Nume). Also, there is no way to set isInExodusMode back to false. (Actually, it exists - urgently develop a new facet with the new code, deploy, and run the fix) The same issue can happen with ERC20 tokens with blacklists, for example USDC .
Another attacker vector with the same principle - avoid the deposit being invalidated. If an ETH deposit by a user is tagged as invalid (during notarizeSettlement ), Nume pays back the deposit. If such a malicious deposit is among valid deposits - there will be no way to remove it, thus it will be a problem to process valid deposits. So the owner will have to treat such a deposit as valid.

title: Attacker can turn on Exodus Mode
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw that allows an attacker to force the Nume protocol into Exodus Mode during the settlement notarisation process. The root cause is the combination of two design mistakes: first, the contract transfers the withdrawal stake to the beneficiary before it finalises the withdrawal queue index, and second, the external functions involved (notarizeSettlement and challengeUserWithdrawal) lack a re‑entrancy guard. When the stake is sent to a malicious contract, the contract’s fallback function can invoke challengeUserWithdrawal while the withdrawal request timestamp has already been cleared and the queue index has not yet been updated. Because the require checks in challengeUserWithdrawal only verify that the supplied queue index is greater than the lastFinalizedWithdrawalsQueueIndex and that the request timeout has passed, the attacker can satisfy these conditions after the timestamp deletion, causing the function to set isInExodusMode to true.
