in the malicious contract. Next the attacker will call VerificationGateway.processBundle() where the bundle is the
single stored operation. This will execute the operation, transferring ETH to the malicious contract.
The malicious contract’s fallback function will be called. Within the fallback function, they may load the operation
from storage and again call VerificationGateway.processBundle(). The operation will be processed a second time
as the nonce has not been incremented and is therefore still valid. Due to executing the operation a second time more
funds are transferred to the malicious contract. The malicious contract may optionally repeat this process, transferring
more ETH each time until there is minimal balance left in the victim’s wallet.
This issue is rated as critical as any bundle with an action that gives control of execution to a third party may be replayed
an infinite number of times. As a result any value transfers may be repeated until there is no value left, draining a wallet
of its assets.

title: Ownership of ProxyAdmin May Be Transferred To Any Wallet
content: The vulnerability consists of an uncontrolled ownership transfer of the shared ProxyAdmin contract through the walletAdminCall function used by BLS wallets. The root cause is that walletAdminCall only verifies that the first argument of a call to ProxyAdmin matches the caller’s wallet address, but it does not restrict which ProxyAdmin functions may be invoked. Because ProxyAdmin inherits from Ownable, the function transferOwnership(address newOwner) is exposed without any whitelist or blacklist. An attacker can craft a call to walletAdminCall that forwards a ProxyAdmin.transferOwnership request, passing the attacker’s wallet address as the newOwner argument. The call satisfies the onlyOwner modifier because the original owner (VerificationGateway) is still the caller at the time of the request, allowing the ownership to be reassigned to the malicious wallet. Once the attacker becomes the owner of ProxyAdmin, they can invoke any admin function on the TransparentUpgradeableProxy instances that the ProxyAdmin manages, including upgrade() and changeProxyAdmin(). This enables the attacker to replace the implementation contract of every BLS wallet that relies on the same ProxyAdmin, effectively inserting malicious code that can drain assets or block legitimate operations. The issue manifests only when a BLS wallet uses walletAdminCall to interact with ProxyAdmin, which is the intended path for legitimate upgrades, making the flaw subtle and easy to overlook. Users of the VerificationGateway protocol, all BLS wallets sharing the same ProxyAdmin, and any funds held by those wallets are at risk. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by SigmaPrime, who noted that the function lacks proper validation of the called selector, a detail that is not obvious from the UI or typical transaction logs. From a user perspective the symptoms may include a wallet suddenly pointing to an unexpected implementation, transactions failing, or funds disappearing without an explicit error message. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted delegate call / admin function exposure” where insufficient access control on a proxy admin leads to ownership hijacking. To remediate, the walletAdminCall logic should either whitelist only the intended ProxyAdmin functions (such as upgrade and changeProxyAdmin) or explicitly blacklist Ownable functions like transferOwnership and renounceOwnership, ensuring that only authorized admin actions can be performed through the wallet interface.
summary:
The function walletAdminCall() is used by BLS wallets to call functions in ProxyAdmin. However, it may be hijacked
to transfer ownership of ProxyAdmin to the wallet.
walletAdminCall() propagates calls from a BLSWallet to ProxyAdmin. The intention is to allow a wallet to call
ProxyAdmin.upgrade() or ProxyAdmin.changeProxyAdmin(). Each of the functions listed in ProxyAdmin.sol have
TransparentUpgradeableProxy as the first parameter.
walletAdminCall() checks that the first parameter of the call to ProxyAdmin is the BLSWallet (i.e. msg.sender). The
check ensures that a wallet cannot change the admin or implementation logic of other wallets, only itself.
However, there are no checks on which ProxyAdmin functions are being called, hence a user may call transferOwnership() which
ProxyAdmin inherits from Ownable. The first parameter of transferOwnership() is address newOwner. Since the first parameter of a ProxyAdmin call must be a BLSWallet the newOwner field will be
the wallet.
As VerificationGateway owns ProxyAdmin, this call passes the onlyOwner modifier and ownership is transferred to
the calling BLSWallet contract.
This is poses a critical risk as ProxyAdmin is the same for all wallets using the VerificationGateway. Once the owner-
ship is hijacked by a malicious BLSWallet instance, it would be possible to call the admin functions of the ProxyAdmin
with arbitrary data. These functions include the ability to change the implementation address of the BLSWallet that
the proxy points to. Changing the implementation contract would allow the attacker to call arbitrary functions on the
wallet and drain all assets.

title: Denial-of-Service (DoS) During Manager Health Checks Affects Liquidations
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs during the manager’s health‑check routine which is invoked by liquidation auctions. The SVI volatility library assumes that its input parameters – strike price, forward price, time‑to‑expiry (tao) and the SVI coefficient a – lie within specific ranges, but the contract does not enforce these constraints before calling getVol. When an option is created with a strike price of zero, or when forwardPrice or tao are zero, or when forwardPrice exceeds the uint56 maximum, the arithmetic inside getVol overflows or divides by zero, causing the function to revert with an overflow or modulo‑zero error. Because the manager’s getMarginAndMarkToMarket function calls volFeeds[marketId].getVol, any revert propagates up to the DutchAuction contract during a bid on an insolvent account. The auction therefore aborts, preventing the liquidation from completing. This effect blocks the protocol’s ability to resolve under‑collateralised positions, leaving insolvent accounts un‑liquidated and potentially exposing the system to loss of funds. The issue is triggered only when a user or option creator supplies the edge‑case parameters, which can be done intentionally by an attacker who creates a zero‑strike option and submits it to the feed. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that attempts to liquidate an account result in a transaction that reverts or completes without any change to balances, giving the impression that “nothing happens” or that “my funds are stuck”. The problem was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime while reviewing the SVI library bounds and the manager’s health‑check logic; it is subtle because the revert occurs deep in the call stack and only under rare parameter values, making it easy to miss in normal testing. The bug belongs to the class of input‑validation and arithmetic‑overflow vulnerabilities that can cause denial‑of‑service in financial smart contracts. To remediate, the contract should enforce non‑zero and within‑range checks for strike, forwardPrice and tao before accepting data, and ensure that the SVI coefficient a is non‑negative (or positive) as required by the library. Adding explicit require statements or sanitising the parameters at option creation and feed acceptance will prevent the overflow and allow liquidation auctions to proceed as intended.
summary:
Configured SVI feed bounds can cause denial-of-service (DoS) during Manager health checks, affecting liquidations.
SVI library calculates volume based on a chosen strike price. Certain values from configured bounds of a, forwardPrice, tao and strike variables will result in reverts in getVol() function reading accepted volume data. Reverts in SVI will prevent users from bidding in auctions on insolvent accounts, affecting liquidations.
Code comments located in the SVI.sol suggest that the following bounds are acceptable:
* @param strike desired strike for which to get vol for, in range [0, inf)
* @param a SVI parameter in range (-inf, inf)
* @param b SVI parameter in range [0, inf)
* @param rho SVI parameter in range (-1, 1)
* @param m SVI parameter in range (-inf, inf)
* @param sigma SVI parameter in range (0, inf)
* @param forwardPrice forward price in range [0, inf)
* @param tao time to expiry (in years) in range [0, inf)
However, the following exceptions will occur if parameters are set within these expected ranges:
• if strikePrice is set to zero, the function will revert with Overflow
• if forwardPrice exceeds type(uint56).max, the function will revert with Overflow
• if forwardPrice or tao are set to zero, the function will revert with division by modulo 0
• if a is set to a negative non-zero number, the function will revert with SVI_InvalidParameters
Since a, forwardPrice and tao variables are set during calls to LyraVolFeed.acceptData() where the feed owner has to approve signers to submit data, potential security implications are limited.
However, strike variable is controlled by those creating new options.
If a user accepts an option with zero value as strike price, it will cause an overflow in all LyraVolFeed.getVol() calculations. Subsequently, any call to StandardManager.getMarginAndMarkToMarket() will fail as well due to volFeeds[marketId].getVol() call on line [679].
During bids on insolvent auctions, the DutchAuction contract makes a call to ILiquidatableManager(manager).getMarginAndMarkToMarket(accountId, false, scenarioId) on line [6676], which will subsequently revert, preventing auctions on insolvent accounts to complete.

title: Liquidator Can Bid With Insufficient Cash
content: The vulnerability is a missing invariant check in the liquidation auction logic that allows a bidder – typically a liquidator – to submit a bid even when the bidder’s cash balance becomes negative after the internal symmetric manager adjustment. The root cause is that the executeBid function calls _symmetricManagerAdjustment on the bidder’s cash asset without verifying that the resulting cash balance remains non‑negative. An attacker can trigger executeBid, cause the adjustment to subtract more cash than the bidder actually holds, and the transaction will still succeed because no revert or require statement validates the post‑adjustment balance. As a result the protocol credits the account being liquidated with additional cash while the bidder’s balance is allowed to dip below zero, effectively creating new cash out of thin air. This breaks the fundamental accounting assumption that cash is conserved, leading to potential insolvency of the protocol and loss of value for all participants. The issue manifests during any liquidation auction where a bid is placed; it does not depend on external conditions other than the presence of a bid with insufficient cash. Users who interact with the auction may notice their cash balance turning negative after a bid, or they may see the liquidated account receive an unexpected increase in cash, both of which contradict the expected behavior that a bid should only be accepted if the bidder can cover it. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, where the logical flow of executeBid was examined and the absence of a post‑adjustment risk check was identified. Because the negative balance is only observable after an internal state change, it can be hard to notice during normal operation, especially if UI components do not display intermediate balances. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check after the symmetric manager adjustment that the bidder’s cash balance is greater than or equal to zero and revert the transaction otherwise; additional risk checks before accepting a bid are also recommended. This class of bug falls under missing balance validation or invariant enforcement, where arithmetic under‑flows are not prevented, leading to unintended asset creation and accounting violations.
summary:
When executeBid() performs _symmetricManagerAdjustment() on the cash asset of the bidder, there is no check that the bidder’s cash balance remains positive after the adjustment. This could result in a negative cash balance after the bid.
The impact is that an attacker can bid on an auction with an insufficient cash balance, and let their cash balance go negative. The account being liquidated would still get an increase to their cash balance. This is eﬀectively printing cash which could make the protocol insolvent.

title: Funds can be Drained from the Protocol by Liquidating an Account During an Asset Transfer
content: The vulnerability is a combination of a re‑entrancy flaw and an unchecked liquidation path that lets an attacker make an insolvent account appear solvent and then extract value that never existed. During a normal asset transfer the protocol first moves the tokens and only afterwards calls a manager hook that performs a risk check. Because the managerData argument can invoke an arbitrary external contract, an attacker can inject a call that starts a liquidation auction for the same account before the risk check runs. The external contract re‑enters the protocol, initiates a Dutch‑auction liquidation, and bids with a second attacker‑controlled account that itself becomes insolvent. Since the liquidation logic does not require the liquidator to pass a risk check, the attacker can transfer the entire liability of the original account to the liquidator, leaving the original account with zero assets and zero liabilities. When control returns to the original manager hook, the risk check now sees an empty, apparently healthy account and passes, allowing the original transfer to complete. The attacker then settles any options or profit‑generating positions that were created by the initial transfer and withdraws the resulting cash, even though no real collateral was ever deposited. From a user perspective the protocol shows a successful transfer and a profit, but the balances of the involved accounts are either empty or negative, effectively causing funds to disappear from the system. The attack works only when managerData is processed before the risk check and when the liquidation mechanism permits a liquidator to become insolvent without additional validation. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the ordering of external calls and the assumptions around liquidation safety. The issue is subtle because the protocol’s accounting appears consistent after the transaction – the risk check passes and no explicit error is raised – making it easy to miss in functional testing. To remediate the problem the protocol should move all external managerData calls to the very end of a transaction after every state change and risk validation, introduce a robust re‑entrancy guard that blocks any nested calls during a transfer, restrict managerData to a whitelist of trusted contracts, and enforce risk checks on accounts that participate in liquidation bids so that a liquidator cannot become insolvent. These changes restore the intended invariant that an account must remain solvent throughout a transfer and that liquidation cannot be used to bypass risk controls, thereby preventing the protocol from losing funds to fictitious profit withdrawals.
summary:
During an asset transfer which would leave an account insolvent, it is possible to execute a reentrancy attack and liquidate that account before the transfer is fully resolved. This renders the insolvent account solvent and thus means that the transfer goes through when it should not. The insolvent account(s) can be abandoned and the positive recipient of assets can withdraw their fictitious profit.
In the following attack scenario, all accounts (Alice, Bob, Cynthia) are owned by a single attacker.
1. Alice sets up a transaction which grants profit to Bob and leaves Alice insolvent. One way of doing this is for Alice to issue Bob with an option which is already expired and which grants Bob significant value, such as a put option at a much higher price than the asset’s price at the expiry time. This can be done on an empty account without requiring any assets to be deposited into the protocol.
However, the effect could also be achieved by transferring out all of the cash asset from an account with a significant existing option liability.
2. This transaction includes a managerData argument which calls an attack contract. This argument can be supplied to subAccounts.submitTransfer(). This function calls _submitTransfer() which transfers all assets without any risk check before calling _managerHook(), which in turn calls StandardManager.handleAdjustment() to perform the risk check. Before the risk check, on line [266], this function calls _processManagerData() with the managerData which Alice submitted. This causes StandardManager to call the function acceptData() on the attack contract.
3. The attack contract starts a liquidation auction on Alice. The attack contract calls dutchAuction.startAuction() to start an auction to liquidate Alice. Alice is insolvent, so an insolvent auction is immediately started.
4. Cynthia bids on Alice’s liquidation auction, and fully liquidates her. The attack contract controls a third account, which we will call Cynthia. Cynthia liquidates Alice by calling dutchAuction.bid() for 100% of Alice’s account.
As we are still within the same single transaction, the liquidation will have a stepInsolvent value of zero, and so the full liability of Alice’s account will be transferred to Cynthia.
Critically, however, there is no risk check on Cynthia during this process. All of Alice’s liabilities have been transferred to Cynthia before Alice has been risk checked, but Cynthia does not need to pass a risk check to execute a liquidation.
5. The attack contract returns control flow to StandardManager, allowing Alice to pass her risk check. StandardManager now performs a risk check on Alice. As Alice no longer has any assets or liabilities, the risk check quickly passes and the attack transaction ends.
6. Bob settles his option and withdraws all his cash profit. Alice is now an empty account. Cynthia is insolvent with no positive assets, but Bob received the profitable side of the option. He can now settle it and withdraw its value in the cash asset.
Note that none of Alice, Bob or Cynthia has ever deposited any tokens into the protocol.
Derive (Formerly Lyra)

title: Bids Can Be Blocked By Sending Option To Liquidator
content: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition in the DutchAuction liquidation flow of the Derive protocol. The executeBid() function assumes that the address submitting the bid (the bidder) holds only the cash asset that will be used to purchase the liquidated position. Because the contract does not perform a risk or asset-type check on the bidder’s balance, an attacker can front-run the transaction that calls executeBid() and transfer a single wei of any non-risk-adding token to the bidder address. When executeBid() runs, the presence of this unexpected token causes the internal balance verification to fail and the call reverts, preventing the auction from completing. The revert occurs only when the attacker’s transfer is mined in the same block before the executeBid() call, making the issue appear intermittent and hard to notice during normal testing. The impact is that liquidations, which are essential for removing high-risk accounts and preserving protocol solvency, can be stalled indefinitely. Users and lenders expect risky positions to be liquidated promptly; instead they see no bids being accepted, auctions remaining open, and the protocol’s risk metrics staying elevated. The attack is permissionless because transferring a token to the bidder does not require any allowance, and the attacker needs only a trivial amount of value. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the assumptions around bidder state. It is difficult to detect because the contract behaves correctly when the bidder holds only cash, and the revert only manifests under a specific front-running scenario. To remediate, the contract should either allow the bidder to hold additional assets and perform a comprehensive risk check after all transfers, or explicitly validate that only the required cash asset is present before proceeding with the bid. By removing the implicit assumption about the bidder’s balance composition, the protocol can restore reliable liquidation execution and maintain its intended risk-management guarantees.
summary:
It is possible to prevent liquidations by frontrunning an executeBid() call.
To provide context, liquidations through the DutchAuction.sol contract are integral to the proper operation of the Derive protocol. This is primarily due to their role in executing risk management processes - liquidating high-risk accounts and, in turn, minimizing the risk of the protocol becoming insolvent.
The issue arises due to the requirement that the bidder must only hold the cash asset when performing a bid. This is due to the high gas costs of performing a risk check during liquidation.
However due to this requirement, an attacker could transfer a non-risk adding asset to the bidder right before the executeBid() function is called, through frontrunning their transaction. If this occurs, the executeBid() function will revert, effectively preventing liquidations from taking place.
The attacker would only need to transfer 1 WEI of an asset to the bidder to perform this attack. Additionally this attack can be performed permissionlessly as the transfer of non-risk adding assets does not require asset allowances.

title: Bids Can Be Blocked By Depositing Tokens To Liquidator
content: The vulnerability is a front‑runable bid blocking condition in the liquidator auction logic. When a liquidator places a bid the contract calls ensureBidderCashBalance to verify that the bidder’s account holds only cash assets. The check is deliberately lightweight to avoid a full portfolio risk evaluation. However, the protocol allows any address to deposit wrapped ERC20 tokens into another address via WrappedERC20Asset.deposit without requiring the recipient’s approval. An attacker can observe a pending bid transaction and, in the same block, call deposit to transfer a non‑cash wrapped token to the liquidator’s account. After the deposit the liquidator’s balance contains a non‑cash asset, causing ensureBidderCashBalance to revert and the bid to fail. This makes it possible to block bids arbitrarily, preventing the liquidator from participating in auctions, which can stall liquidation processes and reduce protocol revenue. The issue affects all liquidators and any participants relying on timely auction settlement. It was identified during a security audit that revisited a previously reported flaw (DRV‑02) which had been fixed for option assets but remained for wrapped ERC20 deposits. The problem is subtle because depositing a token is a normal operation and does not produce an error; the failure only appears later when the bid transaction reverts, making it hard to trace back to the deposit. The correct mitigation is to extend the approval requirement to wrapped token deposits or to modify the cash‑balance check so that it rejects accounts holding any non‑cash assets before allowing a bid. In practice the fix ensures that a liquidator cannot be forced to hold unexpected token types that would invalidate the cash‑only assumption of the auction logic.
summary:
Liquidator bids can be blocked by being front-run with a call to deposit an asset to the liquidator’s account, when
bidding on auctions _ensureBidderCashBalance() is called to ensure a liquidator only has cash in their account. The
check is required for gas reasons as then no portfolio risk check has to be performed on the liquidator.
This leads to a problem where any account can front-run a bid by sending a non-cash asset to the bidder/liquidator,
which results in the bid reverting. This issue was originally highlighted in DRV-02 in the previous security assessment
report, and ﬁxed for Options assets by requiring approval from the receiving account prior to transfer.
However, no approval is required for depositing/wrapping fresh ERC20 tokens into a recipient account, using
WrappedERC20Asset.deposit(). As such, it is still possible to send a non-cash asset (wrapped ERC20 in this case) to an
arbitrary account, which means this vulnerability is still exploitable.

title: Denial of Service on withdrawTokens()
content: The vulnerability resides in the token withdrawal routine of a guild contract where the function withdrawTokens() allows a caller to request a withdrawal of zero tokens. The implementation checks the caller’s locked balance and, if the amount is exactly zero, it decrements a global counter totalMembers using SafeMath subtraction. Because there is no guard against a zero‑amount request, a user with no locked tokens can repeatedly invoke withdrawTokens() with a zero amount, causing totalMembers to be reduced on each call. When totalMembers eventually reaches zero, any subsequent call that would trigger the same decrement (i.e., another zero‑amount withdrawal) causes SafeMath.sub to revert due to an under‑flow, which in turn aborts the entire withdrawTokens() execution. This revert blocks the normal withdrawal path for all users, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate participants cannot retrieve their locked tokens. The issue is discovered during a manual audit of BaseERC20Guild.sol where the conditional decrement was observed without a preceding non‑zero amount validation. It is subtle because the function otherwise appears to work correctly for normal withdrawals, and the zero‑amount edge case is rarely exercised in typical usage, making the bug easy to overlook. The impact is that an attacker can drain the member count to zero, causing the contract to reject further withdrawals and potentially freeze user funds. The affected parties include any token holder that relies on withdrawTokens() to reclaim assets, as well as the protocol itself which depends on an accurate totalMembers metric for governance or reward distribution. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the withdrawal amount is greater than zero before performing any state changes, or alternatively remove the totalMembers counter if it is not essential, thereby eliminating the risky decrement logic. This class of bug falls under improper input validation leading to state‑corruption and denial‑of‑service via integer under‑flow.
summary:
The withdrawTokens() function withdraws locked user tokens from allocated guild contracts. This function fails to check whether a user tries to withdraw zero tokenAmount. If a user has no balance and withdraws zero tokens, totalMembers will reduce by one. This can be seen in the following excerpt from BaseERC20Guild.sol as indicated in the following snippet1:
```solidity
if (tokensLocked[msg.sender].amount == 0) totalMembers = totalMembers.sub(1);
```
A malicious user could launch a DoS attack against the system through repeatedly withdrawing zero tokens until totalMembers == 0. This would prevent other users from withdrawing tokens, due to the aforementioned check causing an Integer Overflow error.

title: Double-voting in BaseERC20Guild
content: The vulnerability is a double‑voting flaw in the BaseERC20Guild family of contracts that manage governance through token locking. When a participant locks ERC20 tokens via the lockTokens() function, the contract records a voting power that can be used to cast a vote on a proposal through setVote(). The contract assumes that the voting power remains bound to the locked tokens for the entire voting period, but the implementation does not automatically revoke a vote when the tokens are withdrawn. If the lock duration (_lockTime) is shorter than the proposal voting window (_proposalTime) – a situation that can arise when a user locks tokens before a proposal is created – the user can withdraw the tokens before the proposal expires, transfer them to a different address, and cast another vote on the same proposal using the same voting power. This effectively allows a single token holder to vote multiple times on a single proposal, breaking the one‑vote‑per‑token principle. The attack sequence is: (1) lock tokens, (2) a proposal is submitted, (3) the user votes, (4) the lock expires while the proposal is still open, (5) the user calls withdrawTokens(), (6) the user transfers the tokens to a new address, (7) the user calls setVote() again from the new address. The impact is a distortion of governance outcomes, enabling malicious actors to sway proposals, potentially approve harmful upgrades, or steal funds indirectly by influencing protocol decisions. The flaw is triggered only when the contract’s configuration permits _lockTime to be less than the active proposal’s voting period, a condition that may be overlooked because the contract checks only that _lockTime >= _proposalTime at deployment, not at runtime for each proposal. All participants in the guild, the protocol’s governance process, and token holders are affected because the integrity of voting results can no longer be trusted. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the relationship between token locking and vote lifecycle. It is subtle because the vote appears to be recorded correctly and the user’s token balance after withdrawal shows zero, giving the impression that the vote has been consumed, while in reality the vote remains active. The bug belongs to the class of “governance double‑spend” or “vote replay” vulnerabilities, where voting rights are reused after the underlying asset is reclaimed. To remediate, the contract should either (a) enforce that a vote is automatically revoked when the associated tokens are withdrawn, (b) prevent token transfers while a vote is active, (c) require a snapshot of voting power at proposal creation that cannot be altered by later withdrawals, or (d) guarantee that the lock period always exceeds the maximum possible voting duration for any proposal. Any of these approaches would ensure that each token can influence at most one vote during its locked period, restoring the intended one‑token‑one‑vote guarantee.
summary: The contract BaseERC20Guild enables users to cast votes on proposals using their voting powers. Voting power is acquired by locking tokens through the lockTokens() function, where the tokens will be locked until lockTime period passes. When a proposal is first submitted, the user can vote on this proposal by calling the setVote() function. Then, after casting their vote, the user can withdraw their tokens by calling withdrawTokens(). The token withdrawal does not revoke their proposal vote. Having their tokens back, the user can transfer the tokens to another account and vote again under the guise of a new user. This allows for double-voting. The scenario above is possible if the user locks tokens before a proposal is proposed, and therefore the lockTime expires before proposalTime passes. In this case, the system configuration where _lockTime >= _proposalTime does not prevent the user from withdrawing tokens before the proposalTime ends.

title: Double-voting in SnapshotERC20Guild
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect ordering of state updates in the snapshot‑based voting contract, which allows a user to retain voting power after their tokens have been withdrawn and then reuse that power on subsequent proposals. The contract records a snapshot of each account’s voting power before the amount of locked tokens is actually modified in both the lockTokens and withdrawTokens functions. Because the snapshot is taken while the old token amount is still stored, the snapshot continues to report the pre‑withdrawal balance even after the tokens have been removed from the guild. An attacker can therefore lock tokens, wait for a proposal to be created (which increments the snapshot identifier), call withdrawTokens to take the tokens out, transfer the tokens to another address, and repeat the process. Each iteration gives the attacker a fresh snapshot that still shows the full locked amount, enabling the same tokens to be counted multiple times across different proposals – effectively a double‑voting or vote‑inflation attack. This flaw manifests whenever a user calls lockTokens or withdrawTokens, because the internal _updateAccountSnapshot call precedes the update of tokensLocked[msg.sender].amount. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, where the unexpected behaviour of votingPower not changing after lockTokens and increasing after withdrawTokens was observed. It can be hard to notice because the snapshot values appear correct at the moment a proposal is created, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when votingPower diverges from the actual token balance. The impact is that governance decisions can be swayed by a single entity that appears to have many votes while holding no tokens, breaking the protocol’s trust model and potentially leading to malicious proposals being approved. Users may see their vote count remain high even after their token balance shows zero, or notice that proposals accept votes from accounts with no locked tokens. To remediate the issue, the snapshot update should be performed after the tokensLocked amount is modified, ensuring that each snapshot accurately reflects the true locked token balance at that point in time. Conceptually, the fix requires aligning the snapshot mechanism with the actual state change so that voting power cannot be decoupled from token holdings.
summary:
The contract SnapshotERC20Guild enables users to cast votes on proposals using their voting powers. Unlike BaseERC20Guild, voting power is managed by a snapshot mechanism. One of the purposes behind most snapshot mechanisms is to prevent people flooding the voting power, after a proposal is created. In SnapshotERC20Guild, the snapshot process has unexpected behaviour:
1. lockTokens(): Calling this function does not increase proposal votingPower unless the user then calls lockTokens() again, or withdrawTokens(). This is due to calling _updateAccountSnapshot(msg.sender) on line [83], before updating the tokensLocked[msg.sender].amount on line [86].
2. withdrawTokens: Calling this function unexpectedly increases the votingPower. This is due to the function calling _updateAccountSnapshot(msg.sender) on line [100] before updating the tokensLocked[msg.sender].amount on line [102].
As a result, a malicious user is able to lock tokens, wait the allocated block.timestamp, and create a new proposal to increment the snapshotId. After this setup, they are able to call withdrawTokens(), which will withdraw the tokens from the guild contract, however the snapshot will maintain voting power as the pre-withdrawal tokensLocked[msg.sender]. After withdrawal, the malicious adversary is able to transfer the tokens to another account and repeat the process, gaining votingPower across multiple accounts that do not hold any tokens. This effectively allows a single user to double vote repeatedly on any future proposal.

title: Snapshot Malfunction
content: The vulnerability is a snapshot malfunction in a governance contract that separates voting logic between a child contract (SnapshotERC20Guild) and a parent contract (ERC20GuildUpgradeable or BaseERC20Guild). The child contract records a snapshot of each voter’s token balance at the moment a proposal is created, intending to use that snapshot to determine voting power later. However, when a user calls setVote or setSignedVote, the child contract forwards the call to the parent contract’s implementation, which checks the current votingPower directly from the token balance instead of the stored snapshot. This mismatch means that if a voter withdraws or transfers tokens after the proposal is created but before casting a vote, the parent contract will see a reduced balance, fail the votingPower check, and revert with an "Invalid votingPower" error. The root cause is the parent contract’s lack of awareness of the snapshot mechanism, leading to an incorrect assumption that the current balance always reflects the intended voting power. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can create a proposal, wait for legitimate voters to prepare their votes, then withdraw tokens from those accounts (or force token transfers) before the voters submit their votes, causing all subsequent vote transactions to revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the governance process; legitimate participants lose the ability to cast votes, proposals may never reach a quorum, and the protocol’s decision‑making can be stalled or manipulated. The condition occurs whenever token balances change between proposal creation and vote submission, which is a common scenario in token‑based systems where users freely transfer tokens. All token holders who rely on the governance mechanism are affected, as are the protocol’s administrators who depend on timely voting outcomes. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, where the logical flow of snapshot handling was examined and the inconsistency between child and parent contracts was identified. The bug is subtle because the child contract appears to perform snapshot checks, giving a false sense of security, while the actual votingPower verification happens deeper in the inheritance chain where snapshots are ignored. This can easily be missed by tests that only verify voting with unchanged balances. To remediate, the votingPower verification should be refactored so that it uses the snapshot data stored in the child contract, either by moving the entire voting logic into the child contract or by exposing snapshot‑aware votingPower checks in the parent contract. In essence, the governance system must ensure that any vote validation respects the snapshot taken at proposal creation, preventing balance changes from invalidating legitimate votes and preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.
summary: In the contract SnapshotERC20Guild, function setVote() and setSignedVote() manage the users’s votes by first checking the snapshot and then calling the parent contract’s setVote() or setSignedVote() function. The contract SnapshotERC20Guild derives from ERC20GuildUpgradeable (or BaseERC20Guild). While snapshots are used in SnapshotERC20Guild, the parent contract ERC20GuildUpgradeable does not have access to the snapshots. For example, SnapshotERC20Guild.setVote() calls the function BaseERC20Guild.setVote() which directly uses the current votingPower before processing further. The same error occurs with SnapshotERC20Guild.setVote() relying on BaseERC20Guild.setSignedVote(). These checks against the parent contract’s votingPower do not take into account applied snapshots in the child contract. If the voters withdraw their tokens after proposal creation and before voting, the parent contract will revert with Invalid votingPower message.

title: Incorrect votingPower Accounting
content: An incorrect voting power accounting bug exists in the SnapshotRepERC20Guild contract that replaces token locking with a snapshot mechanism but fails to override the core accounting function that reports the total amount of tokens considered locked. The contract still calls getTotalLocked, which in the base ERC20Guild implementation returns the amount of tokens that are explicitly locked. Because the derived contract never provides a new implementation, getTotalLocked always returns zero when the snapshot mechanism is used. The governance logic that determines whether a user can create a proposal (votingPowerForProposalCreation) and whether a proposal can be executed (votingPowerForProposalExecution) multiplies the required threshold by the value returned from getTotalLocked. Consequently the required voting power collapses to zero, allowing any address, even one holding a single token, to satisfy the condition and submit or pass proposals. An attacker can therefore craft malicious proposals, trigger their execution, and potentially move funds or change protocol parameters without possessing the intended stake. The issue appears only at the contract level; the front‑end may still display the correct snapshot balance, leading users to believe the governance rules are enforced, which makes the problem hard to notice. It occurs whenever the guild is instantiated with the SnapshotRepERC20Guild implementation and the snapshot token is used, because the overridden functions that should reference snapshot balances are missing. The bug affects all token holders, the guild’s governance process, and any assets that can be controlled through proposals. It was discovered during a security audit that compared the expected snapshot‑based accounting with the actual implementation. To remediate, the voting power accounting functions must be refactored so that getTotalLocked (and any derived helpers) return the snapshot balance of the contract, and the createProposal and endProposal checks must enforce the intended minimum token thresholds based on that snapshot data. This restores the intended economic barrier and prevents unauthorized proposal creation and execution.
summary: Contract SnapshotRepERC20Guild replaces token locking with a snapshot mechanism implemented in the ERC20SnapshotRep token. The guild contract derives from ERC20GuildUpgradeable or BaseERC20Guild and overrides some important functions to set votes and create proposals. The contract however, does not override the votingPower accounting algorithm, for example getTotalLocked() function. This function is used to query the total amount of tokens locked by the contract. totalLocked is then used to determine the minimum amount of tokens required to submit a proposal and to pass a proposal as defined in votingPowerForProposalCreation and votingPowerForProposalExecution respectively. As a result, anyone with an insufficient amount of tokens can propose and pass a proposal, because getVotingPowerForProposalCreation() and getVotingPowerForProposalExecution() will always produce zero.

title: Voting Tally Does Not Count the Zero Action
content: The vulnerability lies in the vote‑tallying routine of a governance contract that determines which action, if any, should be executed after a proposal’s deadline. The routine initializes a variable called winningAction to zero and then iterates over the array of vote totals starting at index one, completely skipping the entry at index zero which represents the "no‑action" or rejection option. The code assumes that if enough votes are cast for the zero‑action entry, the required execution threshold (votingPowerForProposalExecution) will not be met by any other action, causing the default winningAction=0 to correctly indicate a rejected proposal. However, this assumption is not enforced anywhere in the contract configuration. When the execution threshold is set to a value lower than fifty percent, it becomes possible for the majority of voters to select the zero‑action option while a minority (for example thirty percent) votes for a concrete action such as action=1. Because the loop never compares the zero‑action total against the threshold, the minority action can satisfy the threshold and also appear larger than the zero‑action total in the loop, causing the contract to record action=1 as the winning action. An attacker can therefore manipulate the outcome by ensuring the threshold is low and casting a small but sufficient number of votes for a malicious action, effectively overriding the majority’s intent to reject the proposal. The impact is a breach of governance integrity: proposals that should be rejected may be executed, leading to unauthorized changes in sensitive guild or protocol configuration parameters via the setConfig function. This flaw manifests whenever endProposal is called after the proposal deadline while votingPowerForProposalExecution is configured below the fifty‑percent majority level. All participants who rely on the governance process, including token holders, protocol operators, and users of the affected configuration, are potentially affected because the contract may apply changes that were never approved. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of endProposal and the assumptions made in setConfig, noting that the loop start index contradicted the intended default behavior. The bug is subtle because the zero‑action entry is part of the same array as other actions, and developers may assume that initializing winningAction to zero automatically accounts for it, overlooking the fact that the loop never evaluates it. To remediate the problem, the tally loop should start at index zero so that the zero‑action votes are properly considered, or the contract should enforce a configuration rule that requires votingPowerForProposalExecution to be at least fifty percent, thereby guaranteeing that a majority rejection cannot be overridden by a minority. Either approach restores the intended governance semantics where a proposal is only executed when a clear majority supports a specific action, and it prevents the accidental or malicious execution of rejected proposals.

title: Incorrect Parsing of Token Path Between Gearbox and Uniswap
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect parsing of the multi‑hop swap path supplied to Uniswap V3 when called through the Gearbox adapter. Gearbox’s internal function extracts only the first and last 20‑byte token addresses from the path to perform a collateral health check, assuming the path contains exactly two tokens (tokenIn and tokenOut). Uniswap, however, interprets the path as a sequence of token‑fee‑token triples, where each hop consists of a 20‑byte token address, a 3‑byte fee, and the next token address. Because Gearbox ignores the fee bytes and any additional hops, an attacker can construct a path that includes an extra token after the intended output token (e.g., tokenA‑fee‑tokenB‑tokenC). Uniswap will execute the swap only between tokenA and tokenB, discarding tokenC, while Gearbox will read tokenC as the output token for its collateral verification. This mismatch allows the borrower to present a path that passes Gearbox’s health check – the contract believes the swap will receive tokenC as collateral – but the actual swap delivers tokenB, which can be a fake or heavily discounted token created by the attacker. By deploying a malicious ERC‑20 token and a corresponding Uniswap pool, the attacker can force the credit account to trade at an unfavorable price, withdraw the received fake tokens, and ultimately steal value from the pool. The impact is a loss of funds from the Gearbox pool and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees; users may see their balances reduced or missing without any on‑chain error, as the swap transaction itself succeeds. The condition occurs whenever a multi‑hop swap is performed through Gearbox’s adapter and the path contains more than one hop; single‑hop swaps are not affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the Gearbox V1 deployment, where the mismatch between Gearbox’s _extractTokens() logic and Uniswap’s SwapRouter parsing was identified. It is subtle because both contracts successfully decode the byte array according to their own expectations, so no revert or exception is raised, making the bug hard to notice in normal testing. The correct fix is to align Gearbox’s path parsing with Uniswap’s specification, extracting the token addresses at the exact byte offsets used by the SwapRouter (i.e., accounting for the 3‑byte fee between each token) or to validate that the path contains exactly the expected number of hops before performing the collateral check. In broader terms, this is a classic “inconsistent input parsing” or “path‑parsing mismatch” vulnerability that breaks the trust model between a wrapper contract and the underlying protocol, leading to accounting errors and potential fund theft.
summary:
Note, this issue was also disclosed for the Gearbox V1 deployment via Immuni’s bug bounty program during the course of this review. It is further detailed in this post-mortem.
It is possible to manipulate the path parameter passed in to exactOutput() and other functions of UniswapV3.sol adapter to bypass collateral health check on token swaps, leading to theft of funds from the pool.
Uniswap decodes the parameters for each swap pool in a multi-pool path bytes array in the following order: tokenA, fee, tokenB. Each token address is encoded by 20 bytes and the pool swap fee encoded by 3 bytes. Any remaining bytes in the array are ignored, unless large enough (23 bytes for fee + address) to constitute another swap parameter.
Note that tokenA or tokenB could be the output token depending on which Uniswap function is called.
Gearbox uses _extractTokens() to parse only the first and last tokens from the path to run a collateral check and ensure the safety of the swap. The first 20 bytes represent tokenA and the last 20 bytes are read as tokenB.
The difference in parsing methods allows a borrower to craft a malicious path as such: tokenA, fee, tokenB, tokenC.
Uniswap will execute a trade between tokenA and tokenB from this path, and ignore tokenC. However, Gearbox parses tokenC in the place of tokenB for the collateral check.
By deploying a fake ERC20 token and creating a pool for it on Uniswap, an attacker can force a credit account to trade at an unfair price while still passing all of Gearbox’s health and safety checks. The attacker is able to withdraw the stolen tokens by minting fake ERC20 tokens and trading these against their own liquidity pool.

title: Liquidators Can Manipulate Pool’s Proﬁt or Loss Values
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation workflow of the credit protocol, where the function that settles a credit account calculates the account's total value before executing a multicall that can modify the account's balances. Because the snapshot of totalValue is taken prior to the multicall, a liquidator can invoke additional borrowing operations within the same transaction, inflating the borrowed amount with interest while the previously recorded totalValue remains unchanged. This mismatch causes the internal payment calculation routine to treat the difference between the inflated borrowed amount and the stale totalValue as a loss attributable to the pool. Consequently, the pool’s accounting records report a loss that is actually transferred to the liquidator, allowing the attacker to burn treasury‑held diesel tokens at no cost and later recover the tokens they injected into the borrower’s account. The issue manifests only when a liquidation is performed via CreditFacade.liquidateCreditAccount and the contract subsequently calls _multicall after the totalValue snapshot; under these conditions, any extra borrowing performed by the liquidator skews the profit‑and‑loss computation. Users of the protocol, token holders, and the pool’s treasury are affected because funds disappear from the pool without any legitimate repayment, violating the core accounting assumption that liquidation should preserve the pool’s capital. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state‑changing calls and identified that the loss calculation logic in CreditManager._calcClosePaymentsPure does not account for post‑snapshot balance changes. The bug is subtle because the code appears to correctly compute payments when examined in isolation, and the erroneous loss only becomes apparent under the specific sequence of calls used by a malicious liquidator. To remediate the issue, the payment calculation should be performed after all state‑changing operations have completed, or the contract should prevent additional borrowing during liquidation, ensuring that the totalValue used for loss determination accurately reflects the final asset state. This class of bug can be described as an accounting miscalculation caused by a post‑snapshot state change, leading to unintended fund extraction and a breach of the protocol’s financial integrity.
summary:
Liquidators can manipulate the protocol’s proﬁt and loss accounting in
CreditFacade.liquidateCreditAccount(),
which can lead to theft of funds from the pool.
The call to _multicall() is done after totalValue is calculated. Hence, if a liquidator borrows additional funds
before closing the target credit account, totalValue will be under-represented in comparison to
borrowedAmountWithInterest.
This causes CreditManager._calcClosePaymentsPure() to miscalculate the loss amount as
amountToPool >= totalFunds, which means amountToPool = totalFunds. The totalFunds will be less than
borrowedAmountWithInterest, therefore the loss amount will be calculated as
borrowedAmountWithInterest - amountToPool.
This vulnerability allows an attacker to continually burn diesel tokens held by the treasury at no cost to the attacker.
The attacker can recover the tokens that they added to the borrower account.

title: Denial-of-Service (DoS) by Opening a Credit Account on Behalf of the CreditFacade Contract
content: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition that arises when an attacker is able to open a credit account on behalf of the CreditFacade contract in the Gearbox protocol. CreditFacade relies on a multicall mechanism that temporarily transfers ownership of a user’s credit account to the CreditFacade contract so that it can invoke adapter functions, closures and liquidation logic on the user’s behalf. Before the temporary transfer, CreditManager.transferAccountOwnership checks that the address that will receive ownership does not already have an open credit account; this check is implemented as an assert. Because the assert only verifies the absence of an open account, an attacker can deliberately create a credit account whose registered owner is the CreditFacade contract itself. Once such an account exists, any subsequent call to multicall() attempts to transfer ownership to CreditFacade, the assert fails, and the whole multicall reverts. As a result, all functionality that depends on multicall – including adapter calls, position closures, liquidations and any other privileged operations – becomes unusable, effectively freezing user activity on the protocol. The attack can be launched at any time after the malicious credit account is created; it does not require any special privileges beyond the ability to call CreditFacade.openCreditAccount(). The affected parties are all users of the Gearbox protocol, the protocol’s operators, and any third-party contracts that rely on the multicall interface, because their funds become inaccessible and expected actions (e.g., closing a position) silently fail. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit of the CreditFacade and CreditManager contracts, where the auditor noticed that the ownership-transfer assertion does not consider the case where the target address is itself a contract that can open credit accounts. The bug is subtle because the failure only appears when the specific sequence of opening a credit account for CreditFacade and then invoking multicall is executed; normal operation with regular users does not trigger the assert, so the problem may remain hidden until an attacker exploits it. The vulnerability belongs to the class of ownership-transfer assertion misuse or pre-condition violation leading to denial-of-service. To remediate the issue, the openCreditAccount() function should verify that the supplied owner is not the CreditFacade contract, or the transferAccountOwnership() logic should be changed to allow ownership transfer to an address that already holds a credit account, or to use a more permissive check that does not reject the legitimate temporary ownership transfer. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that calls which normally succeed (e.g., executing a multicall to interact with adapters) start reverting with an assertion error, resulting in transaction failed messages, missing expected state changes, and funds that cannot be moved or liquidated. Users expect their operations to complete and their balances to be updated, but instead they see no effect and may suspect a bug or a scam. The protocol’s business logic – which assumes that temporary ownership can always be transferred – is broken, leading to a situation where money is effectively locked while the contract is still operational.
summary:
Malicious actors can create a Denial-of-Service (DoS) condition on the Gearbox protocol by opening new
creditAccount on behalf of creditFacade.
The multicall() functionality of a creditAccount temporarily transfers account ownership to creditFacade to call
various functions on behalf of the owner. There is an assertion in CreditManger.transferAccountOwnership() which
requires that the address receiving ownership does not have an open credit account.
This assertion creates a vulnerability to a denial-of-service attack in which the attacker opens a creditAccount on
behalf of the creditFacade. The creditFacade would then be considered a registered owner of a creditAccount
and any attempts to recieve temporary ownership of accounts via multicall() will fail.
Consequently, any other calls utilizing multicall() will fail (calls to adapters, closures and liquidations, etc).

title: Liquidation Avoidance through Rejecting Native Ether Transfers
content: The vulnerability is a liquidation‑avoidance flaw that arises when a borrower creates a CreditAccount from a contract that deliberately reverts on any incoming native Ether transfer. Gearbox’s CreditManager assumes that, during the closeCreditAccount routine, any remaining collateral that is held as WETH can be unwrapped to Ether and sent to the borrower’s address. The unwrapping is performed by WETHGateway.unwrapWETH which calls a low‑level call to transfer Ether. If the recipient is a contract whose receive() function contains a revert, the Ether transfer fails and the unwrap operation reverts. Because the liquidation path relies on the successful transfer of the unwrapped funds, the revert aborts the liquidation process, leaving the credit account open and the collateral effectively frozen. An attacker can therefore open a credit account from a malicious contract, trigger a liquidation condition, and then block the liquidation indefinitely by causing the Ether transfer to fail. The impact is that the protocol cannot recover the under‑collateralised position, exposing lenders to loss and breaking the accounting guarantees of the system. The issue occurs only when the underlying token is WETH and the borrower’s address is a contract with a rejecting receive() implementation; it does not affect normal externally owned accounts. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the composability of CreditAccounts and the assumptions made in the liquidation flow. The problem is subtle because the failure happens at the very last step of fund transfer, which may not be exercised in typical unit tests that use EOAs. To remediate the issue the protocol should avoid unwrapping WETH when sending remaining funds in a liquidation context, transferring WETH directly instead, or otherwise handling a failed Ether transfer gracefully. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “transfer‑revert” or “fallback‑rejection” vulnerabilities where a contract’s inability to accept Ether breaks downstream logic that assumes successful payment.
summary:
Borrowers can avoid liquidations by creating CreditAccount from a contract address that reverts every time it
receives native ETH transfers.
Gearbox is designed as a composable DeFi protocol. Therefore, it is possible to open a CreditAccount from a
contract address.
This may create issues when CreditManager.closeCreditAccount() attempts to convert remainingFunds into native
ETH and transfer them to the borrower, when the underlying token is WETH. Malicious borrowers could cause
WETHGateway.unwrapWETH() to revert by having the receive() function of a borrowing contract actively revert.
This vulnerability could be exploited to avoid liquidations indeﬁnitely.

title: updateRegisteredErc20() modifies the wrong token
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that is intended to update the oracle address and loan‑to‑value (LTV) for a specific ERC‑20 collateral token. Instead of using the token address supplied as a parameter to locate the correct token identifier, the implementation mistakenly references the global variable that stores the identifier of the most recently registered token. This copy‑and‑paste mistake causes the update logic to write the new oracle address and LTV into the storage slots of the last added token, regardless of which token the caller intended to modify. The root cause is an incorrect mapping key: the function uses the wrong token ID, leading to a mismatch between the UI‑visible token and the on‑chain configuration. An attacker (or any privileged caller) can exploit this by invoking the function with a target token address while the contract silently updates a different token’s parameters. If the affected token is a high‑value asset, the erroneous LTV may make previously solvent vaults appear under‑collateralised, triggering immediate liquidation. Likewise, assigning an oracle address meant for one token to another can cause the price feed to return wildly inaccurate values, causing vaults to be liquidated at a fraction of their true worth. The impact is severe: borrowers can lose their collateral, liquidators may acquire assets at far‑below‑market prices, and the protocol’s risk model is broken. The bug manifests only when the function is called with a token address that does not correspond to the most recently registered token; under that condition the contract updates the wrong mapping entries. Users experience symptoms such as sudden liquidation notices, vault balances dropping to zero, or oracle price feeds showing implausible values for a token that was just updated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, who noted that the parameter token_address is never read inside the function. It is hard to notice because the function signature suggests correct behaviour and the UI may display the intended token, while the underlying storage is altered for a different token, making the misconfiguration invisible without deep inspection. The appropriate remediation is to retrieve the correct token identifier from the token‑address‑to‑ID mapping using the supplied token_address and then apply the oracle and LTV updates to that identifier. This class of bug falls under incorrect identifier usage or parameter misuse, a common pitfall when reusing code without adapting variable references.

title: Inadequate Proxy Implementation Preventing Contract Upgrades
content: The vulnerability stems from an incomplete proxy pattern where the proxy contract forwards calls to a logic contract using DELEGATECALL but does not replicate the constructor‑based initialization performed by the logic contract. In the examined token system the implementation contract expects its owner, name, symbol and decimal values to be set in its constructor. Because DELEGATECALL executes in the context of the proxy, the storage slots belonging to the implementation are never written; the proxy only stores its own admin and implementation addresses. Consequently, when a user interacts with the token through the proxy, the variables that should contain the owner address and token metadata remain at their default values, typically zero. From a user perspective this manifests as a token that appears on‑chain but cannot be transferred, minted, or have its ownership functions called – the UI may show a balance, yet attempts to send tokens or claim ownership result in no action or a revert, and the owner field reads as 0x000…0. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the proxy’s storage layout with the expectations of the implementation contract. It is subtle because the proxy forwards most calls correctly and does not emit obvious errors; only functions that rely on the uninitialized state fail, making the problem easy to miss in functional testing. The impact is critical: the contract becomes effectively unusable, the intended owner loses control, and any downstream applications that depend on the token may be blocked, potentially freezing user funds. The flaw occurs whenever a logic contract relies on its constructor for essential state setup and is linked to a proxy without an explicit initialization routine. To remediate, the implementation should expose an initializer function that can be called once by the proxy after deployment, or the required variables should be stored as immutable constants, or the proxy constructor should directly write the known storage slots for those variables. Any of these approaches ensures that the proxy’s storage contains the correct owner and token metadata, restoring expected behavior and preserving control over the contract.
summary:
The TokenImpl smart contract requires Owner, name, symbol and decimals, of TokenImpl to be set by the TokenImpl constructor.
Consider two smart contracts, contract A and contract B. If contract A performs a delegatecall on contract B, the state/storage variables of contract B are not accessible by contract A.
Therefore, when TokenProxy targets an implementation of TokenImpl and interacts with it via a DELEGATECALL, it will not be able to access any of the state variables of the TokenImpl contract. Instead, the TokenProxy will access its local storage, which does not contain the variables set in the constructor of the TokenImpl implementation.
When the TokenProxy contract is constructed it will only initialize and set two storage slots:
• The proxy admin address ( _setAdmin internal function)
• The token implementation address ( _setImplementation private function)
Hence when a proxy call to the implementation is made, variables such as Owner will be uninitialised (effectively set to their default value). This is equivalent to the owner being the 0x0 address. Without access to the implementation state variables, the proxy contract is rendered unusable.
As stated by the ZeppelinOS documentation [2]:
if your logic contract relies on its constructor to set up some initial state, this has to be redone after the proxy upgrades to your logic contract. For example, it’s common for logic contracts to inherit from Zeppelin’s Ownable contract implementation. When your logic contract inherits from Ownable, it also inherits Ownable’s constructor that sets who the owner is upon contract creation. When you link the proxy contract to use your logic contract, the value of who the owner is from the proxy’s perspective is lost.
Further information can be found in the Solidity documentation which describes how state variables are laid out in storage as well as this blog post [5] which discusses the DELEGATECALL opcode dynamics.
Smart Contract Security Review Summary

title: Variable stakedButUnverifiedNativeETH Is Never Decremented
content: The vulnerability consists of an accounting mismatchin the EigenLayer integration where the contract variable that records the amount of native ETH staked through the protocol, referred to as stakedButUnverifiedNativeETH, is increased when users call the staking entry point but never decreased when those users later withdraw their ETH via the withdrawal workflow. The root cause is that the two withdrawal functions, initiateNativeEthWithdrawBeforeRestaking and claimNativeEthWithdraw, transfer the unstaked Ether to the caller but omit any update to the accounting variable. As a result the protocol’s internal view of total assets continues to include Ether that has already left the system. This inflated asset count is used to calculate the price of the rsETH token, causing the price to be higher than it should be. An attacker or any user can exploit this by simply withdrawing ETH after the price has been overstated; they receive the same amount of Ether they are entitled to, but the protocol records that the same amount is still part of its reserves, effectively creating phantom assets. When subsequent users redeem rsETH at the artificially high price, the protocol must honor withdrawals that exceed its real holdings, leading to a shortfall and potentially catastrophic loss of funds. The issue manifests every time a withdrawal is performed after a stake, because the decrement step is missing, and it affects all participants who hold rsETH as well as the protocol itself, which may become insolvent. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit by SigmaPrime, who noticed that the accounting variable was never written to in the withdrawal paths. Because the variable is internal and not directly exposed to users, the problem can remain hidden; the token price appears normal on the surface, and only a careful comparison of on‑chain asset balances against the token supply reveals the discrepancy. To remediate the bug, the contract should update stakedButUnverifiedNativeETH by subtracting the amount of Ether that is being withdrawn, ensuring that the recorded total assets always reflect the actual funds held by the protocol. This class of bug falls under the broader category of improper state updates or accounting errors, where a state variable that tracks a resource is not correctly synchronized with the real flow of that resource, leading to over‑statement of balances, inflated token valuations, and ultimately loss of economic security.
summary: The incorrect accounting of variable stakedButUnverifiedNativeETH may cause inaccurate rsETH price. Variable stakedButUnverifiedNativeETH in NodeDelegator is meant to track the amount of native ETH staked through EigenLayer. As a result it is incremented when the function stake32Eth() is called. However, when a NodeDelegator withdraws ETH using functions initiateNativeEthWithdrawBeforeRestaking() and claimNativeEthWithdraw() it is not decremented. When the unstaked Ether is then sent to a user who wishes to withdraw, the Ether will still be counted towards the total assets of the protocol even though it is no longer a part of the protocol. This results in the price of rsETH being higher than it should be. When users withdraw assets at this inﬂated rsETH price, the protocol will suffer significant losses.

title: The Value of ethValueInWithdrawal Is Not Normalised To 18 Decimals
content: The vulnerability is a scaling error in the conversion routine that calculates the amount of Ether represented by an EigenLayer asset when minting rsETH. In the function that converts an EigenLayer asset to rsETH, the code multiplies the asset amount (already expressed with 18 decimal places) by the asset price returned by the LRTOracle (also expressed with 18 decimal places). Because both operands are in the 10^18 scale, the product is in the 10^36 scale, but the implementation never normalises the result by dividing by the Ether price (10^18). Consequently the variable ethValueInWithdrawal is stored with an inflated magnitude of up to 10^36. This inflated value is later added to the pool’s ethStakedInEigenLayer counter and participates in the rsETH price calculation performed by LRTOracle.updateRSETHPrice. The price formula multiplies the total asset deposits by the asset‑to‑ETH exchange rate, so the oversized ethValueInWithdrawal drives the rsETH price far above its true market value, potentially by many orders of magnitude. An attacker can exploit this by depositing assets, receiving rsETH at a severely over‑valued price, and later redeeming it for far less Ether than the protocol believes it holds, effectively draining funds. The impact is a broken accounting model: users see rsETH prices that are absurdly high, withdrawals return far less Ether than expected, and the protocol’s total value locked is mis‑reported. The bug manifests whenever convertEigenlayerAssetToRsEth is called, i.e., during any deposit of EigenLayer‑backed assets, and it affects all participants who hold or interact with rsETH, including regular users and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic flow of asset conversion and price aggregation. It is hard to notice because the arithmetic does not overflow; the numbers remain within uint256 limits, so the contract does not revert, and the mis‑scaled values simply produce a wrong but plausible‑looking price. The correct fix is to normalise ethValueInWithdrawal by dividing the product of assetAmount and assetPrice by the Ether price constant (10^18) before it is used in any further calculations, thereby restoring the proper 18‑decimal scaling for all downstream price and accounting logic. In abstract terms, this is a classic decimal‑normalisation bug where two fixed‑point numbers are multiplied without adjusting the scale, leading to an over‑estimation of value and a breach of the protocol’s financial invariants.
summary:
In function convertEigenlayerAssetToRsEth(), the value of ethValueInWithdrawal is not divided by the price of Ether, which will cause the rsETH price calculated in LRTOracle to be much higher than it should. The variable ethValueInWithdrawal on line [117] is calculated as the product of assetAmount and LRTOracle.getAssetPrice(asset), which are both in the scale of 10^18. As a result, ethValueInWithdrawal is in the scale of 10^36. This value would highly impact the price of rsETH. ethValueInWithdrawal is used in LRTDepositPool.getETHDistributionData() as a part of ethStakedInEigenLayer in the following formula:
```solidity
LRTDepositPool.sol
ethStakedInEigenLayer += ILRTConverter(lrtConverter).ethValueInWithdrawal();
```
Then, the function LRTOracle.updateRSETHPrice() calculates the rsETH price based on sum of the function LRTDepositPool.getTotalAssetDeposits() of the different assets as follows:
```solidity
LRTDepositPool.sol
uint256 totalAssetAmt = ILRTDepositPool(lrtDepositPoolAddr).getTotalAssetDeposits(asset);
totalETHInPool += totalAssetAmt * assetER;
```
The variable ethValueInWithdrawal is a part of of the return value of getTotalAssetDeposits(). Therefore, the price of rsETH would be very high and up to 10^36.

title: Elected TSS Nodes Can Act Without Any Deposit
content: An elected threshold signature service (TSS) node can be selected by the BITDAO even after it has withdrawn the insurance deposit that is supposed to guarantee honest behaviour. The root cause is that the contract that records the election result (setTssGroupMember) does not verify that the candidate still holds a sufficient stake in the TssStakingSlashing contract at the moment the election transaction is executed. Because the election transaction is submitted through the public mempool, a malicious node can monitor the pending transaction, submit a withdrawToken call that removes its deposit in the same block, and then let the original election transaction be mined. The node therefore appears in the on‑chain list of active TSS members while its deposit balance is zero, removing any source of funds that could be used for slashing. An attacker can exploit this by timing the withdrawal to precede the election transaction, either by front‑running or by including both calls in the same block with a higher gas price. The impact is that the protocol loses its economic deterrent against inactivity or malicious signing; a compromised or lazy node can continue to participate without risk of being penalised, potentially leading to incorrect signatures, service downtime, or loss of user funds that rely on the TSS service. The condition required for the exploit is the existence of a separate, publicly visible election transaction and a separate withdrawal function that can be called before the election is finalized. All parties that rely on the TSS – the BITDAO, downstream contracts, and end‑users – are affected because the security model assumes that every elected node has collateral that can be seized. The issue was discovered during a manual security review by SigmaPrime, who noted that the election logic does not re‑check the deposit balance after a withdrawal. The bug is subtle because the contract state appears correct at the time the election is scheduled, and only changes between scheduling and execution, a window that is not obvious in static analysis. To remediate, the contract should enforce an atomic check that each elected address still holds the required deposit at the moment setTssGroupMember is executed, or redesign the workflow so that deposit locking and election are performed in a single transaction or via a private transaction relay that prevents mempool observation. By ensuring the deposit cannot be removed without first being deregistered, the protocol restores its ability to slash misbehaving nodes and preserves the intended economic incentives.
summary:
A node can remove its insurance deposit and still be elected as an active TSS node.
TSS nodes are voted for by the BITDAO which then pushes the currently elected nodes on-chain. Nodes that wish
to be voted for must provide a deposit as insurance that they will perform their role honestly if elected. By timing a
withdrawal correctly, a node can remove their deposit and still be elected as an active TSS node. As a result, there is
no means of punishing the node for inactivity or malicious behaviour.
This can occur because election results are published on-chain and so a dishonest node could watch the Ethereum
mempool and frontrun the transaction including their own approval by the BITDAO with a call to withdrawToken().
This has the effect of removing their deposit and still being elected in the BITDAO’s transaction.
As a result the node would no longer have a deposit from which to deduct funds if they are slashed; this means they
are not incentivised to act honestly or timely.

title: Attacker May Steals Stake in stakeWithPermit()
content: The vulnerability resides in the staking function that accepts an off‑chain permit signature. The function receives a 'from' address, a 'to' address, an amount and a deadline, then calls the ERC20 permit method with the parameters (from, address(this), amount, deadline, v, r, s). Because the permit signature does not cover the 'to' argument, the contract never checks that the destination of the newly minted staking shares matches the signer. An attacker who can observe the pending transaction in the mempool can copy the calldata, keep the valid signature, and replace the 'to' field with his own address. By submitting the modified transaction with a higher gas price, the attacker can have it mined before the original one. The permit call still succeeds because the signed data is unchanged, the token transfer is taken from the legitimate 'from' address, but the internal _stake call mints the staking shares to the attacker’s address. As a result the victim loses the right to the staked position and any future rewards, while the attacker gains the shares without providing any tokens. The issue appears only when stakeWithPermit is used with a non‑zero 'to' argument and when an adversary can front‑run the transaction; normal direct staking functions that do not rely on a permit are unaffected.
