The issue manifests only when the contract’s queued balance stays below the depositThreshold while totalActiveDeposits continues to be inflated, a situation that can be deliberately created by an adversary. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the relationship between deposit handling and fee computation and noticed that totalActiveDeposits was updated before the underlying deposit call. The bug is subtle because the contract’s token balance does increase with each tiny deposit, giving the impression that assets are being accumulated, yet the underlying pool never receives them, so the fee logic appears to work correctly until the threshold condition blocks it. The proper fix is to adjust the _deposited function so that totalActiveDeposits is only increased when the queued amount actually exceeds the depositThreshold and is deposited into the sDai pool, or to separate the accounting of queued deposits from active deposits entirely. This class of bug falls under improper state accounting and threshold‑based logic errors that can be exploited to manipulate fee calculations.

title: Attackers can steal unclaimed rewards from GlpStrategy because the accounted balance does not include unclaimed rewards
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the YieldBox GLP strategy where the reported token balance used for share‑to‑amount conversion does not include rewards that have already been harvested from GMX but are still awaiting conversion into GLP. The root cause is that the _currentBalance function adds pendingRewards to the sGLP balance, yet the deposit routine calculates the number of shares to mint before those pending rewards are actually converted, meaning the share‑to‑asset conversion is performed on a lower total amount than the strategy will later hold. An attacker can exploit this by depositing a large amount of assets while unclaimed rewards exist; because the rewards are not reflected in the share calculation, the attacker receives more shares than their proportional contribution warrants. When the attacker subsequently withdraws, the strategy’s balance now includes the previously hidden rewards, so the attacker extracts a disproportionate slice of those rewards. By using flash‑loan capital the attacker can amplify the deposit size, perform the whole sequence atomically, and walk away with a significant portion of the unclaimed rewards. The impact is a loss of protocol‑earned rewards, effectively causing funds to disappear from the strategy and reducing the value available to legitimate users. The issue affects any user interacting with the GLP strategy through YieldBox, as well as the protocol’s overall reward accounting and any role that relies on accurate share accounting. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between YieldBox share logic and the GLP strategy’s balance reporting. The bug is subtle because the pendingRewards variable appears to represent future earnings, yet it already contains harvested tokens, leading to a mismatch that is not obvious from the UI or simple balance checks. From a user perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal may return more assets than expected, or conversely that the protocol’s reward pool shrinks unexpectedly, violating the business rule that rewards should be distributed proportionally to share holders. The recommended fix is to adjust the _currentBalance implementation (or the deposit/withdraw flow) so that the balance used for share calculations accurately reflects all assets that are actually owned by the strategy at the moment of minting, either by harvesting pending rewards before share computation or by excluding already‑harvested rewards from the pendingRewards term. This aligns the accounting model with the intended proportional distribution and prevents the reward‑stealing attack.

title: deposit_ico_in_ata() overwrites the total supply instead of adding to the total amount
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that allows the contract administrator to deposit additional ICO tokens into the program’s associated token account. Instead of increasing the stored total token amount, the code overwrites the existing value with the newly deposited amount by assigning data.total_amount = ico_amount. This assignment discards any previously recorded deposits, effectively resetting the accounting of the ICO supply each time the function is called. The root cause is a simple logic error: using the assignment operator rather than an additive operation. An attacker who controls the admin role can repeatedly call the deposit function with arbitrary amounts, and the contract will report only the most recent deposit as the total supply. Consequently, the protocol’s accounting layer believes fewer tokens are available than actually exist, which can lead to overselling, incorrect price calculations, or the inability to honor refunds because the recorded supply no longer matches the real token balance. The issue manifests whenever the admin invokes deposit_ico_in_ata with a non‑zero ico_amount, a condition that is expected during normal ICO operation. Users, investors, and any downstream contracts that rely on the total_amount field are affected because they receive misleading information about the token pool; for example, an investor may expect a refund proportional to the total supply but receives nothing or an incorrect amount. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the state‑update logic of the deposit routine. It can be hard to notice because the token transfer itself succeeds and the UI may show the transferred tokens, while the internal total_amount variable silently rolls back to the last value, giving the impression that the system is functioning correctly. To remediate the problem, the assignment should be replaced with an additive update (data.total_amount += ico_amount) so that each deposit cumulatively increases the recorded supply, preserving accurate accounting across multiple deposits. This class of bug is a state‑reset or accounting overwrite error, where a cumulative counter is mistakenly overwritten, violating the business rule that the total ICO token supply must be the sum of all deposits.

title: The read() function returns the wrong value because it is not properly scalable
content: The vulnerability lies in the price‑oracle read() function of OracleUniSolo.sol. The function is intended to return the current Uniswap exchange rate between two tokens. Internally it calls a helper _readUniswapQuote with a scaling argument. The contract stores a variable inBase that is already equal to 10 raised to the number of decimals of the input token (inBase = 10 ** inCur.decimals()). However the read() implementation mistakenly passes 10 ** inBase to the helper, effectively applying the exponentiation a second time. This double‑scaling produces a number that is astronomically larger than the intended quote input. When the token has a typical decimal count (e.g., 18), 10 ** inBase becomes 10 ** (10 ** 18), which cannot be represented in a 256‑bit integer and causes an overflow, causing the call to revert or return zero. Even for smaller decimal values the extra factor skews the price dramatically, so the oracle reports a price that is many orders of magnitude off. The incorrect price propagates to any contract that relies on the oracle for collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, fee calculations or swaps. As a result users may see their balances appear to be worth far more or far less than they actually are, liquidations may be triggered incorrectly, and an attacker could exploit the mis‑priced data to drain funds or manipulate market positions. The bug manifests whenever read() is invoked, i.e., any time a downstream contract queries the price, and it affects all participants that trust the oracle, including token holders, lenders, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the arithmetic of the price‑fetching routine. It is subtle because the function is a simple view call and the code appears to use a reasonable naming convention; the error does not produce an obvious compile‑time warning and may pass basic unit tests that only check for successful execution, not for correct scaling. The proper fix is to remove the extra exponentiation and pass the already‑scaled inBase directly to _readUniswapQuote, ensuring the helper receives the correct magnitude and the returned price matches the actual market rate. This correction restores the intended invariant that the oracle returns a value proportional to the true token price, preserving accounting integrity and preventing fund loss.

title: Anyone can update the cluster address Impact: High, because a malicious user would gain access to a very important function. Likelihood: High, the lack of access control makes this function very easy to exploit.
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access control flaw in the contract’s setCluster function, which allows any external account to replace the stored cluster address with an arbitrary contract. The root cause is the absence of a modifier such as onlyOwner that would limit the call to a privileged role; the function contains only a zero‑address check and an event emission before assigning the new address. An attacker can exploit this by simply invoking setCluster with a malicious ICluster implementation. Once the cluster address is under the attacker’s control, any downstream logic that relies on the cluster – for example routing of funds, permission checks, or protocol state updates – can be redirected, causing loss of assets, incorrect accounting, or denial of service for honest participants. The issue manifests whenever the function is called, which is possible from any address because there is no require statement checking the caller’s identity. All users of the protocol, token holders, and any downstream contracts that trust the cluster reference are potentially affected, as the protocol’s core business logic assumes the cluster is a trusted component. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected function visibility and access patterns. It can be hard to notice because the function appears benign, emits a legitimate event, and does not revert for non‑owner callers, so normal transaction monitoring may not flag it as suspicious. To remediate, the function should be protected with an appropriate access control mechanism – typically the onlyOwner modifier from OpenZeppelin’s Ownable contract or a governance‑based role check – ensuring that only the contract’s owner or an authorized governance entity can update the cluster address. This change restores the intended trust model and prevents arbitrary replacement of a critical protocol component, thereby preserving the integrity of fund flows and accounting assumptions.

title: Approvals can be exploited due to insufficient checks in _exitPositionAndRemoveCollateral
content: The vulnerability resides in a helper contract that manages liquidity positions represented as ERC‑721 tokens. The function that exits a position and optionally unlocks the underlying token accepts two boolean flags: one to trigger an exit operation that records the token identifier, and another to trigger an unlock operation that burns the token and sends the underlying assets to a caller‑specified address. When the exit flag is set to false, the code that would normally capture the token identifier (tOLPId) is skipped, leaving tOLPId at its default value of zero. The unlock branch then checks whether a tokenId was supplied, and if so, it assigns that supplied tokenId to tOLPId without verifying that the caller actually owns the token or that the contract is authorized to act on it. The only check performed later is a generic approval test inside the external unlock function, which only requires that the Magnetar contract be approved to manage the token on behalf of its owner. Because many users grant Magnetar a blanket approval for their liquidity tokens when they interact with the protocol, an attacker can craft a call where exit is false, unlock is true, and the tokenId field contains the identifier of any victim’s token. The contract will then invoke the external unlock routine, which burns the victim’s token directly from the victim’s wallet (thanks to the prior approval) and transfers the underlying liquidity to the attacker’s address. This results in the victim losing their liquidity token and the associated funds, effectively “stealing” the token. The issue occurs only when the combination of flags disables the exit path, which bypasses the ownership validation that exists in the exit branch. It is a classic case of missing authorization checks conditioned on mutable control flow, falling under the broader class of improper access control or authorization bypass bugs. From a user perspective the symptom is that a previously held liquidity token disappears from their wallet, their balance shows zero, and they receive no refund or compensation, contrary to the expectation that only their own positions can be unlocked. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the MagnetarMarketModule where the interaction between the boolean flags and the tokenId handling was examined. It can be hard to notice because the unlock logic appears to be guarded by an external contract’s own approval check, leading reviewers to assume that the helper contract does not need additional verification. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit ownership or contract‑address check before performing the unlock, ensuring that the tokenId either belongs to the caller or to the helper contract itself, mirroring the validation performed in the exit path. This would close the authorization gap and prevent arbitrary token hijacking.

title: ProtocolLoses mint() / redeem() FeesDuetoMissingTreasury Collection Mechanism
content: The vulnerability is an accounting omission in the minting and redemption pathways of the protocol. Both the custodianMint and redeem functions calculate a fee correctly, but the implementation simply subtracts the fee from the amount that is minted or returned to the user without ever allocating that fee to a protocol-controlled treasury. The root cause is the absence of a treasury address state variable and the missing transfer logic that would move the deducted fee to a designated revenue account. As a result, whenever a user mints new tokens, the protocol pretends to charge a fee by reducing the minted amount, yet the fee amount is effectively burned because it is not stored or sent anywhere. The same situation occurs during redemption: the user receives less than the gross value because a fee is taken, but the fee never reaches the treasury. This can be exploited by simply invoking mint or redeem as normal; the attacker does not gain extra assets, but the protocol loses all potential revenue from its fee structure. The impact is a systematic loss of funds that should have been recorded as treasury income, leading to a shortfall in protocol financing, possible inability to cover operational costs, and a mismatch between expected and actual treasury balances. The condition occurs on every successful call to mint or redeem, affecting the protocol itself, its treasury, and indirectly token holders who rely on the protocol’s sustainability. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined fee handling logic and noticed that while fee formulas were correct, there was no destination for the collected amounts. It is hard to notice because the user‑facing behavior (receiving slightly fewer tokens) matches the documented fee policy, so the missing revenue does not manifest as an error in user balances. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing revenue collection” or “fee leakage” bugs where calculated fees are not transferred to a designated account. From a user perspective the UI shows the expected fee deduction but the protocol’s treasury balance remains zero, contradicting the expectation that fees accumulate over time. To remediate, the contract should introduce a treasury address variable and modify both custodianMint and redeem to transfer the calculated fee to that address, ensuring proper accounting and preventing silent fund loss.
summary:
The contract implements minting and redemption fees in the
custodianMint()
and
redeem()
functions but fails to properly collect and store these fees for the protocol. During minting, the fee
is simply deducted from the minted amount without being allocated to a treasury. Similarly, during
redemption, the fee is subtracted from the redeemed value without being captured. While the fee
calculations are correctly implemented mathematically, the contract lacks both a treasury address
variable and the logic to transfer these fees to protocol-controlled addresses. This creates a sit-
uation where protocol revenue that should be accruing to the project treasury is effectively being
burned or lost.

The protocol loses all potential revenue from its fee structure as they are not being collected.

title: CALLCODE to withdrawal precompile may lead to fund loss
content: The vulnerability is a withdrawal‑precompile logic flaw that allows funds to disappear without being transferred. The precompile routine accepts any Transfer object that reaches it and creates a Withdrawal message without verifying that the Transfer’s source account actually holds the funds or that the target is correct. When a CALLCODE instruction is used, the EVM creates a Transfer where both the source and the target are set to the calling contract’s address (the context address). Because the precompile does not check that the source balance is reduced, it processes the Withdrawal as if the funds were available, but no value is deducted from the source account. Consequently, the contract reports a successful withdrawal while the underlying balance remains unchanged, effectively creating a situation where the caller believes they have received funds that were never moved. This can be exploited by an attacker who invokes the vulnerable withdrawal function via CALLCODE, causing the precompile to emit a Withdrawal message that appears valid while the actual token or ether stays in the original contract, leading to loss of assets on the L2. The issue manifests whenever the withdrawal precompile is called through CALLCODE or any other call variant that constructs a Transfer with identical source and target addresses, which is permitted by the current implementation. All users of the affected L2 who rely on the withdrawal precompile are at risk, as their funds may be silently drained or become unrecoverable. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the precompile’s handling of Transfer objects and identified that no source‑account validation occurs. Because the precompile’s behavior seems to succeed and no explicit error is thrown, the problem can be hard to notice; the UI may show a successful withdrawal, the user’s balance may appear unchanged, and no obvious revert occurs. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call or precompile misuse vulnerabilities, where insufficient validation of input data leads to accounting inconsistencies. To remediate, the precompile should enforce proper verification of the Transfer object—ensuring that the source account holds sufficient balance and that the target is a legitimate withdrawal address—or the system should restrict the allowed call opcodes to CALL only, thereby preventing CALLCODE from constructing malformed Transfer objects. Implementing these checks restores the invariant that a withdrawal must correspond to an actual debit of the source balance, aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations that a successful withdrawal results in a reduction of their funds and receipt of the withdrawn amount.
summary:
The current withdrawal precompile implementation blindly accepts a Transfer without checking its source and target. When a CALLCODE instruction executes, it creates a Transfer object with the following values:
• source: the context address.
• target: same as source.
The transfer would then be complied by sputnikvm. It may sound like a no-op, but it's an important implementation detail due to EVM's special account existence rules. The fund will not be transferred to the precompile, but the precompile routine is invoked, passed with the above Transfer object. The precompile then blindly creates a Withdrawal message, but the source money is not deducted at all. This is a critical severity issue due to its attack simplicity and impact of fund lose of the L2.

title: Small amount of native token transfer dropped from mempool
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when a contract attempts to transfer an extremely small amount of the native token (for example one wei or 0.000000000000000001 ether) through a precompiled withdrawal function. The kernel that processes blocks copies the current state to a temporary directory, applies the block, and if any transaction causes a failure it discards the temporary state and drops the offending transactions. When the withdrawal amount is below a certain threshold the kernel’s ticket validation logic treats the operation as an "Invalid ticket" and aborts the whole block. Because the block is reverted, the transaction never reaches the mempool and the sender receives no confirmation; from the user’s perspective the withdrawal simply disappears, the expected balance update never happens and no funds are received. The root cause is an unchecked assumption in the withdrawal handling code that the transferred amount will always be above a minimum viable value; the code does not correctly handle under‑flow or rounding when the amount is effectively zero, leading to a ticket that the kernel cannot validate. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can repeatedly submit withdrawal requests with minimal amounts, causing each block that includes such a request to fail and be reverted. As the sequencer drops the failing block, the attacker can flood the system with these tiny withdrawals, preventing legitimate transactions from being included and potentially halting block production. The impact is a loss of availability for the protocol and a denial of service for users who cannot receive refunds or withdrawals; funds are not lost directly but the protocol becomes unusable while the attack persists. The condition appears only when the withdrawal amount is extremely small; larger amounts are processed normally. All participants that rely on the withdrawal precompile – end‑users, custodial services, and any contracts that automate refunds – are affected because their expected receipt of funds is silently dropped. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised edge‑case values and observed that the transaction was not found in the mempool and that the kernel logged an "Invalid ticket" error. It is hard to notice because the transaction simply vanishes without an explicit revert error visible to the caller, and the high gas limit and gas price do not prevent the block from being discarded. The proper fix is to adjust the withdrawal logic to correctly handle zero‑or‑near‑zero amounts, either by rejecting them early with a clear error or by ensuring the ticket generation can accommodate minimal values, and to add explicit validation that prevents the kernel from treating such transfers as invalid tickets. In broader terms this is a classic small‑value handling bug that breaks accounting assumptions and leads to a denial‑of‑service through block reversion.
summary:
When attempting to send a small amount of native tokens (e.g., 0.000000000000000001 ether) using the cast send command to invoke the withdraw_base58 function of a precompile contract, the transaction is being dropped from the mempool. This issue occurs even when providing a high gas limit and gas price. The specific command used is: cast send 0xff00000000000000000000000000000000000001 "withdraw_base58(string)" "tz1PSeFiWEu5Ry9h6PvNnd8EJG51zEB2yA8Y" --value 0.000000000000000001ether --rpc-url https://node.ghostnet.etherlink.com/ --private-key xxxxxx --legacy --gas-limit 20000000 --gas-price 100000000000

The error message received indicates that the transaction was not found and might have been dropped from the mempool: Error: tx not found, might have been dropped from mempool: 0x4023fd45ae7642c231a8cd89acba948cd55bf79edcdb8cc196095db3a8d8059c

In the logs when try to execute a withdrawal with value = 1wei I get: ------------------ Kernel Invocation ------------------ [Info] Going to run an Ethereum transaction - from address: 0x1074...f3eb - to address: Some(0xff00000000000000000000000000000000000001) [Info] Withdrawal to "tz1fp5ncDmqYwYC568fREYz9iwQTgGQuKZqX" [Error] Block 5 failed with 'Invalid ticket'. Reverting. The team introduced a failsafe mechanism in the kernel:
• When the kernel starts to process a block, everything is copied to a temporary directory.
• If the block was successfully applied, we promote the temp directory.
• If the block fails, we revert the blocks and drop the transactions.
The block fails here, because of a kernel bug, therefore we can attack the kernel by spamming these withdrawals. Fortunately as we have a sequencer as frontend it'll probably just drop the transaction because it cannot produce a block with it. But we can always use the delayed inbox to spam it.

title: Mint PerpetualYieldTokens for free by self-transfer
content: An attacker can mint additional PerpetualYieldTokens (PYT) without paying any cost by invoking the token's transfer or transferFrom function to send tokens to their own address. The contract implementation reads the sender's and recipient's balances into temporary variables, then updates the sender's balance to zero before adding the transferred amount to the recipient's balance using the cached recipient balance. When the sender and recipient are the same address, the first write clears the balance, but the second write uses the previously cached balance (which still holds the original amount) and adds the transfer amount again, resulting in the balance being set to twice its original value. This logic flaw originates from operating on stale storage values rather than reading the latest balance after each write. Exploitation requires only a single transaction that calls transfer(A, balanceOf(A)) or an equivalent call via transferFrom. The impact is that any holder can arbitrarily inflate their token holdings, effectively creating free tokens and breaking the accounting guarantees of the yield token system. The bug manifests when a user attempts a self‑transfer, which may appear as a normal operation in the UI; the user will see their balance unexpectedly double, or the protocol may report inflated total supply. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the token contract where the balance update sequence was examined. Because the code path is only exercised for self‑transfers, it can be missed by standard test suites that focus on transfers between distinct addresses, making it subtle to detect. The correct fix is to read the current balance from storage immediately before each write, or to restructure the transfer logic to use a single atomic update that does not rely on cached values, ensuring that when sender and recipient are identical the net change is zero. This class of bug is commonly known as a self‑transfer balance overwrite or mint‑by‑self‑transfer vulnerability, which violates the fundamental invariant that total token supply must remain constant under transfers. From a user perspective the symptom is an unexpected increase in token balance after a self‑transfer, or a situation where the UI shows a higher balance without any deposit. The protocol's accounting assumptions are broken, potentially leading to over‑issuance of yield tokens and loss of trust in the system.
summary:
The PYT.transfer and transferFrom functions operate on cached balance values. When transferring tokens to oneself the decreased balance is overwritten by an increased balance which makes it possible to mint PYT tokens for free. Consider the following exploit scenario:  
• Attacker A self-transfers by calling token.transfer(A, token.balanceOf(A)).  
• balanceOf[msg.sender] is first set to zero but then overwritten by balanceOf[to] = toBalance + amount, doubling A’s balance.

title: Rewards calculation error will result in 0 rewards for users
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the reward‑accumulation formula used by the staking contract. The code adds the product of unaccountedTime and the per‑weight reward rate to the previously accumulated value and then divides the sum by totalWeight using plain integer division. Because both rate and totalWeight are expressed with 18‑decimal fixed‑point precision, the denominator (totalWeight) quickly becomes much larger than the numerator (unaccountedTime * rate), especially as more users stake. When the numerator is smaller than the denominator, the division truncates to zero, leaving rewardsPerWeight_.accumulated unchanged. Consequently, no new rewards are recorded and users receive a reward balance of zero despite the passage of time. The bug manifests whenever unaccountedTime * rate < totalWeight, a condition that occurs frequently because unaccountedTime is only a few seconds or days (a five‑digit number) while totalWeight can be orders of magnitude larger. All stakers, the protocol’s incentive mechanism, and any downstream contracts that rely on the reward distribution are affected because the accounting assumption that rewards grow over time is violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic logic of getUserStakeReward and updateRewardsPerWeight and noticed that the division would almost always round down to zero. It is hard to notice from the UI because the reward balance simply never changes, giving the impression that rewards are not being issued rather than that they are being mis‑calculated. The proper fix is to replace the plain division with a fixed‑point division that preserves precision, such as Solmate’s FixedPointMathLib divWadDown, and to use mulWadDown for the final multiplication. This changes the calculation to a mathematically correct fixed‑point operation, ensuring that rewards accumulate correctly and users see the expected increase in their reward balances.

title: Pool token price is incorrect when there is more than one pending upkeep
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the pool token price that occurs when the contract has more than one pending upkeep (i.e., when there are commits scheduled for future update intervals). The price is derived from the ratio of the token balance to the total supply of pool tokens, but the implementation adds back only the tokens that are burned in the current update interval. Because burn commits are executed immediately at the moment commit() is called, the totalSupply is reduced before the future burns are accounted for. Consequently, when the price is computed for a given interval, the denominator still contains tokens that have already been burned for later intervals, making the price artificially low. An attacker can create or front‑run commits that trigger burns in future intervals, then mint pool tokens at this undervalued price, effectively receiving more pool tokens than the deposited assets merit and draining value from the pool. The issue manifests only when there are pending commits for IDs greater than the current updateIntervalId, a situation that arises when the frontRunningInterval parameter is larger than the update interval and multiple upkeeps are queued. All participants who interact with the pool – including regular users and liquidity providers – are affected because the accounting no longer reflects the true supply, leading to users receiving fewer pool tokens than expected, balances that appear to shrink, or refunds that are missing. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the intended accounting model with the actual Solidity code and noticed that the price formula does not include burn amounts from future intervals. The bug is hard to notice because the UI may still display a non‑zero balance while the underlying price is wrong, and the loss of value can be gradual and only observable after several transactions. The root cause is premature inclusion of burned tokens in the totalSupply without compensating for burns that belong to later intervals, a classic case of incorrect supply accounting in a price oracle. To remediate, the price computation must be adjusted to add back all tokens that have been burned across all pending intervals, or the burn accounting should be deferred until the upkeep for the specific interval is executed, ensuring that the denominator always reflects the true circulating supply. Fixing the calculation restores the invariant that the pool token price accurately represents the ratio of assets to outstanding pool tokens, preventing attackers from exploiting a lower price and protecting users from silent fund loss.
summary:
```solidity
The amount of pool tokens to mint and quote tokens to burn is determined by the pool token price.
This price, for a commit at update interval ID X, should not be influenced by any pending commits for IDs greater than X.
However, in the current implementation price includes the current total supply but burn commits burn pool tokens immediately when commit() is called, not when upkeep() is executed.
// pool token price computation at execution of updateIntervalId, example for long price
priceHistory[updateIntervalId].longPrice = longBalance / (IERC20(tokens[LONG_INDEX]).totalSupply() + _totalCommit[updateIntervalId].longBurnAmount + _totalCommit[updateIntervalId].longBurnShortMintAmount)

The implementation tries to fix this by adding back all tokens burned at this updateIntervalId but it must also add back all tokens that were burned in future commits (i.e. when ID > updateIntervalID).
This issue allows an attacker to get a better pool token price and steal pool token funds.
```

title: Deal tokens are mistakenly burnt for all fiat accounts on principal payout
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect token‑burn calculation in the principal payout distribution routine of a deal contract. The routine is intended to separate fiat‑only payouts from on‑chain payouts and only burn tokens belonging to on‑chain holders. The logic determines the fiat payout amount only when there is a positive on‑chain balance; when all holders are fiat accounts the on‑chain balance is zero, the fiat payout amount is forced to zero. However the total amount of tokens to be burned is still calculated from the requested payoutAmount, and for each holder the contract computes a burn amount proportional to the holder’s balance relative to the total supply. Because the burn calculation does not check the holder’s fiat flag, fiat accounts receive a non‑zero burnTokenAmount even though their payout amount is zero. As a result, when a principal payout is initiated while the deal contains exclusively fiat accounts, the contract iterates over the list of payouts and calls the burn function for every entry, effectively destroying all deal tokens that were issued to fiat participants. This can happen during any scheduled principal payout or any manual trigger of the _initiatePrincipalPayout function when the on‑chain token balance is zero. The impact is that users who have deposited fiat and received deal tokens see their token balance disappear, the protocol’s accounting between fiat and on‑chain portions becomes inconsistent, and the loan may be considered closed prematurely even though the principal has not been repaid. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a normal payout transaction, but after confirmation the user’s token balance is reduced to zero and no fiat refund is received, violating the expectation that “my tokens should remain until the loan ends”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the payout logic, where the auditor observed that the burn calculation does not respect the isFiatAccount flag and that the fiatPayoutAmount branch returns zero when on‑chain balance is zero, yet tokens are still marked for burning. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; it simply burns tokens silently, making the loss easy to miss unless balances are inspected after a payout. The class of bug is a faulty conditional accounting error that mixes off‑chain and on‑chain fund distribution, leading to an unintended token burn. The recommended fix is to compute a single totalPayoutAmount that represents the combined amount to be burned for both fiat and on‑chain portions, then derive the on‑chain and off‑chain payout amounts from that total, ensuring that when the fiat balance is the only source the burn amount for fiat holders is zero. In other words, the burn calculation should be gated by the holder’s fiat flag or by using the total supply after excluding fiat balances, so that no tokens are burned for accounts that are supposed to receive fiat payouts only.

title: TradableStaking: rewards accounting is corrupted
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the staking contract where the per‑user reward checkpoint (previousRewardPerToken) is never set when a new staking position is created. Because the mapping entry defaults to zero, the first time a user calls the claim function the contract calculates the reward as if the user were the very first participant, using the full cumulative reward per token instead of the user‑specific offset. This happens whenever a stake is opened and the contract does not write the current cumulativeRewardPerTokenStored into previousRewardPerToken for that address. An attacker or any regular user can exploit the bug by opening a stake and immediately invoking the reward claim, receiving a reward amount that is far larger than what their stake and time would justify. The impact is a systematic over‑distribution of reward tokens: the protocol’s reward pool is drained faster than intended, token economics are distorted, and honest participants may see their future rewards reduced. The condition is triggered only on the first claim after a stake creation, making the problem subtle; subsequent claims behave normally, so the excess reward can be missed during casual testing. All stakers, the protocol’s treasury, and token holders are affected because the inflated payouts reduce the pool available for legitimate rewards. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the reward‑tracking logic and noticed that the mapping was never initialized. It is hard to notice because the contract still updates balances correctly after the first claim, and the bug does not cause a revert or obvious error – it merely gives users more tokens than expected. To remediate, the contract should initialize previousRewardPerToken for a user to the current cumulativeRewardPerTokenStored at the moment the stake is created, or alternatively store this checkpoint inside the Stake struct and remove the separate mapping. Updating cumulativeRewardPerTokenStored before the initialization and adding comprehensive tests for deposit, withdrawal, and reward calculations will prevent the accounting corruption.
summary:
The TradableStaking contract uses the previousRewardPerToken mapping to keep track of the rewards-per-token, the last time each user updated their rewards. The problem is that this mapping isn't initialized whenever a staking position is created. This means that the first time a user claims rewards, the value of previousRewardPerToken[user] will be zero, so they will receive rewards as if they were the first user to stake their tokens in the contract.
This results in users getting way more rewards than they are entitled to, and the whole system to keep track of rewards will not work.

title: TradableStaking: shares accounting is corrupted
content: The contract contains an accounting bug in its staking routine that corrupts the share ledger. When a user calls the internal _stake function, the code calculates the number of shares that should be assigned to that user (userShares) based on the deposited amount, the current total shares and the pool balance. However, due to a typographical error the contract records the global variable representing the total number of outstanding shares (shares) instead of the calculated userShares. Consequently the stake record for the caller stores a share count equal to the entire pool’s share supply. The same mistake is reflected in the StakeValidated event, which also emits the total shares rather than the user‑specific amount. This flaw occurs on every execution of the staking function, meaning any participant can obtain a stake entry that claims ownership of all shares in the vault. An attacker can therefore withdraw later and receive rewards as if they owned the whole pool, effectively draining the vault’s assets. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after staking a modest amount the UI shows a share balance that matches the total pool, and a subsequent withdrawal returns the entire vault balance, leaving other participants with zero or dramatically reduced balances. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by ThreeSigma, and it can be hard to notice because the contract still updates the total share counter correctly and the balance arithmetic appears sound; only the per‑user share assignment is wrong, which may not be obvious without inspecting the assignment and emitted event. The vulnerability belongs to the class of share‑allocation or accounting bugs where a global state variable is mistakenly used in place of a user‑specific calculation, breaking the invariant that the sum of individual shares equals the total shares. To remediate, the assignment should store uint64(userShares) in the stake record and the event should emit userShares, followed by comprehensive testing of deposit, withdrawal and reward logic to ensure the invariant holds.

title: TradableMarginHandler: can't perform liquidations
content: During liquidation the contract checks a condition that determines whether a position is liquidatable. The condition is marginBalance + (collateralAmount - protocolPercentOfCollateral) <= tradingFeesAccumulated. When this condition is true, the position should be liquidated, but the same condition is used as a guard before performing the arithmetic that updates the user reserve balance. The update adds marginBalance + collateralAmount - totalAmountOwed, where totalAmountOwed = tradingFeesAccumulated + protocolPercentOfCollateral. Because all variables are unsigned integers, the subtraction can underflow when totalAmountOwed exceeds the sum of marginBalance and collateralAmount. The underflow triggers a revert, causing attemptLiquidation() to fail every time the position is actually liquidatable. The root cause is the combination of an unsigned arithmetic underflow and a flawed logic that treats the liquidation‑eligibility check as a safety guard rather than a separate validation step. An attacker or any user trying to liquidate a position will see the transaction revert with no funds transferred, leaving the position permanently stuck in a liquidatable state. This situation can lock user funds, break the protocol’s risk management, and potentially lead to insolvency if many positions become unliquidatable. The bug appears only when the liquidation condition holds, which is exactly the scenario where liquidation is required, making it easy to miss during casual testing because the condition itself looks correct. It was discovered during a formal audit by ThreeSigma, where the underflow was observed in the attemptLiquidation() implementation. The issue belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow combined with improper liquidation guard logic, often referred to as a liquidations revert or funds‑disappearance bug. From a user perspective the UI would show a failed transaction, no refund, and the balance of the position would remain unchanged even though the protocol reports it as liquidatable. To fix the problem the contract should avoid unsigned underflow by using signed integers for the intermediate calculation, by checking the sign of the amount to be added to the reserve balance and performing addition or subtraction accordingly, or by restructuring the liquidation logic so that the eligibility check does not also act as a revert guard. Adding a test case that forces a liquidation scenario and verifies that the reserve balance is updated without reverting would also help prevent regression.

title: TradableMarginHandler: margin account withdraw message will revert on the sideVault
content: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch in how cross‑chain messages are encoded and decoded between the TradableMarginHandler contract and its counterpart side vault. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the handler calls withdrawalValidation which builds a payload using abi.encodePacked("mw", user, selectedToken.token, amount) and forwards it to the side vault via a LayerZero message. The side vault, however, expects the payload to be encoded with abi.encode so that it can decode the fields using standard ABI decoding. Because abi.encodePacked produces a tightly packed byte array without length prefixes, the side vault’s _nonblockingLzReceive function attempts to decode the message as a string and other types, which always reverts. From the user’s perspective the UI may report that the withdrawal transaction succeeded on the source chain, but the tokens never appear in the destination vault, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and creating the impression that funds have vanished. The root cause is an incorrect choice of encoding function that violates the contract’s cross‑chain communication contract, a classic case of message format incompatibility. Exploitation does not require an attacker; any legitimate withdrawal request triggers the failure, effectively locking user funds on the side vault. The impact is critical because users cannot retrieve their assets, the protocol’s liquidity may become stranded, and trust in the system erodes. The issue occurs whenever withdrawalValidation is executed, i.e., for every withdrawal request, and only on the side vault deployed on a different chain where the decoding logic is fixed. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the payload construction and attempted to decode it in a test contract, which immediately reverted. The problem is subtle because the transaction on the source chain does not revert, giving a false sense of success, and the failure only manifests on the remote chain where logs may be less visible. To remediate, the payload should be constructed with abi.encode so that the side vault can correctly decode the message fields, restoring the intended withdrawal flow and preventing funds from being stuck. This class of bug falls under cross‑chain message encoding mismatches, where the sender and receiver disagree on the ABI encoding scheme, leading to decoding errors and transaction reverts.

title: Critical precision loss in slippage protection calculation
content: During token swaps the contract attempts to protect users from excessive slippage by computing an internal minimum output amount. The calculation multiplies the input amount by a constant that should represent the fixed‑point scaling factor (1e18) but mistakenly uses the literal integer 18. Because the scaling factor is off by twelve orders of magnitude, the derived expected output amount is either severely undervalued or rounded down to zero for any realistic swap size. When the expected amount becomes zero, the subsequent slippage protection formula also yields zero, so the contract accepts any user‑provided minimum amount, effectively disabling the slippage guard. An attacker can therefore submit a swap with a tiny minUltiAmount, manipulate the market price of the ULTI/input token pair, and force the contract to execute the trade at a price far worse than intended, draining reserves. The bug appears only when the swap function is called; normal contract interactions that do not involve swaps are unaffected. Users see the symptom that after confirming a swap they receive no ULTI tokens or their ULTI balance remains unchanged even though the input tokens were transferred, leading to apparent loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against the documented formula and noticed the use of 18 instead of 1e18. Because the calculation still compiles and returns a value, the problem does not raise an exception and can be missed by simple testing that does not check edge cases with small expected outputs. The vulnerability belongs to the class of precision‑loss or fixed‑point arithmetic bugs that break financial invariants. To remediate, the contract should replace the constant 18 with the proper 1e18 scaling factor, and consider adding explicit checks that the computed expected amount is non‑zero before applying slippage limits. This restores the intended protection that the output amount cannot fall below the user‑specified minimum adjusted for the maximum allowed slippage, preventing malicious extraction of value from the protocol's reserves.
summary:
The ULTI contract contains a precision error in its slippage protection
mechanism during token swaps (using 18 instead of 1e18). In the
_swapInputTokenForUlti function, the calculation of
expectedUltiAmountWithoutSlippage uses an incorrect scaling factor that
results in a significant precision loss.
function _swapInputTokenForUlti(
uint256 inputAmountToSwap,
uint256 minUltiAmount,
uint256 twap,
uint256 deadline
) private
returns (uint256 ultiAmount)
// 2. Calculate expected output without slippage
uint256 expectedUltiAmountWithoutSlippage = inputAmountToSwap * 18 /
// twap; // @audit should be inputAmountToSwap * 1e18 / twap
// 3. Choose the higher minimum amount between user-specified and
// internal slippage protection
uint256 minUltiAmountInternal = (expectedUltiAmountWithoutSlippage *
(10000 - MAX_SWAP_SLIPPAGE_BPS)) / 10000;
uint256 effectiveMinUltiAmount = minUltiAmount > minUltiAmountInterna
return ultiAmount;
The error leads to:
Precision Loss: Using 18 instead of 1e18 as the scaling factor causes
expectedUltiAmountWithoutSlippage to be drastically undervalued or
rounded down to 0 for most practical input amounts.
Broken Slippage Protection: When expectedUltiAmountWithoutSlippage is
0, minUltiAmountInternal also becomes 0, effectively disabling the
contract's internal slippage protection.
Malicious actors can:
Set a very low minUltiAmount (e.g., 1)
Manipulate the ULTI/Input token price through market operations
Execute swaps with extreme slippage
Extract value from the protocol's reserves

title: The Lowest contributor of the top contributor's list can be removed unfairly
content: The vulnerability is an improper handling of duplicate entries in the top‑contributors rankingused by the contract. The contract maintains a fixed‑size list of the 33 highest contributors and updates it in the _updateTopContributors function whenever a new deposit occurs. When the list is full the algorithm searches for the lowest contribution (minContributor) and, if the new contribution (updatedContribution) exceeds the current minimum, it removes the lowest entry and inserts the new contributor. However, the code does not verify whether the contributor that triggered the update is already present in the list. Consequently, if an existing top contributor makes an additional deposit that is larger than the current minimum, the contract still removes the lowest contributor before adding the same address again. This results in the list losing one distinct entry and ending up with only 32 unique contributors. The root cause is a missing existence check before performing the removal, which belongs to the class of list‑management bugs where duplicate insertion logic is flawed. An attacker can exploit the flaw by repeatedly depositing from an address already in the top list while using a second address to make a minimal deposit that triggers the removal condition. By doing so the attacker can force the lowest legitimate contributor out of the ranking, causing that user to lose eligibility for reward distribution and potentially become a target for denial‑of‑service attacks on the pump function that relies on the list. The impact is that honest contributors may see their reward share drop to zero, their address disappear from the UI leaderboard, and the protocol’s incentive mechanism become skewed. The issue manifests only when the list is full and a top contributor makes a new deposit that is higher than the current minimum, which is a realistic scenario in active fundraising contracts. It was discovered during a manual security review that examined the update logic and noticed the absence of a check for existing members. The bug can be subtle because the contract still records the deposit correctly, so balances appear unchanged, yet the ranking list silently shrinks, making the problem hard to notice without inspecting the list size or reward calculations. To fix the issue the update routine should first attempt to add or update the contributor atomically; only if the contributor is a new entry should the lowest contributor be removed. This ensures that the list size remains constant and that existing top contributors are not penalised by an unnecessary removal. The correction aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that the top‑contributors list always contains the 33 highest distinct contributors and that rewards are distributed accordingly.
summary:
When a new deposit is made the list of top contributors is updated in the
_updateTopContributors function. If the list is full (33 contributors), the
lowest contributor is searched. If the contribution of the current contributor is
greater than the one of the lowest contributor, the lowest contributor is
removed and the current contributor is added to the list.
// Replace lowest contributor if new contribution is higher
if (updatedContribution > minContribution) {
_topContributors.remove(minContributor);
_topContributors.set(contributorAddress, updatedContribution);
However, it is not checked if the current contributor is already on the list. So, if
the current contributor is already on the list, the lowest contributor is unfairly
removed, leaving the list with 32 contributors.
This has several implications:
The lowest contributor can be DoSed for the pump function.
The lowest contributor can be removed from the rewards distribution for top
distributors.
It can be used by a contributor present in the list to occupy another position
by removing the lowest contributor and using a different account to make a
deposit for the minimum amount allowed, even if there were many other
contributors with higher contributions.

title: UBT-1 | Stuck ETH Funds
content: The vulnerability consists of a permanent lock‑up of native Ether that is transferred to the protocol treasury. When the EmergencySafeWithdraw function of a dependent contract such as SquidBetPrizePool is invoked, it forwards Ether to the treasury address, but the treasury contract does not implement any mechanism to move that Ether out, to convert it into the designated funding token, or to allocate it for further use. The root cause is a missing withdrawal or conversion routine in the treasury’s code, which means the contract’s accounting assumes that received Ether can be freely managed, while in reality the balance becomes immutable. An attacker or any user who triggers the emergency withdrawal can cause Ether to be deposited into the treasury, after which the funds cannot be retrieved, effectively disappearing from the protocol’s usable pool. This situation manifests when the emergency withdrawal path is exercised; the treasury’s balance will increase, but the user interface will show no option to claim, withdraw, or exchange the funds, leading to symptoms such as “balance shows zero after expected refund” or “treasury holds ETH but I cannot move it”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the treasury’s public interface and noticed the absence of any payable or withdraw functions. Because the contract compiles without errors and does not revert when receiving Ether, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed when a transaction actually sends Ether to the treasury. The impact is critical: funds become inaccessible, refunds may fail, and the protocol’s financial logic is broken, violating the assumption that all incoming assets are liquid. To remediate, the treasury should be extended with a function that either transfers the Ether to a designated address, swaps it for the funding token, or otherwise allocates it according to the protocol’s accounting rules, ensuring that deposited Ether can be reclaimed or utilized as intended.
summary:
There is no way to withdraw the Ether sent to the treasury. Contracts like SquidBetPrizePool send
ether to the treasury when EmergencySafeWithdraw is called.

title: UBT-2 | Lack of Access Control
content: The contract contains a privilege escalation vulnerability caused by missing access‑control checks on two state‑changing functions that are intended to be restricted to administrators. The functions responsible for removing a budget allocation and for updating a team member's salary do not verify that the caller is an authorized admin, so any external address can invoke them. Because the contract assumes that only privileged accounts can modify financial parameters, the root cause is the absence of a require(msg.sender == admin) or similar modifier. An attacker can call the deletion function to erase an existing allocation, causing the allocated funds to become inaccessible or incorrectly reassigned, and can call the salary‑change function to set a member’s salary to an arbitrary value, including zero, which may result in loss of expected payouts. This can be exploited at any time after deployment, with no special conditions, simply by sending a transaction to the vulnerable functions. The impact includes unauthorized modification of accounting data, potential loss of funds for team members, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s financial governance. Users who rely on the contract to enforce salary guarantees may see their expected payments disappear, while the protocol’s overall integrity is compromised. The issue was identified during a manual security audit when the reviewer noted that the functions lacked any admin‑only modifier. Because the functions appear to perform critical financial updates, the missing check may not be obvious from the UI, making the bug hard to notice until an unexpected change occurs. The proper remediation is to enforce role‑based access control on all functions that modify allocations or compensation, typically by adding an admin‑only modifier or integrating OpenZeppelin’s AccessControl library. This class of bug falls under 'Missing Access Control' or 'Improper Authorization', where privileged operations are exposed to any caller, leading to unauthorized state changes and financial loss.
summary:
Functions deleteAllocation and changeSalary have no Admin requires so anyone can delete an
allocation and change a team member’s salary.

title: UBT-4 | Arbitrary Salary
content: The contract permits a privileged role to modify the per‑period salary that determines how many funding tokens are transferred when a participant calls the withdraw function. Because the function that changes the salary lacks both an upper bound and proper access restrictions, an attacker can set the salary to an extremely large value. When a withdrawal is later executed, the contract calculates the amount to transfer based on this salary. The unchecked large salary either forces the contract to transfer the entire fundingToken balance, effectively draining the pool, or, during the total‑payout computation, triggers an arithmetic overflow that makes the calculated payout incorrect (often zero), preventing legitimate users from receiving their expected funds. This condition occurs whenever the salary variable is updated before a withdrawal or payout calculation. It impacts any user who expects to receive a salary payment, as they may receive nothing while the contract’s funds disappear. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of a salary cap and insufficient access control on the salary‑setting function. Because the overflow only manifests with extreme values, it may not surface during routine testing, making it difficult to detect. The recommended remediation is to enforce a reasonable maximum salary, restrict the salary‑changing function to a trusted role (e.g., contract owner), and employ safe arithmetic (checked math) when performing payout calculations. This vulnerability belongs to the class of unbounded parameter bugs that lead to arithmetic overflow and fund drain, where unchecked user‑controlled values break accounting logic, causing funds to disappear or legitimate payouts to be blocked.
summary:
The salary could be set arbitrarily high before someone calls withdraw to drain the fundingToken
balance. The salary could also be set arbitrarily high to prevent withdrawal during totalpayout
calculation by causing an overﬂow.

title: UB-1 | Total Bets Not Updated
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error where the contract’s internal record of total bets per side is never updated when a user places a bet. The root cause is that the placeBet function does not modify the bets mapping, leaving the stored total for each side unchanged at zero. When a user later calls withdrawGain, the function attempts to calculate the payout by dividing the total reward pool by bets[result.winner]. Because bets[result.winner] remains zero, the division operation triggers a division‑by‑zero exception, causing the transaction to revert. An attacker or any participant can exploit this by simply invoking withdrawGain after a round has been resolved; the call will always fail, preventing any payout from being transferred. The impact is that all funds locked in the betting pool become unrecoverable through the contract’s intended withdrawal path, effectively resulting in a total loss of user deposits. This condition occurs every time a round finishes, regardless of which side wins, because the total bets are never recorded. All users who have placed bets, as well as the protocol that relies on the betting mechanism, are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected state updates and identified that the bets mapping was never incremented. Because the contract does not emit explicit error messages for the division‑by‑zero case, the failure may appear as a generic revert, making it hard to diagnose without reviewing the source. The proper fix is to update the bets mapping inside placeBet, for example by adding bets[_side] += betAmount, ensuring that the total amount wagered on each side reflects the actual deposits. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency bugs that lead to arithmetic exceptions and broken accounting logic. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful bet placement, but later the withdrawal button would either do nothing or revert, and the user would see a zero payout despite having won, violating the expectation that a winning bet yields a reward. The bug breaks the fundamental business rule that the sum of bets determines the share of the reward pool, causing money to disappear from the contract’s accessible balance.
summary:
The bets mapping is not being updated in placeBet. When withdrawGain is called,
.div(bets[result.winner]) would lead to a division by 0 error every time. Therefore, no one would be
able to withdraw their gains, leading to complete loss of funds.

title: UBT-1 | Treasury Cannot Receive ETH
content: The vulnerability is that the treasury contract does not implement a receive() or fallback() function marked payable, which means the contract is unable to accept plain Ether transfers. The root cause is the omission of a payable entry point for the contract, so any transaction that sends ETH without calling a specific payable function triggers the default behavior of rejecting the transfer and reverting. An attacker or any legitimate user who attempts to fund the treasury by sending ETH directly, or by relying on a fee‑forwarding mechanism, will see the transaction fail or the Ether become permanently locked in the sending address. The impact is that protocol fees, rewards, or any other Ether intended for the treasury never arrive, leading to missing balances, zero refunds, and potentially halted economic flows. This condition occurs whenever the contract receives a plain value transfer, which is common in DeFi protocols that forward fees automatically. All participants who expect the treasury to hold Ether—users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting assumptions that the treasury will increase its balance are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the contract’s external interface and noticed the absence of a receive or fallback payable function. Because the contract compiles without errors and the missing function does not raise a warning, the problem can be easy to overlook, especially if tests only call named functions. The bug belongs to the class of “missing payable fallback” or “inability to receive Ether” vulnerabilities, which break the invariant that a contract can accept Ether sent via the transfer or call methods. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction hash while the treasury balance remains unchanged, or the user may receive a revert message stating that the contract does not accept Ether. Users expect their fees to be deposited and later redistributed, but instead the funds stay with the sender or are reverted, effectively causing “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error”. To remediate the issue the contract should be extended with a receive() external payable {} function (or a payable fallback()) so that any plain Ether transfer is accepted and correctly recorded in the treasury’s balance. Adding this entry point restores the intended accounting flow and prevents Ether from being unintentionally rejected.
summary: Because there is no receive or fallback function, any contract that relies on sending ETH to the treasury will face unintended consequences such as stuck fees.

title: Several issues in adding player to raffle list
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect method of adding a participant to a raffle’s address list. The contract iterates over the entire storage array and, for each element that does not match the new address, writes the new address to the position list.length inside the loop. Because storage arrays in Solidity do not automatically expand when an out‑of‑range index is written, the assignment list[list.length] = _address attempts to write to a non‑existent slot, causing the transaction to revert with an out‑of‑bounds error. Even if the write succeeded, the loop logic adds the address on every iteration where the address is not yet found, resulting in the same address being inserted multiple times – once per existing element. As the number of participants grows, the loop executes more iterations, each performing a costly storage write. This linear‑time, storage‑intensive pattern drives gas consumption upward proportionally to the list size. When the list becomes large enough, the required gas may exceed the block gas limit or become prohibitively expensive for users, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition where new participants cannot join. The impact is that users attempting to join may see their transaction revert, lose the gas spent on the failed attempt, and observe that their address is either missing from the participant list or duplicated, breaking the intended one‑entry‑per‑player rule. The issue manifests whenever a user calls the join function with an address that is not already present in the list, especially as the list length increases. It affects all participants, the raffle operator, and any downstream logic that assumes a unique set of entrants for fair winner selection. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the loop and storage write pattern, noting that the code does not use a mapping or a proper existence check before pushing to the array. The problem can be subtle because the contract may appear to work for small lists, masking the underlying inefficiency and duplicate‑entry bug until the list grows. To remediate, the contract should replace the manual loop with a mapping that tracks whether an address has already joined, and use the array’s push method only after confirming uniqueness. This eliminates the need for a costly iteration, prevents duplicate entries, and ensures gas usage remains constant regardless of list size, thereby restoring correct business logic that each participant is recorded exactly once and that the raffle remains accessible to new entrants.

title: First-time raffle entries are double counted
content: The contract implements a raffle where users can purchase multiple tickets for a given raffle ID. When a user buys tickets for the first time, the function creates a ticket struct and assigns the purchased amount directly to the struct field. Immediately after this assignment the code increments the same amount field again with the same value. As a result the user’s ticket balance is recorded as twice the amount they actually paid for. The root cause is an accounting mistake: the initial ticket amount is set to the purchase quantity instead of starting from zero, and the subsequent addition does not differentiate between first‑time and subsequent purchases. This bug can be exploited by any participant who enters a raffle for the first time, because they will receive double the tickets they paid for, inflating their winning probability and unfairly reducing the odds for all other participants. The impact is a distortion of the raffle’s fairness model, potential loss of value for honest users, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions that each ticket corresponds to a single payment. The condition under which the issue manifests is when the mapping entry ticketsBought[msg.sender][raffleid] does not yet contain a record for the given raffle, i.e., on the first purchase for that raffle. All users who join a raffle for the first time are affected, while later purchases behave correctly. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ticket‑buying logic and noticed that the amount field is written twice. It is easy to miss because the code appears to update the ticket count correctly and the double addition only occurs on the first entry, making the bug invisible for subsequent calls. To remediate the issue the ticket struct should be initialized with an amount of zero when the entry does not exist, and the amount should be increased only once after the payment is processed. This aligns the recorded ticket count with the actual number of tickets purchased and restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship between payment and ticket entitlement. The vulnerability belongs to the class of double‑counting or accounting bugs where state is incorrectly initialized and then updated, leading to inflated balances and broken business logic such as “each ticket costs one unit of price”. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that they bought a certain number of tickets, but the contract internally grants them twice that number, causing unexpected high winning chances for the attacker and unexpectedly low chances for other participants. The expectation that buying N tickets yields N entries is violated, resulting in an unfair raffle outcome.

title: User can buy multiple tickets but pay only for one
content: The contract implements a raffle where users spend experience points (XP) to purchase tickets. The function that handles ticket purchases first checks that the caller’s XP balance is sufficient for the requested number of tickets by multiplying the ticket price by the amount requested. However, when the contract actually deducts XP from the user, it calls the internal spendXP routine with only the single‑ticket price, omitting the multiplication by the amount. As a result, a caller can request any number of tickets, pass the balance check, and be charged for only one ticket. This arithmetic omission creates an under‑charging bug, a class of accounting errors where the cost calculation does not match the quantity of goods or services rendered. An attacker can exploit the flaw by calling buyTicket with a large amount value, receiving a proportional increase in raffle entries while the contract records only a single‑ticket fee. The impact is that the protocol’s ticket distribution becomes unfair, the attacker gains a disproportionate chance of winning, and the protocol loses expected revenue because the XP that should have been burned for each ticket remains in the user’s balance. The vulnerability manifests whenever the buyTicket function is executed with an amount greater than one; it does not depend on block timing or external state beyond the balance check. Users are affected because they receive more tickets than they paid for, which may appear as a “free tickets” promotion, while the protocol and other participants suffer from skewed odds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the balance verification logic with the actual state‑changing call and noticed the missing multiplication. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows the number of tickets purchased and the transaction may succeed without reverting, giving the impression that the cost was correctly applied. The bug violates the fundamental business rule that each ticket must cost a fixed amount of XP, breaking the accounting invariant that total XP burned equals tickets sold multiplied by price. To remediate, the spendXP call should be updated to deduct amount * price, ensuring that the XP burned matches the number of tickets purchased and restoring the intended economic model.

title: ClearingHouseLiq::_assertLiquidationAmount() may increase basis points due to negative quoteBalance.amount + insurance
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of a spread position where the contract attempts to compute the maximum basis amount that can be liquidated. The code uses MathHelper.max with a value derived from the expression -( (quoteBalance.amount + insurance).div(liquidationPrice) + 1 ). When the sum of the trader's quote balance and the insurance fund is negative, the division yields a negative number and the outer negation turns it into a positive value. Because MathHelper.max then selects the larger of this positive value and the previously calculated basisAmount, the absolute liquidation amount can be artificially increased. This sign‑error means the contract may liquidate more than the minimum required to close the short spot leg, effectively pulling extra funds from the liquidatee and the insurance pool. The bug is triggered only when a spread position is being liquidated, the spot leg is short, and the combined quote balance plus insurance is below zero – a situation that can arise when the trader is already under‑collateralised. An attacker or an automated liquidator can exploit this by forcing a liquidation under those conditions, causing the protocol to deduct an inflated amount of quote tokens, which may leave the user with a larger loss than expected and can even drive internal accounting into an inconsistent state. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a liquidation that removes more funds than anticipated, sometimes resulting in a sudden drop to zero balance or a missing refund. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, who noted that the mathematical check does not guard against a non‑positive quote balance plus insurance. It is hard to notice because the code appears to perform a sensible max comparison, yet the sign inversion silently inflates the liquidation size only in edge cases. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic sign errors that cause incorrect max/min logic, similar to unchecked negative values leading to over‑estimation of required amounts. To remediate the problem the contract should explicitly verify that quoteBalance.amount + insurance is greater than zero before applying the division, or set basisAmount to zero when the sum is non‑positive, thereby ensuring that liquidation never exceeds the amount needed to cover the short position and preserving the intended accounting guarantees.
summary:
If the position is a spread, it may be liquidated as one up to the minimum absolute value of the spot and perp positions. If the spot is short, the liquidatee + insurance need to have enough quote to buy back the spot position. This check is performed in ClearingHouseLiq::_assertLiquidationAmount():
```solidity
basisAmount = MathHelper.max(
    -((quoteBalance.amount + insurance).div(liquidationPrice) + 1),
    basisAmount
);
```
Note that quoteBalance.amount + insurance may be negative, which would mean that abs(basisAmount) could be increased, leading to incorrect states.

title: Anyone can spend others XP by calling spendXP
content: The vulnerability is a missing access control on the spendXP function of the VaronveStaking contract. spendXP is declared public, which means any external account can invoke it and specify an arbitrary user address whose XP balance will be reduced. The root cause is that the function was intended to be called only by internal contract logic (levelUP and buyTicket) but the visibility modifier was set to public and no require(msg.sender == user) or similar check was added. An attacker can craft a transaction that calls spendXP with the victim’s address and the amount of XP required for a level‑up or ticket purchase, causing the victim’s XP balance to be decremented without their consent. This can be exploited at any time because the contract does not restrict who can call spendXP, so the attack works whenever the contract is live and users hold XP. The impact is that users lose XP, which may prevent them from leveling up, buying tickets, or accessing other features that depend on XP, effectively reducing the utility of their holdings and potentially causing economic loss. From a user’s point of view the UI may suddenly show a lower XP balance or a zero balance after an unexpected transaction, and actions that previously succeeded now fail with insufficient XP. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined function visibility and access control. It can be hard to notice because the function name suggests internal use and there may be no explicit event indicating an external call, so developers might assume only the contract itself calls it. The proper fix is to change the visibility of spendXP to internal (or private) so it cannot be called from outside, or to add an explicit access control check that only allows the contract’s own functions or the XP owner to invoke it.
