This class of bug falls under insecure external function visibility or missing access control, where a privileged operation is exposed publicly and can be abused to manipulate user balances.
summary: In VaronveStaking there's a call spendXP: Which, as the name suggests, spends XP for the user. This is called from levelUP and buyTicket to spend cost for the action. The issue however is that spendXP is public. Hence it can be called by anyone, letting any user spend XP for any other user.

title: Any user can add XP by calling addXP
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized state‑change bug where the function that adds experience points (XP) to non‑fungible tokens (NFTs) is declared public and lacks any access control. Because the function is publicly callable, any address can invoke it directly and specify an arbitrary amount of XP to be credited to any NFT they own. The root cause is the incorrect visibility modifier; the function was intended to be invoked only by internal contract logic (specifically by returnLoserTicketXPs when a user loses a ticket and should be refunded XP), but the developer left it public, allowing external callers to bypass the intended accounting flow. An attacker can exploit the bug by sending a transaction that calls addXP with a large XP value, thereby inflating the XP balance of their NFT without performing any game action. This leads to a distortion of the protocol’s reward and ranking mechanisms, potentially granting the attacker unearned privileges, higher leaderboard positions, or access to XP‑based rewards. The issue manifests whenever a user interacts with the contract, as there is no condition that restricts the call to trusted code paths; therefore, it can be triggered at any time by any externally owned account. All participants who rely on XP as a measure of achievement or as a prerequisite for other contract features are affected, because the integrity of the XP accounting is compromised. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined function visibility and access patterns. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to be part of the legitimate workflow and may not be called directly by the front‑end, leading reviewers to assume it is only used internally. To remediate the issue, the function should be changed to internal or private, or protected with an appropriate modifier (e.g., onlyOwner, onlyAuthorized) that restricts calls to the contract’s own logic. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of “unauthorized external function exposure” or “privilege escalation via missing access control”. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that an NFT suddenly shows a much higher XP balance than expected, and the user may receive rewards they never earned, breaking the trust model of the platform.
summary: Similar to C-01 there is a call addXP: This is called by returnLoserTicketXPs to return XP to the users. The issue is however that it is public and can be called by anyone. Hence any user can add XP to their own NFTs.

title: addXP subtracts XP instead of adding
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that is intended to award experience points (XP) to staked NFTs, commonly named addXP. Instead of increasing the XP balance, the implementation mistakenly decreases it. The code checks whether the current NFT balance is at least the amount to be paid (payPerNFT) and, if so, subtracts that amount from the balance and adds the same amount to a running total called paid. If the balance is lower, it forcibly sets the balance to zero and adds the (now zero) balance to paid. This logic was meant to protect against underflow, but the sign of the arithmetic operation is inverted, causing the NFT to lose XP whenever addXP is called. The root cause is an incorrect arithmetic operation combined with an unnecessary under‑flow guard that masks the error. Exploitation is straightforward: any legitimate or malicious invocation of addXP will reduce the stored XP of each affected NFT, potentially driving the balance to zero. From a user perspective the UI will show XP decreasing after a reward event, or the NFT appearing to have no XP when it should have increased, breaking expectations that a reward transaction should add points. The impact is a loss of earned XP, which may affect downstream mechanics such as level‑up thresholds, reward eligibility, or staking incentives, thereby harming NFT owners and the overall protocol economics. The bug manifests every time the addXP routine is executed, typically during periodic reward distribution, and affects all participants whose NFTs are processed by the function. It was discovered during a manual code audit by CD Security, where the auditor noted that the function name and intended behavior conflicted with the actual state mutation. The issue can be hard to notice because the underflow check prevents a revert, so the transaction succeeds while silently decreasing balances, and test suites may not assert the sign of the balance change. To remediate the problem the function should be redesigned to add payPerNFT to each NFT’s balance, removing the subtraction and the unnecessary balance check, thereby aligning the state update with the intended business logic of rewarding XP. Conceptually this is an accounting sign error – a class of bugs where a credit operation is implemented as a debit, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and leading to unexpected loss of user assets.

title: User can inflate their XP by abusing updateXP
content: The contract implements a staking system where each staked NFT accrues experience points (XP) over time. The XP calculation is performed inside a modifier that adds to the NFT's balance based on the elapsed time since the last balance update, the period length, a per‑period XP rate, a multiplier specific to the NFT, and a bonus that depends on the total number of staked NFTs. The root cause of the vulnerability is that the timestamp field used to measure the elapsed time – lastBalanceUpdateTime – is never refreshed after the XP addition. Consequently, every subsequent call to the modifier treats the entire staking duration as if it were fresh, repeatedly adding the same time‑based amount. An attacker can exploit this by staking one NFT, waiting for some time, and then repeatedly staking and unstaking a second NFT. Each stake/unstake triggers the updateRewardSingleNFT function, which invokes the XP‑updating modifier for the first NFT. Because lastBalanceUpdateTime remains unchanged, each invocation adds XP for the whole original period, inflating the first NFT’s XP balance far beyond what the protocol’s economics anticipate. From a user’s perspective the XP counter jumps dramatically; a user expects a gradual increase but may see their XP surge to unusually high values, potentially leading to higher reward tiers or unlocking privileged features. The impact is a distortion of the reward distribution, allowing malicious participants to claim disproportionate rewards while undermining fairness for honest stakers. The bug manifests whenever a user has at least one NFT staked and performs additional stake/unstake actions on other NFTs, because each action re‑executes the XP update without resetting the timestamp. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the updateXP modifier and noticed that lastBalanceUpdateTime was read but never written. It can be hard to detect in testing because the XP growth still follows a deterministic formula; only the cumulative effect over many calls reveals the abnormal inflation. The proper remediation is to persist the new timestamp after applying the XP delta – i.e., set lastBalanceUpdateTime to block.timestamp – or to redesign the accounting so that only the incremental time since the previous update is considered. This ensures that each call adds XP only for the time that actually elapsed since the last update, preserving the intended economic model and preventing artificial XP inflation.
summary:
A lot of calls in VaronveStaking uses the updateXP modifier which syncs the XP state of the user:
```solidity
NFTs[i].balance += (
    (((block.timestamp - NFTs[i].lastBalanceUpdateTime) /
    period) *
    ((xpPerPeriod * NFTs[i].NFTXPMultiplier) +
    ((NFTs.length - 1) * bonusPerNFTStake)))
);
```
Which essentially takes the time between last update and now and then applies some modifiers. The issue is that lastBalanceUpdateTime is never updated. Hence for each call to this it will add XP since the time the user first staked the NFT. One way of abusing this is to first stake one NFT, then after a while, repeatedly stake and unstake a second NFT. This will cause updateRewardSingleNFT to be called multiple times and greatly inflate the XP for the first NFT.

title: Calling returnLoserTicketXPs will fail
content: The contract implements a raffle where, after the draw, the owner is expected to call returnLoserTicketXPs to distribute experience points (XP) back to participants who did not win. The function is restricted to the contract owner (onlyOwner) and internally calculates the amount of XP per staked NFT using the expression amount / stakedNFTs[msg.sender].length. Because the call originates from the owner, msg.sender refers to the owner’s address, whose stakedNFTs array is empty. Consequently, the divisor becomes zero and the transaction reverts with a division‑by‑zero error, preventing any XP from being returned. This logical flaw means that losers never receive the XP they are entitled to, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and leaving user balances unchanged. The issue manifests only after a raffle finishes and the owner triggers the refund routine, so it may be missed during normal operation. It affects all participants who expect a refund of XP, the protocol’s reputation, and potentially the owner who cannot complete the payout. The vulnerability was identified during a security audit that examined the flow of XP refunds. It is difficult to notice because the division is performed on a dynamic array length that is zero only in the specific owner‑call context, a situation that does not raise compiler warnings. The bug belongs to the class of “division‑by‑zero caused by incorrect use of msg.sender in access‑controlled functions,” which can also be exploited as a denial‑of‑service: if the function were rewritten to use the participant’s address, a malicious user could unstake their NFT just before the call, making the length zero and forcing the same revert. To remediate, the calculation should reference the intended participant address (e.g., _address) and explicitly check that the participant still holds staked NFTs before performing the division. If the length is zero, the contract can safely forfeit the XP or handle the case without reverting, thereby preserving protocol integrity and ensuring that users either receive their XP or are informed of the forfeiture.

title: Cloning a subGauge can result in an uninitialized proxy
content: The vulnerability consists of an uninitialized proxy contract that is created when the GaugeFactory contract clones a subGauge using the Clones.cloneDeterministic function. The factory method createSubGauge deploys a new subGauge instance but, unlike the createGaugeProxyAndSubGauges path, it does not immediately call the subGauge's initialize function. As a result the freshly cloned contract exists on‑chain without any of its critical state variables (such as stakingToken, governance address, reward parameters) being set. This gap creates a window during which any external actor can submit an initialize transaction before the legitimate creator does. An attacker observing the pending transaction can front‑run the initialize call, supplying his own arguments and thereby gaining control over the gauge’s configuration. The exploit proceeds as follows: (1) Alice invokes GaugeFactory.createSubGauge, which clones a subGauge proxy; (2) the proxy is added to a GaugeProxy via GaugeProxy.addSubGauge; (3) Alice later sends a transaction to initialize the subGauge; (4) Bob monitors the mempool, sees Alice’s pending initialize call, and submits his own initialize transaction with malicious parameters that gets mined first. Because the proxy was never initialized by the factory, Bob’s transaction succeeds and he becomes the effective owner or governance of the gauge, able to direct staking rewards, withdraw funds, or otherwise manipulate the gauge logic. The impact is that an attacker can seize control of a newly created gauge, potentially diverting user deposits, altering reward distribution, or freezing legitimate operations. The issue manifests only when a subGauge is created through the createSubGauge path and the subsequent initialize call is not performed atomically; it is invisible to users because the proxy appears to be deployed correctly, but its internal state remains empty until initialized. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the two factory creation flows and noticed the missing initialization step. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; the proxy simply does nothing until initialized, and the front‑run transaction may look like a normal initialization from a different address. The proper remediation is to have GaugeFactory.createSubGauge invoke the subGauge's initialize function immediately after cloning, using the same parameters that would be supplied by the user, thereby eliminating the uninitialized window. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of proxy‑initialization race conditions where a contract is deployed without its constructor‑like setup being performed atomically, allowing an attacker to hijack ownership or configuration through front‑running.
summary: In GaugeFactory::createSubGauge , the Clones::cloneDeterministic method is used to deploy a new subGauge . The problem is, in contrast to GaugeFactory::createGaugeProxyAndSubGauges , in createSubGauge the subGauge is not initialized after cloning, which leaves it vulnerable to a front-running attack. Example scenario: 1. Alice calls GaugeFactory::createSubGauge to deploy a new subGauge 2. The subGauge is added to a GaugeProxy by calling GaugeProxy::addSubGauge 3. Now Alice sends a transaction to call initialize on the subGauge 4. Bob sees Alice's transaction and front-runs it, initializing it with his own supplied arguments ( stakingToken , governance etc), so he controls it

title: Codebase is using a vulnerable Vyper compiler version
content: The vulnerability stems from the use of a Vyper compiler version (0.2.15, 0.2.16, or 0.3.0) that contains a known bug affecting the built‑in @nonreentrant function decorator. The decorator is intended to insert a re‑entrancy guard that prevents a contract function from being called again before the first execution finishes, a standard defensive measure against re‑entrancy attacks. In the affected compiler releases the guard code is omitted during compilation, so functions that appear to be protected in the source code are compiled without any actual protection. This discrepancy occurs because the compiler’s code‑generation step fails to emit the required state‑variable checks for the annotation, effectively rendering the @nonreentrant annotation a no‑op. As a result, any external call made from a function marked @nonreentrant can be re‑entered, allowing an attacker to invoke the same function recursively and manipulate contract state before the original call completes. The issue was discovered during a security audit after a high‑profile exploit in the Ethereum ecosystem that was traced back to the same compiler bug. It is difficult to notice because the source code visibly contains the @nonreentrant annotation, and typical unit tests may not include malicious re‑entrancy scenarios, giving a false sense of safety. The contracts compiled with the vulnerable version – notably GaugeController, LiquidityGaugeV4, and VotingEscrow – therefore lack effective re‑entrancy protection despite the annotation. If an attacker exploits this flaw, they can potentially drain funds, corrupt accounting, or cause unexpected zero balances for users, violating the protocol’s financial guarantees. The vulnerability is classified as a re‑entrancy guard malfunction caused by a compiler defect, a subclass of re‑entrancy bugs where the protective mechanism is silently disabled. To remediate, all Vyper contracts should be re‑compiled with a compiler version that includes the fix (v0.3.1 or later) or the re‑entrancy logic should be implemented manually using a mutex pattern. Upgrading the compiler and redeploying the contracts restores the intended protection and aligns the on‑chain behavior with the developers’ expectations that @nonreentrant functions cannot be called recursively.
summary: A month ago we saw a major exploit in the Ethereum ecosystem due to a bug in the Vyper compiler, as explained here. The Vyper team had the @nonreentrant annotation (or a function decorator) built natively into the language itself, but in version 0.2.15 a bug was introduced, essentially resulting in no reentrancy protection even if the annotation is used on a method. As stated here, "All Vyper contracts that have been compiled with versions v0.2.15, v0.2.16, and v0.3.0 are vulnerable to the malfunctioning re-entrancy guard.". The Vyper files in the repository (apart from BoostDelegationV2 ) all have compiler version 0.2.16, which is also configured in hardhat.config.ts . There are multiple methods marked with @nonreentrant in GaugeController , LiquidityGaugeV4 and VotingEscrow . All of those method are not reentrancy protected.

title: New subGauges can't be used by the protocol
content: The vulnerability is a logical authorization flaw in the gauge factory workflow. When the createSubGauge function of the GaugeFactory contract is called, it deploys a new subGauge contract but fails to register that subGauge with the central GaugeProxy contract. The GaugeProxy contract provides an addSubGauge method that is intended to link a staking token to a subGauge, however this method is restricted to calls originating only from the gaugeFactory or the TLSDFactory. Neither of those contracts contains code that actually invokes addSubGauge during a plain createSubGauge call, so the newly created subGauge remains isolated and invisible to the protocol. This situation occurs whenever a developer or user attempts to extend the system by adding a new subGauge through the dedicated factory method; the transaction succeeds, the subGauge contract exists on‑chain, but the protocol’s registry never records it. From a user perspective the symptom is that after creating a subGauge the UI still shows no new gauge, balances for the intended staking token remain zero, and any attempt to deposit or claim rewards against the supposed new gauge either reverts or silently does nothing because the protocol does not recognize the gauge. The impact is that funds intended for the new subGauge cannot be routed, effectively rendering the subGauge unusable and potentially causing users to lose confidence or waste gas on ineffective operations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the factory’s code paths, where the auditor noticed that createSubGauge does not contain the same addSubGauge call that is present in the createGaugeProxyAndSubGauges function. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not fail and the subGauge contract is deployed, giving a false impression that the gauge is ready for use. To remediate, the createSubGauge implementation should be updated to invoke GaugeProxy(_gaugeProxy).addSubGauge(_stakingToken, subGauge) with the appropriate staking token argument, mirroring the behavior of the combined creation function. This change restores the intended registration flow, ensures that accounting assumptions about gauge availability hold, and prevents the protocol from silently ignoring newly created gauges.
summary: The createSubGauge method in GaugeFactory creates a new subGauge but does not actually add the subGauge to the GaugeProxy as it is done in createGaugeProxyAndSubGauges . Even though the GaugeProxy contract has an addSubGauge method, it is only callable by the gaugeFactory or by the TLSDFactory . Neither contracts have an actual way to directly call the addSubGauge method, which means that even though you can create new subGauge s you can't actually add them to the GaugeProxy in any way.

title: C-1 Unrestricted access to the setVibeFees function in MintSaleBase
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access flaw in the function that configures fee parameters of a token sale contract. The function is intended to be protected by a modifier that only allows the owner of the master contract to change the fee recipient address and the fee percentage. However, the modifier checks only the owner of the master contract and does not verify whether a master contract is actually set. When the contract is deployed as a bare implementation without a master contract, the master‑contract address is zero and the modifier effectively becomes a no‑op, allowing any external account to call the fee‑setting function. An attacker can monitor the deployment of contracts that inherit from this implementation, submit a transaction that calls the fee‑setting function before the legitimate deployment transaction is mined, and change the treasury address to their own wallet while inflating the fee percentage. This results in the protocol diverting a portion of user payments to the attacker, causing users to pay higher fees than advertised and the protocol to lose revenue. The issue manifests only when the contract is used as an implementation without a master contract, a situation that is easy to overlook because the function appears to be protected. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the access control logic of the modifier. The bug is hard to notice because the code path is rarely exercised in tests that always deploy through a master contract. To remediate, the modifier should include an explicit check that, if no master contract is present, only the contract owner may pass, for example by requiring msg.sender == owner() when the master contract address is zero. This restores proper access control and prevents arbitrary fee manipulation. The class of bug is an incomplete access‑control check that leads to privilege escalation and financial loss, violating the business assumption that fee parameters can only be set by trusted governance.
summary: ThesetVibeFees function within the MintSaleBase contract is protected by the onlyMasterContractOwner modifier. However, anyone can call this function if the contract is the implementation contract itself, meaning it has no master contract. An exploiter via this vulnerability can monitor the deployment transactions of the MintSaleBase inheritor contracts and submit their transaction before deployment, thereby setting the vibeTreasury field to their address and arbitrarily increasing the value of the feeTake field. Consequently, the owner of the masterContract must reset the values back and re-establish the fee parameters of the affected copy.

title: Anyone can change the base URI
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted public function that allows any address to modify the base URI of an ERC‑721 collection. When the collection is created through the launchpad, the deployer supplies an initial IPFS hash that is stored as the base URI. However, the contract defines a function setbaseUri that writes a new string to the internal _baseuri variable and is marked as public with no access‑control checks. Because the function lacks a modifier such as onlyOwner or a role‑based guard, any external account can invoke it at any time after deployment. An attacker can therefore call setbaseUri and replace the original metadata location with a malicious or empty URI. This change is reflected in the tokenURI calculation, so all token metadata – images, descriptions, attributes – are fetched from the attacker‑controlled location. From a user’s perspective the expected artwork or information suddenly disappears or shows unrelated content, leading to confusion, loss of trust, and potential devaluation of the NFTs. The impact is primarily on token holders, creators, and marketplaces that rely on the integrity of the metadata; the tokens themselves remain owned by the original addresses, but their displayed representation can be altered without consent. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that inspected the contract’s public interface and noted the absence of any access‑control modifier on a state‑changing function. It can be hard to notice because the UI may still display the token, while the underlying metadata silently points to a different source, making the problem appear as a simple content glitch rather than a security breach. The proper remediation is to restrict the setbaseUri function to authorized roles, typically the contract owner or a designated admin, by adding an appropriate modifier (e.g., onlyOwner) or integrating a role‑based access control system. This aligns the function with the broader class of “unauthorized state‑change” bugs where critical configuration parameters are exposed to the public, violating the business assumption that only the collection creator can define where token metadata is hosted.

title: C-1 Insecure Liquidity Valuation with Oracle Updates
content: The vulnerability is an insecure liquidity valuation flaw that arises because the LPManager contract calculates share amounts for addLiquidity and token amounts for removeLiquidity using the price reported by a Pyth oracle at the exact moment the function is executed. The root cause is that the oracle price can be updated by any user atomically within the same transaction, and the contract does not enforce any time‑based separation or historical price reference before using the price for accounting. An attacker can therefore submit a transaction that first updates the oracle to a low price, adds liquidity at that artificially depressed price, then updates the oracle again to a higher price and immediately removes the same liquidity, receiving more underlying tokens than were contributed. This sequence can be performed in a single atomic transaction, creating a flash‑loan‑style arbitrage opportunity that extracts value from the pool without any visible re‑entrancy. The impact is a rapid loss of funds from the protocol, reduced pool balances, and unfair outcomes for honest liquidity providers who see their shares devalued or their balances disappear. The condition under which the exploit works is when the protocol permits oracle updates and liquidity operations in the same block without a delay or price smoothing mechanism. All participants that rely on the pool – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions that the pool’s token value reflects a stable market price are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between oracle update functions and liquidity management, noting that the price is taken directly from the oracle state without any historical guard. The flaw can be hard to notice because the price appears correct after the transaction completes, and there is no explicit error or revert; the loss is manifested only as a discrepancy between expected and actual token balances. To remediate the problem, the contract should introduce price epochs of a duration equal to the maximum allowed oracle age and use the highest price from the last two epochs when minting shares on addLiquidity, and the lowest price from the last two epochs when calculating token payouts on removeLiquidity. By anchoring calculations to a bounded historical window, abrupt short‑term price manipulations become ineffective, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the liquidity vault. From a user’s perspective, the bug manifests as a situation where a user adds liquidity expecting a fair share of the pool, but after a single transaction the received tokens are either zero or far less than anticipated, effectively causing funds to disappear. The vulnerability belongs to the class of oracle manipulation and price‑stabilization bugs that break accounting invariants in DeFi protocols.
summary:
This issue has been identified within the addLiquidity and removeLiquidity functions of the LPManager contract.
Because Pyth oracles can be updated atomically by users in the same transaction, it is possible to supply liquidity at a low price and subsequently remove it at a higher price, all within a single transaction. This creates an arbitrage opportunity that can rapidly extract value from the protocol.
The issue is classified as critical severity because it allows attackers to exploit sudden price changes for profit, potentially causing substantial losses to the protocol.

title: C-2 Incorrect Remainder Allocation in Market-Only Orders
content: The vulnerability originates in the order placement routine of the market‑only trading path. When a caller submits an order with the marketOnly flag set to true, the contract deliberately skips inserting the order into the on‑chain order book, because market‑only orders are expected to be fully executed immediately. However, the accounting logic still computes a variable called remainShares as the original quantity minus the number of shares that were actually executed. For a true market‑only order the correct remainder should be zero, because any unfilled portion is discarded. By leaving the subtraction unchanged, the contract records a non‑existent leftover share balance. These phantom shares are subsequently added to the per‑token reserve mapping (lobReservesByTokenId) and are included in the aggregate reserve calculation performed by _getReserves. The result is that the protocol reports a total reserve amount that is larger than the real assets held. This overstatement can be triggered whenever a market‑only order is placed, and it persists until the phantom shares are unintentionally consumed by later operations. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a higher available liquidity or larger pool balance than actually exists, leading users to believe they can withdraw more funds than are truly available. Liquidity providers therefore face the risk that the pool becomes insolvent, because the accounting layer believes there are assets that are not present. The issue was uncovered during a systematic security audit that examined the order‑matching and reserve‑tracking code paths. It is difficult to notice because the discrepancy is hidden inside aggregated reserve numbers rather than being exposed as an explicit error, and the contract does not emit any warning when the remainder is incorrectly calculated. The proper remediation is to explicitly set remainShares to zero for any order where marketOnly is true, thereby preventing phantom shares from entering the reserve accounting and ensuring that the reported total balance matches the actual token holdings. This change restores the invariant that reserves equal on‑chain token balances and eliminates the risk of inflated liquidity figures that could lead to financial loss.
summary:
This issue has been identified within the _placeOrder function of the ProxyLOB contract.
When marketOnly is set to true the order is not included into IOnchainTrie within the IOnchainLOB.placeOrder, but the code still calculates remainShares as quantity - executedShares, instead of correctly setting it to zero. As a result, these non-existent leftover shares are added to lobReservesByTokenId and factored into _getReserves, ultimately inflating the protocol's reported total balance. Since _getReserves then shows a value higher than what truly exists, this discrepancy can lead to insolvency of the protocol.
The issue is classified as critical severity because overstated reserves severely undermine the protocol's financial stability, risking potential losses for liquidity providers.

title: C-3 Improper Bid Trie Reference Causing Reserve Overstatement
content: The vulnerability is an improper handling of the order identifier when processing bid orders in the _claimOrder function of the ProxyLOB contract. In this system the least‑significant bit of an orderId signals which on‑chain trie should be consulted: a zero‑ending bit selects the bid trie, while a one‑ending bit selects the ask trie. When the function is invoked with isAsk set to false (indicating a bid), the implementation fails to mask or convert the orderId before querying the trie. As a result the contract looks for the order in the wrong trie, treats the bid as non‑existent and returns zero values for the claimed amount. Because the claimed amount is never deducted from the protocol’s internal reserves, the total reserves appear larger than the actual assets held. This overstatement propagates through subsequent accounting calculations, inflating the reported asset balances of the protocol. The flaw can be triggered whenever a user or an attacker calls _claimOrder with a bid orderId that ends with a one‑bit, which is the normal encoding for bids. The attacker can repeatedly submit such claims, each time receiving no settlement while the contract’s reserve accounting remains unchanged, effectively creating phantom assets. The issue primarily affects the protocol’s financial integrity, liquidity providers and any participants who rely on accurate reserve figures for pricing or withdrawal decisions. It was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, where the logical mismatch between orderId encoding and trie selection was identified. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; it simply returns zero, which can be mistaken for a legitimate “no‑funds” condition, making the overstatement hard to detect without deep inspection of the accounting flow. To remediate the bug, the _claimOrder logic must be updated to correctly mask or shift the orderId when isAsk is false, ensuring that bid orders are looked up in the bid trie and that their amounts are properly deducted from reserves. Conceptually, the fix restores correct key derivation for data structures, preventing state inconsistencies that lead to reserve overstatement and preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary:
This issue has been identified within the _claimOrder function of the ProxyLOB contract.
When isAsk = false (a bid), the final bit of the orderId indicates the relevant on-chain trie (bid trie expects a zero-ending bit). However, _claimOrder does not convert or mask the orderId before querying the trie, causing the bid order to appear non-existent and returning zero values. This erroneously inflates the contract's reserves by failing to correctly match and settle claimed amounts from the reserves of the claimed order.
The issue is classified as critical severity because it can produce a chain of incorrect calculations that ultimately overstate the protocol's asset balances.

title: C-4 Double-Counted Fees in Partial Bid Claims
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that occurs in the claimOrder routine of the ProxyLOB contract when a bid order is only partially executed. When a user places a bid (isAsk = false) the contract transfers the full amount calculated as quantity * price plus a passive payout commission into the liquidity order book (LOB) and records this total in the internal mapping lobReservesByTokenId. If the order is later partially filled and claimOrder is called with only_claim set to false, the contract correctly returns the unfilled portion of the fee to the LPManager, but it fails to subtract that returned amount from lobReservesByTokenId. As a result, the function _getReserves continues to include fees that are no longer held by the LOB, inflating the reported reserve balance. This double‑counting can cause the protocol to believe it has more assets than it actually does, potentially leading to insolvency when withdrawals or settlements are performed based on the overstated reserves. The bug manifests only after a partial execution followed by a claim that does not request a full settlement, making it easy to miss during casual testing because the on‑chain token balances appear correct while the internal accounting diverges. It was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, which examined the logic of fee handling and reserve calculations. Exploitation could involve an attacker deliberately creating many partially filled bids, triggering the faulty claim path to inflate the global reserve counter, and then withdrawing more funds than are truly available. Users may notice symptoms such as a bid that was only partially filled still showing a full fee lock in the UI, unexpected “insufficient liquidity” errors on withdrawal, or balances that appear higher than the actual token holdings. The issue belongs to the class of double‑counted accounting bugs where a value is added to a ledger but not removed when it is refunded or reclaimed. To remediate, the claimOrder implementation must update lobReservesByTokenId by subtracting the fee amount that is returned to the LPManager, ensuring that the reserve mapping always reflects the true amount of assets held by the LOB. This conceptual fix restores consistency between external token balances and internal reserve accounting, preventing the protocol from operating on incorrect balance assumptions.
summary:
This issue has been identified within the _claimOrder function of the ProxyLOB contract.
When placing a bid (isAsk = false), the contract transfers quantity * price + passivePayoutCommission into the LOB and records the same total in lobReservesByTokenId.
However, if the order is partially executed, and claimOrder is invoked with only_claim = false, the unfulfilled portion of the fee is returned to the LPManager but is never subtracted from lobReservesByTokenId. Consequently, _getReserves continues to count fees that no longer remain, causing an inflated reserve calculation.
The issue is classified as critical severity because overstating reserves can lead to protocol insolvency if the system operates on incorrect balance assumptions.

title: C-5 Missing Price Factor in Claimed Shares Calculation
content: The vulnerability is an accounting miscalculation in the claimOrder function of the ProxyLOB contract that occurs when the isAsk flag is false. Instead of converting the number of claimed shares into their monetary value using the current price, the implementation subtracts (totalClaimedShares + passiveFee) multiplied only by the token‑Y scaling factor from the reserves. Because the price multiplier is omitted, the contract records a smaller reduction than the true value of the claimed shares, which inflates the protocol’s reported reserve balance. The root cause is a logical error: the price factor that should translate share quantity into token value is missing from the subtraction expression. An attacker can trigger the flaw by invoking claimOrder with isAsk set to false, claiming a set of shares, and allowing the contract to update its internal accounting with an understated debit. The excess reserves remain in the contract and can later be withdrawn or used to manipulate pricing, effectively allowing the attacker to extract more value than entitled or to present a false picture of liquidity. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s balance sheet, potentially leading to over‑issued tokens, loss of funds for honest participants, and erosion of trust in the system. The condition under which the bug manifests is specific to the claimOrder path where isAsk is false; all other claim paths are unaffected. Users who claim shares, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself are affected because the reported balances no longer reflect the true state of assets. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by MixBytes, where the auditors identified that the subtraction formula did not include the price term. Because the reserves appear larger rather than smaller, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple balance checks, making it hard to notice without detailed accounting verification. From a user perspective the symptom may be that a claim transaction seems to leave the contract with more funds than expected, or that the UI shows a higher reserve balance after a claim, contradicting the user’s expectation that the reserve should decrease by the claimed amount. This class of bug belongs to arithmetic or accounting errors where a conversion factor (price) is omitted, leading to an incorrect formula. To remediate the issue the subtraction should be rewritten to multiply totalClaimedShares by the current price before adding the passive fee and applying the scaling factor, i.e., (totalClaimedShares * price + passiveFee) * scalingFactorTokenY. This ensures that the claimed amount is correctly valued and removed from the reserves, restoring accurate accounting and preventing the inflated balance exploit.
summary:
This issue has been identified within the _claimOrder function of the ProxyLOB contract.
When isAsk = false, the current code subtracts (totalClaimedShares + passiveFee) * scalingFactorTokenY from the reserves without multiplying totalClaimedShares by price.
Consequently, the actual value of the claimed shares is not correctly accounted for, resulting in a higher-than-accurate reserves value.
The issue is classified as critical severity because it leads to a miscalculation of the claimed token's worth, which inflates the protocol's reported balances.

title: Users can get NFTs for as little as 1 wei Wizzard_audit.md
content: The vulnerability is a classic push‑payment flaw in the auction contract where the highest bid amount is sent to the previous bidder using a direct transfer before the contract state is updated. The root cause is the use of a payable(item.highestBidder).transfer call without handling the case where the recipient contract cannot receive ether (for example, it lacks a receive or fallback function). When a malicious contract becomes the highestBidder, any subsequent call to placeBid or endAuction triggers a transfer that always fails, causing the whole transaction to revert. This prevents the contract from updating the highestBidder and highestBid fields, effectively locking the auction (brick) or allowing the malicious bidder to win the NFT with a minimal amount such as 1 wei because the owner may end the auction and the refund to the malicious contract fails. The impact is that legitimate bidders cannot outbid the malicious contract, the auction may never be closed, and the NFT may be transferred for far less than its intended price, resulting in loss of expected revenue and potential loss of user trust. The condition under which this occurs is when the highestBidder address points to a contract that does not implement a payable fallback, and the contract follows a push‑payment model. All participants in the marketplace – bidders, token owners, and the protocol itself – are affected because funds can become stuck and the auction logic is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of ether in placeBid and endAuction and identified that external calls are made before state changes. It is hard to notice because a failed transfer simply reverts the transaction, which may be interpreted as a normal failure of a bid rather than a systemic flaw, and developers often assume that transfer will always succeed for externally owned accounts. The recommended remediation is to replace the push pattern with a pull‑payment design: record the amount owed to each outbid participant in a mapping and provide a separate withdraw function that lets users claim their refunds. Additionally, the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern by updating internal state before making any external calls, and use call{value: amount}("") with proper error handling instead of transfer. This change eliminates the possibility of a malicious contract blocking the auction and ensures that funds are safely retrievable, preserving the intended auction economics.

title: C-1 Several reentrancy scenarios
content: During token transfers the protocol interacts with ERC‑20 tokens that may implement ERC‑777 style hooks. When the contract calls token.transfer or token.transferFrom, a malicious token can invoke a callback (tokensReceived) that executes arbitrary code in the calling contract. The LOB contract updates the user's balance only after the external call, so the contract is left in an inconsistent state while the callback is running. An attacker can therefore re‑enter vulnerable external functions such as withdraw or placeOrder before the balance is corrected, causing the same tokens to be transferred or accounted for twice. This classic re‑entrancy pattern results in double‑spending: the attacker withdraws tokens, re‑enters the contract and withdraws again, or deposits tokens and re‑enters placeOrder to spend the same amount multiple times. The bug manifests when the protocol is deployed on networks that support tokens with transfer hooks, or when a user supplies a malicious token contract. From a user’s point of view the expected outcome – a single token transfer matching the deposited amount – is violated; users may see their balance unchanged while the protocol sends out tokens repeatedly, or they may notice that their deposited tokens are spent without a corresponding balance reduction. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which flagged the lack of a checks‑effects‑interactions pattern and the absence of a re‑entrancy guard on mutable external functions. Because most ERC‑20 tokens do not exhibit callback behaviour, the problem can be subtle and may only appear when a specially crafted token is used, making it hard to detect through ordinary testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of re‑entrancy bugs where external calls are made before internal state is updated. To remediate, the contract should apply a non‑reentrant modifier (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant) to all public and external functions that modify state and perform external calls, and it should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern by updating the trader’s balance before invoking token.transfer. Implementing these changes prevents the contract from being re‑entered while its state is inconsistent, thereby eliminating the double‑spending risk.
summary:
The issue is identified within the LOB contract.
Some ERC-20 tokens implement extensions, such as the ERC-777 standard, that allow an account to gain
execution control during token transfers. As the protocol is planned to be deployed on several networks and
support various tokens, it may encounter issues related to these types of tokens.
If an attacker gains control during a token transfer, they can launch a "reentrancy" attack against the protocol
by following these steps:
1. Set up send/receive hooks.
2. Perform an action that causes the protocol to send or receive tokens.
3. Execute additional calls to the protocol, exploiting the inconsistent state from step 2 to gain profit.
At a minimum, the following scenarios can be exploited:
• Withdraw tokens, reenter the protocol, and withdraw the same tokens again, effectively double-spending.
• Deposit tokens, reenter the protocol with the placeOrder function, and double-spend the tokens.
This issue is classified as critical severity because it can lead to significant financial loss through double-
spending.

title: C-2 Incorrect Condition for post_only Orders
content: The vulnerability is a logical condition error in the order‑matching routine that classifies post‑only bid orders as executable when they should remain passive. In the contract’s post‑only handling block the if statement checks the price identifier against the best offer using a comparison that is reversed, so the condition is true for any price that would normally keep the order off the book. Because the condition is always satisfied, the function returns a non‑zero value and the order is treated as a market order, triggering the commission logic that is intended only for taker trades. This flaw originates from a sign inversion in the comparison operator, a classic example of an incorrect conditional guard that misclassifies order intent. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug simply by submitting a post‑only bid; the contract will automatically execute the order against the current ask price and deduct the taker commission, even though the user explicitly requested a passive placement. The impact is financial loss: users see unexpected commission deductions, balances may drop, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that post‑only orders incur no fees are violated. The issue manifests whenever a post‑only bid is placed, regardless of market depth, because the faulty condition does not depend on external state beyond the best offer price. All participants who rely on post‑only semantics – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s fee model – are affected. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit where the auditor inspected the order‑matching logic and noticed the inverted comparison; the existing test named testPostOnly failed to catch it because it only verified that the function returned a value, not that the execution path matched the intended passive behavior. The problem is subtle because the contract still compiles and appears to process orders, so the unintended fee deduction can be mistaken for normal market activity. To remediate, the condition must be flipped so that the function returns early only when the price would cross the spread, preserving the post‑only guarantee and preventing commission charges on passive orders. Conceptually, the fix restores the correct classification of order types and aligns the contract’s behavior with the expected accounting model where post‑only orders never incur taker fees.
summary:
The issue is identified within the OnchainLOB.sol#L230 function of the LOB contract.
There is a critical vulnerability in the post_only order handling logic. The incorrect condition in the if
statement means that post_only bid orders will always be executed, causing the bidder to pay commissions
that are not intended for passive orders in this architecture. This can lead to unintended financial costs for
users.
The test named testPostOnly provided by the developers does not catch this issue because it does not
properly check the execution path.
The issue is classified as critical severity, because it can lead to significant unintended financial consequences
for users placing post_only orders.

title: C-3 Potential Data Corruption in Trie Structure
content: The vulnerability resides in the matchesNode routine of a trie‑based order storage contract. The function attempts to locate an order identifier within a matching node and, if it appears to exist, proceeds to update the subtree that stores the order data. However, the implementation neglects to examine the boolean flag that indicates whether the identifier was actually found before performing the update. Consequently, when matchesNode is invoked with an order_id that is not present in the node, the code still overwrites or inserts data into the subtree based on an assumed match. This omission breaks the fundamental invariant that each node’s key set must accurately reflect the stored orders, leading to structural inconsistency and eventual data corruption. An attacker or a malformed user input can trigger the faulty path by supplying a non‑existent order_id, causing the contract to corrupt the trie’s internal mapping. The corrupted trie may return incorrect balances, drop orders, or mis‑route funds, which can manifest to users as missing refunds, zero balances after a successful deposit, or orders that never appear in their history. The issue occurs whenever matchesNode is called without a prior existence check, which is typical during order lookup, cancellation, or settlement operations. All participants that rely on the trie for accounting – including regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the corrupted state can lead to loss of funds or incorrect accounting. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logical flow of the trie library and identified the missing verification step. Because the contract does not revert on the erroneous update, the corruption can remain silent, making it difficult to detect without explicit state validation or extensive testing. To remediate the problem, the matchesNode logic should first verify the found flag and only modify the subtree when the order_id is confirmed to exist; otherwise it should abort or skip the update. This change restores the trie’s consistency guarantees and prevents accidental overwriting of unrelated data, thereby protecting the protocol’s accounting integrity and user funds.
summary:
The issue is identified within theTrieLib.sol#L780-L795 function of the Trie contract.
There is a critical vulnerability where the matchesNode function checks if the order_id potentially exists in
the matching node, but it doesn't verify the found boolean value before updating the subtree. If the order_id
does not actually exist in the matching node, it can lead to a violation of the validity and consistency of the trie,
resulting in data corruption and potential loss of funds.
The issue is classified as critical severity because it can cause severe data corruption and financial loss.

title: C-4 Incorrect accounting of commissions
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the order placement routine where the commission amount is recorded twice: once as the explicit commission charge and a second time as part of the trader's token_y balance. This double‑counting originates from a logic flaw in the placeOrder function that adds the calculated commission to the market maker’s token_y accounting while also storing it as a separate commission variable. Because the same value is subtracted from the trader’s balance and then added back to the market maker’s accounting, the internal ledger shows more commission than is actually transferred on‑chain. An attacker controlling the market maker role can submit orders that trigger this path, causing the protocol to credit the market maker with extra tokens that were never taken from users, effectively generating profit without cost. The impact includes state inconsistency between recorded commissions and real token flows, potential loss of user funds, and contract malfunction such as unexpected reverts when balances become negative or mismatched. The condition occurs each time an order is executed and the commission calculation branch is taken, i.e., for any non‑zero commission scenario. All participants that rely on correct accounting – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because their displayed balances may not reflect the true economic outcome. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that inspected the accounting logic of the OnchainLOB contract. It can be hard to notice because the external token transfers appear correct; only the internal accounting variables diverge, which may not be visible without deep state inspection. The bug belongs to the class of double‑counting or misallocation errors, where a monetary value is added to two separate accounting entries, violating the invariant that total tokens in the system equal the sum of user balances plus collected commissions. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include receiving a smaller net amount than expected, seeing a zero or unexpectedly low balance after a trade, or observing the market maker’s balance increase without a corresponding trade fee. The contract’s business logic assumes that commissions are deducted from the trader and held separately; the double entry breaks this assumption and can be exploited for profit. The proper fix is to ensure that the commission amount is deducted from the trader’s token_y balance exactly once and recorded only in the dedicated commission storage, removing any addition of the same amount to the market maker’s token_y accounting. This restores a single source of truth for commission accounting and prevents the market maker from gaining unearned tokens.
summary:
In the OnchainLOB.sol#L261 function, the total_commission value is accounted for twice: once as the
commission and once as the token_y value of the trader. This duplication can lead to incorrect commission
accounting and potential contract malfunction due to mismatched accounted and actual balances. Additionally,
it may allow the market maker account to exploit the commission system for profit.
This issue is rated as critical severity as it may lead to malfunction due to contract state inconsistency and
enable the market maker to gain undesired profit.

title: Direct Loss of Rewards on Re-Staking
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the reStake function of the DiscreteStakingRewards contract. The function is supposed to transfer a user’s earned rewards back into the user’s staked balance so that the rewards are compounded. To achieve this it clears the earned reward amount and then calls the external stake function with the reward amount. Because stake is an external call, the execution context changes and msg.sender becomes the contract itself (address(this)) during the call. Consequently the stake function records the reward as belonging to the contract rather than to the original caller. The user’s earned rewards are therefore moved to an internal balance that is not associated with any external address and there is no mechanism for the contract to withdraw or claim those self‑staked tokens. The loss occurs whenever a user invokes reStake while having a positive earned reward. The impact is that the user’s expected increase in staked balance never materialises; instead the rewards disappear from the user’s perspective, the UI may still show the earned amount before the call but after the transaction the user’s stake remains unchanged and the earned amount is reset to zero. This breaks the accounting assumption that earned rewards are either claimable or can be compounded for the same user. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the flow of reward handling and noticed that the external call altered the caller identity. It can be hard to notice because the function name and comments suggest correct behavior and the contract does not emit an event indicating that the rewards were transferred to the contract itself. The proper fix is to avoid the external call and directly increase the caller’s staked balance and total supply within the same execution context, ensuring that the reward amount is credited to the user and not to the contract.
summary: The reStake() method of the DiscreteStakingRewards contract intends to add a user’s (msg.sender) earned rewards to their staked balance instead of claiming those rewards. This is done by clearing the user’s earned rewards and forwarding them to the contract’s stake() method. However, the stake() method is called externally and therefore the msg.sender will be the contract itself (address(this)) during the stake call. Consequently, the user’s earned rewards are re-staked on behalf of the contract instead of the user and are therefore lost. Furthermore, the re-staked rewards become stuck, since there is no way for the contract to redeem those “self-staked” amounts.

title: User Claimable Reward Tokens Can Be Locked
content: The vulnerability originates from the use of a uint8 variable to store the protocol's current epoch counter. Because a uint8 can only represent values from 0 to 255, the counter overflows when the protocol attempts to advance past the 255th epoch. The overflow is not caught or handled, so the increment operation reverts, preventing the _endEpoch routine from completing. As a result the contract cannot finalize epoch 255 and cannot create epoch 256, effectively freezing the reward‑distribution logic. An attacker (or any user) can trigger the overflow simply by performing an action that calls addYeetVolume, which internally invokes _endEpoch, once the currentEpoch value is already 255. The transaction then reverts, leaving the contract in a state where no further epochs can be closed. Because rewards are calculated per epoch and the getClaimableAmount function only sums rewards for epochs that are strictly less than the current epoch, users are unable to claim any reward for the final epoch and the loop never progresses beyond the stuck epoch. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that a reward is pending, but any claim transaction returns 0 or fails, creating the impression that funds have disappeared. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the entire protocol: all future reward accruals stop, existing pending rewards become unclaimable, and the protocol’s economic incentives break down. All participants—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s governance—are affected because the core accounting assumptions (that epochs advance monotonically) are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the data types used for epoch tracking and identified that the chosen type could not accommodate the intended lifespan of the system. It is hard to notice in normal testing because the overflow only occurs after 255 days of operation, a period that is rarely simulated in unit tests. To remediate the problem the epoch counter should be stored in a type that can safely grow for the expected lifetime of the protocol, such as uint256, or the contract should implement explicit overflow checks and a fallback mechanism that allows the system to continue operating after the maximum value is reached. A more extensive redesign could eliminate per‑epoch mappings altogether and aggregate rewards in a single balance per address, thereby removing the need for a continuously incrementing epoch index and avoiding the overflow risk entirely.
summary: In the Reward.sol file, the currentEpoch variable is defined as a uint8, which means it can only hold values from 0 to 255. Since each epoch lasts for a day, the maximum epoch possible is indeed 255. However, this setup could potentially lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) scenario for the entire protocol. This issue arises because when the epoch reaches 255, any attempt to increment it further, like during the addYeetVolume() function that calls _endEpoch() internally upon yeeting, will cause an overflow, resulting in a revert. Therefore, ending the 255th epoch is impossible. The getClaimableAmount() function loops through each epoch. However, it is important to note that although the maximum value of currentEpoch is 255, no amounts can be claimed beyond that point because no new epochs can be finalized. Attack Scenario To understand better the vulnerability let’s look at the following example: 1. The currentEpoch is 255. 2. Alice yeets and now participates in epoch 255 and userYeetVolume[currentEpoch][user] += amount; mapping will update Alice’s data for the current epoch. 3. Once Epoch 255 concludes, the protocol attempts to increment the value, but hits a roadblock—it’s unable to proceed. Consequently, the protocol stalls, unable to advance to the next epochs. 4. Alice tries to claim her rewards for epoch 255 but the tx will return 0, because epoch < currentEpoch is going to be false.

title: Gas calculation frequently uses unchecked free variables
content: The vulnerability consists of unsafe gas accounting in the zkEVM implementation where several opcodes – notably CALLDATACOPY, CODECOPY, EXTCODECOPY and the internal memory‑expansion helper – compute their gas cost using a free variable that is not constrained or validated. The formula 3*((C+31)/32) is applied directly to the remaining gas counter, where C represents the size of the data being copied. Because C is supplied by the caller and no overflow or bounds checks are performed, an attacker can provide a value that makes the subtraction underestimate the true cost. When the contract later executes the out‑of‑gas jump (JMPN outOfGas) the check may be bypassed, allowing execution to continue with insufficient gas or causing an unexpected revert. This can be exploited by crafting a transaction with a large calldata payload that triggers the faulty calculation, leading to either a silent out‑of‑gas failure (the transaction reverts and the user sees no refund or a zero balance) or, in some edge cases, state changes that occur without the proper gas charge, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The impact is critical because it affects any contract that relies on those opcodes in the affected zkEVM version (0.5.2.0, Polygon‑Hermez), potentially causing funds to be locked, transactions to fail intermittently, and overall loss of confidence in the protocol’s reliability. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by Spearbit, who noted that the arithmetic is performed in the VM’s arithmetic state machine without any safety checks, making the bug hard to notice from the outside – it only manifests as occasional out‑of‑gas reverts that do not follow the expected gas consumption pattern. To remediate the problem the free variable must be bounded and the gas formula must be recomputed using safe arithmetic with explicit overflow protection, matching the specification for each opcode. In practice this means replacing the unchecked expression with a deterministic calculation that validates the size of the copied data before subtracting gas, and adding proper checks in the memory‑expansion routine so that the gas counter cannot be under‑estimated.
summary:
An example in opCALLDATACOPY where unconstrained free variables are used to calculate the word-size cost:
GAS - 3 => GAS :JMPN(outOfGas)
GAS - ${3*((C+31)/32)} => GAS :JMPN(outOfGas) ; Arith
In some places, like opRETURNDATACOPY these are mostly performed using the arithmetic state machine:
;${3*((C+31)/32)}
C+31 => A
;(C+31)/32
A
:MSTORE(arithA)
:MSTORE(arithB)
:CALL(divARITH)
$ => A
:MLOAD(arithRes1)
; Mul operation with Arith
; 3*((C+31)/32)
:MSTORE(arithA)
A
:MSTORE(arithB)
:CALL(mulARITH)
$ => A
:MLOAD(arithRes1)
GAS - A => GAS
:JMPN(outOfGas)
Under tag 0.5.2.0 a number of instances remain, including opCALLDATCOPY, opCODECOPY, opEXTCODCOPY, and the saveMemGAS utility affecting memory expansion. Polygon-Hermez: All unsafe computations has been ﬁxed in PR #199 and PR #221.

title: Memory alignment malleability
content: The vulnerability is a memory‑alignment malleability issue caused by a constant polynomial (referred to as BYTE_C4096) that is expected to represent a single byte value in the range 0‑255 but fails to wrap around after reaching 255. Because the constant does not apply a modulo‑256 operation, the variable inV can take on values larger than a byte. When the contract later stores this value using the low‑level MSTORE8 opcode, the oversized value causes the opcode to write an extra most‑significant bit into the memory slot immediately preceding the intended byte. This off‑by‑one write corrupts the adjacent memory location, shifting data and breaking the assumed byte‑wise layout. The root cause is the missing wrap‑around (or masking) logic for the constant, which allows values outside the 8‑bit range to propagate into memory operations that are designed for single‑byte storage. An attacker can exploit this by crafting input that forces inV to exceed 255, triggering the malformed MSTORE8 write. The resulting memory corruption can alter critical state variables such as balances, counters, or cryptographic commitments, leading to incorrect accounting, unexpected zero balances, or loss of funds. The bug manifests only when the contract processes inputs that produce a value greater than 255 for the affected polynomial, which may be rare and therefore easy to miss during normal testing. Users experience symptoms such as their balance appearing unchanged after a deposit, refunds returning zero, or transaction receipts showing unexpected values. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the handling of low‑level memory writes and identified the lack of a wrap‑around constraint. Because the problem resides in a low‑level assembly instruction, it does not generate obvious Solidity‑level errors and can remain hidden until a specific edge case is triggered. To remediate the flaw, the constant should be constrained to a byte by applying a modulo‑256 operation or by explicitly casting to uint8 before any MSTORE8 usage, ensuring that only the least‑significant 8 bits are stored. This class of bug falls under memory‑alignment or storage‑layout vulnerabilities where improper handling of byte boundaries leads to data corruption and potential financial loss.
summary: The constant polynomial BYTE_C4096 does not wrap around after value 255 as it should, allowing inV to have values above a byte, which may carry over and cause an MSTORE8 to write a 1 before the given byte in memory.

title: Incorrect BYTE implementation
content: The vulnerability concerns an incorrect implementation of the EVM BYTE opcode (opBYTE) where the range check performed before extracting a byte from a 256‑bit word only validates the lowest byte of the index (B0) and ignores the higher bytes (B1‑B7). Because the specification requires that any index greater than 31 must result in a zero value, the implementation should reject any non‑zero high‑order bits. In the flawed version, if an index such as 0x100000001 is supplied—where B0 equals 1 and B1 equals 1—the opcode incorrectly returns the first byte of the source word (e.g., 0xa0) instead of zero. This occurs during execution of the BYTE instruction when the contract or client passes an out‑of‑range index with non‑zero high bytes. The root cause is a missing validation of the full 256‑bit index, leading to a logical error where the opcode’s guard clause only checks B0. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a transaction that supplies a malicious index, causing the opcode to return an unexpected non‑zero byte. That unexpected value can be used in subsequent arithmetic or conditional checks, potentially bypassing access controls, mis‑calculating token amounts, or corrupting accounting logic. The impact includes incorrect state transitions, loss or misallocation of funds, and violation of business rules that assume a zero result for out‑of‑range indices. Users, developers, and protocols that rely on precise byte extraction—such as token contracts, parsers, or cryptographic primitives—are affected because they may observe balances that do not match expectations, refunds that are partially missing, or contract logic that behaves unpredictably. The issue was discovered during a security audit (by Spearbit) that examined the opBYTE implementation against the formal specification and identified a counter‑example not covered by the standard Ethereum State Tests; however, some client implementations (e.g., evmone) have unit tests that catch the bug. The bug is subtle because the opcode still returns a plausible byte value, making it hard to notice without targeted tests that include high‑byte indices. To remediate, the implementation should replace the faulty range check with a comprehensive validation, such as using a subtraction‑based check (:SUB) that ensures the index is within the 0‑31 range, and add dedicated unit tests for cases where high bytes are set. This correction aligns the opcode’s behavior with the EVM specification and prevents the erroneous non‑zero return that can lead to financial inconsistencies.
summary: In opBYTE, the argument range check 31 - B => D :JMPN(opBYTE0) is incorrect because this only checks B0. If any of B1–B7 are non-zero, the result of opBYTE must be 0 but may be other value in this implementation. Counter example: • A = 0xa0a1a2a3a4a5a6a7a8a9b0b1b2b3b4b5b6b7b8b9c0c1c2c3c4c5c6c7c8c9d0d1, • B = 0x100000001, i.e. B0 = 1, B1 = 1, • The result should be 0 but is 0xa0. This case or similar are not covered by the Ethereum State Tests, but various implementations cover it via unit tests (like evmone).

title: Test failures in VMTests/vmPerformance/loopExp (potential issue in EXP)
content: The issue is an incorrect implementation of the exponentiation (EXP) opcode in the zk‑EVM, which manifests as failures in the official Ethereum VM performance test suite (VMTests/vmPerformance/loopExp). The root cause is a deviation from the Ethereum specification in how the EXP operation computes results or accounts for gas, likely related to the handling of large exponent values or the internal zk‑counters used for proof generation. An attacker can exploit this deviation by submitting a transaction that includes a carefully crafted EXP expression; because the opcode produces a wrong result, the contract’s arithmetic may be corrupted, leading to mis‑calculated balances, failed refunds, or other accounting errors. The impact is severe: contracts that rely on exponentiation for token math, interest calculations, or cryptographic primitives may produce incorrect state, potentially causing funds to disappear or become unrecoverable. The vulnerability appears only when the EXP opcode is exercised with inputs that trigger the faulty path, such as loops that repeatedly call EXP or large exponent values, which is why it is exposed by the loopExp performance test but may remain hidden in ordinary usage. All users of the zk‑EVM, including developers deploying smart contracts, auditors reviewing code, and end‑users interacting with affected contracts, are potentially affected because the underlying virtual machine may produce wrong outcomes. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that executed the full Ethereum test vector suite against the zk‑EVM implementation; the loopExp test consistently threw an error, indicating a mismatch with the reference behavior. Because the failure occurs deep inside the VM execution engine, it can be difficult to notice from the UI – users may see unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or transactions that revert without a clear reason. To remediate, the EXP opcode must be brought back into compliance with the Ethereum Yellow Paper: the exponentiation algorithm should correctly handle arbitrary‑size operands, the gas cost must follow the spec, and any zk‑specific counters must be updated accurately. After fixing the opcode, the VM tests should pass, confirming that exponentiation behaves as expected and that contract arithmetic remains reliable.

title: opJUMP/opJUMPI reading position out of code bounds
content: The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds read in the virtual-machine implementation of the opJUMP and opJUMPI instructions. The code that validates a jump destination compares the length of the contract bytecode with the destination using the condition bytecodeLength < jumpDst. Because the comparison is reversed, a destination equal to the exact length of the bytecode (jumpDst == bytecodeLength) passes the check and the VM subsequently attempts to fetch the opcode at code[bytecodeLength]. Since valid indices run from 0 to bytecodeLength-1, this read accesses memory outside the compiled contract. The root cause is an off-by-one error in the bounds-checking logic. An attacker can craft a transaction that forces the EVM to execute a JUMP or JUMPI to the last byte of the code, causing the VM to read undefined data. Depending on how the underlying execution environment handles the out-of-bounds value, the jump may resolve to an invalid opcode, cause a revert, or be interpreted as a different instruction, potentially allowing the attacker to alter control flow, skip security checks, or cause loss of funds. The issue manifests only when a jump destination is exactly equal to the bytecode size, a situation that typical unit tests may not cover, making it hard to notice. All contracts executed on the affected zkEVM, including those on Polygon-Hermez, are exposed because the VM is shared across deployments; any user interacting with a vulnerable contract may experience unexpected reverts or, in worst cases, loss of assets. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit by Spearbit, who identified the incorrect comparison. Because the out-of-bounds read does not immediately throw an exception, the symptom from a user’s perspective can be a transaction that appears to succeed but results in no state change, a zero balance after a supposed transfer, or a silent failure where the contract behaves incorrectly. The bug belongs to the class of jump destination validation errors or off-by-one bounds checks that break the fundamental accounting assumption that code execution stays within the defined bytecode. The recommended fix is to replace the condition with jumpDst < bytecodeLength and to route any invalid destination to a dedicated error handler (e.g., JMPNC(invalidJump)). This ensures that any attempt to jump outside the code will be caught before the VM reads memory, preserving execution integrity and preventing the described exploit.
summary:
The check for jump destination being within code bounds is done as bytecodeLength < jumpDst.
In case dst == bytecodeLength it proceeds to fetch bytecode at position code[bytecodeLength].

title: Incorrect check for calldata overrun in CALLDATACOPY
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect bounds check performed before executing the CALLDATACOPY opcode. The intended safety condition is to ensure that the sum of the calldata offset and the number of bytes to copy (size) does not exceed the total length of the transaction calldata, i.e., offset+size < txCalldataLen. In the examined implementation the registers are populated incorrectly: the register A holds txCalldataLen+size while register B holds the offset, and the comparison therefore evaluates txCalldataLen+size < offset. This reversed inequality does not prevent an overrun because it can be satisfied even when offset+size exceeds the calldata length. The root cause is a logical error in the assembly‑level code that swaps the operands of the comparison, likely due to a copy‑and‑paste mistake or misunderstanding of the underlying virtual machine semantics. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a calldata payload where the offset is small and the size is large enough that offset+size goes beyond the actual calldata. Because the faulty check passes, CALLDATACOPY will read beyond the supplied calldata buffer, pulling undefined or attacker‑controlled data into memory. This can corrupt the contract’s internal state, cause incorrect calculations, or enable the attacker to manipulate subsequent logic that relies on the copied data. The impact is severe: the contract may execute with malformed inputs, leading to loss of funds, broken accounting, or a breach of protocol invariants, which is why the issue is classified as critical risk. The condition occurs every time the vulnerable contract executes a CALLDATACOPY operation that relies on this check, typically in functions that parse external input.
