The bug is subtle because the order appears to revert normally, yet the hidden retry silently creates a pending order that later executes, making the profit look like a legitimate trade. The vulnerability belongs to the class of order‑handling and replay bugs where stale execution data is reused, violating the accounting assumption that each trade is settled at the current market price. To remediate, the contract should not retry orders that fail with EMPTY_POSITION_ERROR_KEY; instead it must reject them outright and require the user to open a valid position before submitting a decrease order, ensuring that price data is refreshed for each new order and that no pending orders can be exploited for arbitrage.
summary: The custom handling for the Keys.EMPTY_POSITION_ERROR_KEY allows users to create MarketDecrease orders that continue to revert and be retried until the user creates a position. The MarketDecrease order would then be executed at the prices of the block in which the decrease order was created. This way a user can submit a long MarketDecrease for an empty position, and wait until the price of the index token decreases before submitting a MarketIncrease order and realizing risk-free profits from the exchange.

title: ORDU-1 | Cancelled Order In beforeOrderExecution Callback
content: The vulnerability is a logic and re‑entrancy flaw that allows an order to be cancelled inside the beforeOrderExecution callback while the same order continues to be processed. The callback returns the user’s collateral and removes the order entry from the orderStore, but the execution flow does not stop; it proceeds to create a new position using the original collateral delta and USD size. This mismatch between the stored order state (removed) and the runtime execution (position created) creates a deficit in the orderStore balances, breaking the accounting invariants of the exchange. The root cause is that the cancelOrder function can be invoked during the same transaction that is supposed to execute the order, and there is no re‑entrancy protection or consistency check between the storage update and the cached parameters used later in the call stack. An attacker or a malicious contract can trigger cancelOrder from within the beforeOrderExecution hook, causing the order to be marked as cancelled and the funds to be refunded, yet the protocol still records a position as if the order had been fulfilled. The impact is that the exchange ends up with positions that have no backing collateral, leading to potential loss of funds, incorrect user balances, and systemic accounting errors that affect all participants, including liquidity providers and other traders. The condition occurs whenever an order is processed and the beforeOrderExecution callback is executed; if the callback includes a call to cancelOrder, the bug is triggered. It was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team through targeted testing of the order lifecycle and observing that the orderStore balances diverged after a cancellation inside the callback. The issue is hard to notice because the UI may show that the order was successfully cancelled and the user received a refund, while a hidden position appears in the system, and the deficit only becomes apparent when aggregate balances are reconciled. To remediate, the protocol should forbid order cancellation while the same order is being executed, for example by moving cancelOrder logic to a separate orderHandler component protected by a non‑reentrant modifier, and by ensuring that any cached execution parameters are refreshed after state changes so that storage and runtime views remain consistent. This class of bug falls under order‑lifecycle race conditions and re‑entrancy vulnerabilities that break accounting guarantees, resulting in symptoms such as users receiving a refund but later seeing an unexpected open position, balances that appear to disappear, or missing funds in the exchange’s accounting ledger.
summary: In the beforeOrderExecution callback it is possible to cancel the order prior to processing which returns funds to the user and removes the order from the orderStore. However, the order will still execute and create a position with the initial collateral delta and USD size. This results in a deficit in the orderStore balances which causes accounting issues across the entire exchange.

title: GLOBAL-1 | shouldUnwrapNativeToken DoS
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by the misuse of a boolean flag that indicates whether a native token should be unwrapped during liquidation and auto‑deleveraging (ADL) operations. The flag, named shouldUnwrapNativeToken, is set to true for both liquidation and ADL orders under the assumption that the contract receiving the unwrapped native token is able to accept it. However, the protocol does not verify the actual capability of the recipient contract to receive native tokens. When a position is opened by a contract that lacks a payable fallback function or otherwise rejects incoming native token transfers, any subsequent liquidation or ADL that attempts to unwrap the token will trigger a revert. The root cause is the reliance on the flag to decide transaction success without performing a safe‑transfer check, effectively allowing an attacker to create a position that cannot be decreased. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a contract that deliberately rejects native token transfers, opening a position through that contract, and then waiting for the protocol to attempt liquidation or ADL. When the protocol executes the order, the unwrap call fails, the transaction reverts, and the position remains open indefinitely. The impact is that the affected position becomes frozen, preventing liquidators from reducing risk, potentially leading to systemic exposure if the position is under‑collateralised. This condition occurs only when the flag is true and the recipient is a non‑payable contract, which is a realistic scenario for contracts that deliberately block native token receipt. Users, liquidators, and the protocol itself are affected because expected collateral returns are not delivered and the protocol’s risk‑management mechanisms are bypassed. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test reproducing the revert. It can be hard to notice because the flag appears innocuous and the failure manifests only in edge cases where the recipient contract is specially crafted. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a liquidation attempt that instantly reverts, leaving the balance unchanged and giving the impression that the position cannot be closed or that the protocol is malfunctioning. The expected behaviour—successful liquidation and return of collateral—is violated, resulting in “funds disappear” or “position cannot be decreased” symptoms. To remediate, the shouldUnwrapNativeToken logic should be refactored so that it no longer determines transaction viability; the protocol should either set the flag to false for liquidation and ADL orders or perform a safe‑transfer that gracefully handles non‑payable recipients, ensuring that a failure to unwrap does not revert the entire order.
summary: The shouldUnwrapNativeToken flag can be exploited by users to create positions that cannot be decreased by liquidations or ADL orders. For both liquidation orders and ADL orders the shouldUnwrapNativeToken flag is set to true, however the position can be created by a contract that is unable to receive the native token, causing the order execution to revert.

title: ORDU-2 | Uncancellable/Unfreezable Order
content: The vulnerability is an uncancellable and unfreezable order condition that arises when the protocol attempts to refund a user in the native blockchain token during a cancel or freeze operation. The refund logic assumes that the destination address can always receive native tokens, and it performs a direct transfer (or low‑level call) without checking whether the call succeeds. If the user’s address is a smart contract whose fallback function reverts or otherwise refuses incoming native tokens, the refund transaction fails, causing the entire cancel or freeze transaction to revert. As a result the order remains in an active state and cannot be cancelled or frozen by the user. An attacker can deliberately deploy a contract that rejects native token transfers, place an order using that contract as the recipient, and then repeatedly attempt to cancel or freeze the order. Each attempt reverts, keeping the order pending until the market moves in a favorable direction, at which point the attacker allows the order to be executed and captures profit without bearing the intended risk. The impact is that users can manipulate the order lifecycle to obtain risk‑free trades, undermining the economic assumptions of the protocol and potentially harming other participants who rely on timely order cancellation or freezing. The issue manifests only during the cancel or freeze pathways and only when the refund address is a contract that cannot accept native tokens, making it easy to miss in testing that primarily uses externally owned accounts. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, which provided a proof‑of‑concept that demonstrates the revert behavior. Because the failure occurs deep inside a low‑level transfer, it may not surface as an obvious error in the UI; users simply see that their order does not cancel and no refund is received, leading to confusion. The recommended mitigation is to avoid sending native tokens directly to the user; instead the protocol should credit the user with a wrapped version of the native token (WNT) or employ a safe‑transfer pattern that handles failed transfers gracefully, ensuring that cancellation and freezing can always complete regardless of the recipient’s contract code. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of unsafe external‑call refunds and improper handling of token transfer failures, which can break business logic that assumes refunds always succeed.
summary: In the process of cancelling or freezing an order, the executionFee is paid to the keeper and a native token refund is issued to the user. However, the address of the user can point to a contract that is unable to accept the native token, causing the cancellation or freezing to revert. This way, the user may cause their order execution to revert and be retried until they wish their order to be executed – enabling risk free trades with knowledge of how the market moved after their order was created.

title: DPU-1 | Open Interest Errantly Increased
content: The vulnerability resides in the market utility routine that updates the open interest measured in tokens. When a trader reduces a position, the contract receives a positive sizeDeltaInTokens that represents the amount of tokens being removed from the market. Instead of decreasing the open‑interest counter, the routine mistakenly adds this positive delta, causing the open‑interest value to grow even though the position is shrinking. This accounting error propagates to the calculation of profit‑and‑loss, funding rates and the market’s reserve balances, because all of those formulas rely on an accurate open‑interest figure. An attacker can trigger the bug by submitting a decrease order, inflating the reported open interest and consequently manipulating funding payments or reserve allocations to their advantage. The issue manifests only during the execution path that handles position reductions; normal position openings are unaffected. Anyone who interacts with the market – traders, liquidity providers, or the protocol itself – may see unexpected behavior such as higher than expected funding charges, missing refunds, or balances that appear to shrink without a corresponding trade. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit where a test case demonstrated that after a decrease call the open‑interest metric increased instead of decreasing. Because the metric is a high‑level aggregate, the problem can be subtle and may not raise an immediate alarm; the market may simply appear to have growing activity. To remediate the bug the size delta should be negated before applying it to the open‑interest counter, effectively subtracting the tokens that are being removed. In broader terms the defect belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a sign inversion leads to incorrect state updates, breaking the invariant that open interest must reflect the net amount of outstanding positions. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after closing a trade the protocol reports a larger open‑interest, the expected refund is zero or lower than anticipated, and the overall market accounting no longer matches the trader’s intuition, violating the fundamental business rule that decreasing a position reduces exposure.
summary: The call to MarketUtils.applyDeltaToOpenInterestInTokens applies the positive sizeDeltaInTokens to the open interest in tokens while the position is being decreased by that amount of tokens rather than increased. This incorrectly represents the accounting of the decrease order and perturbs all open interest, pnl and reserves accounting for that market.

title: DPU-2 | Incorrect Impact Calculation
content: The vulnerability is an accounting miscalculation in the price impact logic of the market contract. The contract determines the amount of price impact to apply (priceImpactAmount) by using the raw order size parameter (sizeDeltaUsd) instead of the adjusted order size (adjustedSizeDeltaUsd) that reflects fees, slippage or other reductions applied before the trade is executed. Because the adjusted size can be considerably smaller than the original size, the impact that is recorded in the pool’s accounting differs from the impact that the trader actually experiences. As a result the protocol may credit the impact pool with more funds than were truly transferred, while simultaneously reducing the main pool amount based on the smaller adjusted size. This double‑counting creates a discrepancy where funds appear to disappear from the user’s perspective, balances may become lower than expected, and the overall market accounting no longer balances. The flaw is triggered whenever an order is subject to adjustments – for example when fees are taken, when the order is partially filled, or when price limits cause a reduction in the executed size. Any trader, liquidity provider, or downstream protocol that relies on the pool’s accounting can be affected because the pool may hold less capital than it believes, potentially leading to under‑collateralisation or loss of funds. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test showing that the impact pool and the main pool could be charged simultaneously for the same trade, effectively double counting the same amount. The bug is subtle because the contract still emits a price impact value that looks plausible; only a deeper inspection of the internal state reveals the mismatch. To remediate, the priceImpactAmount calculation must be based on the adjustedSizeDeltaUsd value, ensuring that the impact applied to accounting matches the actual size of the trade. This aligns the accounting with business logic that assumes impact is proportional to the executed trade amount, prevents double counting, and restores the integrity of the pool’s balance sheet.
summary: The calculation of the priceImpactAmount is computed with the params.order.sizeDeltaUsd, however the price impact that the user actually experiences is based on the adjustedSizeDeltaUsd which can be significantly smaller than the params.order.sizeDeltaUsd. This way the impact that is applied to the accounting for the pool and the impact that actually takes place can be significantly different and cause the market to start double counting funds in both the impact pool and the poolAmount.

title: DPU-3 | Incorrect Fee Decrement
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee decrement logic that results in a double‑charging of users. In the fee settlement routine the contract is supposed to subtract the amount that will be sent to the user (outputAmount) from the total fee (totalNetCostAmount). However, the implementation sets values.outputAmount to zero before performing the subtraction, so the fee is calculated against a zero output and then the full fee is also taken from the user’s collateral. This logical error occurs whenever the contract processes a trade that involves a fee, especially when the fee amount is large, because the mistaken zeroing of the output amount amplifies the loss. An attacker or any user interacting with the exchange can be exploited by simply executing a normal trade; the contract will silently deduct the fee twice, leaving the user with a reduced balance and possibly no tokens received. The impact includes significant asset loss for traders, unexpected accounting discrepancies within the market, and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees that fees should only be taken once from the intended source. The bug is discovered during a security audit that examined the fee accounting path and noticed that the output amount was cleared before the fee subtraction, a subtle mistake that does not raise an immediate error flag and therefore can be hard to notice in normal operation. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or zeroed token receipt despite a successful transaction and a fee that appears higher than expected, violating the expectation that the fee is taken only from the output amount. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of accounting or fee‑calculation errors where state variables are overwritten before they are used in arithmetic, leading to double‑charging or loss of funds. The recommended remediation is to perform the subtraction of values.outputAmount from the fee first, and only after the fee has been correctly reduced set values.outputAmount to zero, thereby preserving the intended single‑charge behavior and restoring correct market accounting.
summary: In the condition where the values.outputAmount is intended to be subtracted from the fee amount, the values.outputAmount is set to 0 before being subtracted from the fee amount, causing the fee to be taken from both the outputAmount and the user’s collateral. In the case of large fees, this can lead to significant loss of assets for users interacting with the exchange, and can potentially cause unexpected accounting within a market.

title: DPU-4 | Wrong Token Amount Applied
content: The vulnerability is a token‑type mismatch in the pool accounting logic. When a trader closes a position the system calculates a net profit‑or‑loss amount (pnlAmountForPool). If the position is losing, the amount represents collateral tokens that must be returned to the pool; if the position is winning, the amount represents profit tokens (pnlToken) that must be removed from the pool. The function that updates the pool balance, however, always treats the amount as collateral regardless of its actual token type. Consequently, when a profit is realized the contract subtracts a pnlToken amount from the collateral token balance, corrupting the pool’s accounting. This can be triggered whenever a user realizes a gain, causing the pool’s collateral reserve to be reduced by an amount of a different token, which may lead to insufficient collateral for future positions, incorrect payout calculations, and potentially loss of user funds. The issue appears during the settlement step after a position is closed, and it affects any participant who relies on the pool’s accounting – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended token flow with the actual state changes in the test suite. The bug is subtle because the contract emits no explicit error; the mismatch only shows up as a drift in the pool’s token balances over time, which may be missed until a large discrepancy surfaces. The correct fix is to make the accounting routine detect the token type of the amount being removed and apply the delta to the corresponding token balance, ensuring that profit tokens are deducted from the profit pool and collateral tokens from the collateral pool. In abstract terms this is a classic “wrong asset applied” accounting flaw, similar to using the wrong currency in a financial transaction. From a user’s perspective the symptom can be that a trader who should receive a profit finds their balance unchanged or sees the pool’s collateral unexpectedly depleted, leading to failed withdrawals or reduced margin capacity. The deviation violates the protocol’s invariant that the sum of collateral and profit tokens in the pool must equal the total value locked, breaking the accounting guarantees that underpin the synthetic product.
summary: The pnlAmountForPool is either the collateralToken if the user realized losses or the pnlToken if the user realized gains. However the applyDeltaToPoolAmount treats this amount as collateralToken no matter what, therefore perturbing the accounting of the pool by applying a pnlToken amount to a collateralToken amount.

title: PPU-1 | Open Interest Value Uninitialized
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that prepares the next open‑interest parameters for a market. Two variables, representing the projected long and short open‑interest balances, are declared but not given explicit initial values. The code only assigns a new value to one of them depending on whether the incoming request is for a long position; the other variable retains its default Solidity value of zero. Because the market’s price‑impact formula uses both the long and short open‑interest figures, a missing initialization causes the calculation to treat one side of the market as having no exposure. This mis‑representation leads to nonsensical price‑impact numbers, extreme slippage, or even trades being executed at rates far from the expected market price. The bug appears whenever the getNextOpenInterestParams function is called, which is on every trade that updates open interest. Any user, trader, or liquidity provider interacting with the market can be affected, as the protocol may charge incorrect fees or allow arbitrage opportunities that drain funds. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the flow of open‑interest data and noticed that one of the variables remained untouched in certain branches. It can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and runs; the erroneous zero value only manifests in edge cases where the opposite side of the market has non‑zero exposure, making the price‑impact output look wildly out of range. Exploitation can follow a simple scenario: an attacker submits a trade that triggers the branch where the short open‑interest is left uninitialized, causing the price‑impact calculation to assume zero short exposure. The resulting price may be artificially favorable, allowing the attacker to open a large position at a discounted rate and later unwind it for profit, effectively stealing value from the pool. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a zero balance for one side of the market, or a trade may unexpectedly revert or settle with a huge loss, contradicting the expectation that the market price reflects true supply and demand. The root cause is a classic uninitialized‑state bug, where default zero values are unintentionally used in critical arithmetic. The recommended remediation is to initialize both projected open‑interest variables with the current on‑chain values before applying any delta, ensuring that the price‑impact formula always receives accurate inputs. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting logic that both sides of the market must be considered for fair pricing and risk management.
summary: In the getNextOpenInterestParams function the nextLongOpenInterest and nextShortOpenInterest variables are not initialized from the default values and only one is set in either of the params.isLong cases. This drastically misrepresents the open interest balance of the market and yields nonsensical price impact calculations.

title: MKTU-1 | Impact Pool Included In Pool Value
content: The vulnerability is a double‑counting accounting error in the market’s pool valuation logic. The function that reports the total pool value adds the balance of the position impact pool to the net pool value, even though the impact pool only holds a notional amount of synthetic index tokens that should be treated as a separate liability. When a trader suffers a negative impact, the protocol transfers index tokens from the trader into the impact pool and simultaneously records a negative profit‑and‑loss (PnL) for that trader. Because the getPoolValue routine adds the impact pool’s notional amount, the same loss is reflected twice: once as the tokens moved into the impact pool and again as the trader’s negative PnL. This double counting inflates the reported pool value while the actual assets backing market tokens are lower. The error manifests whenever a negative‑impact trade occurs and the pool value is queried, typically during depositors’ withdrawal calculations. As a result, depositors may be unable to withdraw the full amount of MarketTokens they own, effectively causing funds to disappear or become locked. Traders also see an unexpected loss because the pool’s accounting does not match the economic reality of their positions. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by the Guardian team, which reproduced the problem with a proof‑of‑concept test that showed the pool value diverging from the true asset balance after a negative impact event. The bug is subtle because the pool’s reported value still appears reasonable, masking the underlying deficit until a withdrawal or a detailed accounting audit is performed. Conceptually, the fix is to exclude the position impact pool from the net pool value calculation, treating it as a separate liability rather than part of the pool’s assets. By doing so, the accounting system correctly reflects the actual collateral backing market tokens, preventing double counting, ensuring that users receive the expected withdrawal amounts, and preserving the integrity of the protocol’s financial model.
summary: In the getPoolValue function, the position impact pool value is added to the value of the pool. However the position impact pool is comprised of a notional value of synthetic index tokens, therefore it should not be added to the pool value. When a trader is negatively impacted, two things happen: indexTokens are taken from the trader and allocated to the position impact pool. The trader immediately experiences a loss on their PnL. This results in the pool accounting for this negative impact amount twice. Once for the indexTokens that are allocated to the position impact pool. And a second time for the negative PnL that the trader has just experienced. This double counting invalidates the market’s accounting system and does not allow depositors to withdraw all of their MarketTokens.

title: MKTU-2 | Funding Fees Partially Paid
content: The vulnerability originates in the funding calculation routine that determines how much funding fee each position must pay per unit of collateral size. The function divides the total funding amount denominated in USD by the aggregate open interest of both long and short sides and then assigns the resulting per‑size value to each collateral token. This approach is appropriate when users are receiving funding because they can claim fees in both the long and short tokens. However, when users are required to pay funding, they are only able to pay with the collateral token that matches their position direction. By still dividing the funding amount by the total open interest of the entire side, the contract spreads the payable amount across a larger base than actually contributes, causing each payer to remit only a fraction of the fee that should be owed. Consequently, the pool records a full funding amount as claimable while only a partial amount is collected, creating a persistent accounting deficit. Over time this deficit can erode the pool’s solvency, potentially leading to market insolvency. The issue was uncovered during a targeted audit that exercised funding claim and payment flows and observed that the net funding collected was consistently lower than the net funding credited. The bug is subtle because the contract still reports correct funding amounts in the public view functions, and the discrepancy only manifests during the payment step, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate, the funding per‑size calculation for the paying side must be based on the open interest that is actually able to provide the required collateral token, rather than the total open interest of the side. In practice this means using the open interest of positions that hold the specific collateral token when computing the payable portion, ensuring that the full funding fee is transferred into the pool and that accounting remains balanced. This class of bug falls under incorrect fee distribution or mis‑allocation of financial obligations, where a formula assumes symmetric payment capabilities that do not exist, violating the protocol’s accounting invariants and expected user experience of receiving or paying the full funding amount.
summary: In the getNextFundingAmountPerSize function, the fundingAmountPerSizePortion values are calculated by dividing the corresponding fundingUsd by the open interest of both longs and shorts. This is done to get a value that is to be received/paid for each collateral type for each position direction. This logic makes sense in the case where users are being paid the funding fees since they are able to claim both the long and short tokens. However users are only able to pay the fundingAmountPerSizePortion value for their respective collateral token. This errantly reduces the amount the fundingAmountPerSizePortion that is paid for each corresponding collateral token as the amounts are divided by the entire open interest of the side that is paying funding fees. As a result, only a portion of the funding fees are being paid while the entire amount can be claimed, and a deficit in the pool accounting is created which will force markets into insolvency over time.

title: MKTU-3 | Unclaimable Collateral
content: The contract contains a logic error in the collateral‑claim routine that makes the claim function permanently revert for users who have never claimed before. The function checks that the adjusted claimable amount is strictly less than the amount the user reports as already claimed, and if this condition is not met the transaction is reverted. Because a fresh claimant reports a claimed amount of zero, the adjusted claimable amount – which is always a positive number representing the collateral the protocol believes is owed – can never be less than zero. Consequently the require statement fails and the transaction reverts, preventing the user from receiving any of their collateral. The root cause is an inverted inequality: the contract should revert only when the adjusted claimable amount is smaller than the already‑claimed amount, not when it is larger or equal. This bug is discovered during a manual audit that examined the claim flow and noticed that the condition could never be satisfied on a first claim. It is easy to miss because the check appears to protect against over‑claiming, yet the test suite did not include a scenario where claimedAmount is zero. When exploited, the impact is that legitimate users are unable to withdraw their collateral, effectively locking funds in the contract. Any participant who relies on the claim function – including traders, liquidity providers, or any role with vested collateral – is affected. The failure manifests from the user’s perspective as a transaction that always reverts with no error message indicating insufficient balance, leading to confusion such as “my claim transaction fails every time” or “my collateral never arrives”. The business logic that collateral should be claimable after a position is closed is broken, violating the protocol’s accounting guarantees. To remediate, the conditional check must be inverted so that the transaction reverts only when adjustedClaimableAmount is less than claimedAmount, allowing a zero‑claimedAmount claim to succeed and restoring the intended flow of collateral withdrawal.
summary: When users attempt to claim their collateral, the adjustedClaimableAmount is asserted to be < the claimedAmount, otherwise the tx reverts. However if a user has not claimed any of their collateral the claimed amount will be 0 and therefore the adjustedClaimableAmount cannot be strictly less than the claimedAmount. Therefore users are unable to claim their collateral.

title: DPCU-1 | Wrong Token Amount Applied
content: The vulnerability is a token‑type mismatch that occurs during the liquidation of a position when the remaining collateral becomes negative. The getLiquidationValues routine calculates a value called pnlAmountForPool on line 347, but this value is derived strictly from the collateral token amount. The function then returns pnlTokenForPool, which the caller assumes represents the profit‑and‑loss token. In scenarios where a trader’s position is still profitable yet the overall collateral value falls below the minimum collateral requirement because the price of the collateral token has depreciated, the liquidation logic will still be triggered. Because the profit token (shortToken for a short position or longToken for a long position) can differ from the collateral token, the contract ends up applying a short‑token amount as if it were a long‑token amount, or vice‑versa. This misallocation drastically perturbs the pool’s accounting for the pnl token, potentially draining the pool, creating an insolvent market, or causing extreme losses for market depositors. The bug is triggered only when a liquidation is executed while the position is in profit but the collateral value is insufficient, a condition that can be reproduced by manipulating token prices to push the collateral value below the required threshold. It was discovered by the Guardian audit team through targeted testing that forced a profitable liquidation and observed the incorrect token transfer. The issue is subtle because liquidation still appears to succeed and the contract does not emit an explicit error; instead the pool’s internal balances become inconsistent, which may only be noticed after significant fund loss. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include receiving no profit after liquidation, seeing their deposited balance shrink unexpectedly, or observing the market pool balance drop to near zero. The root cause is the failure to distinguish between collateral and profit token amounts in the liquidation value calculation. To remediate, the getLiquidationValues function must be adjusted to correctly compute and return the profit‑and‑loss token amount when a trader is liquidated in profit, ensuring that the token type used for the pool update matches the actual pnl token and preserving the market’s accounting invariants.
summary: In the case where the remainingCollateral for a position is negative during a liquidation, the getLiquidationValues function is called. The values.pnlTokenForPool is used in the returned values. However the values.pnlAmountForPool computed on line 347 is strictly a collateral token amount. A position may be in profit and still be liquidated due to the minCollateralUsdForLeverage combined with a depreciation in the user’s collateral token price. Therefore the pnlTokenForPool may be different from the collateral token, in which case a shortToken amount could be applied as a longToken amount or vice-versa. This will drastically perturb the poolAmount for the pnlTokenForPool in such a way that could leave the market insolvent or simply cause extreme loss for the market depositors.

title: CBU-1 | Malicious Revert Bytes
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service style bug that arises when a contract receives a revert reason from an external callback and copies the returned bytes into memory inside a catch block. The root cause is that the catch clause unconditionally loads the entire reasonBytes array, regardless of its size, and then processes it with a utility that extracts the revert message and also includes the raw bytes in an emitted event. Because Solidity stores dynamic byte arrays in calldata and copying them to memory incurs a cost proportional to their length, an attacker can craft a malicious callback contract that reverts with an arbitrarily large reason string. When the victim contract executes the callback, the gas required to copy and parse the oversized reasonBytes can exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. This can be exploited in two ways: (1) an attacker can toggle the callback contract between a benign implementation and a malicious one, creating a risk‑free trade by first causing the keeper’s execution transaction to fail (burning the attacker’s gas) and then allowing it to succeed when the revert payload is removed; (2) a front‑runner can observe a pending keeper transaction in the mempool, switch the callback contract to the malicious version just before the keeper’s call, and force the keeper’s transaction to exceed gas limits, leading to a failed execution. The impact is that legitimate orders may never be executed, users may see no refunds or missing balances, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about successful callbacks are broken because the contract assumes that any revert reason can be safely handled. The issue occurs whenever the contract interacts with third‑party callbacks that may revert, and the catch block does not impose a size limit on the reason data. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the error‑handling logic of the keeper’s callback flow and identified that the reasonBytes were copied without validation. The bug is hard to notice because the revert reason is typically small, so developers may not anticipate a large payload, and the gas exhaustion manifests only under malicious conditions. To remediate, the contract should avoid loading the external revert reason into memory altogether, or at least cap its size before copying, and should not rely on parsing or emitting the raw reasonBytes. This class of bug falls under unchecked external data handling leading to gas exhaustion and denial‑of‑service, where the contract’s error‑handling path can be weaponized to disrupt normal protocol operation.
summary: In each callback function the bytes memory reasonBytes returned from the third party callback contract in the event of an error is loaded into memory in the catch case. reasonBytes can be potentially very large and therefore extremely gas intensive when it is copied into memory. Furthermore, the catch block continues to perform computation with reasonBytes, first parsing the error message with ErrorUtils.getRevertMessage and also emitting an event that contains reasonBytes. An attacker may simply implement a callback contract that reverts with an extremely large reasonBytes so that the execution tx would require more gas than the block gas limit. The attacker can then toggle the callback contract to no longer revert when they want their order to be executed successfully, enabling a risk-free trade. In another attack, a trader could observe the keeper’s execution tx in the mempool and front-run it to toggle the callback contract to revert with a large reasonBytes. This would cause the keeper’s execution tx to consume an unforeseen amount of gas and likely run out of gas and fail. The attacker could leverage this in a similar manner to create a risk-free trade opportunity.

title: GLOBAL-1 | Homogeneous Markets Double Count Value
content: The vulnerability is a double‑counting accounting error that appears when a synthetic market is configured with the same token used as both the long and the short backing asset. In the getPoolValue routine the contract reads two cached values – cache.longTokenAmount and cache.shortTokenAmount – and adds them together under the assumption that they represent distinct token balances. When the long and short tokens are identical, both cached variables reference the exact same token amount, so the pool’s total value is inflated by roughly 100 %. This mis‑count propagates to several validation functions such as validateReserve, validateMaxPnl and validatePoolAmount, which also sum the two identical amounts and therefore accept incorrect state. The same flaw exists in the getNextFundingAmountPerSize calculation, where open interest is summed twice, producing erroneous funding fee numbers. The bug can be exploited by creating a homogeneous market (longToken == shortToken), depositing funds, and then relying on the overstated pool value to open larger positions, receive excessive funding payouts, or trigger liquidations based on wrong collateral ratios. The impact is that users may see a pool value that is double what they actually supplied, funding fees may be paid out incorrectly, and the protocol’s risk parameters become unreliable, potentially leading to loss of funds for liquidity providers or traders. The condition occurs whenever the protocol allows markets with identical backing tokens; it is not limited to a specific transaction but is inherent to the accounting logic. All participants who interact with such a market – depositors, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions that underlie safety checks are broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team, which provided a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrates the double counting. It is hard to notice from a user interface because the displayed balances may appear normal while the internal accounting is silently inflated, and the discrepancy only surfaces in funding calculations or when extreme positions are taken. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid the creation of markets where the long and short tokens are the same, or redesign the accounting paths so that a single backing token is only counted once for each side, adjusting all validation and funding formulas accordingly. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “double‑counting accounting errors” that break financial invariants, leading to situations where users expect a correct refund or fee but receive zero or an unexpected amount, and where the protocol’s accounting model no longer matches its business logic.
summary: When using the getPoolValue function for markets with identical long and short backing tokens, the cache.longTokenAmount and cache.shortTokenAmount represent the same token amount. However both of these token amounts are counted in the value of the pool. Therefore the deposited pool value is doubled. Additionally, several validations e.g. validateReserve, validateMaxPnl, and validatePoolAmount among others are immediately invalidated as they errantly count the same exact token amount for both the short and long side. This way the single backing token pool is effectively double counted as backing both long positions and short positions. Similarly open interest in these markets is double counted in the getNextFundingAmountPerSize function, producing a completely invalid calculation for funding fees.

title: ORDU-1 | Unbounded swapPath Length
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded swapPath length in the order creation logic of the exchange contract. When a trader creates an order, the contract accepts an arbitrary array of token addresses that define the multi‑hop swap route, but it does not enforce any maximum size for this array. Because each hop in the swapPath consumes additional gas, an attacker can craft a swapPath that is extremely long, causing the total gas required for order execution to approach or exceed the block gas limit when combined with a callback that also consumes near the maximum callback gas allowance. Under these conditions the order cannot be executed in the current block, so it remains pending. The attacker can later toggle the callback contract to consume only a small amount of gas, allowing the same order to be executed with stale market prices. By controlling when the order becomes executable, the attacker can perform risk‑free trades that profit from price differences while other participants see no execution or delayed settlement. The impact includes potential financial gain for the attacker, denial‑of‑service for other users because pending orders occupy block space, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that orders are executed promptly with up‑to‑date prices. The issue occurs whenever an order is created without a length check on the swapPath, which is true for all users of the platform. It was discovered during a security audit that exercised edge‑case inputs and observed that the contract accepted swapPath arrays of arbitrary size, as demonstrated in the provided proof‑of‑concept test. The problem is hard to notice because typical usage employs short swap paths, so the gas explosion only appears with deliberately crafted inputs that are not covered by standard unit tests. To remediate, the contract should enforce a reasonable maximum number of hops in the swapPath (for example, five or ten) and also limit the gas that a callback may request, thereby preventing gas‑limit manipulation attacks and restoring the expected behavior that a market order either executes immediately with current prices or fails with a clear error.
summary: When creating an order there is no validation that the swapPath is under a certain max length. This allows malicious users to create risk-free trades on the exchange. Notably, among other ways, a trader may submit a MarketIncrease order with a swapPath that puts the order just over the block gas limit when combined with a callback that consumes nearly the entire maxCallbackGasLimit. When a trader wishes the trade to be executed using outdated prices, they can toggle the callback contract to only consume a very small amount of gas, enabling the order to be executed and recorded in a block.

title: DPCU-2 | LimitDecrease Gamed With EmptyPosition Error
content: The vulnerability is a logic error in the handling of limit decrease orders when a trader removes all collateral from an open position. The contract throws an EmptyPosition error when the remaining collateral amount becomes zero, but this error is classified as retryable. Because the error is retried, an attacker can craft a two‑step sequence that turns a normal limit decrease into a risk‑free trade. First, the attacker opens a LimitDecrease order that halves the position size in USD while simultaneously withdrawing all collateral, causing the order to revert with EmptyPosition and be placed in the retry queue. While the order is pending, the attacker submits a MarketDecrease order that reduces the remaining position size by another half, leaving the position with a non‑zero size but still zero collateral. When the original LimitDecrease is finally retried, the contract now sees a position that can be closed without violating the EmptyPosition check, so it closes the position and returns no error. The attacker therefore receives the full value of the position without having to provide any collateral, effectively executing a profit‑making trade with no risk. The root cause is the misuse of the EmptyPosition error for a situation that should be considered an InsufficientCollateral condition; the former is designed to be retried, while the latter should abort permanently. Exploitation requires the ability to submit both limit and market decrease orders and to set collateral to zero, which is possible for any trader with sufficient permissions on the platform. The impact is that a malicious participant can extract value from the protocol without exposing capital, undermining the economic guarantees of the system and potentially draining liquidity that honest users rely on. The bug manifests as repeated EmptyPosition reverts for limit orders, confusing users who expect their order to execute but see it stuck in a retry loop. It was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with an automated proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the repeatable failure. The issue is subtle because the EmptyPosition error is a legitimate response for genuine under‑collateralisation, so developers may assume the retry behaviour is appropriate. To remediate, the contract should revert with an InsufficientCollateral error when remainingCollateralAmount is zero; this error is not retried, preventing the attacker from leveraging the retry mechanism. Additionally, the order validation logic should reject any decrease that would leave a position with zero collateral, ensuring that the accounting invariants of the protocol are preserved and that users receive the expected outcome of either a successful trade or a clear, non‑retryable failure.
summary: Removing all of the collateral from a position will result in the EmptyPosition error, which will be retried for LimitDecrease orders. An attacker can leverage this by creating a LimitDecrease order that initially only reduces their position.sizeInUsd by half, but reduces their collateral to 0. The LimitDecrease will continue to result in the EmptyPosition error until the attacker creates a MarketDecrease order that reduces the size of their position by half. Now when the original LimitDecrease is executed, it will close the position and no longer revert with the EmptyPosition error. A malicious trader can leverage this to make a risk-free trade with their LimitDecrease.

title: MKTU-4 | 60 Decimals Of Precision Causes Overflow
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow caused by mixing 60‑decimal precision values with 18‑decimal market token amounts in the pool valuation logic. In the getPoolValue routine the contract stores the accumulated borrowing fees in a cache variable that is scaled to 60 decimal places. When the protocol later applies the borrowingFeeReceiverFactor, the result still carries 60 decimals. During a withdrawal, the function marketTokenAmountToUsd multiplies the reported pool value (inflated by the 60‑decimal fee) by the amount of market tokens the user wishes to redeem, which is only expressed with 18 decimals. Because the two numbers are not aligned, the multiplication exceeds the 256‑bit integer limit and wraps around, producing an artificially low pool value. Consequently the calculation that determines how many market tokens the LP should receive returns a dramatically reduced amount, so the LP sees a shortfall or even a zero payout. This condition is triggered only after borrowing fees have been accrued and an LP initiates a withdrawal; before fees are accumulated the mismatch does not manifest. The affected parties are liquidity providers who expect to receive a proportional share of the pool, as well as the protocol itself which may end up with unaccounted‑for funds. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that inspected the precision handling in the fee accounting code. It is subtle because the overflow does not revert; the contract continues execution with wrapped values, making the symptom appear as a simple “my withdrawal amount is much lower than expected” rather than a contract bug. The root cause is the use of an excessively high decimal precision for fee storage without normalising it before arithmetic with other 18‑decimal quantities. To remediate, the fee cache should be stored using the same 18‑decimal basis as other monetary values, or the factor‑application step must explicitly down‑scale the result to 18 decimals before it participates in further multiplications. Aligning decimal precision eliminates the overflow risk and restores correct accounting, ensuring that users receive the market tokens they are entitled to.
summary: In the getPoolValue function, the cache.totalBorrowingFees utilizes 60 decimals of precision, therefore Precision.applyFactor(cache.totalBorrowingFees, cache.borrowingFeeReceiverFactor) will have 60 decimals of precision. Whenever an LP wants to withdraw after borrowing fees have been accumulated, the call to marketTokenAmountToUsd in WithdrawalUtils.sol would overflow since the pool value is multiplied by the market token amount which has 18 decimals of precision. Furthermore, the amount of market tokens depositors receive will be drastically reduced as the pool value is inflated.

title: GSU-1 | Missing Swap Gas Estimation
content: The vulnerability is an under‑estimation of gas required for withdrawal operations that involve token swaps. The function that calculates the gas limit for executing a withdrawal (estimateExecuteWithdrawalGasLimit) only accounts for the base withdrawal logic and completely ignores the additional gas that will be consumed when the contract follows either the longTokenSwapPath or the shortTokenSwapPath to convert assets before sending them to the user. Because the keeper – the entity that funds the transaction with native gas – is reimbursed based on the estimated gas, the omission means the keeper is not compensated for the extra gas spent on the swap step. This can be exploited whenever a user requests a withdrawal that triggers a swap; the keeper pays the full gas cost, receives no reimbursement, and its native token balance is gradually depleted. If an attacker repeatedly initiates such swap‑enabled withdrawals, the keeper’s balance can be drained quickly, causing the protocol to lose the ability to pay for further transactions and potentially halting exchange functionality for an extended period. The issue manifests only when the withdrawal path includes a token swap, so ordinary withdrawals appear normal and the problem may be missed during casual testing. It affects the protocol’s keeper contract, the overall health of the exchange, and indirectly the users who rely on timely withdrawals. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit where the test suite demonstrated that the estimated gas limit was insufficient for swap‑enabled withdrawals, leading to failed reimbursements. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑estimation omissions, where a contract’s accounting logic does not reflect all execution branches, breaking the assumption that the reimbursed gas equals the actual consumption. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that withdrawals that should include a token conversion either fail or are delayed because the keeper runs out of native tokens, contrary to the expectation that the system will always have enough gas to process the request. The correct mitigation is to extend the gas‑estimation routine to include the extra steps of both the long and short swap paths, mirroring the approach already used for deposit operations, thereby ensuring the keeper is properly reimbursed for the full cost of the transaction.
summary: The estimateExecuteWithdrawalGasLimit does not account for either the longTokenSwapPath or the shortTokenSwapPath, therefore the keeper will not be remunerated for users using the swap feature on withdrawals. This will lead to the protocol keeper being unexpectedly drained of the native token, potentially stopping execution on the exchange for a period of time. The gas draining can occur due to regular exchange usage or can be easily leveraged by an attacker to maliciously drain the keeper.

title: IPU-1 | Rounding Leads To Risk Free Trade
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract calculates the token amount for a limit increase order in the increasePosition function. When a user submits a long position request, the contract converts the desired USD size (sizeDeltaUsd) into a token amount (sizeDeltaInTokens) by applying a rounding‑down operation. If the supplied sizeDeltaUsd is just one wei below the trigger price, the rounding can produce a token amount of zero. The contract then throws an EmptyPosition error, causing the transaction to revert. In a market with very low open interest, an attacker can deliberately craft such a borderline sizeDeltaUsd, causing the order to revert initially. By subsequently manipulating the open interest – for example by adding or removing liquidity to change the price impact – the attacker can lower the execution price. A lower execution price changes the conversion rate so that the same sizeDeltaUsd now yields a non‑zero sizeDeltaInTokens after rounding, allowing the previously failing limit order to succeed. Because the attacker can pair this with a large initialCollateralDeltaAmount and a swap path that exploits stale price feeds, they can execute a trade that yields profit without exposing themselves to market risk, effectively a risk‑free arbitrage. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a limit increase transaction that fails with an “EmptyPosition” error, even though the user supplied a non‑zero USD amount; the expectation that the order would be placed is violated. The impact is that the protocol can lose funds when the attacker’s trade is settled, and liquidity providers may see their pool balances altered without a corresponding market move. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated the rounding edge case and the subsequent price‑impact manipulation. It is difficult to notice because rounding to zero is a rare event that only occurs at the extreme edge of the price curve, and the subsequent price manipulation step is not obvious from a simple code review. The bug belongs to the class of “rounding‑to‑zero arithmetic errors combined with price‑impact manipulation”, a subtle form of accounting inconsistency that breaks the assumption that a non‑zero USD size always results in a non‑zero token size. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum USD size (for example 1e30 wei, roughly $1) before performing the conversion, reject any order that would round to zero, or adjust the rounding logic to guarantee a positive token amount when the USD size is positive. This prevents the attacker from creating a revertable order that can later be turned into a profitable, risk‑free trade.
summary: In increasePosition, the sizeDeltaInTokens is rounded down for long positions. An attacker can provide a sizeDeltaUsd that is 1 wei less than their triggerPrice and have their sizeDeltaInTokens rounded to 0. In this case a LimitIncrease would revert with the EmptyPosition error. The attacker can make a LimitIncrease long for a niche market with low open interest where it is easy to manipulate the price impact by controlling the open interest. The attacker can then manipulate the open interest such that their LimitIncrease long is positively price impacted, meaning their executionPrice is decreased. A reduction in the executionPrice would cause the sizeDeltaInTokens to no longer be rounded to 0, and the order to no longer revert with an EmptyPosition error. The attacker can leverage this with a large initialCollateralDeltaAmount and a swapPath that allows them to take advantage of outdated prices for a risk-free trade.

title: CON-1 | _validateRange Prevents Critical Values Being Set
content: The vulnerability resides in a private validation routine that is intended to enforce numeric limits on configurable protocol parameters. Instead of checking the supplied value, the routine immediately reverts when it encounters specific keys that represent the swap fee factor and the position fee factor. Because the function does not perform any range comparison and simply aborts for those identifiers, any transaction that attempts to set or update these critical fee parameters will fail. The root cause is a misplaced revert statement that treats the presence of the key as an error condition rather than evaluating the actual numeric input. This logic error can be triggered whenever the contract’s governance or admin functions call the generic parameter‑setting method with the fee‑related keys. When the call reaches the validator, the transaction is reverted, leaving the stored fee values unchanged. From a user’s perspective the protocol appears to ignore attempts to adjust fees: the UI may still display the old fee percentages, users may notice that their expected fee reductions never materialize, or that the fee remains at a default or previously set value despite a successful governance proposal. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the protocol’s economic controls; the governance cannot react to market conditions, correct mis‑configurations, or implement fee‑related upgrades, potentially leading to revenue loss, market imbalance, or even a scenario where an initially set extreme fee cannot be lowered. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit where the reviewer inspected the validation function and observed that it contains hard‑coded reverts for the fee keys without any value checks. Because the function’s name suggests safety checking, the problem can be subtle and may not surface in standard unit tests that only cover typical parameter updates. To remediate the bug, the validator should be rewritten to accept the fee keys and perform proper numeric range checks (for example, ensuring the fee factor stays within a predefined minimum and maximum) instead of unconditionally reverting. This change restores the ability of authorized actors to modify fee parameters while still protecting against out‑of‑bounds values, aligning the contract’s behavior with its intended business logic of configurable, bounded fees.
summary: The _validateRange function does not perform any validation on the value, but rather reverts for specific keys such as the Keys.SWAP_FEE_FACTOR and Keys.POSITION_FEE_FACTOR. This restricts the protocol from setting these crucial values for the exchange.

title: GLOBAL-3 | Referral Codes Used To Game Orders
content: The vulnerability is a mutable‑parameter exploit in the fee‑discount mechanism of the ExchangeRouter. When a trader creates a LimitIncrease order, the contract calculates the required net cost (fees.totalNetCostAmount) at execution time using the trader’s current referralCode, tier and traderDiscountFactor. Because the contract permits the trader to update their referralCode at any moment by submitting a new order, the discount factors can be changed after the order has been placed but before it is executed. An attacker can therefore submit an order whose fees exactly match the initial collateral, causing the execution to revert with an EmptyPosition error. By waiting for a favorable price movement and then changing the referralCode (or the tier) so that the discount reduces the net cost, the same order no longer reverts and is executed with insufficient collateral. This allows the attacker to open or increase a position without providing the required margin, effectively bypassing the protocol’s accounting checks. The issue manifests to users as an order that initially fails with an EmptyPosition error and later succeeds after the trader changes a referral setting, or as positions that appear with zero or unexpectedly low collateral. The bug is hard to notice because updating referral codes is an intended feature for legitimate discount changes, and the fee calculation is deferred, so the mismatch between the snapshot at order creation and the value used at execution is not obvious. The problem was discovered during a security audit through targeted testing that demonstrated the ability to manipulate the referralCode and observe the change in execution outcome. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑mutation or fee‑snapshot bugs where mutable parameters are applied at a later stage, breaking the invariant that fees must be fixed at order submission. The recommended mitigation is to freeze the totalRebateFactor and traderDiscountFactor for any order that is already pending, effectively taking a snapshot of the discount parameters at order creation and preventing any subsequent updates from affecting the execution of that order.
summary: A trader is able to update their referralCode at any time by creating a new order through the ExchangeRouter. A malicious trader can submit a LimitIncrease where the fees.totalNetCostAmount will be their exact initialCollateralDeltaAmount, yielding an EmptyPosition error on execution. The malicious trader can then allow the LimitIncrease to be executed once they see that prices have moved in their favor by updating their referralCode so that their fees.totalNetCostAmount is discounted and now the order will no longer revert with the EmptyPosition error. This attack can also be executed if the tier or traderDiscountFactor is updated on a trader’s current referralCode as well.

title: GLOBAL-4 | positionIncreasedAtBlock Used To Game Orders
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract tracks the block number at which a position was last increased, stored in the positionIncreasedAtBlock field, and uses this value to restrict the price range for LimitIncrease, LimitDecrease and StopLossDecrease orders. The logic assumes that once a position has been increased, the block number will only move forward, thereby preventing orders from being executed with price data that predates the increase. However, the contract does not consider the situation where a trader closes the position entirely; closing a position resets positionIncreasedAtBlock to zero. Because the validation for the aforementioned order types only checks the current value of positionIncreasedAtBlock, an attacker can deliberately close the position after an initial order has been filled, causing the block marker to revert to zero. After the reset, a second limit order that was previously rejected because its valid descending price range started before the original block number now appears valid, allowing it to be executed with a stale price that is favorable to the attacker. The exploit proceeds as follows: (1) the attacker creates two LimitIncrease orders with the same trigger price; (2) the first order executes, setting positionIncreasedAtBlock to the current block (e.g., 100); (3) the second order is rejected because its allowed price range is defined as descending from before block 100; (4) the attacker waits for the market to move in their favor and then closes the position using a MarketDecrease order, which resets positionIncreasedAtBlock to zero; (5) the previously rejected LimitIncrease order now passes validation and executes at the out‑of‑date price, yielding a risk‑free profit. This flaw can be exploited by any trader who can open multiple limit orders and subsequently close the position, and it becomes effective whenever the market moves in the trader’s direction after the reset. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: users can obtain profit without providing the intended risk, potentially draining liquidity and undermining fairness. The issue was discovered during a formal audit, with a proof‑of‑concept test script demonstrating the exact sequence of calls. It is difficult to notice because the positionIncreasedAtBlock variable appears to be a benign state marker, and resetting it to zero is not flagged as an error by the existing checks. To remediate the problem, the contract should record the block number of the most recent position closure and incorporate this value into the validation logic for LimitIncrease, LimitDecrease and StopLossDecrease orders, ensuring that orders cannot be executed using price data that predates either the last increase or the last closure. Alternatively, the protocol could make positionIncreasedAtBlock immutable after the first increase or require that any reset only moves forward, thereby preserving the monotonicity needed for correct price‑range enforcement. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a limit order that was expected to remain pending or be rejected suddenly fills after the position is closed, resulting in an unexpected gain or, conversely, causing other participants to see their orders unfairly bypassed. This behavior violates the business logic that limit orders should only be executable within a price window that reflects the current state of the position, breaking the intended accounting and risk model of the platform.
summary: LimitIncrease, LimitDecrease, and StopLossDecrease orders depend on the positionIncreasedAtBlock for the price ranges that they can be executed with. A malicious trader may take advantage of past prices by closing their position to reset the positionIncreasedAtBlock to 0. Consider the following attack: 1. A trader makes two LimitIncrease orders with the same triggerPrice. 2. The first one is successfully executed and the positionIncreasedAtBlock is set to 100. 3. The second one is not executed since the valid descending price range is from before the positionIncreasedAtBlock. 4. The trader waits and observes that price moves in their favor, and then closes their position with a MarketDecrease order. Therefore resetting the positionIncreasedAtBlock to 0. 5. Now the second LimitIncrease is able to be executed with the out of date price range, enabling a risk-free trade.

title: CON-1 | Missing Keys In Conﬁg
content: The vulnerability is a configuration omission in the contract initialization routine where three critical parameters are not registered in the initAllowedBaseKeys function. The missing keys are the minimum position size expressed in USD, the maximum profit‑and‑loss factor that can be applied to deposits, and the maximum profit‑and‑loss factor that governs the auto‑deleveraging (ADL) mechanism. Because these keys are absent, the contract falls back to default values, typically zero, which disables the intended safety checks. As a result, traders can open positions of any size, including amounts far below the intended economic threshold, and the system does not cap the PNL factor for deposits, allowing arbitrarily large profit or loss calculations. Likewise, the ADL safeguard that should limit exposure when a position’s loss exceeds a defined factor is ineffective, so extreme losses are not automatically reduced. The exploit can be carried out simply by submitting a trade that would normally be rejected or limited; the contract accepts it and computes payouts based on unbounded formulas, potentially draining user balances or exposing the protocol to systemic risk. The impact is that users may lose funds unexpectedly, the protocol’s risk parameters are bypassed, and the overall financial integrity of the platform is compromised. The condition occurs at deployment or any upgrade that invokes initAllowedBaseKeys without supplying the missing entries, meaning the bug is present from the moment the contract becomes live. All participants—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the missing constraints apply globally to every trade. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s documented configuration schema with the actual initialization code and identified the absent entries. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit explicit errors; the defaults silently disable the checks, and only extreme edge cases reveal the problem through abnormal loss or profit outcomes. To remediate, the initAllowedBaseKeys function should be updated to include the three missing keys with appropriate non‑zero default values that reflect the protocol’s risk policy, thereby restoring the intended minimum position size enforcement, PNL factor caps, and ADL limits. This class of bug falls under missing configuration or parameter validation errors, where critical business‑logic constants are omitted, leading to accounting inconsistencies and violation of the platform’s economic assumptions. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as “my position opened with a tiny amount even though the UI said there is a minimum”, “my profit was huge and my balance exploded”, or “my loss was not reduced by ADL and my funds vanished”. The expectation that the system would enforce size and risk limits is therefore not met, resulting in money disappearing or unexpected zero‑balance outcomes.
summary:
Several critical keys are missing from the initAllowedBaseKeys function:
MIN_POSITION_SIZE_USD
MAX_PNL_FACTOR_FOR_DEPOSITS
MAX_PNL_FACTOR_FOR_ADL

title: DPCU-1 | Unliquidatable Position Due To getLiquidationValues
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the liquidation routine of a synthetic market contract. In the function that calculates liquidation values, the variable that tracks the profit‑and‑loss amount allocated to the pool (pnlAmountForPool) is overwritten with a new value even when a swap from the pnl token to the collateral token has already consumed the previous amount. Because the previous pnlAmountForPool is not credited back to the pool, the market’s internal token balance becomes inconsistent with the expected delta. When a liquidation transaction reaches the final market token balance check, the mismatch triggers a revert, preventing the liquidation from completing. As a result a position that should be liquidated remains open and the market records a shortfall, effectively creating bad‑debt. The bug manifests only when a liquidation path includes a swap of the pnl token before the final accounting step, a scenario that is not obvious during casual testing and therefore can be missed. It was discovered during a formal audit where a proof‑of‑concept test reproduced the revert condition. From a user perspective the expected outcome – the position being closed and the collateral returned – does not happen; instead the transaction fails, the user sees no refund, and the position appears unchanged, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The issue belongs to the class of state‑reset or delta‑mis‑application bugs that break accounting invariants in financial smart contracts. To remediate the problem the contract should add logic that, when a swap has occurred, applies the previously consumed pnlAmountForPool back to the pool using the market utility function, thereby restoring the correct balance before the final check. This change re‑establishes the invariant that total pool tokens equal the sum of all accounted deltas, allowing liquidations to succeed and preventing the creation of unbacked debt.
summary:
In the getLiquidationValues function the values.pnlAmountForPool is reset to a new value, although
the previous value may have been used in a swap from the pnlToken to the collateralToken.
This causes mis-accounting in the market and causes a revert with the market token balance check
upon liquidation. Therefore positions can be unliquidatable, yielding a potentially catastrophic
amount of bad-debt for the market.

title: DPCU-2 | Mis-Accounting When Swap Fails
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑accounting flaw that appears when a leveraged position holds unrealized profit that should be converted into the collateral token to cover outstanding borrowing or funding fees, but the internal swap operation fails. The contract’s liquidatability check incorrectly treats any positive profit‑and‑loss (PnL) as additional collateral, allowing the position to remain open even though the total fees exceed the actual collateral backing the trade. When the swapProfitToCollateralToken call reverts because pool limits, reserve constraints, or maximum‑PnL checks are violated, the protocol does not have a fallback path. Consequently, auto‑deleveraging (ADL) orders revert, liquidation logic only considers the raw collateral and ignores the unpaid fees, and the trader loses the entire profit while the protocol must absorb the shortfall. Liquidity providers see the market pool balance drop abruptly by the amount of the unpaid borrowing fees, and users who submit decrease orders expecting to use their profit to pay fees find those orders cancelled or frozen. This situation occurs whenever a position’s profit is large enough that converting it would exceed pool capacity or breach reserve rules, typically under high‑volume or volatile market conditions. The bug affects any trader with a leveraged position whose accrued fees are greater than the collateral, as well as the protocol’s liquidity pool and overall financial health. It was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation and ADL pathways, where the auditor observed that the isPositionLiquidatable function adds positive PnL to the collateral calculation without verifying that the swap can actually succeed. The issue is hard to notice because the failed swap is not exposed directly to the user; instead, a generic revert later in the ADL or liquidation flow masks the underlying accounting error, leading to unexpected loss of profit and frozen orders. The proper remediation is to enforce that a position may only be opened or remain open when the sum of its collateral and any realizable profit after a successful swap is sufficient to cover all outstanding fees, and to allow liquidation paths that treat a fee shortfall as a loss of collateral rather than causing a transaction revert. In broader terms, this belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting of derived collateral” or “swap‑dependent collateral validation” bugs, where the system assumes a successful token conversion without checking for failure conditions, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and exposing users to unexpected fund loss.
summary:
Positions in profit with unpaid borrowing/funding fees that are greater than the position’s collateral
open the exchange up to several high-impact issues when the swapProfitToCollateralToken swap
fails. These positions are able to exist since the isPositionLiquidatable check factors positive PnL as
collateral that would purportedly always be able to cover these fees.
However swapProfitToCollateralToken will commonly fail whenever the validatePoolAmount,
validateReserve, or validateMaxPnl checks fail as a result of the swap, causing the following issues:
Positions in large profit would be un-ADL-able since the ADL order would revert on line 224 as
the collateral is not sufficient to cover the fees alone.
Liquidations for these positions result in the user losing all of their profit since the execution
enters getLiquidationValues.
Liquidations for these positions result in the protocol having to cover a potentially large deficit
between the position’s collateral and the unpaid funding fees.
The pool value for market depositors sees a stepwise jump down from the potentially large
unpaid borrowing fees.
Decrease orders expecting to be able to use their profit to pay fees will be cancelled/frozen

title: DPCU-1 | Position fundingFeeAmountPerSize Errantly Reset
content: The vulnerability is a state‑reset bug that occurs when a position pays the total cost amount excluding funding using any secondary token. In that situation the contract replaces the entire fees structure with a freshly instantiated, empty object. Because the empty fees object does not contain the previously stored latestFundingFeeAmountPerSize value, the position’s fundingFeePerSize field is overwritten with zero. The protocol then assumes that the position has never accrued any funding fees and consequently charges the full amount of funding fees that have accumulated since the market opened.
